exp.0:0:
It says that Solomon, the son of David, was strengthened and firmly established in his kingdom. The reason is that the Lord his God was with him and made him very great. The phrase about being strengthened means that his rule was established and secure. The phrase about being greatly magnified means that he was exalted in a very great measure, exceedingly.

This is the beginning of 2 Chronicles. The narrator, whom Jewish tradition often identifies with Ezra (this is not certain), writes for a people who were returning from exile. He wants to remind them that Solomon's greatness came from God. Right after this, we see that Solomon gathers the people and goes to Gibeon, where the tabernacle was, to seek the Lord.

For today: true success and stability come from God's presence, not only from our own effort. Before seeking to grow, let us first seek that God would go with us, as Solomon did when he turned to Him.
exp.0:2:
He says that Solomon went with all the congregation of Israel to the "high place" at Gibeon, a raised place where worship took place. There stood the tabernacle, the sacred tent that Moses, the servant of the Lord, had made in the wilderness.

It is the account of the Chronicler, written for a people who were returning from exile. At the start of Solomon's reign, the text shows him seeking God together with the leaders of the people. The ark was in Jerusalem, but the tabernacle and the bronze altar still remained at Gibeon. That is why Solomon went there to worship. The Bible does not explain every detail of this arrangement, so it is wise not to assume more than the text says.

Before making big decisions, seek God first. Solomon did not begin with plans of his own, but with worship, and he did it accompanied by others. Today we can begin our goals and responsibilities by praying and seeking God, if possible together with our family or our church.
exp.0:5:
This verse says that Solomon went up to the bronze altar, which stood before the tabernacle at Gibeon, and there offered a thousand burnt offerings to God. A burnt offering was a gift that was burned whole on the altar, as a sign of complete surrender. The sacred tent where God met with his people is the tabernacle of the congregation.

The writer of Chronicles tells us that Solomon, newly made king, gathered the leaders of Israel to seek God. The ark was in Jerusalem, but the altar and the tabernacle made in the time of Moses were in another place. After this offering, God appeared to him that night and offered to give him whatever he wished.

Before making important decisions or taking on new responsibilities, it is wise to seek God with a humble and surrendered heart. He sees the attitude of those who come to worship him.
exp.0:11:
God tells Solomon that he grants what Solomon asked for: wisdom and knowledge, that is, understanding and insight to govern well. In addition, he promises what Solomon did not ask for: riches, possessions (goods and property) and glory (honor and fame). He says that no king before him had anything like it, and none after him will have the like.

God speaks at Gibeon, where the tabernacle was. Solomon had just offered sacrifices and asked for wisdom to guide such a numerous people. God was pleased that he did not ask for riches, fame, or the defeat of his enemies, but for help to serve others well.

For today: before asking for things for ourselves, we can ask God for wisdom to carry out well what he has entrusted to us, whether in the family, at work, or in the church. He also knows how to give us what we need, though not always in the way we expect.
exp.0:12:
This verse says that Solomon left the high place at Gibeon, where the tabernacle was, and returned to Jerusalem. There he began to reign over Israel. A high place was a hill where worship took place, and the tent of meeting was the sacred tent where worship was offered to God.

The writer of Chronicles tells this right after God granted Solomon wisdom, riches and glory. Solomon had gone to Gibeon to offer sacrifices, and there God answered him. Now he returns to Jerusalem to govern, already with that promise received. The text shows that his reign began after an encounter with God.

For today: before taking on a great task, take time to seek God and ask Him for wisdom. Then return to your responsibilities with humility, trusting that He will guide you in everyday life.
exp.0:14:
This verse says that, in the time of Solomon, silver and gold were so abundant in Jerusalem that they looked like ordinary stones. Cedar, a fine and costly wood, was also as plentiful as the sycamore trees that grow untended in the low fields.

Here the chronicler speaks, writing the history of Israel after the exile. He wants to show that God fulfilled what he promised Solomon when Solomon asked for wisdom: God also gave him riches and honor. It is a description full of emphasis, not necessarily an exact figure.

For today: what we have is a gift from God, not the center of life. Solomon received abundance, but the true blessing was his wisdom. We can ask God for direction first, and use with gratitude and generosity what He entrusts to us.
exp.1:2:
Solomon sends a message to Huram, king of Tyre, and asks for his help. He reminds Huram that he had already sent cedar wood to Solomon's father David, so that David could build a house and live in it.

Solomon is speaking, the new king of Israel. He has just decided that he will build the temple for the Lord and also a palace for his kingdom. He has already gathered thousands of workers, but he needs good timber, which was plentiful in Lebanon. So he turns to an old friendship that his father had built.

For today: God often carries out his plans with the help of others. Recognizing that we need other people, and valuing the good relationships we have inherited or built, is an act of wisdom and humility.
exp.1:5:
This verse says that no one is able to build God a house worthy of him. The heavens, even the highest heavens, cannot contain him. That is why Solomon asks who he is to build a house for him. He says it would only be to burn incense, that is, to burn incense as an act of worship. "Contain" here means to hold or encompass.

Solomon, king of Israel, speaks in a message to Hiram, king of Tyre. He asks for help with timber and craftsmen to build the temple. Solomon makes clear that the temple will be large, but he acknowledges that God is greater than any building.

For today: we can serve God with effort and excellence, but with humility. Nothing we do makes him depend on us. Let us serve with gratitude, remembering that he is the one who gives us the opportunity to worship him.
exp.1:6:
Solomon asks Hiram, king of Tyre, to send him a skilled craftsman. He must know how to work gold, silver, bronze and iron, and also dyed cloth: purple and scarlet (reds and purples) and blue. In addition, he must be able to engrave and carve, working alongside the craftsmen of Judah and Jerusalem whom David had already prepared.

Solomon is speaking as he prepares to build the temple. He has just said that God is so great that even the heavens cannot contain him. Even so, he wants to build with excellence, because the work is meant to honor God. He asks help from another kingdom, since he needs skills that he lacks.

For today: serving God deserves the best of our effort, and we do not have to do it alone. Recognizing what we lack and asking for help, with humility, is a form of wisdom.
exp.1:7:
Here Solomon asks Hiram, king of Tyre, to send him cedar, fir and pine from Lebanon. He says that Hiram's servants know how to cut that timber, and that his own servants will work alongside them.

Solomon is preparing to build the temple in Jerusalem. He acknowledges that God is so great that even the heavens cannot contain him, and yet he wants to honor him with a house. So he asks for help from someone who has the experience and the resources, and he offers to pay for the work.

For today: serving God does not mean doing everything alone. We can recognize our limitations, ask for help, and work as a team, with humility and with honesty in our agreements.
exp.1:8:
Here Solomon asks King Hiram of Tyre that his workers prepare a large amount of timber for him. The word "prepare" in this verse means to get something ready for use. The word "wonderful" means admirable, something that causes wonder. Solomon explains that the temple will be very great and extraordinary.

Solomon is speaking, as he sets out to build the temple for the Lord. He writes to Hiram because the workers of Tyre were skilled at cutting cedar in Lebanon. In exchange, Solomon promises wheat, barley, wine, and oil. He asks for help instead of doing everything alone.

When God places a great work on our hearts, we do not have to do it by ourselves. We can ask for help, value the talents of others, and plan with order, always seeking that what we do honors God.
exp.1:9:
Here Solomon offers King Hiram of Tyre a payment for the work of his men who will cut the timber. He promises twenty thousand measures of wheat and twenty thousand of barley, and twenty thousand baths of wine and twenty thousand baths of oil. The measure and the bath were ancient units, one for dry goods and one for liquids. Their exact equivalence is debated, but they were very large quantities.

Solomon speaks as he prepares to build the temple. He writes to Hiram to ask for cedar from Lebanon and for skilled men to cut it. Solomon does not simply ask for a favor; he offers fair pay in food and drink. Hiram later answers with praise to the LORD.

For today: when someone works for us or with us, we should pay them with justice and generosity. Serving God is no excuse for neglecting honest dealing with others.
exp.1:11:
Hiram praised the God of Israel, who made heaven and earth. He acknowledged that God had given King David a wise son, a man of understanding, discernment and careful judgment, someone who thinks well and acts with care. That son, Solomon, would build a house for the Lord and also a house for his kingdom.

Hiram was king of Tyre, a Phoenician city near Israel. He answered a letter from Solomon, who had asked him for timber and workers for the temple. Hiram had enjoyed a good relationship with David. We do not know for certain how far his faith in the Lord went. His words may be respect and courtesy, or they may be a sincere recognition that the Lord was a powerful God.

For today: recognize and celebrate the gifts God gives to others, even when they are not from your own circle. And if you have wisdom or talent, use it to serve God and help others, not only for your own benefit.
exp.1:13:
This verse describes the craftsman whom King Hiram of Tyre sends to Solomon. His mother was from the tribe of Dan, and his father was from Tyre. He knew how to work gold, silver, bronze and iron, as well as stone and wood. He also mastered dyed fabrics: purple, blue, fine linen and deep red. He could carve figures and create whatever design was requested, and work alongside Solomon's workmen and those who had belonged to David.

It is Hiram, king of Tyre, who speaks in a letter answering Solomon, who had asked for help building the temple. Hiram acknowledges the God of Israel and sends an expert for that work. Some note that in 1 Kings 7:14 his mother is described as being from Naphtali; the Bible does not explain this, and several solutions have been proposed.

For today: God uses ordinary talents and skills when they are placed at the service of his work. Offer what you know how to do, with excellence and humility, and work in unity with others.
exp.1:14:
It says that King Hiram asks Solomon to keep what was promised: to send to his workers the wheat, the barley, the oil and the wine that Solomon himself had offered. The workers are Hiram's own men, and Solomon is the one Hiram addresses with respect. These were staple foods of the time.

The speaker is Hiram, king of Tyre, in a reply letter to Solomon, who was preparing to build the temple in Jerusalem. Hiram sends a skilled craftsman and commits to cutting timber from Lebanon. In return, he asks for these foods for those who would do the work. It is a clear agreement between two kings.

For today: keeping what we promise is a way of honoring others. Whether at work, in the family or in the church, paying on time and doing what was agreed reflects the character of God, who is always faithful.
exp.1:16:
Solomon took a census of the foreigners who lived in Israel, that is, those who were not descendants of Jacob. Earlier, his father David had already counted them. The result was 153,600 men. The word "found" here means that they were counted or turned out to be that number.

The writer of Chronicles describes Solomon's preparations to build the temple. He had just asked King Hiram of Tyre for timber from Lebanon. For the heavy labor he needed workers, and the next verse shows that he organized these foreigners as burden-bearers, stonecutters, and overseers. Some scholars note that this shows foreigners working on God's project, though the text does not say how they felt.

God uses people from different backgrounds in his work. Today we might ask ourselves: whom am I leaving out of my church or community? Let us value and make room for those who come from other places, for they too have gifts to serve.
exp.1:17:
It says that Solomon organized the foreigners who lived in Israel for the building of the temple. Seventy thousand carried materials, eighty thousand cut stone or wood in the mountains, and three thousand six hundred were overseers, that is, foremen or supervisors who watched over and directed the work of the people.

The writer of Chronicles tells how Solomon prepared the work of the temple in Jerusalem. Earlier, Solomon had asked King Hiram of Tyre for cedar wood from Lebanon. Then he counted the foreigners living there, following the census that David had taken. It is the same group of 153,600 people. The list shows a large work, well organized and with clear roles.

For today: God often does his work with order and with the participation of many. Ask yourself what concrete task you can take on in your church or family, even if it seems small, and do it with steadiness.
exp.2:0:
It says that Solomon began to build the temple in Jerusalem, on Mount Moriah. That place had been pointed out to David, his father, and David had prepared it on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite. A threshing floor was a flat piece of ground where grain was beaten to separate it from the husk.

Here the chronicler speaks, recounting the history of Israel after the exile. He wants to remember that the temple was not an improvised idea, but something God directed and David prepared. Some believe Moriah is the same mountain where Abraham was tested with Isaac (Genesis 22), although the text does not state this directly. Ornan is also called Araunah in 2 Samuel 24.

For today: God often uses the work of one generation to bless the next. Prepare in faith what others will continue, and value what others prepared for you.
exp.2:1:
It says that Solomon began to build the temple on the second day of the second month, in the fourth year of his reign. The text gives a precise date, as if it wanted to record that the work had a real and orderly beginning.

The book of Chronicles was written by an author who is not named in the text, and it was addressed to a people who were returning from exile. It wanted to remind them that the temple was the center of their faith. That is why it tells in detail how Solomon raised the house of God on Mount Moriah, in the place David had prepared. The book of 1 Kings 6:1 also places the beginning in the fourth year of Solomon.

For today: the important things of life with God are built with steady steps and with order. If there is something God has placed on your heart, begin, even with a simple first day, and continue with perseverance.
exp.2:2:
Here we are told that Solomon built the temple following exact measurements. The house of God was sixty cubits long and twenty cubits wide. A cubit was an ancient unit of measure, roughly the length of the forearm, about 45 centimeters, though its exact size is debated.

The narrator is the Chronicler, who writes after the exile to remind the people how the first temple was raised. Solomon built it on Mount Moriah, where David had prepared the site. Recording the measurements shows that the work was done with order and care, and it helped a people who had been struck down to remember their heritage of worship.

For today: God values what is done with order and dedication. Whether in prayer, service, or work, offer him your best, without improvising or doing things halfway.
exp.2:3:
This verse says that Solomon built at the entrance of the temple a porch, that is, a covered space at the front. It was twenty cubits long, the same as the width of the house, and one hundred and twenty high. A cubit was an ancient measure, roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the fingers. Inside, the porch was overlaid with pure gold.

Here the chronicler speaks, retelling the history of Israel for the people who returned from exile. He wants them to remember the temple, the place where God was worshiped. The numbers may vary: some scholars believe the height of one hundred and twenty cubits may have been a copying error, and there is no certain agreement.

For today: God deserves the best of us. Offer Him your time, your attention, and your heart with care, not what is left over.
exp.2:5:
He decorated the house with precious stones for beauty, not only for their value. The gold used was gold of Parvaim. No one knows for certain where Parvaim was; it could be a place, or simply a way of naming gold of very high quality.

Here the chronicler speaks, recounting how Solomon built the temple in Jerusalem. He describes it in such detail because the people, returning from exile, needed to remember that God should be the center of their lives and their worship.

For today: let us give God our best, not what is left over. It can be our time, our gifts, or our attention. In this way we show that He is precious to us.
exp.2:6:
It says that Solomon covered the whole inside of the temple with gold: the roof beams, the thresholds (the lower part of the doors), the walls and the doors. He also had cherubim, figures of heavenly beings, carved on the walls.

The writer of Chronicles, who writes after the exile, tells how Solomon built the temple in Jerusalem. The details of gold and beauty show that this place was holy, set apart for worshiping God. The cherubim call to mind God's presence, as in Eden and over the ark. How many details the temple had, and what each one meant, is understood in several different ways.

For today: God deserves the best from us. We can ask ourselves what part of our time, talent and attention we give to God with love and care, not with what is left over.
exp.2:7:
Solomon built the most holy place, the innermost room of the temple. It measured twenty cubits in length and twenty in width, that is, about nine meters on each side. A cubit was an ancient unit of measure, roughly the length of the forearm. Everything was covered with fine gold, six hundred talents. A talent weighed several dozen kilograms, so it was a very large amount of gold, although the exact calculation is not known.

The account comes from the Chronicler, who wrote after the exile, traditionally perhaps Ezra. He wanted to remind the people of the greatness of the temple and that God lives among his people. The most holy place held the ark of the covenant, a sign of God's presence.

Today, this passage invites us to give God our best, not what is left over. Today we can draw near to Him with confidence through Christ, so let us set apart quality time to pray and worship.
exp.2:8:
This verse says that the nails used in the temple weighed fifty shekels of gold in total. A shekel was a unit of weight, about eleven or twelve grams, though the exact calculation is debated. It also says that Solomon overlaid the upper chambers with gold. In other words, even small details, like the nails, received care and value.

The speaker is the Chronicler, an unknown author, although Jewish tradition connects him with Ezra. He writes after the exile, to remind the people how the temple that Solomon built was. He wants them to value the worship of God and his house. He describes the gold in such detail because the temple was the place where God met his people.

For today: God is interested in the small things. We can offer him excellence even in what no one sees, such as work done with honesty or a sincere prayer in private.
exp.2:9:
It says that Solomon made two cherubim inside the most holy place, the innermost room of the temple, and overlaid them with gold. "Cherubim" are angelic beings who serve God. The phrase about their form is difficult: the Hebrew word is rare, and other translations describe them as carved work or sculpted work.

The one telling the story is the chronicler of Israel, who writes after the exile. He describes how Solomon built the temple to remind the people that God chose to dwell among them. The cherubim guarded the place where God's presence was, and they recall the garden of Eden and the ark of the covenant.

Today, this invites us to take God's presence seriously. We can give him our best time and our whole heart, approaching him with reverence and, at the same time, with gratitude, because he wants to be close to us.
exp.2:10:
This verse says that each cherub had two wings of five cubits, that is, ten cubits in total. A cubit was an ancient unit of measure, about 45 centimeters. One wing touched the wall of the temple and the other touched the wing of the other cherub, so between the two they covered twenty cubits of width. The cherubim are spiritual beings who attend the presence of God.

The writer of Chronicles describes the temple that Solomon built in Jerusalem. These figures stood in the most holy place, where the ark of the covenant was kept. The writer gives precise measurements to remind the people that this place was sacred and that God was worshiped there with order and reverence.

For today: draw near to God with respect and with calm. Before praying or reading the Bible, take a moment to remember that you are standing before a holy God who also covers you and cares for you.
exp.2:11:
This verse describes the wings of the two cherubim that Solomon made for the most holy place. Each cherub had two wings of five cubits (a cubit is roughly half a meter). One wing touched the wall of the temple, and the other touched the wing of the other cherub. In this way, together the two covered a width of twenty cubits.

The writer of Chronicles, probably writing after the exile, goes through the construction of Solomon's temple in detail. He wants to remind the people that God dwelt among them in an ordered and holy place. The cherubim stood beside the ark of the covenant, where God's presence was made known. Their exact form is not known with certainty.

For today: God cares about the details and wants us to draw near to Him with reverence. Today we can pray with respect and gratitude, knowing that Christ opened the way into his presence.
exp.2:12:
This verse says that the outstretched wings of the two cherubim together measured twenty cubits across. A cubit was an ancient unit of measure, roughly half a meter. The cherubim stood on their feet, facing inward, that is, toward the house, toward the main part of the temple. The word "cherubim" refers to angelic beings that appear in the Bible near the presence of God.

Here the chronicler speaks, recounting how Solomon built the temple in Jerusalem. These cherubim were in the most holy place, where the ark of the covenant was. This is told in such detail because the temple was the center of Israel's worship. Scholars do not fully agree on exactly how these figures looked.

For today: God cares about the details of his worship. We can approach him with respect and reverence, facing his presence with humility, and not with carelessness or haste.
exp.2:14:
The verse says that Solomon made two pillars in front of the temple. Each one was thirty-five cubits high, and on top of each was a capital, a decorative piece at the upper part, five cubits high. A cubit was an ancient unit of measure, roughly the length of the forearm. Some scholars note that 1 Kings 7:15 speaks of eighteen cubits, and there are several possible explanations, such as that the figure here adds together the height of both pillars, but there is no certainty.

Here the chronicler speaks, the one who recounts the building of the temple in Jerusalem. He wrote for a people who were returning from exile and needed to remember the greatness of their house of worship. The pillars received the names Jachin and Boaz, and their exact meaning is debated.

For today: Solomon took care over every detail in raising a place for God. We can ask ourselves whether we offer God our best in time, effort, and attention, not the leftovers.
exp.2:15:
It says that Solomon made chains and placed them on the capitals, that is, the upper part of the columns. Then he put one hundred pomegranates on those chains. But the text is difficult: the parallel passage in 1 Kings 7 places the chains on the outer columns, so it is not known with certainty what they were like.

The writer of Chronicles describes how Solomon built the temple in Jerusalem. He wants his people to remember that worship of God was carried out with order, care, and beauty. The pomegranates may have been an ornament that spoke of abundance, though the Bible does not explain their meaning here.

For today: God cares even about small details. Let us do our work, service, and prayer with diligence and gratitude, as an offering to Him.
exp.3:0:
It says that Solomon ordered a very large bronze altar built for the temple. It measured twenty cubits in length, twenty in width, and ten in height. A cubit was roughly the length of the forearm, about 45 to 50 centimeters, so the altar was about 9 or 10 meters on each side and nearly 5 meters high. It was an altar for offering sacrifices.

Here the chronicler speaks, telling the history of Israel after the exile. He describes in detail the building of the temple under Solomon. He wanted to remind his people that worship of God was the center of their identity. This altar stood in the courtyard, where the people drew near to God through sacrifice.

For today: drawing near to God calls for reverence and devotion. Today Christians believe that Christ made the complete sacrifice, so we can approach with confidence, but also with gratitude and a heart willing to offer our lives to him.
exp.3:2:
This verse describes the base of the "sea," a huge bronze basin in the temple. Beneath its rim were figures of oxen, ten for each cubit (a cubit is roughly half a meter), going all the way around the sea. There were two rows of oxen, made in one piece with the basin. Being cast together means they were poured in the same mold.

The chronicler tells this, probably writing after the exile, to remind the people how Solomon built the temple. The details show the order and care with which the place of worship was prepared. Some think the water was used for the cleansing of the priests; the parallel passage later on suggests this.

For today: God values what is done with care and dedication. We can serve him with excellence in the small things, and seek every day to be clean and renewed before him.
exp.3:7:
He made ten tables and placed them in the temple, five on the south side and five on the north side. He also made a hundred bowls of gold. The word "bowls" refers to wide vessels or cups, probably used in the temple service, perhaps for sprinkling the blood of the sacrifices, though the text does not make this clear.

The author of Chronicles, who writes after the exile, describes in detail the temple that Solomon built. Earlier he speaks of basins and lampstands, also in groups of ten. His purpose seems to be to remind the people that the worship of God had order, beauty, and care. Scholars are not sure what each table was used for, but they were connected to the worship.

For today: God deserves our best, and also order and care. We can ask ourselves what part of our prayer life, service, or congregation most needs more attention and sincere dedication, not for appearance, but out of love for Him.
exp.3:10:
He says that Huram, the craftsman sent from Tyre, made the bronze vessels for the temple: pots (large kettles), shovels (for removing the ashes from the altar), and basins (bowls for catching the blood or the water). With this, he finished all the work he had done for King Solomon in the house of God.

The author of Chronicles, writing after the exile, goes through the construction of the temple in detail. He wants to remind the people who were returning to their land that the worship of God was carried out with order, care, and devotion. The text does not speak of God or of a character, but of the chronicler who narrates the work.

God is concerned with the small things as much as with the great. Even shovels and basins are mentioned in his house. Do your daily work with care, even when it seems humble, and offer it to God.
exp.3:13:
This verse tells that Huram made the stands, which were bronze bases or carts with wheels, and on them he placed the basins, that is, the large fonts or laver basins. The priests used those basins to wash what was offered in the sacrifices (2 Chronicles 4:6).

The passage is part of an account that describes, in great detail, the objects made for Solomon's temple. The author, whom tradition calls the Chronicler, writes after the exile, and he wants the people to remember that their worship had order and special care. That is why he lists each piece, even though it may seem technical.

For today: God cares about the details of our service. We can do small and hidden tasks with diligence and without boasting, because humble work also serves God.
exp.4:1:
This verse tells how Solomon gathered in Jerusalem the elders of Israel, the leaders of the tribes, and the heads of the families. He wanted them to bring the ark of the covenant, the sacred chest that symbolized God's presence, from the city of David, called Zion, to the temple that had just been completed.

The writer of Chronicles, who tells the history of Israel, is the one narrating. Solomon had just finished the temple and had placed in it the offerings that his father David had dedicated. What remained most important was to set the ark in its place. That is why he summoned the whole leadership of the people, so that the act would involve the entire nation.

For today: the most valuable part of any project is the presence of God, not the building or the resources. Before considering something finished, invite him to be at the center of your home, your work, or your church.
exp.4:3:
This verse tells that all the leaders of Israel came, and that the Levites lifted up the ark of the covenant. The ark was the sacred chest that represented God's presence among his people. Here "took up" means they carried it in order to move it.

The book of Chronicles tells the story of Israel, and here it describes the dedication of the temple that Solomon had built. The ark was being moved from the city of David to the new temple. It was the Levites who were to carry it, since God had entrusted that service to them. This took place at the feast in the seventh month, when the people gathered.

For today: drawing near to God calls for order, reverence, and unity. We can ask ourselves how we serve together in our church or family, each doing with respect the task entrusted to us, so that God may be the center of everything.
exp.4:4:
This verse tells how they brought up the ark, the tent where God met with his people, and all the sacred items. The priests and the Levites were the ones who carried them.

The writer of Chronicles tells about the dedication of Solomon's temple. All of Israel was gathered for the feast in the seventh month. The Levites carried the ark, as the law of Moses directed, because it was a symbol of God's presence. Some think the tent came from Gibeon, but the text does not give those details.

For today: approach God with respect and order, without treating his presence as something ordinary. Also, serve as a team, because here each person did the task that belonged to them.
exp.4:9:
This verse says that inside the ark of the covenant there were only the two stone tablets that Moses placed there at Horeb, another name for Mount Sinai. With them God had made his covenant, that is, his agreement, with Israel after bringing them out of Egypt.

The author of Chronicles tells how Solomon brought the ark into the new temple. It makes clear what the ark contained at that time. Hebrews 9:4 also mentions Aaron's rod and the manna, and it is not easy to know how these texts fit together. The people were returning from exile when this was written, and it reminded them that God was still faithful to his covenant.

For today: God keeps his word. What is essential in our lives is not buildings or rituals, but his Word. Today you can spend a few minutes reading it and putting it at the center of your day.
exp.4:11:
This verse describes the Levite singers and musicians, from the families of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun, together with their sons and brothers. They were dressed in fine linen and stood on the east side of the altar, with cymbals, harps, and lyres (stringed instruments similar to a small harp). With them were one hundred and twenty priests blowing trumpets.

The writer of Chronicles recounts the dedication of the temple that Solomon built. The ark of the covenant was already in its place, and everyone was preparing to praise God. The musicians were organized and set apart for this service. Then, when all of them praised together as one voice, the cloud of God's glory filled the house.

God delights in worship that is prepared, orderly, and united. Today we can serve in the church with dedication and harmony, not seeking attention for ourselves, but honoring God together with what we know how to do.
exp.4:12:
This verse says that the priests blew the trumpets and the singers sang together, as one, in unity. They praised and gave thanks to the Lord, acknowledging who He is. Their song declared: "For he is good, and his mercy endureth forever." Then a cloud filled the temple. The word "filled" here means to fill completely.

This happens when Solomon dedicates the temple and the priests have just placed the ark of the covenant in its place. The text tells it as narration; it is not the speech of any particular person. The Levite singers and the priests with trumpets were worshiping in good order. The cloud signals God's presence, as in the tabernacle in the days of Moses. The priests could no longer minister because of that cloud.

For today: united and sincere worship, centered on the goodness and mercy of God, prepares us to recognize His presence. We can begin the day by thanking Him for who He is, not only for what He gives us.
exp.4:13:
This verse says that the priests could not continue their work in the temple because a cloud filled the house. That cloud showed that the glory of the Lord, that is, his powerful and holy presence, was there. The word "filled" here means filled completely, and "minister" means serving or performing the worship.

The writer of Chronicles recounts the moment when Solomon finished the temple and the ark of the covenant was brought in. While the Levites and priests praised God with music and sang that his mercy endures forever, the cloud filled the place. It was like the cloud that filled the tabernacle in the time of Moses. With it, God showed that he accepted that house.

For today: sometimes our plans and religious routines must stop before God. Praise him sincerely, and let his presence matter more than your schedule or your performance.
exp.5:5:
God says that he chose Jerusalem as the place where his name would be, that is, where his presence would be honored and sought by the people. He also says that he chose David to rule over Israel.

Solomon, son of David, is speaking on the day the temple is dedicated. He is recalling a promise of God. Before David, God had not designated any city or any king. Solomon wants to show that the temple and David's line come from God's choosing, not from a human plan.

For today: God acts on his own initiative and keeps what he promises. When you make plans or serve God, remember that he is the one who calls and sustains the work. You can rest in his faithfulness and give thanks because he keeps his word.
exp.5:9:
Solomon says that God fulfilled what he promised. He takes the place of his father David as king of Israel, and he has already built the temple to honor the name of the Lord. Here, "house" refers to the temple.

Solomon speaks at the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem, in front of all the people. He reminds them that David wanted to build it, but God told him that his son would do it. Solomon presents the temple as the result of God's faithfulness to his word, not only of his own effort.

Today we can learn to look with gratitude at how God has been faithful in our lives. When we wait for one of his promises, we can trust that his timing and his way of doing things are good. We can also recognize those who began something before us, such as parents, teachers, or brothers and sisters in the faith.
exp.5:10:
Solomon says that in the temple he built he has placed the ark, the sacred chest where the covenant of the Lord with Israel was kept. The name of God is one that the reader will find in the verse as "the Lord", and the word for making a binding agreement or pact is what the covenant itself refers to, so the sentence about the meaning of the old wording can be left out. The tablets of the law were inside the ark, and for that reason it was a symbol of God's promise to his people.

Solomon speaks before the whole congregation, on the day he dedicates the temple. He has just recalled that God kept his word to David, his father, and now he wants to show that the temple is not merely a building, but the place where the memory of the covenant is kept. Then he kneels down and begins his prayer.

For today: God keeps what he promises. Before asking him for anything, we can remember his promises and thank him for his faithfulness, as Solomon did. This strengthens our trust and prepares us to pray with humility.
exp.5:14:
Solomon tells God that he has kept what he promised to his father David. "Kept" here means that God held firm to his word. The phrase about speaking with his mouth refers to the promise made in words, and the phrase about fulfilling it with his hand refers to making it happen through deeds. The phrase about it being "this day" means that the fulfillment was visible.

Solomon prays before all Israel, kneeling with his hands spread out, at the dedication of the temple. God had promised David that his son would build the house of the Lord. Now the temple is finished, and Solomon acknowledges that it was God who accomplished it. With that gratitude, he asks that God continue to keep his promises to David's family.

For today: when you doubt, remember how God has already been faithful to you. Recalling what He has fulfilled strengthens confidence for what you are still waiting for.
exp.5:19:
What it says: Solomon asks God to keep his eyes open toward the temple, always, day and night. It is the place where God said he would put his name, that is, where his presence and his authority would be acknowledged. Solomon also asks God to hear the prayer that he himself offers there. Here Solomon refers to himself with humility as God's servant.

Context: Solomon speaks at the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem, in front of all Israel. He knows God is so great that not even the heavens can contain him, so he does not ask that God be shut up inside the building. Rather, he asks God to listen to the prayers directed toward that place, as God had promised.

For today: We can pray with the same humility and confidence. God is great, but he is also near and attentive. Today, before asking for something, take a moment to acknowledge who God is, and trust that he truly hears you.
exp.5:20:
Solomon asks God to hear the prayers that he and the people of Israel make in the temple. God dwells in heaven, and from there he can hear. But Solomon asks for something more: that, when he hears, he also forgive.

Solomon is praying at the dedication of the temple he has just built. He knows the people will fail, and so he asks not only that God listen, but that he be merciful. Some think the temple was a place toward which prayer was directed, not a place that could contain God, since Solomon himself recognizes that the heavens cannot contain him.

For today: when you pray, do not fear coming to God with your failures. Ask him for forgiveness sincerely, trusting that he hears and is compassionate.
exp.5:21:
This verse begins one of the situations that Solomon presents to God in his prayer. It says that if someone wrongs his neighbour, and he is required to take an oath, and that oath is brought before the altar in the temple... (the sentence is left open and is completed in the next verse).

Solomon is praying at the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem. He asks that God hear from heaven the prayers made in that place. Here he imagines a conflict between two people, where one denies having done harm and swears before God. Solomon asks God to act justly, punishing the guilty and defending the innocent.

For today: when there is a conflict, the truth matters because God sees it. We can ask him to do justice instead of lying or taking revenge, and we can be honest in what we say.
exp.5:22:
This verse says that God hears from heaven and acts as a just judge. He gives the wicked what they deserve: the consequences of their evil ways fall back on their own heads. He declares the righteous innocent and treats them according to their righteousness.

King Solomon is speaking, in the prayer at the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem. He is asking that if someone accused of a wrong swears before the altar that they are innocent, God himself would settle the case, because He sees what human judges cannot see.

For today: when you suffer injustice and cannot prove the truth, hand the matter over to God in prayer. He sees everything and judges with justice. In this way you can let go of revenge and live with honesty yourself.
exp.5:24:
This verse is part of a prayer. Solomon asks God to hear from heaven, to forgive the sin of Israel, and to bring them back to the land he gave to them and to their fathers.

The one speaking is King Solomon. He has just finished building the temple and prays in front of all the people to dedicate it. In this part he asks that if Israel sins, is defeated, and then repents, confesses the name of God, and prays toward the temple, God would forgive them and restore them.

For today: when we fail, we do not have to hide from God. We can return to Him sincerely, acknowledge what we have done, and ask for forgiveness, trusting that He hears and restores those who repent.
exp.5:25:
This verse speaks of a drought. It says that if the heavens are shut up and there is no rain because the people have sinned against God, and then they pray toward the temple, acknowledge God's name, and turn from their sins, this happens when God corrects them through that hardship.

Solomon is praying at the dedication of the temple. He asks that God hear his people when, after failing, they return to him. In that time rain was vital for the harvests, and the Bible presents drought as one of the warnings of Israel's covenant (Deuteronomy 28).

For today: when you go through a difficulty, do not turn away from God. Stop, pray sincerely, acknowledge whatever needs to be corrected in your life, and return to him. Not every difficulty is punishment, but God always welcomes whoever comes back to him with humility.
exp.5:26:
This verse says that God listens from heaven to the prayer of his people. When they acknowledge their sin, God forgives them, teaches them how to live well, and sends the rain back to them.

Here Solomon is speaking. He is praying at the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem. He asks that if Israel sins and suffers drought as a result, God would hear them when they pray toward that place and turn back to him. Solomon knows the people can fail, and he trusts in God's mercy.

For today: when you fail, do not hide from God. Return to him sincerely, confess what you have done, and ask him to guide you. He does not only forgive; he also shows the good way so that you can keep moving forward.
exp.5:27:
This verse lists several calamities that could fall on Israel: famine, contagious disease, crop-destroying blights, an invasion of locusts or aphids, and enemy attacks that besieged their cities. The Hebrew-derived plant diseases that once spoiled wheat, and the insect that damaged crops, are all covered by the verse's broad list of blasting, mildew, and caterpillars. At the end, Solomon adds "whatsoever sore or whatsoever sickness there be," so that nothing is left out.

Solomon speaks at the dedication of the temple. He prays before the whole people and asks God to listen when his people, in the middle of their distress, turn to him and pray facing that house.

For today: we do not need to wait until everything is in order before we pray. When a crisis comes, whether of health, money, or fear, we can come to God honestly, acknowledge our failures if there are any, and trust that he listens.
exp.5:28:
This verse says that God hears any prayer or request, whether it comes from one person or from all of Israel. It speaks of someone who recognizes their sore (their wound, their problem) and their grief in the heart, and for that reason spreads out their hands toward the temple. Spreading out the hands was a gesture of prayer and of need.

Here Solomon is speaking, in the prayer when he dedicates the temple in Jerusalem. He asks that God would attend to those who pray toward that place in times of famine, plague, war, or sickness. The request continues in the next verse: that God would hear from heaven and forgive.

For today: you don't need a perfect prayer or beautiful words. God looks at an honest heart. When something hurts you, bring it to him with sincerity, just as it is, and trust that he hears you.
exp.5:29:
This verse says that God hears prayers from heaven, which is the place where he lives. Solomon asks him to forgive and to deal with each person according to his way of living, because God knows the heart. The phrase "you will give to each one according to his ways" means that God answers each person justly. The word "dwelling place" refers to the place where God resides.

King Solomon is speaking in the prayer at the dedication of the temple. He is asking that, when the people suffer hunger, plagues, or attacks from enemies and pray facing the temple, God will hear and forgive. He acknowledges that only God sees what is within a human being.

For today: when you pray, you do not need to pretend or use beautiful words. God already knows your heart. Speak to him with sincerity, acknowledge your faults, and trust that he hears and can forgive.
exp.5:30:
This verse says that God hears and forgives his people with a purpose: that they revere him with awe and live according to his will all their lives in the land he promised to their ancestors. The phrase about the land refers to the surface of the earth. Here "fathers" means the ancestors of Israel.

It is King Solomon speaking, during his prayer at the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem. He is asking that God hear the prayers of those who turn toward that place with a sincere heart. His desire is that God's forgiveness produce in the people a faithful and obedient life.

For today: when God forgives you, his goal is not only to relieve your guilt, but to draw you closer to him. Today, after praying, ask for help to take one concrete step of obedience in your daily routine.
exp.5:31:
This verse speaks of the foreigner, that is, someone who is not part of the people of Israel. That foreigner comes from a distant land because he has heard of the greatness of God, of his power and of his action to save and protect. He comes to pray in the temple.

The speaker is King Solomon, in the prayer he offers when he dedicates the temple he built in Jerusalem. He asks God to listen not only to Israel, but also to foreigners who pray there. The following verse explains the purpose: that all peoples may know God's name and revere it.

For today: God has a heart open to all people. We can imitate him by welcoming with kindness those who come from other places or cultures, and by praying that they too may come to know him.
exp.5:32:
He says that God hears from the heavens, where he dwells, and answers whatever the foreigner who calls out to him asks for. The purpose is that all the peoples of the earth may come to know his name, honor him as Israel does, and know that the temple bears his name. The phrase about the surface of the earth refers to the ground, and the idea of fearing God here means revering him with respect and trust.

King Solomon is speaking in his prayer at the dedication of the temple he built in Jerusalem. He asks that God also attend to foreigners who travel from distant lands drawn by his reputation. It shows that from the very beginning God's heart was open to all nations.

For today: if God hears the outsider, he also calls us to welcome with respect those who come from elsewhere. Today you can pray for an immigrant or visitor you know, and treat them with concrete kindness.
exp.5:40:
Here Solomon asks God to "arise," that is, to come and settle in the newly built temple, his resting place, together with the ark, the symbol of his power. He asks that the priests be clothed with salvation, surrounded by deliverance and protection, and that the faithful people of God, the saints, rejoice in goodness, that is, enjoy his kindness.

The one speaking is King Solomon, at the end of his long prayer to dedicate the temple in Jerusalem. He has just asked that God hear, forgive, and attend to his people. These words close the prayer and recall a similar psalm (Psalm 132:8-9).

For today: before asking things for ourselves, we can ask God to be at the center of our life, our family, and our church. When He dwells among us, His protection and His goodness come with Him.
exp.5:41:
It says that Solomon asks God not to reject his anointed, that is, the king chosen by Him. Turning away the face means not turning one's back on him or withholding His favor. He also asks God to remember the mercies of David, that is, the acts of kindness and faithfulness David showed toward God, although some understand it to refer to the promises of kindness God made to David.

Solomon is finishing his prayer at the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem. He has just asked that God would dwell there with the ark, and that His priests and His people would live under His blessing. Now he bases his request on the covenant God made with David. Some see Solomon himself as the anointed one here, and others also see a look toward the future Messiah.

For today: when you pray, do not rely on your own merits, but on the faithfulness of God and on what He has promised. You can come near with confidence, reminding Him of His promises.
exp.6:0:
As soon as Solomon finished his prayer, fire came down from heaven and completely consumed the burnt offering and the sacrifices. Then the visible presence of God, called the glory of the Lord, filled the temple.

It is the account of the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem. Solomon had just prayed, asking that God would dwell there and listen to his people (2 Chronicles 6). The writer tells how God answered. The verses that follow say that the priests could not enter, and that the people bowed down and praised God for his goodness and his mercy that endures forever.

For today: God hears sincere prayer and answers in his own way and in his own time. Pray with humility, and when you see his work, respond as Israel did: with worship and thankfulness, remembering that his mercy endures forever.
exp.6:1:
It says that the priests could not go into the temple because the glory of the Lord had completely filled it. "Filled" here means full, and "glory" refers to the visible, powerful presence of God, shown so strongly in this moment that no one could pass inside.

The writer of Chronicles recounts the dedication of the temple that Solomon built. He had just finished his prayer, and God answered with fire from heaven on the sacrifice. This recalls what happened when the tabernacle was dedicated in the time of Moses. The text shows that God accepted the house and that He Himself came to dwell among His people. Afterward, everyone bowed down and worshiped Him.

For today: before we bring our requests or serve God, it is worth pausing with reverence and awe before His presence. God is not a tool for us; He is holy and good. We can draw near to Him with humility and gratitude.
exp.6:4:
This verse says that King Solomon offered an enormous number of animals as sacrifices: twenty-two thousand oxen and one hundred and twenty thousand sheep. With that offering, the king and all the people dedicated the temple, which here is called "the house of God." To dedicate means to set something apart for God's use and honor.

The one telling the story is the writer of Chronicles, who recounts the opening of the temple in Jerusalem. Shortly before, the fire and glory of God had come down, and the people bowed down to worship. The numbers are very large, and we do not know exactly how these sacrifices were divided, but the text aims to show a huge and thankful celebration.

For today: when God helps us, responding with gratitude comes naturally. We do not need to offer animals, but we can dedicate to God our time, our gifts, and our hearts with joy and generosity.
exp.6:8:
It says that on the eighth day the people gathered in a solemn assembly. Before that they had spent seven days dedicating the altar and another seven days celebrating the feast. The word for the gathering means a sacred meeting, and the word for the observance means a special religious festival.

This is the chronicler's account of the dedication of the temple in the time of Solomon. All Israel was gathered, from north to south. According to the context, the feast coincided with the seventh month, and the people were sent home on the twenty-third day. Some scholars connect it with the Feast of Tabernacles, although the text does not give all the details. The purpose was to give thanks to God and to offer him the temple.

For today: after celebrating and giving thanks, it is good to pause and gather calmly before God. We can set aside time to thank him for his blessings, rather than rushing from one activity to another without reflection.
exp.6:11:
This verse says that God appeared to Solomon one night and spoke to him. He assured him that he had heard his prayer and that he had chosen the temple as the place where sacrifices would be offered. "House of sacrifice" means a place where the people drew near to God with offerings.

The Lord speaks, and he answers Solomon after Solomon finished the temple and dedicated it with a great prayer. The people had already gone home glad. God confirms that he approved the work and that the temple would be a place of meeting with him. What follows are warnings and promises for his people.

For today: God listens when we pray sincerely. We can speak to him with confidence, knowing that he desires to draw near to us and to answer.
exp.6:12:
God says he could shut up the heavens so that there is no rain, or command the locust (an insect similar to a grasshopper that devours crops) to destroy the harvest, or send pestilence, which is a disease that spreads among the people. These are three examples of hardships that could fall upon the people. The sentence is left open, and verse 14 completes it.

God himself speaks. He appears to Solomon at night, after he has finished the temple and heard his prayer. God answers him that he has chosen that place and explains how he will act if the people suffer because of their disobedience. These words were addressed to Israel, under the covenant with God.

For today: when difficult times come, it is good to stop and ask God whether there is something in our hearts that needs correcting. Not every difficulty is a punishment, but we can always draw near to him with humility and sincerity.
exp.6:18:
This verse begins a warning from God. It says that if the people turn away, meaning they stop following Him and abandon His laws and commands, and go off to serve and worship other gods, there will be consequences. His rules and instructions are the statutes and commandments. The other gods are the gods of other nations, not the true God.

God is speaking to Solomon, after he finished building and dedicating the temple. Earlier God had promised to establish his throne if he walked faithfully, as David did. Now God presents the other side: faithfulness brought blessing, and rebellion would bring the loss of the land and the temple, as the following verses say.

For today: God does not look only for beautiful words, but for a faithful heart. Today the "other gods" can be money, success, or pride. Ask yourself honestly what holds first place in your life, and return to God with humility.
exp.6:19:
God says that if the people abandon him, he will uproot them from the land he gave them. He will also reject the temple he set apart for his name and turn it into a thing of mockery and scorn among all nations. Being set apart means being dedicated to God. The idea of cutting off and casting out from his presence means that God will withdraw his favor and his presence from that place.

God speaks to Solomon after the dedication of the temple. He promises blessing if the people remain faithful to him, but he also warns them seriously. The problem he describes is not a small mistake but turning away from him to worship other gods. Later, the history of Israel and Judah shows the fulfillment of this warning, though each reader may understand the historical details in different ways.

For today: spiritual privileges do not replace a living faith. Ask yourself what things compete with God in your heart, and return to him with sincerity.
exp.7:4:
It says that Solomon rebuilt the two cities called Beth-horon, one in the upper part and the other in the lower part. He left them well protected, with walls, gates, and bars. The "bars" were thick crossbeams of wood or metal used to secure the gates. "Rebuilt" means that they already existed and he raised them up again or improved them.

Here the chronicler, who narrates the reign of Solomon, speaks. After finishing the temple, Solomon devoted himself to strengthening the kingdom with cities for defense, for storage, and for chariots. Beth-horon lay on an important route toward Jerusalem, so protecting it made sense. Scholars agree that it was a strategic area.

For today: peace and prosperity do not take care of themselves. Just as Solomon diligently cared for what God had entrusted to him, we too can wisely protect our faith, our family, and our habits, trusting in God while we do what is ours to do.
exp.7:5:
This verse continues the list of Solomon's building projects. It says that he built Baalath and all the store cities where he kept supplies and weapons. He also built cities for his chariots and for his horsemen. In addition, he built whatever he wished in Jerusalem, in Lebanon, and throughout all the land he ruled.

The one who records this is the Chronicler, a writer who lived after the exile, whose purpose was to remind the people of how great Solomon's kingdom had been. After finishing the temple, Solomon devoted effort to organizing and strengthening his nation. The text shows a prosperous, secure, and well-established kingdom, just as God had promised.

God also values orderly work and careful planning. Building, organizing, and caring for what has been entrusted to us can be a way of honoring him. But it is good to remember that our works, however great, are worth more when they come from a life placed in God's hands.
exp.7:6:
This verse speaks of the peoples who still lived in the land of Israel: the Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites. They were remnants of the ancient nations of Canaan and did not belong to the people of Israel. The sentence is left open and is completed in the next verse, where it says that Solomon made them tributaries, that is, that they had to pay taxes or work for him.

The book of Chronicles recounts the reign of Solomon and highlights his great building works. The author is unknown, although Jewish tradition often names Ezra. It was written for a people returning from exile, reminding them of their history and identity. Here it is told how Solomon organized his kingdom, and it is made clear that the Israelites were not put to work as servants.

For today: God calls us to protect the dignity of people, especially when we have power or authority. We can ask ourselves whether we treat with justice those who depend on us.
exp.7:8:
This verse says that Solomon did not use the Israelites as servants or forced laborers in his building projects. They served in other ways: they were soldiers, leaders, captains, and commanders of the chariots and the horsemen.

The phrase about the horsemen refers to the cavalry, the soldiers who fought on horseback.

Here the narrator of Chronicles, who tells the story of Solomon, is speaking. The verse before it says that the peoples who remained in the land, such as the Hittites and the Amorites, were made to work for him. This verse makes a contrast: the Israelites had a different role in the kingdom. Some scholars note that the account in Kings is more complex, so not everything is explained in the same way there.

Each person has a place and a distinct function, and all are valuable. Today we can ask ourselves how we treat those who work alongside us: with dignity and fairness, recognizing their gifts and not only their usefulness.
exp.7:10:
Solomon moved Pharaoh's daughter, his wife, from the city of David to a house he had built for her. Solomon explained that she should not live in David's palace, because the places where the ark of the Lord had come were holy.

The speaker is the narrator of Chronicles, quoting Solomon's words. This took place when he had finished his building projects. The text says nothing more, so some think Solomon felt respect for the holiness of the ark. Others believe he also recognized how delicate this marriage to a foreign woman was. The Bible does not fully make this clear.

For today: Solomon cared for what was sacred and set limits on his household. We can ask which places, habits, or decisions need more respect for God, and look after them with care and sincerity.
exp.7:12:
This verse says that Solomon had the sacrifices offered to God on the days that were appropriate, as Moses had commanded. That included the sabbaths, the new moons (the beginning of each month), and the yearly feasts. The three great feasts were the feast of unleavened bread (bread without yeast, which recalled the departure from Egypt), the feast of weeks, and the feast of tabernacles.

Here the chronicler speaks, recounting how Solomon organized worship in the newly built temple. He followed the Law of Moses and also the order that his father David had left for priests and Levites. The author wants to show that worship in Jerusalem was carried out with order and obedience.

For today: God deserves a constant place in our lives, not only when we feel encouraged. We can set aside regular times to pray, read the Bible, and gather with other believers, with a grateful and sincere heart.
exp.7:14:
This verse says that the priests, the Levites, and the keepers of the treasures did not turn aside from what King Solomon had commanded. Turning aside from an order means disobeying it or drifting away from it. The phrase "any matter" refers to any task or concern at all, not only religious ones.

Here the narrator of Chronicles speaks, recounting how Solomon organized worship in the temple. Solomon followed the arrangement that his father David had left, and what Moses had commanded. The author wants to show that, in this time, service to God was carried out with order and faithfulness.

For today: obedience and order serve God when they are practiced with consistency. Try to be faithful in what falls to you, both in spiritual matters and in everyday things such as money and work.
exp.8:1:
This verse says that Solomon answered all the questions of the queen of Sheba. She put her doubts and problems to him, and he explained them one by one. Here "explain" means make clear or make known. There was no subject so difficult that Solomon could not make clear.

The account tells that the queen of Sheba travelled to Jerusalem because she heard of Solomon's fame. She wanted to test him with hard questions. The text does not say what those questions were. What it does show is that Solomon's wisdom, which the Bible presents as a gift from God, left her amazed, as the following verses make clear.

For today: when you have difficult questions, bring them honestly to God and to wise people. He is not troubled by our doubts. Ask for wisdom and seek godly counsel, without fear of asking.
exp.8:2:
This verse says that the queen of Sheba, after hearing Solomon's answers, saw with her own eyes two things: his wisdom and the palace he had built. The word "saw" here means to observe carefully. The sentence is left open and is completed in the next verse.

The account tells of the visit of a foreign queen to Jerusalem. She had heard of Solomon's fame and wanted to test it with hard questions. The chronicler describes what she saw. Sheba was a distant kingdom, but scholars do not fully agree on its exact location; it is usually linked with southern Arabia.

For today: do not rely only on what others say about God. Seek with sincerity, ask your questions, and observe his work. Real wisdom shows in what is said, and also in how things are lived and built.
exp.8:9:
This verse tells that the servants of Huram, king of Tyre, and the servants of Solomon went to fetch gold from Ophir. On their return they also brought algum wood and precious stones. Algum wood is a fine timber; it is not known with certainty what tree it was, and some think it could be sandalwood.

The text is a narrative, and no character speaks. It leads into the visit of the queen of Sheba, who praised God and gave Solomon gold, spices and jewels. The account shows the wealth of his reign. It then says that this wood was used for the steps of the temple and of the palace, and for harps and lyres for the singers.

For today: the best we receive can be put at the service of God. Our resources, talents and opportunities can be used to worship him and to help others, and not only for our own benefit.
exp.8:11:
This verse says that King Solomon gave the queen of Sheba everything she desired and asked for, even more than what she had brought him as a gift. Then she returned to her own land with her servants.

Here the speaker is the narrator of the book of Chronicles, who summarizes the end of the queen's visit to Jerusalem. Shortly before, the text speaks of Solomon's wealth and wisdom. The account shows his great generosity and reputation, and how his fame reached other nations. It does not say in detail what she asked for, so we should not invent it.

For today: generosity is not about giving the least we can, but about giving with joy and abundance, according to what we have. We can ask ourselves whom we might bless today with our time, help, or resources, and do it without expecting anything in return.
exp.8:12:
This verse says that each year Solomon received about six hundred and sixty-six talents of gold. A talent was a very large unit of weight; many scholars calculate it at about 30 to 35 kilograms, although the exact figure varies. It was an enormous amount of wealth. The phrase "came to Solomon" means that it reached him as income each year.

The book of Chronicles, written for the people of Israel after their return from exile, highlights here the greatness of Solomon's reign. It comes after the visit of the queen of Sheba, who was amazed by his wisdom and his riches. The author narrates; God does not speak directly. It shows how God kept his promise to bless Solomon.

For today: wealth can be a blessing, but it is not the most important thing. Solomon himself later wrote that everything is fleeting if one lives without God. Let us ask for wisdom to use well what we have and to share it generously.
exp.8:14:
This verse tells that King Solomon had two hundred large shields made, of gold beaten into thin sheets by hammer. Each one held six hundred shekels of gold. The shekel was an ancient unit of weight, and the total in kilograms is calculated in different ways.

The writer of Chronicles, who wrote long after Solomon's time, describes here the wealth and splendor of Solomon's reign. He has just spoken of the gold that came each year from neighboring merchants and kings. These shields were more for display and ceremony than for war. With them the writer shows how greatly Israel had prospered under Solomon.

For today: wealth can impress, but it is not a secure foundation. Later, in 2 Chronicles 12, these shields were lost. Put your trust in God, who does not change, and use what you have with gratitude and generosity.
exp.8:15:
The verse says that King Solomon made three hundred small shields of beaten gold, that is, gold worked by hammering. Each shield carried three hundred shekels of gold (a shekel weighed about eleven or twelve grams). Solomon placed them in the house of the forest of Lebanon, a building in his palace where he kept objects of great value.

The one telling this is the chronicler, who looks with admiration at Solomon's enormous wealth. It comes after the mention of the larger shields, and before the description of his ivory throne. These were shields of luxury more than of war, and they displayed his splendor before other kings.

For today: wealth can shine brightly, but it is not the most important thing. Solomon had gold to spare and still needed wisdom and faithfulness to God. Ask yourself today where you place your trust: in what you have, or in God.
exp.8:16:
This verse says that King Solomon had a large throne built from ivory, meaning the hard, white material of elephant tusks. He then covered it with pure gold. It was a very costly throne and beyond the ordinary.

Here the narrator of Chronicles speaks, describing the wealth and glory of Solomon's reign. This book was written for a people returning from exile, and it reminded them of the splendor of the kingdom that God had blessed. The passage also shows how much wealth Solomon had, although scholars debate whether the account only admires his glory or also hints at a warning.

For today: Everything valuable we have comes from God and is on loan. Let us make sure our possessions serve to honor him and bless others, not to feed pride.
exp.8:17:
This verse describes the throne of King Solomon. It had six steps to climb, and a footstool of gold, that is, a base to rest the feet on. On both sides of the seat there were supports to lean on, and next to them stood two lions.

The writer of Chronicles tells of the greatness of Solomon's reign. After speaking of the gold shields, he describes the ivory throne covered with pure gold. The lions and the steps gave an impression of power and authority. The text stresses that no other kingdom had anything like it, and that gold was so plentiful that silver was hardly valued.

For today: Solomon's wealth and power were impressive, but they were temporary. We can thank God for what he gives us and use it with humility, remembering that the true King is God, and that our security lies not in what we have, but in him.
exp.8:18:
This verse says that Solomon's throne had twelve lions, placed on the six steps, six on one side and six on the other. Together with the two lions beside the arms of the seat, the throne was surrounded by figures of lions. The text adds that nothing like it was ever made in any kingdom.

Here the chronicler is recounting the reign of Solomon, probably for the people who were returning from exile. He wants to show the splendor of Israel when the king sought God. The number twelve may recall the twelve tribes, though the text does not explain this, so it is a possible interpretation.

For today: human greatness, however brilliant, is passing. Use what God has entrusted to you with gratitude and humility, and remember that the true throne belongs to God.
exp.8:20:
It says that King Solomon had a fleet of ships that sailed to Tarshish together with the servants of Hiram, king of Tyre. Every three years they came back loaded with gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks. The word for the apes in the original is simply "apes," and the word for the peacocks is probably a reference to peacocks or other exotic birds; scholars are not sure of the exact meaning. It is also not known for certain where Tarshish was.

The Chronicler tells this to show how enormous Solomon's wealth was, right after describing his throne and his gold tableware. In this way he prepares the next comment: that Solomon surpassed all the kings in riches and in wisdom, gifts that the text says God gave him.

For today: riches and success can be blessings, but they are not the most important thing. Solomon was admired above all for the wisdom God gave him. We can ask God for wisdom before possessions, and use what we have with gratitude and generosity.
exp.8:21:
This verse says that King Solomon was greater than all the other kings of the known world, both in riches and in wisdom. To say he surpassed others is to say he went beyond them. The mules used for carrying loads, and the faraway trading place, are not mentioned in the verse you are reading, and scholars are not sure where that trading place was.

The Book of Chronicles was written after the exile in Babylon, and Jewish tradition attributes it to Ezra, though this is not certain. The narrator remembers Israel's golden age to encourage the people who were returning to their land. The text makes clear that Solomon's wisdom came from God, not from himself.

Riches can impress, but wisdom is worth more. Ask God for wisdom to decide well in everyday life, and remember that everything good you have is a gift from him to be used in serving others.
exp.8:23:
This verse says that the visitors who came to see Solomon did not come empty-handed. Each one brought a gift: objects of silver and gold, clothing, weapons, perfumes and spices, horses and mules. The mules mentioned here are animals used for carrying loads. And this happened year after year, that is, on a steady basis.

The text is part of the Chronicler's account of Solomon's reign. It comes right after saying that kings from all over the earth sought to hear the wisdom God had given him. The gifts show the respect he earned and how great his reputation was. It is the author who is telling the story, not Solomon.

For today: true influence comes from what God places in the heart, not from what a person boasts about. Let us ask God for wisdom and use it to serve, for people draw near to someone who has something good to teach.
exp.8:24:
It says that Solomon had four thousand stalls, that is, stables, for his horses and war chariots. He also had twelve thousand horsemen, soldiers on horseback, stationed in the "chariot cities" and in Jerusalem, near the king.

The writer of Chronicles, writing long after, sums up Solomon's greatness: wisdom, wealth and power. But the Law warned that the king should not multiply horses (Deuteronomy 17:16). Also, 1 Kings 4:26 gives a different figure, and it is not known with certainty why the numbers differ.

Today we can enjoy what God gives us without placing our security in it. Resources, savings or plans help, but only God truly sustains. Ask yourself: in what do I rest more, in what I have or in the Lord?
exp.8:25:
This verse says that Solomon ruled over many kings. His territory extended from the river, which is almost always understood to be the Euphrates, to the land of the Philistines, along the Mediterranean, and to the border of Egypt. More than a kingdom with fixed borders, it was a dominion over neighboring peoples who paid him tribute.

The narrator, the Chronicler, writes after the exile to encourage a people who were starting over. He reminds them of the period of greatest peace and prosperity for Israel, when God kept his promises to David. The yearly gifts, the horses, and the chariots show that power.

For today: what we have, whether much or little, is a gift from God and not a guarantee. Use it with humility and wisdom, and do not place your trust in your resources, but in God.
exp.8:26:
This verse says that in the time of Solomon silver was as common in Jerusalem as stones on the road. It also says that cedars, a very valuable wood, were as plentiful as the sycamore trees, which are wild fig trees that grew without care in the low plains, that is, in the lowlands or low-lying land.

Here the narrator of Chronicles describes the wealth and power of Solomon's kingdom. It is an account that looks back, probably to encourage a people who had lived through hard times. It shows God's blessing on Solomon, although the later account of the kings also shows that this abundance brought risks and failures.

For today: abundance can be a blessing from God, but it is not the most important thing. We can give thanks for what we have, use it generously, and take care that it does not take the place of God in our hearts.
exp.8:29:
This verse says that Solomon was king in Jerusalem and ruled over all the tribes of Israel for forty years. "Reigned" means that he governed as king. "Jerusalem" is the city of Jerusalem, the capital. The phrase "over all Israel" shows that his kingdom included the whole people.

Here the chronicler, the author of Chronicles, is summarizing the life of Solomon. Before this, he mentions the records of the prophets Nathan, Ahijah, and Iddo, where the rest of his history was kept. Afterward he tells of Solomon's death and that his son Rehoboam succeeded him. In this way the author closes this reign and prepares for what comes next.

For today: our years are also limited. Solomon had great achievements, but his time came to an end. It is worth asking ourselves how we use the years God gives us, and living them with wisdom, faithfulness, and thought for what we will leave to others.
exp.9:0:
It says that Rehoboam, son of Solomon, went to Shechem (this is how the name is written today). There all Israel had gathered to make him king.

This is the opening of the account of the division of the kingdom. The one telling the story is the writer of Chronicles, writing for a people who were returning from exile. Shechem was an important place for the northern tribes, and many think Rehoboam went there because he needed their acceptance. The text does not explain all his reasons.
