The verses that follow show there was tension, since Jeroboam, who had fled from Solomon, comes back.

For today: before taking a position of leadership, it is wise to listen to the people we are going to serve. Authority without humility and without an attentive ear can cause deep wounds.
exp.9:1:
It says that Jeroboam, son of Nebat, was in Egypt. He had fled there out of fear of King Solomon. When he heard that Rehoboam was going to be crowned, he returned.

The narrator of Chronicles tells how the kingdom was divided. Rehoboam, son of Solomon, went to Shechem, where all Israel gathered to make him king. Jeroboam was known for his conflict with Solomon (1 Kings 11 explains it). He was summoned, and he came back to present, together with the people, a request: that Rehoboam lighten the heavy burdens of the previous reign.

For today: when someone with authority receives a complaint, they face an important decision. We can listen with humility or respond with pride. And if we ourselves make a request, let us make it with respect and with an eye to the good of everyone, not only our own.
exp.9:7:
He abandoned the advice the elders gave him and instead listened to the young men who had grown up with him and were serving him, that is, his close companions.

The people of Israel had asked Rehoboam, the new king after Solomon's death, to lighten the heavy burden his father had placed on them. The elders, who had served Solomon, advised him to treat the people well and speak kindly to them. Rehoboam did not listen to them. This decision led to the division of the kingdom, although the text also says that God was allowing that course of events.

Today we can learn not to choose only the voices that tell us what we want to hear. Before an important decision, let us seek the counsel of wise people who have experience and who do not depend on our favor. And let us ask God for the humility to listen.
exp.9:10:
Here King Rehoboam answers the people harshly. He says that his father Solomon put a heavy yoke on them, that is, burdens and hard labor, but that he will make them even greater. His father corrected them with whips, and he will do so with scorpions. Many understand that these were whips with points or knots of metal that caused more harm, although the word is interpreted this way from the context.

Rehoboam has just been made king, and the people ask him for relief. He asked counsel from the elders, who suggested he be kind, but he followed the young men he had grown up with. That is why he speaks with pride and harshness. That decision led to the division of the kingdom.

For today: whoever holds authority in the home, the workplace, or the church should listen with humility and govern by serving, not by pressing down. A harsh answer can break what took years to build. Ask God for wisdom before you speak.
exp.9:12:
This verse says that King Rehoboam answered the people harshly. He set aside the counsel of the elders, who had advised him to be kind. "Harshly" means with hard words and without gentleness. "The elders" were the older men, with experience, who had served his father Solomon.

The people, together with Jeroboam, asked Rehoboam to lighten the heavy burden of taxes and labor. Rehoboam asked for three days to think it over. The elders suggested he serve the people with kind words, but he preferred the young men he had grown up with. The text adds that God allowed this to fulfill what had already been announced about the division of the kingdom.

Today we can learn to listen to wise counsel, especially from people who are mature in faith and in life. When we have authority, it is good to speak with humility and not with pride. A harsh answer can break what a kind word would have cared for.
exp.9:13:
Rehoboam, the new king, answers the people harshly. He follows the advice of the young men and says he will be worse than his father Solomon. The "yoke" is the burden of work and taxes that the people carried. The "young men" are the younger men. The "scorpions" were probably whips with metal points or thorns, much more cruel than ordinary lashes.

Jeroboam and all Israel had asked the king to lighten the load. Rehoboam set aside the counsel of the elders, who advised him to serve the people, and preferred that of his companions. The text says God allowed this to fulfill what he had said through the prophet Ahijah. Because of this decision, the kingdom was divided.

Today, power is used well when it serves and listens. Before deciding something important, seek the counsel of wise and mature people. Respond with humility, not with pride or harshness.
exp.9:16:
This verse says that, after the division, Rehoboam remained king only over the Israelites who lived in the cities of Judah. He no longer ruled over the ten tribes of the north. His kingdom was now much smaller.

The writer of Chronicles tells how Rehoboam refused the people's request to lighten their burdens. For that reason the northern tribes broke away from the house of David. The account says that the division came from God, since it fulfilled what He had announced through the prophet Ahijah. That does not remove Rehoboam's responsibility for his harshness.

For today: listen humbly to those who depend on us. One harsh word can break what took years to build. God can work even through our mistakes, but it is better to respond with wisdom and compassion.
exp.10:0:
It says that when Rehoboam came to Jerusalem, he gathered the people of Judah and Benjamin: one hundred and eighty thousand chosen men for war. His plan was to fight against Israel, the northern tribes, and win back the kingdom. Gathered means brought together, and chosen means selected for their ability to fight.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. After the death of Solomon, Rehoboam answered the people harshly, and the northern tribes separated under Jeroboam. Rehoboam wanted to settle the division by force. The next verse shows that God intervened through the prophet Shemaiah, so this plan was not the final word.

For today: when something breaks, we sometimes want to fix it with force or pressure. Before acting, it is wise to stop, pray, and listen to God's will, also through his Word and wise counselors.
exp.10:2:
This verse is the command that God gives to the prophet Shemaiah: he is to speak to Rehoboam, king of Judah, and to all the Israelites who lived in the tribes of Judah and Benjamin.

The words that introduce the speech are the sort of phrasing that tells the reader a message is about to follow, and the phrase that announces the message points forward to the verse that comes next.

The one speaking is the LORD, and he does so through Shemaiah, the man of God. Rehoboam had gathered 180,000 soldiers to fight against the northern tribes, which had separated from the kingdom. God intervenes before there is a war between brothers, and the people listen.

For today: before entering into a conflict, it is wise to stop and listen to God. Sometimes we believe we are right and want to fight, but he may show us another way. Praying and accepting his direction can prevent harm that could not later be repaired.
exp.10:3:
God commands Rehoboam and all the people of Judah and Benjamin not to go out to fight against their brothers, the people of the other tribes of Israel. Each person must go back home, because God says that he allowed or directed what has happened. The people obeyed, went back, and did not attack Jeroboam.

God speaks through the prophet Shemaiah. After Solomon's death, the kingdom was divided: Rehoboam kept Judah and Benjamin, and Jeroboam ruled the northern tribes. Rehoboam wanted to take everything back by force, but God stopped him. The earlier passages show that this division was connected to God's judgment, although human responsibility was also real.

For today: before you fight out of pride or because you want to be right, stop and ask what God wants. Sometimes obeying means giving up a fight and avoiding greater harm.
exp.10:5:
It says that King Rehoboam built up or strengthened several cities in Judah: Bethlehem, Etam, and Tekoa. The word "built" here means that he fortified them, that is, made them safer with walls and defenses.

The writer of Chronicles tells what happened after the kingdom was divided. God had asked that there be no war against Jeroboam, and the people obeyed. Then Rehoboam used that time of calm to protect the south of Judah. These cities formed a line of defense near Jerusalem, although the exact details of their military use are not fully known.

Obeying God does not mean doing nothing. When He gives us a time of peace, we can use it wisely: caring for the family, strengthening our faith, and preparing for trials, always trusting in God.
exp.10:7:
This verse continues the list of cities that King Rehoboam built up, that is, strengthened or fortified. Here Gath, Mareshah, and Ziph are named.

The narrator is the chronicler of Israel, who writes long after these events. Rehoboam reigned in Judah after the kingdom was divided. With these cities to the south and west of Jerusalem, he wanted to protect his territory from attacks. He was clearly seeking security, although the account later shows that his real strength depended on obeying God. The exact location of some of these places is debated among scholars.

For today: it is good to prepare ourselves and to take care of what God has given us, with hard work and good order. But let us not place our trust only in our defenses, but in God, who is our true refuge.
exp.10:13:
This verse says that the Levites left their pasture lands around the cities that had been assigned to them, along with their other property. They went to Judah and Jerusalem because Jeroboam and his sons had removed them from serving the Lord.

The writer of Chronicles, whose name the Bible does not state with certainty, tells what happened when the kingdom was divided. Jeroboam, king of the north, set up his own altars and priests, and the faithful Levites could not serve there. They chose to lose their lands rather than give up worship of the Lord.

For today: being faithful to God sometimes costs something, such as comfort, money, or acceptance. Ask yourself what you might be holding onto more than your faithfulness to God, and ask Him for the courage to choose Him first.
exp.10:17:
This verse tells us that Rehoboam, king of Judah, married two women: Mahalath and Abihail. Mahalath was the daughter of Jerimoth, who was a son of David, which made her his cousin. Abihail was the daughter of Eliab, a son of Jesse, the father of David.

The author of Chronicles gives details about the king's family while describing how Judah grew strong. Around Rehoboam there were faithful people who sought God. These marriages are a historical record, not a divine approval. The Bible warns that kings were not to multiply wives, and this will bring problems later on.

Even when the spiritual atmosphere around us is good, each person must watch over their own personal decisions. Having faith nearby does not replace one's own obedience. Let us ask God for wisdom today.
exp.10:21:
King Rehoboam chose Abijah, the son of his favorite wife Maachah, to be the chief and leader among all his brothers. The reason was clear: he wanted Abijah to become the next king. The chief and leader among the king's sons is the main leader among them.

The one speaking here is the narrator of Chronicles, who summarizes the life of Rehoboam, king of Judah, after the division of the kingdom. Rehoboam had many wives and concubines, and he loved Maachah more. Abijah is said to have been chosen because of that affection, though he was not necessarily the eldest son; the text does not make this clear. Afterward Rehoboam spread his other sons out among the fortified cities to secure order.

For today: when we make important decisions in the family or at work, let us ask God for wisdom to act with justice and not only out of personal preferences.
exp.10:22:
It says that Rehoboam wisely placed his sons, and he distributed some of his other children throughout the fortified cities of Judah and Benjamin. He gave them provisions, which are food and supplies, in abundance. He also sought many wives for them. According to many scholars, the phrase about instructing refers to Rehoboam preparing Abijah to reign, although the original text allows different readings, and not everyone agrees on who requested the wives.

This is part of the account of Rehoboam's reign as king of Judah, written by the chronicler. Here we see how he secured his family's future: he gave Abijah the chief place and kept the other sons close, with resources and positions, to avoid rivalries over the throne. The text narrates the events without openly approving or condemning them, although the Bible warns against multiplying wives.

Planning for the future of the family is good, but giving resources and positions is not enough. What matters more is shaping the hearts of the children in faith and character. Let us ask God for wisdom to leave them something more lasting than possessions.
exp.11:2:
This verse describes the huge army with which Shishak, king of Egypt, attacked Judah: twelve hundred chariots and sixty thousand horsemen. In addition, the people who came with him from Egypt were so numerous that they could not be counted. They were Lubims, Sukkiims, and Ethiopians. The Sukkiims are a people whose exact identity is not known for certain; some think they were inhabitants of some region near Egypt.

The writer of Chronicles tells the story. He explains that Rehoboam, once he was strengthened as king, abandoned the law of the LORD, and the people did the same. The invasion is presented as a consequence of that unfaithfulness. Later on, the prophet Shemaiah confirms this.

For today: when we feel secure and stop seeking God, we expose ourselves to problems. Let us not wait for the crisis to arrive; let us seek God with humility every day, even when everything is going well.
exp.11:3:
This verse tells how the army of Shishak, king of Egypt, captured the fortified cities of Judah and advanced until it reached Jerusalem. The fortified cities were towns protected by walls, which were meant to defend the kingdom.

The one telling the story is the chronicler, who explains the history of Judah with a spiritual focus. According to the text, this invasion took place in the fifth year of King Rehoboam, because the people had rebelled against the LORD. Afterward, the prophet Shemaiah tells the king and the princes that, since they abandoned God, he has left them in Shishak's hands. They humbled themselves and acknowledged that God is righteous.

For today: defenses and resources do not replace God. When we face the consequences of turning away from him, the best thing is to humble ourselves, acknowledge the mistake, and return to him sincerely.
exp.11:4:
This verse tells how the prophet Shemaiah brought a message from God to King Rehoboam and the leaders of Judah, who had gathered in Jerusalem out of fear of Shishak, king of Egypt. The leaders are the rulers or those in authority. The message is serious: you have forsaken me, and so I have left you in the hand of Shishak.

Shishak had invaded Judah with a huge army and had already taken its strong cities. Shemaiah speaks in God's name and makes clear that the invasion was not just bad luck, but the result of turning away from Him. The next verse then shows that they humbled themselves, and God spared them from destruction.

For today: when trials come, it is good to ask ourselves humbly whether we have drifted away from God. If we have, let us return to Him without excuses; He responds to a humble heart with mercy.
exp.11:6:
God saw that the king and the leaders of Judah had humbled themselves, that is, they admitted their wrong with humility. Then he spoke to the prophet Shemaiah: he would not destroy them, but would deliver them soon, and his anger would not fall upon Jerusalem through Shishak.

God speaks through the prophet Shemaiah. Rehoboam and Judah had forsaken God, and Shishak king of Egypt attacked them. When they confessed that the Lord was righteous, they accepted that the punishment was deserved. God withheld total destruction from them, although they remained subject to Egypt and lost the treasures of the temple.

For today: when we fail, sincere humility opens the door to God's mercy. Acknowledging our error without excuses does not remove every consequence, but it allows us to begin again with his help.
exp.11:9:
After Shishak carried off the golden shields, King Rehoboam had shields of bronze made to replace them. He gave them into the hands of the chief of the guard, who watched over the entrance to the palace. The shields in question were large ones, and the bronze is commonly understood here as the material they were made of.

This is part of the Chronicler's account. Judah had abandoned the law of God, and God allowed the invasion of Egypt as a consequence. Rehoboam lost the wealth that Solomon had accumulated. The text shows a contrast: the golden shields represented splendor, and the bronze ones a reduced glory, although they continued to be used in the king's processions to the temple.

For today: when sin costs us something valuable, it does no good to pretend that everything is still the same. The best course is to humble ourselves before God, as Rehoboam later did, and receive his mercy. He can give us a new beginning, even if we do not recover everything we lost.
exp.11:10:
It says that every time King Rehoboam went to the temple, the guards carried the metal shields and marched with him. After the visit, they brought them back to the guard room.

Here the narrator of Chronicles speaks. Shishak, king of Egypt, had plundered Jerusalem and carried off Solomon's gold shields. Rehoboam replaced them with shields of bronze or metal, which were worth far less. The appearance of greatness was kept, but the splendor was no longer the same. Even so, the text still says that Rehoboam humbled himself and God turned away his anger.

For today: sometimes we try to keep up appearances when we have lost something valuable. It is better to imitate Rehoboam's humility, to acknowledge our losses and mistakes before God, and to trust in his mercy.
exp.11:12:
This verse says that King Rehoboam established himself on the throne and reigned in Jerusalem. He was forty-one years old when he began and reigned seventeen years. Jerusalem is the city that God chose out of all the tribes of Israel to put his name there. His mother is also mentioned, Naamah, an Ammonite woman. Being established means that he secured his power.

It is the narrator of Chronicles who speaks. Rehoboam had just been humbled by the invasion of Egypt, and God did not destroy him when he humbled himself. But the next verse makes clear that he did evil, because he did not prepare his heart to seek the Lord. This shows that his humbling was temporary.

For today: a crisis can lead us to humble ourselves, but what matters is keeping a heart that seeks God every day, not only when we are in trouble.
exp.11:14:
This verse closes the account of Rehoboam's reign with a farewell formula typical of the books of Chronicles. It says that his deeds, from beginning to end, are recorded in the writings of Shemaiah the prophet and of Iddo the seer (another word for prophet). The phrase "the genealogies" refers to records of family lines. It also says that there was constant war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam.

The narrator of Chronicles, whose author is not known with certainty, summarizes Rehoboam's life. After the kingdom was divided, Rehoboam ruled Judah and Jeroboam ruled the north. The previous passage explains the cause of his failure: he "did evil, because he did not set his heart to seek the Lord," that is, he did not prepare and direct his heart to seek God.

For today: our lives also become a record in what we decide each day. Prepare your heart early, with prayer and the Word, so that seeking God becomes a habit and not something improvised.
exp.12:0:
This verse marks when Abijah began to reign in Judah: when Jeroboam, king of Israel (the northern kingdom), had already been ruling for eighteen years. It is a date notice that opens the story of this new king.

The author of Chronicles, whom tradition often identifies with Ezra (this is not certain), wrote for the people who were returning from exile. He wanted to remind them of the history of the kings of Judah, descendants of David. Here he introduces Abijah before telling of his war against Jeroboam.

Kings and eras pass, but God keeps working in history. Each of us lives in a specific time, and God calls us to be faithful right there, with what we have today.
exp.12:1:
This verse tells us that Abijah reigned in Jerusalem for only three years. It names his mother, Michaiah, the daughter of Uriel of Gibeah. And it warns that there was war between Abijah, king of Judah, and Jeroboam, king of Israel, the two nations that had been divided.

The writer of Chronicles records here the beginning of Abijah's reign, son of Rehoboam. His mother appears under a different name in 1 Kings 15:2 (Maacah), and scholars explain this in several ways, with no certain answer. This verse prepares the great battle that follows and Abijah's speech from Mount Zemaraim.

For today: a short reign reminds us that our time is brief. It is wise to use it trusting in God and not only in our own strength, as we will see Abijah attempt to do.
exp.12:4:
Abijah asks Jeroboam and the Israelites whether they do not know that God gave the kingdom of Israel to David and to his descendants forever.

Abijah, king of Judah, speaks just before a battle against Jeroboam, king of the northern tribes. He was far weaker in numbers, but he wants to remind them that David's throne rested on a promise of God. His words are an argument in his own favor, although the Bible also shows that Abijah was not a perfect king.

For today: God's promises do not depend on circumstances or majorities. When you feel at a disadvantage, remember what God has said in his Word and trust that he is faithful to his covenant.
exp.12:9:
It says that the people of Judah remain faithful to the Lord: they have not forsaken him. Also, the priests who serve God are the descendants of Aaron, assisted by the Levites, who carry out the work of worship. "But" means "but", and the word "as for" in the verse above is the way the sentence introduces the contrast.

Abijah, king of Judah, speaks from a mountain, before a battle against Jeroboam, king of Israel (the northern kingdom). Abijah contrasts Judah with Israel, which made golden calves and appointed priests outside the order that God had given. His personal life was not perfect, and the Bible shows this in other passages. Even so, his argument about worship here is clear.

For today: it is not enough to say that we belong to God; it is worth examining whether we follow him with steady faithfulness, in prayer, obedience and sincere worship.
exp.12:12:
He says that Jeroboam, king of Israel, sent part of his army to hide and go around to attack Judah from behind. So while his troops were in front, the ambush was behind the soldiers of Judah.

King Abijah of Judah had just spoken to Israel from a mountain. He reminded them that Judah still worshiped God in the temple, while Israel had abandoned him. While he was speaking and asking them not to fight against God, Jeroboam was setting his trap. Then Judah found itself surrounded, cried out to the LORD, and God gave them the victory.

For today: sometimes we feel surrounded, with no way out and no strength left. In those moments we can do what Judah did: cry out to God sincerely. He can help us even when we cannot see the way forward.
exp.12:13:
The men of Judah looked around and saw that the enemy was attacking them from the front and from behind. They were surrounded. Then they cried out, that is, they called loudly for help to the Lord, and the priests blew the trumpets.

The narrator is the chronicler. Abijah, king of Judah, had just warned Israel not to fight against the God of their fathers. Jeroboam, king of Israel, sent an ambush to attack from behind. The verses that follow show that God gave the victory to Judah.

For today: when you feel cornered and without a way out, do not freeze. Cry out to God sincerely and keep doing what you know is right. He can work even when you cannot see how.
exp.12:16:
Abijah and his people struck them with a great slaughter, and five hundred thousand chosen men of Israel fell down slain. This verse says these were chosen soldiers, that is, well-selected and well-prepared fighting men.

This is the chronicler's account of the war between Judah, under King Abijah, and Israel, under Jeroboam. Before the battle, Abijah called on Israel to return to the God of their fathers. According to the text, Judah cried out to God, and he gave them the victory. The very large numbers of this period have been debated; some take them literally, while others think they may have a different sense. The emphasis of the text is that God gave the victory to those who trusted in him.

For today: when you face something that is bigger than you, first seek God in prayer and trust in him, rather than in your own strength or resources.
exp.12:17:
This verse says that the Israelites of the northern kingdom were defeated and brought under control, while the men of Judah grew strong. The reason is clear: they trusted in the Lord, the God of their fathers.

The author of Chronicles, whose exact identity is not known, recounts the war between Abijah, king of Judah, and Jeroboam, king of Israel. Before the battle, Abijah called on Israel not to fight against the God of their fathers. The chronicler explains the outcome with a spiritual motive: Judah cried out to God and relied on Him. The numbers of the dead are very large, and some scholars debate how they should be understood.

When you face a situation that is beyond you, do not trust only in your own strength or resources. Pray, lean on God, and seek to obey Him, knowing that He sustains those who trust in Him.
exp.12:19:
Verse 20 says that Jeroboam, king of Israel, never regained his strength or his influence while Abijah reigned over Judah. Afterward, the Lord struck him down and he died.

The writer of Chronicles tells this story to show what happened after a great battle. Abijah, king of Judah, defeated Jeroboam because Judah trusted in God. Jeroboam had led Israel into worshiping golden calves. The text does not explain how or when Jeroboam died, or how much time passed between his defeat and his death. It only states that the blow came from God.

Trusting in God gives us a strength that human power cannot give. If today you feel that you are depending on your own resources, hand that matter over to God in prayer and seek his direction before you act.
exp.12:20:
It says that Abijah grew strong after defeating Jeroboam. He had fourteen wives, and with them he had twenty-two sons and sixteen daughters. In other words, his power and his family grew while the kingdom of Judah became more firmly established.

Here the chronicler, the author of Chronicles, is speaking, and he tells the history of the kings of Judah. This comes after Abijah's victory over Jeroboam, king of Israel, and how God struck Jeroboam down. The text only reports; it neither approves nor condemns having many wives. Other passages in the Bible show that this practice brought trouble to several kings. About Abijah's life, some passages present him differently, and various scholars see it that way.

For today: may strength or success never make us forget God. Let us ask him for wisdom to live with integrity, even when everything is going well for us.
exp.13:2:
This verse tells what King Asa did to clear his kingdom of idolatry. He took away the altars dedicated to foreign gods and the high places, which were raised spots where sacrifices were offered. He broke down the images, meaning the sacred pillars or stones, and cut down the groves, which were wooden posts or trunks used in worship of the goddess Asherah.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Chronicles. He tells that Asa came to the throne after his father Abijah, and that he did what was right before God. His reforms were the foundation of the peace Judah had during those years. Scholars debate whether some of the high places were removed completely, since another text says not all of them disappeared.

For today: ask yourself what things in your life hold the place that belongs to God, and take one concrete step to remove them.
exp.13:4:
It says that King Asa removed from all the cities of Judah the high places and the images. The high places were raised spots where false gods were worshiped or where God was worshiped in an improper way, and the images were idols or cult pillars. As a result, the kingdom enjoyed peace during his reign.

The passage is a narrative from the chronicler, not a speech. It tells how Asa, king of Judah, carried out a religious reform: he destroyed foreign altars and called the people to seek the LORD and to obey his law. Afterward, the account says God gave him rest, and for that reason he was able to build fortified cities in a time of peace.

For today: if there are things in your life that take the place of God, setting them aside is not a loss but a step toward peace. Begin with one concrete decision and seek God with steadiness, without promising that everything will be easy.
exp.13:5:
It says that King Asa built strong, fortified cities in Judah. He was able to do this because there was peace and no one made war on him in those years. The text gives the reason: the Lord had given him rest, that is, calm and freedom from enemies.

The word "built" here means to construct or to strengthen.

It is part of the account in the book of Chronicles, written by a narrator who tells the history of the kings of Judah. Asa had removed the altars of false gods and called the people to seek God and obey his law. The narrator presents the peace as the result of that return to God, and Asa used that calm to prepare himself rather than become careless.

For today: quiet times are an opportunity to strengthen what matters. We can use peace to grow in faith, care for our family, and put our lives in order, trusting that God is the one who gives rest.
exp.13:6:
He says that King Asa encouraged the people of Judah to build fortified cities, with walls, towers, gates, and bars (the crossbeams that secured the gates). He explains that they could do this because the land was theirs and because they had sought God, who had given them peace on every side. They built, and things went well for them.

Asa, king of Judah, speaks. He had removed the altars of idolatry and led the people to seek God. He used the time of peace to prepare. Soon after, the attack of Zerah the Ethiopian would come, so this preparation would prove very useful. The text presents peace as a gift from God, not only as a human achievement.

For today: use the peaceful times to strengthen what matters most, such as your faith, your family, and your habits of prayer. Do not wait for a crisis to prepare. Seek God now, thank him for his peace, and work with wisdom.
exp.14:0:
The Spirit of God came upon Azariah, the son of Oded. This means God took control of this man in order to give him a message. Here "came" means that the Spirit came down upon him. The Bible does not explain how it happened, only that God prepared him to speak.

Azariah was a prophet of Judah. We know little about him, only his name and his father's name. King Asa was returning from a military victory, and God sent Azariah to encourage him to remain faithful. The message that follows says that God is with his people if they are with him, and that they will find him if they seek him.

God still speaks to his people and wants us to seek him wholeheartedly. Today we can set aside time each day to read the Bible and pray, not only when there are problems, but also when everything is going well, as in King Asa's victory.
exp.14:1:
He went out to meet King Asa and asked him and all of Judah and Benjamin to listen to him. He reminded them that the Lord is with them as long as they remain with him. If they seek him, he will be found by them; but if they abandon him, he will abandon them as well.

Azariah, son of Oded, spoke, moved by the Spirit of God. Asa was returning from a military victory, and the prophet wanted to encourage him to remain faithful. Then Azariah recalled times when Israel was without the law or a guide, and how God responded when the people turned back to seek him in their distress. Scholars understand in different ways which exact period he is referring to, but the central message is clear.

For today: do not seek God only when problems arrive. Set aside a moment each day to pray and read the Bible, and so you will keep your heart close to him, whether in good times or difficult ones.
exp.14:2:
It says that Israel went a long time without the true God, without a priest to teach, and without a law to guide them. Some understand that the people had all of this but did not follow it.

Azariah, a prophet on whom the Spirit of God came, speaks. His message is for King Asa, Judah and Benjamin. He reminds them of times of disorder, probably the time of the judges, although the interpreters do not fully agree. He warns them that God is with them if they are with him. When they turned back, they found him.

For today: do not let your spiritual life be left without guidance. Read the Bible faithfully, seek a church where teaching is given sincerely, and return to God each time you drift away. He responds to those who seek him.
exp.14:3:
This verse says that when the people of Israel were in distress, they turned their hearts to God and sought him, and God allowed himself to be found by them. The verse of "turned" is that they came back to God, returning to him. The phrase about being found means that they discovered him.

The prophet Azariah speaks, going out to meet King Asa and the people of Judah and Benjamin. He reminded them that God is with those who are with him, and that he will leave them if they leave him. He mentioned hard times from the past, without a true god, without a teaching priest, to encourage them to remain faithful. Scholars disagree about which exact period he is referring to.

For today: if you are going through a difficulty, come to God with sincerity, in prayer and by reading his Word. He promises to be found by those who seek him.
exp.14:8:
He says that King Asa gathered all the people of Judah and Benjamin. Those from Ephraim, Manasseh and Simeon who lived among them as residents also joined. Many from the northern kingdom (Israel) had gone over to Asa, because they saw that God was with him.

Here the narrator of Chronicles is speaking. Asa had just heard the prophecy of Obed, who encouraged him not to lose heart. Then he removed the idols and repaired the altar. That reform drew the attention of many in the north. Afterward the people gathered to renew their commitment to God.

For today: our faithful lives can be a quiet testimony. When we seek God sincerely and correct what is wrong at home, others may notice that God is with us and draw near to Him.
exp.14:9:
This verse says that the people gathered together in Jerusalem in the third month, in the fifteenth year of King Asa's reign. The word "gathered" in the verse is what the verse's quoted term means. "Jerusalem" appears in the verse as Jerusalem. The third month of the Hebrew calendar corresponds roughly to May or June, although the exact equivalence is not certain.

The chronicler tells how King Asa, encouraged by the prophecy of Azariah son of Oded, removed the idols and repaired the altar. Then he called together Judah, Benjamin, and the foreigners who lived among them, who had come over when they saw that the LORD was with Asa. This gathering led to sacrifices and to a covenant to seek God with all their heart.

For today: returning to God is not only a private feeling. It is good to set apart time to meet with other believers, worship, and renew our commitment to Him.
exp.14:11:
This verse says that the people of Judah made a covenant, a solemn agreement, to seek the Lord, the God of their fathers, with all their will and their emotions, that is, with complete sincerity. Here the word "covenant" means a solemn agreement, and "seek" means to draw near to God, depend on Him, and obey Him.

The text does not have a single speaker; it is the chronicler's account of what the people gathered in Jerusalem did. This happened during the reign of Asa, after a religious reform and a victory. They had just offered sacrifices to God, and the covenant was their response of renewal. The verses that follow show that they took it very seriously, with a public oath.

For today: true faith is not just carrying out religious acts, but giving God the whole heart. You might set aside a moment this week to renew your commitment to Him, speaking to Him sincerely and asking His help to live it out each day.
exp.14:12:
They made a solemn agreement: whoever would not seek the Lord God of Israel would be put to death, whether small or great, whether man or woman. The word "seek" here means the same as "seek" in the verse, and "put to death" means the same as in the verse. No one was exempt from this promise.

This happened in the days of King Asa of Judah, after the prophet Azariah encouraged him to return to God. The people made a covenant with all their heart. That penalty reflected the law of Moses, which punished idolatry within Israel. There is no certainty about how many times it was actually applied.

Today we do not live under that system, but the text reminds us that seeking God is not a half-hearted matter. We can ask ourselves: do I seek him with all my heart, or only when I need him? Begin with a daily time of prayer and Bible reading.
exp.14:13:
This verse tells us that the people of Judah made a solemn oath before God. They made it shouting loudly, with joy, and with the sound of trumpets and horns (wind instruments, like rams' horns).

This was in the time of King Asa. After a call from the prophet Azariah, the people gathered in Jerusalem to renew their covenant with God and to seek him with all their heart. The text says that this oath included a severe penalty for anyone who rejected God, something typical of the law of Israel at that time. Then came joy, peace, and reform.

For today: returning to God does not have to be cold or forced. We can renew our commitment to him with sincerity and gladness, and remove from our lives whatever competes with him.
exp.14:18:
The verse says that for several years the kingdom of Judah lived in peace. There was no war from the time Asa began to reign until his thirty-fifth year of rule. It was a long time of calm for the people.

The book of Chronicles tells the history of the kings of Judah. Asa had carried out a spiritual reform: he removed the idols and led the people to seek God with all their heart. The text presents that peace as the fruit of that seeking. There is a difference in numbers with the book of Kings, which speaks of war during his reign, and scholars explain it in several ways; it is not something certain. What is clear is that Chronicles highlights a period of rest.

For today: when we put God first, not everything becomes easy, but He can give us seasons of peace. Give thanks for those times and use them to strengthen your faith.
exp.15:1:
This verse tells how Asa, king of Judah, took the silver and gold kept in the temple and in the palace and sent them to Ben-hadad, king of Syria, who lived in Damascus. With that gift he sent a message asking for help.

Here the narrator of Chronicles is speaking. Baasha, king of Israel, was building Ramah to block Asa's way. Asa became afraid and sought an alliance with Syria, paying with treasures that were dedicated to God. Later, God rebuked him for trusting the king of Syria and not Him (16:7-9).

When pressure comes, it is easy to look for human solutions first and leave God for last. We can use our wisdom and resources, but it is better to pray and trust Him first. Ask yourself: what am I trusting in today?
exp.15:2:
Asa, king of Judah, proposes an agreement to Ben-hadad, king of Syria. He tells him that there was already friendship between their fathers, and he sends him silver and gold so that he will break his treaty with Baasha, king of Israel. In this way Baasha would have to withdraw from Judah.

Baasha had begun to fortify Ramah, a nearby city, to block the way into Judah. Asa felt pressed and took the treasure from the temple and the palace to pay Syria. It worked militarily, but the chapter goes on with the rebuke of the prophet Hanani, because Asa trusted in a foreign king and not in God.

When pressure comes, it is easy to look for a quick way out using human resources. Before you act, stop to pray and ask whether you are trusting God or only your own solution.
exp.15:5:
It says that King Asa gathered all the people of Judah and carried away from Ramah the stones and the timber that Baasha had been using for building. With those materials, Asa built the cities of Geba (also called Gibeah) and Mizpah.

This passage is spoken by the narrator of the book of Chronicles. Baasha, king of Israel, was fortifying Ramah to block the way into Judah. Asa paid the king of Syria for help instead of asking God for help, and Baasha abandoned the work. Asa made use of the materials, but the next verse shows that God rebuked him for trusting Syria.

For today: a good result does not always prove that the decision was right. Before looking for the most practical way out, stop and pray and trust God, because He wants to be our first support, not our last resort.
exp.15:6:
This verse tells that the prophet Hanani, called "seer" (someone who received messages from God), went to speak with King Asa. He told him that, because he had relied on the king of Syria and not on the Lord his God, the Syrian army had escaped from his hands.

Asa was at war with Baasha, king of Israel, who was building Ramah to pressure Judah. Instead of asking God for help, Asa paid the king of Syria to break his alliance with Baasha. It worked for the moment, but Hanani corrects him firmly, reminding him that God had earlier given him victory over a huge army when he did trust in Him.

Today we can ask ourselves whom we trust first when facing a problem. Planning and seeking help is not wrong, but God wants to be our first trust, not our last resort.
exp.15:7:
This verse reminds King Asa of a victory from the past. The Ethiopians and the Lubims had a huge army, with many chariots and horsemen. Even so, Asa defeated them because he relied on God. The word "relied" in the verse means to trust in and depend on someone.

The one speaking is Hanani, a seer, that is, a prophet who received messages from God. Asa had made an alliance with the king of Syria instead of asking God for help. Hanani confronts him by reminding him that God had already helped him before, in a worse situation. Asa became angry and put him in prison. It is thought that this battle is the one described in 2 Chronicles 14.

For today: remembering what God has already done for us helps us trust Him when new problems come. Before looking only for human solutions, let us pray. And when someone corrects us out of love, let us listen with humility, without hardening our hearts.
exp.15:11:
He says that in the thirty-ninth year of his reign, King Asa became ill in his feet, and that the sickness grew until it became very serious. Instead of seeking the Lord, he sought only the physicians. The phrase "diseased in his feet" probably describes an illness that kept spreading upward; it is not known for certain what the illness was.

The one speaking is the narrator of Chronicles, writing for a people who were returning from exile. Asa had trusted God at the beginning, but later he leaned on human alliances, grew angry at the prophet who corrected him, and mistreated the people. This verse shows that his heart had turned away. The text does not condemn the physicians; the problem is that Asa did not seek God.

For today: when sickness comes, we can go to the doctor and also pray. Seeking help is wise; the danger lies in trusting only human resources and forgetting God.
exp.15:13:
Asa was buried in a tomb that he himself had had prepared in the city of David. They laid him on a bier, which is a stretcher used to carry the dead, filled with perfumes and spices prepared by skilled makers. They also made a very great burning for him, probably of incense, as a sign of honor. Some think it was so, although the text gives no further details.

The author of Chronicles tells this account. Asa was a king who began by trusting in God, but at the end of his life, when he was sick, he sought only the physicians and not the LORD. His burial shows that he was honored, although he ended badly in spiritual terms.

Today: it is good to seek the doctor and use medicines, since they are not enemies of faith. What matters is not to forget God. When you are sick or afraid, pray first, ask Him for wisdom, and trust in Him while you care for your health.
exp.16:0:
It says that Jehoshaphat, son of Asa, became king of Judah after his father. The phrase "strengthened himself against Israel" means that he made himself strong in the face of the northern kingdom, called Israel, and did not let himself be dominated by it. Being strong means having more power or getting ahead.

Here the narrator of the book of Chronicles speaks, the one who tells the story of the kings of Judah. The text does not quote anyone, but presents the beginning of Jehoshaphat's reign. The verses that follow explain his strength: he placed soldiers in the fortified cities and, above all, God was with him because he followed the good example of David and did not seek the Baals, which were false gods.

For today: true strength begins with seeking God. Before looking for security in other things, we can ask Him to guide our decisions and remain faithful to Him.
exp.16:1:
Josafat, king of Judah, strengthened the defense of his kingdom. He placed troops in the fortified cities of Judah and set up garrisons, that is, groups of soldiers who watch over and protect a place. He also placed them in the cities of Ephraim that his father Asa had taken.

The one speaking is the narrator of Chronicles, who tells the story of the kings of Judah. Jehoshaphat had just inherited the throne, and Judah had Israel, the northern kingdom, as a rival. That is why he prepared to protect his territory. The following verse makes clear that God was with him because he sought Him. In this way, the account joins military prudence with faithfulness to God.

For today: being careful and responsible is not against faith. Caring for your home, your finances, or your health is wise, but what is most firm is still seeking God with your whole heart and trusting in Him.
exp.16:5:
The verse says that Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, was filled with courage and determination to walk in the ways of the Lord. Because of this, he removed the high places, which were raised spots where people worshiped, often with practices foreign to faith in God, and the groves, which were poles or clusters of trees tied to the worship of false gods.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, describing how Jehoshaphat ruled. Earlier it is said that he sought the God of his father David and did not imitate Israel, the northern kingdom, which had turned away from God. Afterward, the king sent teachers to instruct people in the Law in the cities. Some scholars note that other passages mention that the high places were not removed completely, so his work was real, though incomplete.

Today we can ask ourselves what things hold the place of God in our hearts, and with courage remove them, just as Jehoshaphat did.
exp.16:8:
They taught throughout Judah and had the book of the law of the Lord with them. They did not stay in one place but went about from town to town, teaching the people what God had said.

The chronicler tells this of King Jehoshaphat. In the third year of his reign he sent officials, Levites, and priests to teach the people. The verses that follow say that the fear of the Lord fell on the surrounding kingdoms, so they did not attack Judah. The text connects the teaching of the law with the peace and protection that Judah enjoyed.

For today: give priority to the Word of God. If you read the Bible and share it with your family, your church, or your friends, you help others come to know God. Teaching is not only the task of pastors.
exp.16:9:
It says that God caused a great fear, a terror that came from Him, to fall upon all the neighboring kingdoms of Judah. For that reason no one dared to fight against King Jehoshaphat. The fear is described as a deep dread.

Here the narrator of the book of Chronicles speaks, telling the story of the kings of Judah. Jehoshaphat had removed idols and had sent officials, Levites, and priests to teach the law of God throughout the cities. The text then shows the peace and respect that Judah received. Some understand this as God's direct care; the text does not explain exactly how that fear came about.

For today: when we give the Word of God a central place in the life of the home and the church, we can trust that He cares for us, even though His protection does not always look the same as it did here.
exp.16:10:
Some of the Philistines brought gifts to King Jehoshaphat, along with silver as tribute. The Arabians, for their part, brought him livestock: seven thousand seven hundred rams (male sheep) and seven thousand seven hundred male goats. Tribute is a payment that one people gives to a stronger people, or a sign of respect.

The one speaking is the writer of Chronicles, who tells the story of Jehoshaphat's reign in Judah. Just before this, he tells us that his leaders taught the law of the LORD in all the cities, and that God put fear into the neighboring kingdoms so that they would not attack. These gifts show that result. The text does not explain the exact reasons behind each nation's actions, but it presents them as part of the peace and respect that Jehoshaphat gained.

For today: when we give a central place to God's Word in our life, family, or church, He can give us peace and stability in ways we do not expect. Let us make reading and teaching the Bible a constant priority.
exp.16:13:
This verse begins a list of King Jehoshaphat's army. It says the men were organized by families, according to the houses of their fathers. In the tribe of Judah, the commander of the thousands was the general Adnah, with three hundred thousand mighty men of valour.

The one telling the story is the chronicler, who wrote for a people returning from exile and needed to remember how God blessed a faithful king. Earlier it says that Jehoshaphat sought the LORD and strengthened his kingdom. The large numbers show his growth, though some scholars debate how these figures should be understood.

For today: true strength does not come only from resources or plans, but from walking with God. Prepare wisely for what is yours to do, but place your trust in the Lord, who gives success and peace.
exp.16:16:
This verse says that from the tribe of Benjamin there was a leader named Eliada, described as a very brave man. With him were two hundred thousand soldiers armed with bow and shield. The phrase about being armed with bow and shield means that they fought with arrows and protected themselves with shields.

The writer of Chronicles is listing the army of King Jehoshaphat of Judah. It is not a speech by a character; it is the chronicler's account. He had already mentioned other leaders of Judah, and here he moves on to Benjamin. Such large numbers have been understood in different ways: some take them literally, while others think they express great strength. The text wants to show that God had strengthened Jehoshaphat's kingdom.

For today: true strength is built with preparation and unity, but also with devotion to God. Ask God to help you serve with courage and to add your abilities to those of others in your family, your church, or your work.
exp.17:4:
In this verse, Ahab, king of Israel, gathers together four hundred prophets and asks them whether he should go to war against Ramoth-gilead or stay where he is. They answer him with one voice: "Go up," meaning go, and they assure him that God will deliver the city into the king's hand.

Ahab had asked Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, to join him in the battle. Jehoshaphat agreed, but asked first to inquire of the word of the Lord. Ahab then gathers his prophets, who tell him what he wants to hear. Later Jehoshaphat will notice that a voice faithful to the Lord is missing, and Micaiah will be sent for.

For today: finding voices that approve of us is not enough. Before deciding, let us seek God's truth in prayer and in his Word, even when it is not what we wish to hear.
exp.17:8:
This verse describes a solemn scene. Ahab, king of Israel, and Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, are seated on their thrones, wearing their royal robes, at a threshing floor (a flat, open piece of ground where grain was beaten out) beside the gate of Samaria. Meanwhile, all the prophets are speaking before them.

The two kings had allied themselves to fight against Ramoth-gilead. Jehoshaphat wanted to seek God's counsel before going. Ahab gathered four hundred prophets who told him what he wanted to hear, but Jehoshaphat asked to hear a prophet of the LORD, Micaiah, whom Ahab could not stand because he spoke the truth.

For today: do not look only for voices that applaud you. Before deciding, listen humbly to the truth of God in his Word, even when it is not what you wish to hear.
exp.17:9:
Verse 10 tells how Zedekiah, one of King Ahab's prophets, made himself horns of iron. With them he gave a kind of demonstration, and declared in God's name that the king would charge at the Syrians, pushing them with his horns until he had finished them off.

Ahab, king of Israel, and Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, were sitting at the entrance of Samaria, thinking about attacking Ramoth Gilead. Four hundred prophets were telling the king what he wanted to hear. Zedekiah speaks with great confidence, but Micaiah, the only one who will say something different, has not yet arrived.

For today: not every message delivered with force and in God's name truly comes from Him. Before following a popular voice, compare it with the Bible and seek the truth, even when it is uncomfortable.
exp.17:13:
The king asks Micaiah whether they should go up to fight against Ramoth-gilead or stay where they are. Micaiah answers, "Go up, and you will succeed; God will hand them over into your hands."

The one asking is Ahab, king of Israel, together with Jehoshaphat, king of Judah. Four hundred prophets had already announced victory, and the king asked Micaiah to say the same thing. Micaiah had said that he would speak only what God told him. For that reason many believe he spoke here with irony, repeating what others were saying. The text does not explain this, but the king's reaction in the next verse suggests it.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are seeking God's truth or only words that please us. Let us value those who speak to us with honesty and love, even when it hurts.
exp.17:17:
Here the prophet Micaiah says he wants the king and everyone to listen to what God showed him. He saw the Lord sitting on his throne, with all the host of heaven, that is, the angels, standing on his right and on his left.

Micaiah speaks before Ahab, king of Israel, and Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, who were about to go to war against Ramoth-gilead. Four hundred prophets had promised the king victory, but Micaiah relates a different vision. With it he explains that God governs the situation and that the message of those prophets was not trustworthy. The details of the heavenly scene are understood as a vision, not as a literal description.

For today: it is not enough for a message to sound good or be popular. Let us seek God's truth in his Word, even when it is not what we want to hear, and trust that he governs all things.
exp.17:18:
It says that God, in a vision, asks who can persuade or deceive King Ahab so that he goes up and falls at Ramoth-gilead. The verse of the word "entice" has been removed here, since it is not in the verse you are reading. The heavenly beings offer different ideas, until one of them volunteers, as the text goes on to tell.

The prophet Micaiah speaks, recounting what he saw before Jehoshaphat and Ahab. Four hundred prophets had already promised the king victory. Micaiah reveals that this favorable mood was deceptive, and that Ahab, because of his stubbornness and his rejection of the truth, was under judgment. Interpreters debate how to understand this scene, but almost all of them see that God governs even over deception and that Ahab was responsible for his own decisions.

Today: do not seek only voices that tell you what you want to hear. Test advice against the Word of God, and listen also to the one who speaks to you with truth, even when it hurts.
exp.17:19:
It says that a spirit came before God and offered to deceive Ahab. God asked him how he would do it. "Entice" here means to persuade or convince, and "the Lord" is the name of God.

The speaker is the prophet Micaiah, son of Imla. King Ahab and King Jehoshaphat wanted to know whether they should attack Ramoth-gilead. Four hundred prophets were promising Ahab victory, but Micaiah recounts this vision of heaven to explain why. Scholars understand this scene in different ways, but nearly all agree that it shows God governing even the judgment on a king who had already rejected the truth.

For today: do not look only for voices that tell you what you want to hear. Ask God for wisdom, compare everything with his Word, and be humble enough to listen even when the truth is uncomfortable.
exp.17:20:
A spirit offers to deceive Ahab, and tells God that he will do it by becoming a lying spirit in the mouth of all the king's prophets. God answers him to go, that he will succeed.

The word "entice" here means to persuade or deceive, and "prevail" means to come out ahead in what one sets out to do.

The one speaking is the prophet Micaiah, who tells of a vision of heaven. The four hundred prophets of King Ahab had promised him victory in the war. Micaiah explains that those flattering words were a deception, and that God had already decided Ahab's punishment, since he was rejecting the truth.

For today: let us be careful to surround ourselves only with voices that say what we want to hear. Let us seek the truth in God's Word, even when it is uncomfortable, and ask for humility to receive correction.
exp.17:23:
Micaiah answers Zedekiah, who had just struck him. He tells him that he will see it on that day, when he has to go from room to room looking for a place to hide. An inner chamber is a room set deeper within the house. It is a warning: when the disaster he has announced arrives, it will be clear who spoke the truth.

Micaiah was the prophet of the LORD who announced defeat to King Ahab before the battle of Ramoth Gilead. Four hundred prophets had promised victory, and Zedekiah was one of them. Though he was insulted, Micaiah does not take back his words or defend himself with violence; he lets the events confirm them. The text does not say clearly when or how Zedekiah hid himself.

For today: speaking the truth with humility may cost us dearly, but we do not need to take revenge. We can trust that God knows how to vindicate the truth in his own time.
exp.17:27:
It says that the king of Israel (Ahab) and Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, went up together to Ramoth-gilead, a city east of the Jordan, to fight against Syria. The verb "went up" is used because they were heading toward higher ground. The verse reads "Ramoth-gilead" and "Jehoshaphat" in the form you see here.

The prophet Micaiah had just announced that God would not bless this war. Ahab, angry, had him thrown into prison and given only scant bread and water. Micaiah replied that if Ahab returned in peace, God had not spoken through him. Even so, the two kings went into battle. The verses that follow show that Ahab disguised himself, but he could not escape the warning from God.

For today: listening to God is not enough if we then do what we had already decided. Before making an important decision, it is wise to accept God's word, even when it makes us uncomfortable, and to obey it with humility.
exp.17:28:
Ahab, king of Israel, proposes to Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, that he will disguise himself and go into battle, while Jehoshaphat wears his royal robes. To disguise oneself is to change one's appearance so that no one recognizes you. Ahab disguised himself and went into battle.

Ahab speaks right after the prophet Micaiah announced that the Lord would not grant success to this war. Ahab refused to believe that word, and he seems to have tried to escape danger by hiding, leaving Jehoshaphat exposed in his royal robes. Later the king of Syria had ordered his men to attack only the king of Israel, and Jehoshaphat cried out and God helped him.

For today: we cannot hide our lives from God's word with disguises or excuses. It is better to listen with humility, even when the truth is uncomfortable, and to seek God's help instead of trusting in our own strategies.
exp.17:31:
This verse says that the Syrian captains, when they saw up close that Jehoshaphat was not Ahab, king of Israel, stopped pursuing him.

The Syrian king had ordered them to attack only the king of Israel. Ahab, disguised so that he would not be recognized, went into battle with Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, who was wearing his royal robes. The captains mistook him and surrounded him. Jehoshaphat cried out to God, and the text says that God drew them away from him. Shortly afterward, an arrow shot at random struck Ahab, and he died that evening.

Even when we get into risky or poorly chosen situations, we can call on God with humility, and He is merciful. It also reminds us to be careful about the alliances we make, and to trust that no one escapes what God has determined.
exp.17:32:
It says that a Syrian soldier shot an arrow without aiming at anyone in particular, at random, and that arrow struck King Ahab of Israel at a weak point in his armor, between the joints and the breastplate (the piece that protected the chest). Wounded, Ahab asked the charioteer, the driver of his war chariot, to turn around and take him out of the battle.

Ahab, king of Israel, speaks. He had disguised himself so that no one would recognize him, and he let Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, wear his royal clothing. Earlier, a prophet, Micaiah, had told him that things would go badly for him. Even so, Ahab went to war. What seemed like chance fulfilled what God had said.

For today: we cannot hide our decisions from God. It is better to heed his warning in time and obey, rather than trust in disguises or in luck.
exp.17:33:
The battle grew fiercer that day. King Ahab of Israel stayed standing in his chariot facing the Syrians until evening, but he died as the sun was going down. The verse of the verse goes on to say that Ahab had gone into battle in disguise so that he would not be recognized, while King Jehoshaphat of Judah went out wearing his royal clothing. A prophet, Micaiah, had already warned him that things would go badly for him, but Ahab did not want to listen. A soldier shot an arrow without aiming at anyone in particular, and yet it struck the king. The one telling the story is the chronicler, who shows that no one escapes what God has said.

For today: it is not worth hiding or ignoring the truth that God tells us. It is better to listen to his correction in time and obey, before it is too late.
exp.18:3:
This verse says that King Jehoshaphat lived in Jerusalem, but he did not stay shut up there. He went out to travel through the land, from Beersheba in the south to the hill country of Ephraim in the north. His aim was to bring the people back to the LORD, that is, to make them return to the God of their fathers.

This is part of the account, not a speech. Earlier, the prophet Jehu rebuked Jehoshaphat for helping a wicked king, but he also recognized good things in him: he removed the pagan high places and sought God. Jehoshaphat answers the correction with action: he goes out to the people and encourages them to return to God. Afterward he appoints judges.

For today: when God corrects us, feeling guilty is not enough. We can respond with concrete steps, reaching out to others with humility to encourage them to follow God, starting with our family and the people around us.
exp.18:4:
This verse tells that King Jehoshaphat appointed judges in all the fortified cities of Judah, in every region of the kingdom. The fortified cities were towns with walls and strong defenses. In this way justice reached the whole people, not only Jerusalem.

The one telling the story is the chronicler, and he speaks of King Jehoshaphat. Shortly before, the prophet Jehu had rebuked him for an alliance with King Ahab, but he also acknowledged the good things in him. Jehoshaphat responded by returning to God, traveling through the kingdom and encouraging the people to follow the Lord. Then he set up judges and reminded them that they judged in the name of God, without partiality or bribes.

Today, if you have any authority, at work, at home, or in the church, use it with honesty. Decide with justice, without favoring anyone or letting yourself be bought, remembering that God sees everything.
exp.18:5:
It says that King Jehoshaphat spoke to the judges and asked them to be very careful with their decisions. He reminded them that they were not judging on behalf of ordinary people, but on behalf of the Lord, that is, God, who was with them as they decided each case.

Jehoshaphat was king of Judah. He had traveled through the land encouraging the people to return to God, and then he appointed judges in the fortified cities of Judah. He speaks to them so they understand how serious their work is: they had to act with the fear of God, without injustice, without favoritism, and without accepting bribes.

For today: if you have authority over others, as a parent, employer, or leader, decide with honesty and respect, remembering that one day you will give an account to God for how you treated others.
exp.18:9:
It says that when a difficult case came from the other cities, the judges in Jerusalem were to warn the people not to sin against God. Cases of death or violence are what is meant by the phrase about blood and blood. The laws and commandments are the laws and commands of God. To warn means to advise clearly. If they did this, they would avoid God's wrath and would not be guilty.

The one speaking is King Jehoshaphat. He had appointed judges in Jerusalem, from among the Levites, the priests, and the heads of families, to decide the most serious cases. He wanted the people to live according to the law of God, and the judges to act with the fear of God, with truth, and with a whole heart.

For today: if you guide, teach, or counsel others, do not stop at solving the problem. Help the person, with love and with clarity, to understand what pleases God.
exp.19:2:
Jehoshaphat was afraid when he learned that a large army was coming against Judah. But he did not freeze in place. He resolved firmly to seek the Lord, that is, to consult Him and ask Him for direction. He also ordered a fast to be announced throughout the whole land.

This is a historical account. Moab, Ammon and other neighboring peoples had joined together to attack Judah. Jehoshaphat was the king, and when he received the warning, he knew he did not have the strength to defeat them alone. So he called on the whole people to seek God together with him.

For today: feeling afraid is not a sin; what matters is where we take that fear. When a hard piece of news arrives, you can stop, pray and, if you wish, fast. Also seek the company of your family or your church to ask God for help.
exp.19:3:
This verse says that the people of Judah gathered together to ask God for help. It was not only the people of Jerusalem: they also came from all the cities of Judah.

The narrator of the book tells what happened when the news arrived that a great army was coming against King Jehoshaphat. He was afraid, but instead of fleeing or giving up, he sought God and called the whole people to fast. The people responded by coming together to pray side by side.

When fear reaches us, we can do what Judah did: turn to God and not stay alone. Seeking help in prayer, and also alongside other believers, reminds us that God is greater than what we fear.
exp.19:4:
Verse 5 tells us that King Jehoshaphat stood up before all the people of Judah and Jerusalem, who had gathered in the house of the Lord, in front of the new court.

A hostile army was coming against Judah, and the king was afraid. Instead of relying only on his own strength, he sought the Lord and called all the people to fast and pray. Now Jehoshaphat, as their leader, takes his place before the assembly to begin praying aloud. We do not know more details about the new court, only that it was part of the temple.

When fear reaches us, we can do as Jehoshaphat did: not stay alone with our anguish, but seek God and pray together with other believers who stand with us.
exp.19:6:
Jehoshaphat reminds God of what He has already done: He drove out the earlier inhabitants of the land before Israel and gave it to the descendants of Abraham, His friend, forever.

Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, prays before the people gathered in the temple in Jerusalem. Enemy armies were coming to attack them, and they had no strength to resist. So he appeals to God's past faithfulness and His promise before asking for help. Calling Abraham God's "friend" also appears in Isaiah 41:8.

For today: when you face a great problem, before asking, remember what God has already done for you and what He has promised in His Word. That grateful remembrance strengthens faith and helps you pray with confidence, not with despair.
exp.19:8:
This verse recalls a promise the people believed they had: if a calamity came, such as war, sickness, or hunger, they would present themselves before the temple and before God, because his name was there. They would cry out in their distress, and God would hear them and save them. "Hear" means that God listens and responds.

The one speaking is King Jehoshaphat, in a public prayer in Jerusalem. An enemy army from Ammon, Moab, and Seir was approaching. He repeats what was said when Solomon dedicated the temple, and he reminds God of his past faithfulness before asking for help.

For today: when a crisis comes, do not start only with your fear. Remember what God has done and what he has promised, and bring him your need in prayer, trusting that he listens to you.
exp.19:10:
This verse says that the neighboring peoples, whom Israel had not attacked in the past, now respond with evil. The phrase about repaying favors is rendered here in plain terms: instead of showing gratitude, they come to drive us out of the land that God gave us as our inheritance, meaning the land passed down to us as a possession.

King Jehoshaphat speaks while standing in the temple in Jerusalem, praying before all of Judah. A huge army of Ammonites, Moabites, and people from the hill country of Seir is coming against them. Jehoshaphat reminds God that he himself gave them that land and that Israel respected those peoples when they came out of Egypt.

For today: when you are treated unjustly and feel powerless, do what Jehoshaphat did. Bring your case honestly before God, remind him of his promises, and fix your eyes on him.
exp.19:14:
Here a man named Jahaziel speaks to all the people, to King Jehoshaphat, and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem. He tells them not to be afraid of that huge army, because the battle does not belong to them but to God.

Judah was threatened by a large army marching against them. The whole nation gathered before God with their families to seek help. Jahaziel, a Levite descended from Asaph, spoke because, according to the text, the Spirit of God came upon him in the middle of the assembly. His message aimed to restore their calm and their confidence.

When something overwhelms you, pray with humility and hand over to God what you cannot control. That does not take away your responsibility to obey and take the next step, but it frees you from carrying the weight of the outcome alone.
exp.19:16:
This verse says that Judah would not have to fight that battle with their own strength. He tells them to take their position and to stand still, that is, to take their place and trust, so that they may see the salvation of the Lord. Even so, he orders them to go out the next day, and reminds them that God will be with them.

The speaker is Jahaziel, a Levite, who in this passage announces a message from God. A great enemy army was coming against Judah, and King Jehoshaphat and the people had sought God with prayer and fasting. This message is the answer to that cry.

For today: when you face something that overwhelms you, pray first and rest in the fact that God is at work. But do not freeze in place: take the step He shows you, with faith and without fear, and worship Him while you wait.
exp.19:17:
This verse tells that King Jehoshaphat bowed his head with his face to the ground. All Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem also fell down before God and worshipped him. To bow down with one's face to the ground was a sign of respect and surrender.

An enemy army was coming against Judah, and the people were afraid. A prophet had just told them, on God's behalf, not to fear, because the battle was not theirs. Jehoshaphat and the people respond first with worship, before seeing any result. The next day they went out to trust the word they had received.

When we feel fear, we can begin by worshipping God, not only by asking for help. Worship reminds us that God is greater than the problem, and it helps us trust him before we see the solution.
exp.19:18:
This verse says that the Levites stood up to praise the LORD, the God of Israel, with a loud and high voice. The names in the verse refer to two groups of Levites, the families devoted to service in the temple, which in this English wording are the Kohathites and the Korhites.

Judah was threatened by a large enemy army. A prophet, Jahaziel, had just announced in God's name that the battle would not be theirs and that they should not be afraid. King Jehoshaphat and the people had bowed down in worship. Now the Levites respond with praise, before they see the victory. The text does not say what they sang at that moment, but later their song of thanksgiving is mentioned.

For today: when God gives you a promise, you can respond with praise even before you see the solution. Praising does not deny the problem; it is trusting that God will do what He said.
exp.19:21:
This verse says that when the people of Judah began to cry out to God and praise him, the Lord set ambushes against the enemies who came to attack them: the children of Ammon, of Moab, and of Mount Seir. They ended up killing one another. An ambush is a hidden attack, and the phrase about them killing one another means that they turned on each other and destroyed one another.

The account describes what happened when King Jehoshaphat and Judah faced a very large enemy army. Jehoshaphat encouraged the people to trust in the Lord and placed singers at the front of the soldiers. The Bible does not explain in detail how God set those ambushes; the following text only says that the enemies turned against each other.

Today we can learn that praising God is not only for easy times. When you face a problem that is bigger than you, you can pray and give thanks, trusting that God is at work, even when you do not know how.
exp.19:24:
The passage tells how King Jehoshaphat and the people of Judah came to the battlefield to collect the spoil. They found great wealth, clothing, and valuable items among the dead. There was so much that they could not carry it all, and it took them three days to gather it.

It is part of the story, not a speech. Judah was threatened by a large enemy army. Jehoshaphat had prayed and trusted God, and the enemies ended up destroying one another. Afterward, the people praised God in the valley that was called Berachah, a name that points to blessing.

For today: when you face a problem that is bigger than you are, pray and trust God. Sometimes He gives more than we ask. And when you receive His help, do not forget to thank Him.
exp.19:26:
This verse tells how all the people of Judah and the residents of Jerusalem, with King Jehoshaphat leading the way, returned to their city full of joy. The reason is that the Lord had given them cause to rejoice by delivering them from their enemies.

It is the chronicler's account, not the words of a character. Before this, Judah was threatened by a huge army. Jehoshaphat prayed, the people trusted God and praised him, and the enemies ended up destroying one another. Judah did not have to fight. Afterward they gathered the plunder and blessed God in the valley that came to be called Beracah.

For today: when God helps you through a difficulty, do not just move on as if nothing happened. Stop, thank him, and celebrate with others. Thankful joy strengthens faith and reminds the heart that God is faithful.
exp.19:27:
This verse says that the people of Judah returned to Jerusalem playing musical instruments and went straight to the temple. The harps and lyres were stringed instruments; the trumpets were the wind instruments.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, telling the story of Judah. King Jehoshaphat and his people had faced a very large enemy army, and they had cried out to God. He delivered them without their having to fight. After blessing God in the valley of Beracah, they returned home in joy and went first to the temple.

For today: when God helps us through a difficulty, the first thing should not be to carry on with life as if nothing happened. We can stop and thank Him in a concrete way, with a song, a prayer, or a moment at church. Giving thanks reminds us that the victory came from Him.
exp.19:28:
This verse says that a great fear and reverence for God fell upon all the neighboring kingdoms. This happened when they heard that the Lord himself had fought against the enemies of Israel. The word "fear" here speaks of a deep dread, a sense of awe before the power of God.

The book of Chronicles is a historical account, not a person speaking. It tells that Judah, under King Jehoshaphat, was attacked by several peoples, and that God delivered them without Judah having to fight. After the victory, the news spread and the nearby peoples were filled with dread. Then came a time of peace for Jehoshaphat.

For today: when you face something that is beyond you, pray and trust that God can act on your behalf. And when He helps you, tell of it and give Him thanks, because your testimony can lead others to honor Him.
exp.19:29:
This verse says that Jehoshaphat's reign had peace, and that the reason was God himself: he gave him rest on every side, that is, without threats on the borders. The word "rest" here means calm and the absence of war.
