The speaker is the narrator of Chronicles, who summarizes what happened after the victory God gave Judah over the armies that had come to attack it. The people had prayed and praised God, and then returned to Jerusalem with music to give thanks. The neighboring nations heard what had happened and were filled with fear. The text presents the peace as the result of God's action, not only of military strength.

For today: when you face a pressure you cannot resolve, bring your need to God with prayer and thanksgiving. He can give you rest, even if it does not always come in the same way.
exp.19:30:
This verse is an official summary of Jehoshaphat's reign. It says that he began to reign at thirty-five years old, that he ruled for twenty-five years in Jerusalem, and that his mother's name was Azubah, daughter of Shilhi.

Here the narrator of the book of Chronicles is speaking, not a character in the story. After telling of the victory God gave the people and the rest that followed, the writer closes the account with this kind of record, which is common in the stories of the kings. He then explains that Jehoshaphat followed the way of his father Asa, but the high places were not removed, and the people had not yet fully turned their hearts to God.

For today: a life can have good results and still need a more wholehearted devotion. Ask God to help you obey him not only outwardly, but with all your heart.
exp.19:31:
This verse says that King Jehoshaphat followed the example of his father Asa. He did not turn away from that path, and he did what was pleasing to God. The sentence about the name of God and the phrase meaning what he approves as just do not apply here, so they are removed.

Here the writer of Chronicles sums up the reign of Jehoshaphat in Judah. He describes him as a faithful king, to whom God gave peace. But the text that follows adds a realistic note: the high places, where worship was offered, were not taken away, and the people had not yet given their whole heart to God.

For today: following a good example is valuable, but imitation alone is not enough. We can learn from faithful people and, at the same time, ask God that our own hearts be sincere toward him. Consider which habit of faith you want to keep up steadily.
exp.19:32:
This verse says that, although Jehoshaphat did what was right, the high places remained standing. High places were places of worship on the hills, where many people worshiped improperly, sometimes mixing faith with pagan customs. The phrase about the people not having prepared their hearts means that the people had not yet fully turned back to God.

The speaker is the chronicler, who summarizes Jehoshaphat's reign. He acknowledges his successes, but also his limits. Other passages say that Jehoshaphat removed the high places (17:6), so some believe that he removed some and others returned, or that the reform was left incomplete. The text does not fully explain this.

For today: outward changes are not enough if the heart does not turn to God. Ask him to help you surrender to him your motives, desires, and hidden habits as well.
exp.19:35:
This verse says that Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, joined himself with Ahaziah, king of Israel, to prepare ships that would go to Tarshish. The word "make" in the verse means to build or equip them. The ships were built at Ezion-geber, a port by the Red Sea. Tarshish was a distant place of trade; no one knows for certain where it was.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, recounting the end of Jehoshaphat's reign. Earlier he praises him as a king who sought God, but now he points out a mistake: Jehoshaphat joined himself with Ahaziah, a king who did not honor God. Then the prophet Eliezer warns him that God would destroy that work, and the ships were broken. A good king can also err in choosing whom he partners with.

For today: before making an important business deal or alliance, pray and ask whether that union will draw you closer to God or farther from him. Also listen to the wise counsel of faithful people.
exp.19:36:
It says that a prophet named Eliezer warned King Jehoshaphat that God would destroy what he had done, because he had joined himself with Ahaziah. Soon after, the ships were broken and could not set sail toward Tarshish. Joining oneself with someone means partnering with them or doing business together; ships are the vessels in the verse, and Tarshish was a distant place of trade whose exact location is not known for certain.

Eliezer speaks here, a prophet about whom we know nothing more. Jehoshaphat was a king who generally followed God, but he entered a business partnership with Ahaziah, king of Israel, whom the text describes as wicked. God used the prophet to show him that this alliance did not please Him. There is a parallel account in 1 Kings 22, with some different details.

For today: before we partner with someone in an important business or project, let us pray and ask for wise counsel. A good goal is not enough if the partnership pulls us away from God or puts our faith at risk.
exp.20:2:
Before he died, Jehoshaphat gave his other sons gifts of silver, gold, and valuable things, along with walled cities in Judah. But the kingdom he gave to Jehoram, because he was the oldest son, the firstborn.

The author of Chronicles, writing as a narrator, explains how Jehoshaphat arranged his inheritance. The brothers received wealth and protection, and Jehoram received the throne by custom. The next verse shows the contrast: as soon as Jehoram felt secure, he killed his brothers. So we see that a good inheritance does not guarantee a good heart.

For today: we can leave our children possessions and good plans, but the most important thing is to shape their character and faith. And if we receive more, let us use it to care for our family, not to harm it.
exp.20:3:
This verse tells how Jehoram, son of King Jehoshaphat, came to the throne of Judah. Once he was secure and in control, he put to death all his brothers with the sword, along with some of the leaders of the people. The quoted phrase about being raised up to the kingdom is not explained further here, and the rest of the wording needs no comment.

This is the narrator of Chronicles speaking, who tells the story of the kings of Judah. Jehoshaphat had divided goods and cities among his other sons, but he gave the kingdom to Jehoram because he was the eldest. Even so, Jehoram saw his brothers as a threat. The following text explains part of the background: he married the daughter of Ahab and followed evil ways.

For today: power and insecurity can harden the heart. We can ask God to teach us to care for our family, not to see others as rivals, and to be careful about whom we join ourselves to, because those influences shape us.
exp.20:5:
It says that Jehoram, king of Judah, did not follow the example of David, but that of the kings of the north, that is, of Israel. He copied the ways of the house of Ahab, because he married Ahab's daughter. The phrase "he wrought that which was evil in the eyes of the Lord" means that he did things that God saw as wrong. "He walked in the way of the kings of Israel" is a way of saying that he lived as they did.

The writer of Chronicles tells this to a people returning from exile who needed to understand what leads a kingdom to fall. Jehoram had killed his brothers, and the account shows how his alliance with the house of Ahab drove him into further wickedness. Even so, the next verse reminds us that God kept his promise to David.

For today: friendships, marriage, and alliances shape us. It is worth asking ourselves who influences our decisions, and asking God for wisdom so that we are drawn closer to him.
exp.20:7:
This verse tells how, during the reign of Joram, king of Judah, the land of Edom (called here Idumea) rebelled. It no longer wanted to remain under the rule of Judah, and it set up its own king.

The text has no speaker; it is the chronicler who recounts the history. Joram had turned away from God by following the bad example of the kings of Israel, influenced by his marriage to the daughter of Ahab. The account connects that unfaithfulness with the loss of control over his territories, saying that Libnah also rebelled because he had abandoned the LORD. Even so, God preserved the house of David because of his promise.

For today: bad decisions and bad influences gradually take away our stability. But God's faithfulness remains firm, so we can return to Him and surround ourselves with influences that draw us closer to Him.
exp.20:10:
This verse says that King Jehoram built high places in the mountains of Judah, that is, raised places for worshiping other gods. The word here about the people turning away speaks of spiritual unfaithfulness: leaving God to follow other gods. Jehoram did not only turn away himself, but pushed the people of Jerusalem and Judah to do the same.

The one telling the story is the chronicler, who explains why Judah suffered rebellions and trouble. Jehoram had married a daughter of the family of Ahab, and the Bible links his conduct to that influence. Shortly afterward, the prophet Elijah sent him a letter rebuking him for this sin.

For today: those who have influence, in the home, at work, or in the church, also draw others along by their example. Let us ask God that our lives lead people toward Him and not away from Him.
exp.20:16:
The Philistines and the Arabs attacked Judah, entered the country, and carried off all the possessions found in the king's house. They also took the king's sons and wives. Only Jehoahaz, the youngest son, was left.

The writer of Chronicles presents this as the result of the wickedness of Jehoram, king of Judah. Earlier, the prophet Elijah had sent him a letter announcing judgment for turning away from God and leading the people into idolatry. This attack is part of that punishment. The text says that God stirred up the spirit of these peoples against him. In this way, the author shows that God governs even the enemies of his people.

For today: our choices have consequences, and turning away from God can cost us dearly, even what we hold most dear. It is wise to heed warnings in time, to return to Him, and to care for our home with faithfulness.
exp.20:17:
After all the invasions and family losses, God struck King Jehoram with a disease in his bowels that had no cure. The word for the inner organs of the abdomen is what the text names here, and the phrase means that he was punished with a blow.

Here the chronicler speaks, recalling the history of the kings of Judah. Jehoram had killed his brothers, worshiped idols, and turned away from God (2 Chronicles 21:4, 11). Earlier, the prophet Elijah had sent him a letter announcing this judgment (21:12-15). The text presents his sickness as the result of his wickedness, and his death was sad, with no one mourning him.

For today: God takes our decisions seriously, but he is also patient and warns us so that we will change. Let us not harden our hearts. If God speaks to us through his Word or through someone else, let us listen and return to him in time.
exp.20:18:
This verse says that King Joram's sickness lasted two years, until his bowels came out and he died in great pain. His people did not make a burning in his honor, that is, the fire of perfumes and spices that was made to honor dead kings, as had been done for his ancestors.

Here the narrator of Chronicles speaks. Joram, king of Judah, had left the way of God, had married into a family that promoted idolatry, and had killed his brothers. The text presents the sickness as a judgment of God. He died without being mourned.

For today: our decisions leave a mark. More than fame or power, what matters is living in such a way that God and others remember with gratitude how we walked. There is still time to return to Him with humility.
exp.21:0:
The inhabitants of Jerusalem (the people of the city) made Ahaziah, the youngest son of Jehoram, king. The older sons had died, because a band of raiders (the troop) that came with the Arabians to the camp had killed them all. That is why the kingship fell to him.

The writer of Chronicles tells how this king of Judah came to the throne. Earlier, in 2 Chronicles 21, it says that Jehoram lost almost all his sons in an attack. Later we see that Ahaziah followed the evil path of the house of Ahab, counseled by his mother Athaliah.

For today: our decisions are shaped by those who advise us. Let us seek wise voices that draw us closer to God, and not only those who tell us what we want to hear.
exp.21:1:
The verse says that Ahaziah began to reign in Jerusalem at forty-two years old, and that he reigned only one year. His mother was named Athaliah, the daughter of Omri. There is a known difficulty: 2 Kings 8:26 says he was twenty-two years old. Some think this is an error in copying the numbers; others think it is counted in a different way. It is not known for certain.

Here the one speaking is not a character; it is the chronicler who recounts the history of the kings of Judah. The Arabs had killed Ahaziah's older brothers, and for that reason the youngest son came to the throne. Athaliah came from the family of Ahab, king of the north, known for its wickedness, and she influenced her son to do what was evil.

For today: the voices that advise us shape our decisions. Let us seek counselors who bring us closer to God, and not those who push us toward evil.
exp.21:2:
This verse says that Ahaziah, king of Judah, followed the same path of wickedness as the family of King Ahab, who ruled the northern kingdom of Israel. The reason the text gives is that his own mother, Athaliah, counseled him to act wickedly, that is, without reverence for God.

The author of Chronicles recounts the history of the kings of Judah. Ahaziah came to the throne young, after invaders had killed his older brothers. His mother was a daughter of Omri and part of the house of Ahab, known for its idolatry. By uniting the royal families through marriage, that influence reached as far as Jerusalem. The text points out that the advice he received did not help him but led him to his ruin.

For today: notice who advises you and what effect their words have on your life. Seek counsel that brings you closer to God, and do not let yourself be carried along only by those who have influence over you.
exp.21:3:
The verse says that Ahaziah, king of Judah, did evil in the sight of God, just like the family of King Ahab. The reason is that, after his father Joram died, the people of Ahab's house became his counselors, and their advice led him to ruin.

The one speaking is the chronicler, who reviews the history of the kings of Judah. Ahaziah was a grandson of Omri, and his mother, Athaliah, belonged to Ahab's family. Because of this kinship, the influence of Israel entered the palace of Judah. The chronicler wants to show where the king's downfall came from: the voices he listened to.

For today: the people we listen to most shape our decisions. It is worth asking ourselves who our counselors are and seeking wise voices that bring us closer to God and do not lead us to destruction.
exp.21:4:
The verse says that Ahaziah, king of Judah, followed the counsel of Ahab's family. For that reason he went to war alongside Joram, king of Israel, against Hazael, king of Syria, at Ramoth-gilead. There the Syrians wounded Joram.

The writer of Chronicles tells the story of the kings of Judah. Ahaziah was Ahab's grandson through his mother, Athaliah, and she advised him to do evil. After his father's death, other counselors from that same house led him down the wrong path. The account shows how bad company drew him into a war and to his downfall.

For today: pay close attention to who your counselors are. The voices you listen to most shape your decisions. Seek advice from people who love God and who tell you the truth, even when it is not what you want to hear.
exp.21:8:
It says that Jehu ordered a search for Ahaziah, king of Judah, who was hiding in Samaria. They caught him, brought him before Jehu, and killed him. But they buried him, because they remembered that he was the grandson of Jehoshaphat, a king who sought God with all his heart. At the end it says that Ahaziah's family no longer had the strength to keep hold of the kingdom.

Context: It is the narrator of Chronicles who tells this, looking back at the history of Judah. Jehu had been anointed to destroy the house of Ahab, and Ahaziah was tied to that house through his family and his alliances. The text says that his downfall came from God. The details of his death are told differently in 2 Kings 9, and it is not easy to harmonize them with certainty.

For today: The sincere faith of a person can leave a mark on their descendants and on those who remember them. Let us live seeking God with all our heart, for our example can be a blessing that lasts longer than our lives.
exp.21:9:
It says that Athaliah, the mother of King Ahaziah, when she saw that her son was dead, arose and had all the royal descendants of Judah put to death. She wanted to keep the throne for herself.

The writer of Chronicles tells this as history. Ahaziah died at the hands of Jehu, and his family was left weak. Athaliah, a daughter of the house of Ahab, took advantage of the power vacuum. Even so, the account goes on to show that God watched over the line of David: Jehosheba hid the little Joash in the temple. How each political detail should be understood is not explained further, but the text makes clear that wickedness did not have the final word.

When someone acts with ambition and violence, it can seem that everything is lost. But God can use brave and humble people to protect what He has promised. Trust that He is still at work, even in silence.
exp.21:10:
Her name is Jehoshabeath, the daughter of King Jehoram. She took Joash, the young son of the late King Ahaziah, and secretly drew him out from among the king's sons who were being killed. She hid him and his nurse in a bedchamber, probably a room where the beds were kept. In this way she saved him from Athaliah. She was the wife of the priest Jehoiada and the sister of Ahaziah (it is understood that she was a half-sister, since Athaliah would not have been her mother).

It is the narrator of Chronicles who tells this. After her son's death, Athaliah wanted to wipe out the whole royal family of David. But David's line could not disappear, because God had promised a king from that family.

God often protects his promises through the brave acts of ordinary people. Jehoshabeath had no power, but she acted in time and at her own risk. Today you might ask yourself whom you can quietly care for or defend, trusting that God uses your small act.
exp.22:0:
In the seventh year, Jehoiada the priest made a bold decision. He made a covenant with five military leaders, called centurions, who were captains of groups of one hundred soldiers.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, telling the story of Judah. Athaliah, the queen, had been ruling for six years after killing the royal family. Jehoiada had hidden the child Joash, heir of David. Now he was preparing to present him as the rightful king. The texts do not say everything Jehoiada thought, but it is clear that he wanted to protect God's promise to David.

For today: when you know something is right, do not act alone. Seek faithful and trustworthy people, and move forward together with courage and prayer. God often works through people who unite to do what is right.
exp.22:1:
They went around all over Judah, traveling through the whole region, and gathered the Levites from all the cities of Judah, along with the leaders of Israel's families, and they came to Jerusalem.

This verse says that the five military commanders who joined Jehoiada toured all of the territory of Judah. They gathered the Levites from all the cities and the heads of Israel's families, and everyone came to Jerusalem.

The narrator of Chronicles tells this. Jehoiada was the priest, and in the seventh year of the reign of the usurper Athaliah he decided to act. He had been hiding the young Joash, David's heir, in the temple. Before proclaiming him king, he needed the support of religious leaders and of the families of the people.

For today: important and difficult decisions are not carried out alone. Jehoiada sought unity and backing before he acted. We can ask God for wisdom and seek the counsel of faithful, mature people in our community.
exp.22:2:
This verse tells that all the people gathered made a solemn agreement with the young king Joash inside the temple. Jehoiada, the priest, showed them the boy and reminded them that, according to God's promise to the family of David, one of David's descendants was to reign. A covenant means a solemn commitment. The king's son here refers to Joash.

Jehoiada speaks after Athaliah, the mother of the previous king, seized the throne by force and nearly destroyed the royal family. Joash had been saved and was hidden in the temple for six years. Now Jehoiada gathers leaders and Levites to restore the rightful throne, relying on God's promise.

For today: when things look dark, God still keeps his promises. We can make serious commitments with other believers to support what God has said, and act with courage and together, not alone.
exp.22:3:
Jehoiada gives precise instructions. A third part of the priests and Levites who were beginning their weekly turn in the temple was to keep watch over the entrances. The ones who guard the gates are the keepers of the doors. Those who came in for their weekly shift were the ones arriving to carry out their turn of service.

The one speaking is the priest Jehoiada. The leaders of Judah had gathered in the temple and made a covenant with the young Joash, the king's son, to protect him and crown him. Athaliah was then reigning, and the plan aimed to restore the line of David, according to God's promise. Each group receives a specific task.

For today: God often works through people who faithfully carry out a simple task. Ask yourself which door has been entrusted to you today: your family, your work, or your church. Guard it with responsibility and as part of a team.
exp.22:6:
It says that the Levites will form a circle of protection around the young king, each one with his weapons in his hand. Anyone who tries to enter the temple without permission must be put to death. The guards must stay with the king at all times, going with him wherever he goes.

The priest Jehoiada is speaking. Queen Athaliah had seized the throne of Judah, and Jehoiada secretly protected Joash, David's rightful heir. Now he is organizing priests, Levites, and leaders to crown him. The weapons came from the temple treasury, which had belonged to King David. Jehoiada acts with care, so that the temple remains a place set apart for God.

For today: when what is right must be defended, do it with order, courage, and respect for what is sacred. Think about whom you need to protect or accompany, and do so with faithfulness and steadiness.
exp.22:8:
Jehoiada the priest handed over to the commanders of hundreds the spears, the small shields, and the large shields that had belonged to King David and were kept in the temple. Large shields are the ones that covered the whole body, and the commanders of hundreds are the leaders of groups of one hundred men.

Jehoiada was leading a plan to protect young Joash, the rightful heir of David, and to crown him. Until then Athaliah had been reigning, after seizing the throne. The writer of Chronicles emphasizes that the weapons were David's, which underlines the continuity of the royal line. We also do not know in detail how long they had been stored there.

For today: God can use what others have left safely kept, along with brave leaders, to restore what is right. Ask yourself what heritage of faith you have within reach, such as prayer, the Word, or the example of others, and use it with courage and good order to serve God.
exp.22:12:
Athaliah enters the temple and sees the young king Joash standing by his pillar at the entrance. The princes and the trumpeters surround him, and all the people celebrate with music and praise. Athaliah tears her clothes in sign of distress and cries out, "Treason, treason!"

The account tells what happens when the priest Jehoiada crowns Joash, David's rightful heir, who had been hidden away. Athaliah had seized the throne and ruled by force. Now she accuses others of treason, even though she herself had taken power. The text does not say what she was thinking, but her reaction shows that her control was collapsing.

God works even when evil seems to dominate for a long time. We can trust that he keeps his promises and rejoice when what is right is restored. It is also good to examine our hearts: do we defend our place at any cost, or do we accept the order God establishes?
exp.22:19:
The text says that the priest Jehoiada gathered the captains of hundreds, the nobles, the governors, and all the people. Together they brought the king, the young Joash, down from the house of the Lord. They entered through the high gate into the king's house and set him on the throne.

Here the account is told by the chronicler, not by a character in the story. For years Athaliah had reigned after seizing the throne. Jehoiada had secretly protected Joash, the rightful heir of David, and arranged this moment with order and the support of everyone. The chronicler shows that the temple and the line of David remained important to God.

For today: when something unjust needs to be set right, it is wise to act with patience, order, and unity, not only with courage. Seek wise counsel, take care of what God has placed in your hands, and do things with integrity, trusting that He sustains his work.
exp.22:20:
This verse says that all the people of the land rejoiced and that the city was quiet after Athaliah was put to death with the sword. The phrase rendered here as "rejoiced" means they celebrated with joy. The word for "quiet" means calm and free from disturbance.

This is part of the historical account in Chronicles, not a speech. Athaliah had taken the throne of Judah by violence. The priest Jehoiada protected the young boy Joash, the king's son, and crowned him in the temple. With Athaliah dead, the people saw an end to a time of oppression and idolatry. The text does not explain every detail of their feelings, but it shows relief and hope.

For today: when God brings an end to injustice or to a difficult time, we can thank him with joy. We can also pray and act with courage and order so that justice and sincere worship take root in our homes, our church, and our community.
exp.23:0:
This verse says that Joash was only seven years old when he began to reign over Judah, and that he ruled for forty years from Jerusalem. It also mentions his mother, Zibiah, who was from Beersheba, a city in the south of Judah.

This is the narrator of the book of Chronicles, who tells the story of the kings of Judah. Joash came to the throne as a child, after a very dark and violent time in the kingdom. The following verse explains that he did what was right while the priest Jehoiada lived, since Jehoiada guided him. This suggests that his course depended greatly on that guide.

For today: God uses people of every age, but we all need good counselors. Seek to surround yourself with wise people, and also cultivate your own faith, so that it does not depend only on others.
exp.23:4:
King Joash is said to have gathered the priests and the Levites. He ordered them to go out to the cities of Judah to collect money from all Israel, so that the temple could be repaired each year. But the Levites did not hurry, and they did not take the matter seriously.

Here King Joash is speaking. He wanted to repair the temple, which had been damaged and plundered in the days of the wicked Athaliah. He had followed the priest Jehoiada, and now he takes the lead. His command was clear, but those responsible did not act with urgency. For that reason, later on, the king calls for Jehoiada and asks him why the work was not being done.

For today: a good desire is not enough; steady perseverance is needed. If God places a service on your heart, begin it with order and devotion, without leaving it for later. And if you have a responsibility in the church, carry it out with joy.
exp.23:5:
King Joash called for Jehoiada, the chief priest, and asked him a question that sounds like a rebuke: why had he not made sure that the Levites brought in the collection that Moses had commanded? That collection was to be gathered in Judah and in Jerusalem for the tabernacle of witness, that is, the place of worship where God's presence was.

Here the king speaks, and he wanted to repair the temple. He had asked the priests and Levites to gather money every year, but they did not hurry. The temple had fallen into ruin because Athaliah and her followers had damaged it and had used holy things for their idols. So the king calls his spiritual leader to account.

For today: if God has entrusted us with something, such as serving, giving, or caring for the church, let us not put it off. Let us ask for help to act with diligence and to answer for our responsibilities with humility.
exp.23:6:
This verse explains why the temple was in poor condition. Athaliah, a wicked queen, and her sons had damaged the house of God. Furthermore, they took the things that were set apart for the service of the Lord and used them for idols, that is, for false gods. The dedicated things are those given over to God.

The author of the book explains the reason for King Joash's command. He asked the priests and Levites to gather money to repair the temple, but they did not hurry. Athaliah had ruled Judah after killing much of the royal family, and her household neglected the worship of God. For that reason the temple urgently needed repairs.

For today: God deserves the first and the best, not what is left over. We can ask ourselves whether we are caring for what belongs to God: our time, our offering, and our life of prayer. If something has been neglected, we can always begin again with diligence.
exp.23:7:
This verse says that King Joash gave the command to make a chest, that is, a large box to receive offerings. They set it outside, beside the gate of the temple. "House of the Lord" refers to the temple in Jerusalem.

The king had spoken with the priest Jehoiada because the temple had been neglected and damaged. The Levites had not collected the offering that Moses had established for the service of God. Earlier, Athaliah and her followers had plundered the temple and used sacred things for idols. So Joash looked for a simple, orderly way to gather what was needed to repair it.

Today we can learn that serving God also involves organization and order. If something in your church or in your spiritual life has been neglected, take a concrete step to restore it: a simple plan, consistency, and a heart willing to give with joy.
exp.23:9:
This verse says that the leaders of the people and all the people rejoiced to be able to give toward the temple. They would bring their offering and put it into the chest until it was full.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. King Joash had ordered the house of the LORD to be repaired, because it had been neglected and was falling into disrepair. He placed a chest at the gate of the temple and sent word throughout Judah that people should bring the offering that Moses had required. The people responded gladly, and with that money the workers who repaired the temple were paid.

Giving to God willingly, without pressure, brings joy and blesses others. Today we can ask ourselves: do I give with joy and consistency to the work of my church and to help those in need?
exp.23:11:
King Joash and the priest Jehoiada would hand over the money collected to those in charge of the work on the temple. With that money they hired stonemasons (those who cut and shape stone), skilled workers (laborers or builders), ironworkers (those who work iron), and workers in bronze and other metals. All of them repaired the house of the Lord.

This is a narrative passage, not a speech. The writer of Chronicles tells how the temple had fallen into disrepair and how the people had given their offerings gladly, putting them into a chest. Joash and Jehoiada worked together so that this money would be used well in the restoration.

For today: when we give to the work of God, it is worth doing so with order and honesty. Churches and leaders should manage resources with transparency, and each person can give their money or their skill with joy.
exp.23:12:
This verse says that the workers in charge labored diligently and that, thanks to their hands, the repair of the temple advanced until it was finished. The phrase that restored the house of God to its condition means they brought it back to its original state, and the word meaning they made it firm means they left it steady and secure.

It is part of the account in the book of Chronicles, which tells how King Joash and the priest Jehoiada arranged an offering to repair the temple, which had been neglected. The money was gathered into a chest and used in an orderly way. This verse shows the result: the work was completed because the people labored and the money was managed well.

For today: God often uses faithful and honest people to sustain his work. We should serve with loyalty in ordinary tasks, without seeking applause, and take care with integrity of what has been entrusted to us.
exp.23:13:
When they had finished the repairs to the temple, some money was left over. They brought it to King Joash and to the priest Jehoiada, and with it they made articles for the worship of the Lord: vessels for the service, bowls (the exact meaning of the word is uncertain, and they may have been cups or basins), spoons, and vessels of gold and silver. In addition, burnt offerings were being presented continually, sacrifices that were burned whole, all the days of Jehoiada.

This is part of the chronicler's account of the restoration of the temple under the young King Joash, guided by the priest Jehoiada. The people had given offerings for the work, and everything was handled with order. The verses that follow show that after Jehoiada's death the king turned away, so Jehoiada's influence was key.

For today: when we manage resources for the church or for our work, we can be honest and generous. What is left over can be dedicated to serving God and others, and steady faithfulness, like Jehoiada's, leaves a mark on others.
exp.23:15:
This verse tells us that Jehoiada, the priest, was buried in the City of David, the place where the kings were laid to rest. He was given this honor because he had done good in Israel, both toward God and toward his house, that is, toward the temple and its service.

Here the narrator of the book sums up Jehoiada's life. He guided the young King Joash and helped restore the temple. But the text that follows shows something sad: after Jehoiada died, the leaders led the king toward idolatry. This shows how deeply his life had influenced the nation.

For today: value and thank the people who guide you in faith, but do not depend on them alone. Make sure your love for God is your own, so that it remains firm even when no one is there to walk with you.
exp.23:17:
They abandoned the house of the Lord, the God of their ancestors, and began to worship the sacred poles or trees dedicated to a false goddess called Asherah, along with carved images, that is, idols. Because of this sin, God's punishment came upon Judah and Jerusalem.

The chronicler tells what happened when the priest Jehoiada died, the man who had guided King Joash well. The officials of Judah persuaded him, and the king listened to them. God sent prophets to them, but they paid no attention. The king's faith seemed to depend on a good adviser, not on a conviction of his own.

For today: it is not enough to lean on the faith of others, such as that of our parents or a pastor. Let us cultivate our own relationship with God, and be careful about who we keep company with, because bad influences can lead us away little by little.
exp.23:19:
The Spirit of God came upon Zechariah, that is, it clothed him or filled him with power to speak. Standing before the people, he asked them why they were disobeying the commandments of the Lord, and he warned them that this would not lead them to anything good. Their breaking of God's law was plain, and his message was clear: if you forsake God, He will also forsake you.

Zechariah was the son of the priest Jehoiada, who had protected and guided King Joash. But after Jehoiada's death, the people and the king turned back to idols. God sent prophets, and they would not listen. Zechariah spoke as a final call, and for that reason he was stoned by the king's command.

For today: let us not ignore loving warnings. If someone corrects us with the Word of God, let us listen with humility and return to Him before sin hardens us.
exp.23:20:
This verse tells how the leaders of Judah secretly agreed against Zechariah and killed him by stoning. They did it by the command of King Joash, in the court of the temple. A plot made in secret by several people to do harm is what the verse describes, and to stone someone means to pelt him with stones until he dies.

The narrator is the chronicler, who recounts the downfall of King Joash. Zechariah, son of the priest Jehoiada, had spoken on behalf of God and warned that forsaking the Lord would bring abandonment. Instead of repenting, the king killed the son of the man who had protected him as a child. Soon after, the army of Syria invaded Judah.

For today: when an honest word makes us uncomfortable, let us not silence it out of pride. Let us ask God for humility to listen to it, even when it hurts, and to be thankful toward those who have helped us.
exp.23:23:
This verse says that the army of Syria came with only a small company of men, yet still defeated a much larger army from Judah. The reason is that God allowed it, because the people had forsaken the Lord, the God of their fathers.

The Chronicler explains why this happened. Joash had been protected by the priest Jehoiada, but after Jehoiada died he turned away from God. He even had Zechariah, the son of Jehoiada, put to death, and Zechariah, as he died, asked that the Lord would see it and call them to account. The author sees the defeat as a response to that unfaithfulness.

For today: true strength is not found in numbers or resources, but in walking close to God. Let us remember with gratitude those who helped us, and keep our faith firm even when those people are no longer with us.
exp.23:24:
It says that when the Syrian army left, it left King Joash very ill. Then his own servants made a conspiracy against him, because he had shed the blood of the sons of Jehoiada the priest. They struck him down in his bed and he died. They buried him in the city of David, but not in the tombs of the kings.

The writer of Chronicles recounts the end of Joash's reign. Earlier, Joash followed God while the priest Jehoiada lived. Afterward he turned away from God and ordered the death of Zechariah, son of Jehoiada (2 Chronicles 24:20-22). The text presents the defeat by Syria and his death as the consequence of having forsaken the Lord.

For today: it is not enough to have good counselors for a season; our faith must be personal and firm. And we should remember with gratitude those who helped us, rather than repaying good with evil.
exp.23:25:
This verse names the two men who conspired against King Joash: Zabad, son of an Ammonite woman named Shimeath, and Jehozabad, son of a Moabite woman named Shimrith. "Conspired" means they secretly agreed together to harm him.

The writer of Chronicles is telling how the reign of Joash ended. He had ordered the killing of Zechariah, son of the priest Jehoiada, and he had turned away from God. After that, his own servants attacked him. The text presents his end as the result of having abandoned the LORD. The foreign origins of the conspirators are mentioned, but the text does not explain why.

For today: when we turn away from God and hurt others, sooner or later there are consequences. It is better to recognize our wrong in time, ask forgiveness, and return to Him.
exp.23:26:
It says that the rest about King Joash's sons, the many burdens laid on him, and the repair and restoration of the house of God are written in the story of the book of the kings. After his death, his son Amaziah reigned in his place.

This closes the account of King Joash of Judah. The chronicler, writing to a people returning from exile, summarizes his reign and points to other sources. Joash began well, under the guidance of the priest Jehoiada, and repaired the temple. But later he turned away, and his own servants conspired against him. It is not known with certainty which book "the book of the kings" refers to here; it is not necessarily our 1 and 2 Kings.

For today: it is not enough to start well. Good achievements can be overshadowed if we stop being faithful. Let us ask God for perseverance and surround ourselves with people who help us stay firm to the end.
exp.24:0:
This verse says that Amaziah was twenty-five years old when he began to reign as king of Judah. He reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Jehoaddan, and she was from Jerusalem.

Here the narrator of the book of Chronicles speaks, presenting basic facts about each king, such as his age, the length of his reign, and his mother. In this way the reader places Amaziah within the line of the kings of Judah. The text that follows makes clear that he did what was right, but not with a whole heart.

For today: God looks at more than our beginnings or our good actions; he looks at the heart. We can ask him to give us a sincere obedience and not a half-hearted one, so that what we do on the outside reflects what is within.
exp.24:3:
He says that King Amaziah punished the men who had murdered his father, but he did not put their children to death. He followed what God commanded in the law of Moses: parents were not to die for the sins of their children, and children were not to die for the sins of their parents. Each person answers for his own sin.

The writer of Chronicles describes how Amaziah began to reign in Judah. In many nations there was an old custom of wiping out the entire family of a guilty person. Amaziah did not do this, and he obeyed Deuteronomy 24:16. Even so, the previous verse makes clear that he did what was right, though not with a wholehearted heart, meaning his obedience was only partial.

God is just: he does not hold a person guilty for the wrongs of others. Today we can avoid judging someone for what their parents or family did. It also reminds us to be honest about our own choices, without blaming others.
exp.24:4:
Amaziah gathers all the people of Judah and organizes them by families. He appoints leaders over large groups (commanders of a thousand) and over smaller groups (commanders of a hundred). He counts the men twenty years old and up and finds three hundred thousand chosen warriors, ready to fight with spear and shield.

The one speaking here is the narrator of Chronicles. Amaziah has just established himself as king and has acted justly by not putting the children to death for the sins of their fathers. Now he prepares for a war against Edom. His plan seems sensible, but soon he will hire soldiers from Israel, and God will correct him through a prophet.

For today: planning with order and effort is good, but it is not enough. Before trusting our own resources, it is wise to ask God whether we are on the right path and to be willing to change course.
exp.24:5:
This verse says that King Amaziah of Judah hired soldiers from the kingdom of Israel, the northern kingdom. They were a hundred thousand mighty men, and he paid them a hundred talents of silver. The phrase about hiring them means he engaged them and paid them to fight. A talent was a very large unit of weight, and its exact value in kilograms is calculated in different ways.

Here the narrator of Chronicles speaks. Amaziah already had three hundred thousand men from Judah and Benjamin, but he wanted to strengthen his army with extra help to attack Edom. In the next verse, a man of God warns him not to do this, because God was not with Israel at that time, and because victory depends on God, not on the number of soldiers.

For today: sometimes we look for security in resources, connections, or money, even when we already have what we need. Before we secure our plans with human help, let us ask God and trust that strength comes from Him.
exp.24:8:
Amaziah, king of Judah, worries about the money. He had paid one hundred talents (a large amount of silver) to hire soldiers from Israel. The prophet tells him that God can give him much more than what he has lost. "Man of God" means prophet, and "the Lord" is the name of God.

Amaziah was preparing to fight against Edom (the descendants of Seir). A prophet warned him not to take the Israelites with him, because God was not with them at that time. The king hesitated, thinking about his investment. The prophet reminded him that God is the one who gives victory or defeat, and that his provision is greater than any loss.

Obeying God sometimes costs money, time, or comfort. Before you cling to what you have already lost or invested, ask yourself what God wants from you today. You can trust that He takes care of you, even though He does not always return things to you in the same way.
exp.24:9:
This verse tells that King Amaziah sent away the soldiers he had hired from the kingdom of Israel (Ephraim). They left very angry at Judah, full of fury.

Amaziah, king of Judah, was getting ready to fight against Edom. He had paid one hundred talents of silver to Israelite troops, but a man of God warned him not to take them, because God was not with that army. Amaziah obeyed, though he lost his money. The Bible does not say why they were so angry, but later they attacked cities of Judah (v. 13).

For today: obeying God can cost us money, comfort, or good relationships, and it is still the right thing to do. God can give us more than what we lost, as the prophet said.
exp.24:11:
This verse tells that the army of Judah captured alive another ten thousand men of Seir, that is, of Edom. They took them to the top of a cliff and threw them down from there, and all of them were dashed to pieces. To cast someone down from a height means to throw them off a steep drop. It was a very harsh way of treating the defeated.

Here the chronicler is speaking, recounting King Amaziah's war against Edom. Earlier, Amaziah had obeyed a prophet and sent home soldiers from Israel. God gave him the victory. But the text only describes this event; it does not say that God commanded that cruelty. Soon after, we see that Amaziah brings back the gods of Edom and worships them.

For today: a victory does not prove that everything we do is right. After a success, it is wise to guard the heart, to be humble, and to remain faithful to God, without letting pride or hardness toward others take hold of us.
exp.24:12:
This verse says that the soldiers whom Amaziah had sent back, so that they would not fight with him, attacked several cities of Judah, from Samaria as far as Beth-horon. They killed three thousand people and carried off much plunder.

The chronicler tells what happened after Amaziah, king of Judah, obeyed a prophet and sent away the soldiers he had hired from Israel. They were angry about losing the battle and their pay. Some scholars debate the exact area that "Samaria" covers here, but the general sense is a violent raid on the border.

Obeying God can bring costs and difficult reactions from others. Even so, his way is safer than ours. Trust in Him, and do not let the fear of losing something lead you to disobey.
exp.24:15:
What it says: While the prophet was speaking, King Amaziah angrily interrupted him. He asked whether he had been made a counselor of the king, and told him to stop, or they would kill him. The prophet stopped, but first he said that God had determined to destroy him for doing this and for not listening to his counsel.

Context: Amaziah had defeated the Edomites, but he brought their gods home and worshiped them. God, angry, sent a prophet to correct him with a question: why seek gods that could not save their own people? The king answered with a threat instead of repenting. The text shows that his pride later led him into a disastrous war.

For today: When someone corrects us based on God's Word, let us not respond with anger or pride. Let us listen with humility, pray, and examine our hearts, because a timely correction can save us from serious consequences.
exp.24:19:
It says that King Amaziah would not listen to Joash's warning. The text gives the reason: the matter came from God, who wanted to hand them over into the hands of their enemies. The cause was that Judah had sought after the gods of Edom.

The writer of Chronicles explains why Amaziah ignored advice that seemed wise. Joash, king of Israel, had answered him with a parable of the thistle and the cedar, and warned him not to seek a fight. Amaziah had just defeated Edom and had become full of pride. Moreover, he had worshiped the idols of the defeated people, and the text sees the defeat as a consequence of that.

For today: when pride or a bad decision closes our ears, it is wise to stop and listen to sound counsel. A victory is no excuse for turning away from God.
exp.24:20:
It says that Joash, king of Israel (the northern kingdom), went up with his army to face Amaziah, king of Judah (the southern kingdom). They met face to face, that is, directly opposite each other, at Beth-shemesh, a city that belonged to Judah.

Amaziah had defeated Edom and felt proud. Joash warned him not to get into trouble, but Amaziah would not listen. The text explains that God allowed that defeat, because the people had turned to the gods of Edom. This is understood as God's judgment for their idolatry.

When success fills us with pride, we stop listening to advice, even when it comes from unexpected people. Let us ask God for humility, and remember that He corrects us when we turn away from Him, so that we return to seeking Him alone.
exp.24:21:
This verse tells us that the army of Judah was defeated in battle by the army of Israel. The soldiers fled, and each one ran back to his home.

No one speaks here; it is the narrator who relates what happened. Amaziah, king of Judah, had challenged Joash, king of Israel, and would not listen to his warning. The text explains that God allowed this defeat because Amaziah and the people had sought the gods of Edom, that is, idols.

For today: when a decision of ours pulls us away from God, it also makes us deaf to good counsel. If you notice that you are walking in pride or giving room to other things before God, stop, pray, and listen with humility. God corrects so that we will return to him.
exp.24:22:
It says that Joash, king of Israel, captured Amaziah, king of Judah, at Beth-shemesh and led him to Jerusalem. There he had about four hundred cubits of the city wall broken down, from the gate of Ephraim to the corner gate.

The chronicler is telling the story of the kings here. Amaziah had defeated Edom and, in his pride, challenged Israel. Joash warned him not to do it, but Amaziah would not listen. The text says this came from God, because Amaziah had sought out the gods of Edom (2 Chronicles 25:14-20). Judah lost the battle, and the broken wall left Jerusalem without defense.

For today: pride blinds us and makes us reject wise counsel. After a success, it is good to ask God for humility and to listen to those who warn us sincerely.
exp.24:24:
This verse says that Amaziah, king of Judah, lived fifteen more years after Joash, king of Israel, died. In other words, Amaziah outlived the man who had defeated and humbled him. The same thing is said in 2 Kings 14:17.

Here the chronicler is not describing a scene but giving a detail of time. It comes right after Amaziah's defeat at Beth-shemesh, when Joash of Israel captured him, broke down part of the wall of Jerusalem, and carried off treasures. The text will later say that Amaziah turned away from the LORD and that they killed him at Lachish. The author connects his downfall with his turning away from God.

For today: living many years does not mean that everything is well inside. How we live matters more than how long we live. Even after a failure, God invites us to return to Him and not to harden our hearts.
exp.25:0:
It says that all the people of Judah chose Uzziah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king in place of his father Amaziah. Uzziah is the same person called Azariah in 2 Kings. The phrase "took" here means that they chose him or brought him to the throne, and "made him king" simply means they placed him on the throne.

This is part of the chronicler's account of the kings of Judah. Amaziah had died, and the people acted so that the house of David would stay on the throne. The verse does not say who proposed Uzziah or give the political details of that moment, so it is not wise to assume them. The book will later show his long reign of fifty-two years, with successes and also a fall.

For today: God can use young people with little experience, but they need good counsel. If you are young, seek wisdom and humility. If you are older, support and guide the younger ones with patience and a good example.
exp.25:2:
Uzziah (called Uzzías in this version) was only sixteen years old when he began to reign in Jerusalem. He reigned for fifty-two years, a very long time. His mother's name was Jecoliah, and she was from Jerusalem.

The speaker is the chronicler, the author of Chronicles, whose name is not stated with certainty. He tells how the people of Judah chose Uzziah as king after the death of his father Amaziah. By giving the new king's age and his mother's name, the author introduces him and shows that the line of David still sat on the throne. The verses that follow say that God prospered him as long as he sought God.

God can use a young person who truly seeks him. But starting well is not enough: Uzziah's success was tied to seeking God. Today, whatever your age, make prayer and the Word a daily habit.
exp.25:3:
This verse says that Uzziah, the young king of Judah, did what pleases God, following the example of his father Amaziah. The phrase that is right in the sight of the Lord means what God considers right.

Here the chronicler summarizes the reign of Uzziah, which began when he was sixteen years old and lasted fifty-two years. The verses that follow explain that God prospered him while he sought the Lord with the guidance of Zechariah. Note that the Bible also shows that Amaziah had failings, so this praise is a general assessment, not a perfect one.

For today: what we do now can inspire others, but each person must seek God personally. Give thanks to those who set a good example for you, and ask God for a heart that seeks Him every day, not just out of family custom.
exp.25:6:
This verse says that God helped King Uzziah in his wars against three neighboring peoples: the Philistines, the Arabs who lived in Gur-baal, and the Meunites.

Gur-baal is an uncertain place, and all we can tell is that it was an area where Arabs lived.

The passage is the chronicler's account, which tells the history of the kings of Judah. Here it explains that Uzziah's military successes were not due to his own merit alone. They came from the fact that he sought God while he was guided by Zechariah, a man who understood the visions of God. The passage shows the connection between seeking God and receiving his help.

Today we can learn that the achievements of life are more solid when we receive them as help from God. Let us seek him every day and surround ourselves with wise people who bring us closer to him.
exp.25:7:
This verse says that the Ammonites brought gifts to Uzziah, who was king of Judah. These gifts were a kind of tribute, that is, a payment that a weaker people gives to a stronger one. In addition, Uzziah's reputation reached as far as the border of Egypt, because he had become very powerful.

The speaker is the chronicler, who tells the history of the kings of Judah. Earlier he explained that God helped Uzziah in his wars against the Philistines, the Arabs, and the Ammonites. Afterward he shows how Uzziah strengthened Jerusalem and took care of the land. The text presents his power as the fruit of that help from God.

For today: if God gives us success, influence, or good results, let us remember where they come from. We can thank him and use what we have with humility and responsibility, without relying only on our own strength.
exp.25:10:
This verse says that King Uzziah (also called Azariah) had a well-organized army. The soldiers went out to war in groups, according to a list made by Jeiel the scribe (the secretary who kept the records), by Maaseiah, a governor or official, and by Hananiah, one of the king's officers.

Here the writer of Chronicles, who tells the story of the kings of Judah, is speaking. He shows that Uzziah prospered: he built towers, dug cisterns, cared for the land, and organized his army. The text just before says that God helped him while he sought the Lord. Later, his pride led to his downfall.

For today: order, planning, and teamwork are good things. But they must not lead us to trust only in our own strength. Let us plan with wisdom, and place our trust in God.
exp.25:13:
He says that King Uzziah equipped his whole army with what was needed for war. He gave them shields, spears, helmets, and body armor, bows, and slings for hurling stones. It was a complete and well-organized preparation.

The writer of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition often identifies with Ezra (this is not certain), tells how God blessed Uzziah with strength and fame while he sought the LORD. This verse shows his good management. But the text goes on with a warning: when Uzziah grew strong, his heart filled with pride, and he went into the temple to burn incense, something that was not his place to do.

Preparing ourselves and organizing our lives well is good and wise. But strength, success, or talent should never lead us into pride. May each achievement remind us that we depend on God and keep us humble and thankful.
exp.25:14:
It says that King Uzziah had machines of war built in Jerusalem, designed by skilled experts or engineers. They were placed on the towers and on the fortified corners of the wall. They served to shoot arrows and large stones. His fame spread far because he was helped in a remarkable way, and so he became powerful.

It is part of the Chronicler's account of Uzziah's reign (also called Azariah). Just before, his great army and weapons are described. The writer shows how God prospered him while he sought the Lord. But the next verse announces the turn: with strength came pride, and his fall.

For today: achievements and abilities are blessings, but they can become a trap if we forget where they come from. When something in your life goes well, thank God and keep your heart humble and dependent on Him.
exp.25:15:
It says that Uzziah, when he was already strong and powerful, became filled with pride, and this led him to his ruin. He rebelled against God by entering the temple to burn incense on the altar of incense. Incense was the sweet-smelling smoke burned as an offering, and to say he was lifted up means that he thought himself superior.

The narrator of the book tells the story of Uzziah, king of Judah. He had enjoyed many successes: a well-equipped army and defensive machines in Jerusalem. But the law reserved the burning of incense only for the priests, the descendants of Aaron. For that reason, the priest Azariah and eighty others confronted him right away.

For today: success can make us feel that we no longer need limits or advice. We can ask God for a humble heart and listen respectfully to those who correct us with love.
exp.25:16:
This verse says that the priest Azariah entered the temple after King Uzziah, accompanied by eighty priests of the Lord.

Here the narrator is speaking, not a character. Uzziah was a strong and famous king, but his success filled him with pride. He entered the temple to burn incense, something the law reserved for the priests descended from Aaron. Azariah and the priests followed him to stop him and correct him, out of love for obedience to God.

For today: success can make us proud without our noticing. Let us learn to respect the limits God sets, and to listen humbly to those who correct us with courage and respect, even when we hold power or experience.
exp.25:17:
This verse says that the priests confronted King Uzziah (also called Azariah or Ozias). They told him that burning incense to God did not belong to him, but to the priests, the descendants of Aaron, set apart for that work. They asked him to leave the sanctuary. They warned him that this would not bring him honor before God.

It speaks of the priest Azariah together with eighty brave priests. The king had had great success, but his heart had been filled with pride. He entered the temple to do something that the law of Moses reserved for the priests. They corrected him to guard the holiness of worship and also the king himself.

For today: success can make us proud and make us believe that the rules are not for us. Let us be humble, respect the limits God sets, and receive with gratitude the correction of those who love us.
exp.25:19:
Azariah the chief priest and the other priests looked at King Uzziah and saw leprosy on his forehead. The sentence that explained the quoted word has been removed. The priests quickly drove him out of the temple, and the king himself hurried to leave, because he understood that God had struck him.

The account tells that Uzziah, a king who had enjoyed great success, wanted to burn incense in the temple. That duty was reserved for the priests descended from Aaron. Azariah and the priests confronted him, but the king became angry. Then the leprosy appeared. Because of that disease, he lived apart until he died, and his son Jotham ruled in his place.

For today: success can make us proud and lead us to believe that the rules are not meant for us. When someone corrects us with respect, it is wise to listen and humble ourselves, instead of becoming angry. God takes care that we seek him in his way.
exp.25:20:
This verse tells how the life of King Uzziah (also called Azariah) ended. He was a leper until he died. He lived in a separate house, because he could no longer enter the temple of the Lord. Meanwhile, his son Jotham took charge of the palace and governed the people. The word "leper" refers to a serious skin disease, which under the law of Moses required a person to live apart from others.

The writer of Chronicles tells the story of the kings of Judah. Uzziah had been very successful, but his heart had filled with pride. He entered the temple to burn incense, something reserved for the priests, and became angry when he was warned about it. Then God struck him with leprosy.

For today: success can make us proud and lead us to believe we do not need correction. Let us ask God for a humble heart, and listen with respect to the advice of wise people, even when it makes us uncomfortable.
exp.26:0:
This verse says that Jotham was twenty-five years old when he began to reign over Judah, and that he ruled for sixteen years from Jerusalem. It also names his mother, Jerusha, the daughter of Zadok. The old spellings "Jerusalem" and the older form of the verb in the source are simply the same city and word as in the verse you have read, so no further note is needed.

The one speaking is the Chronicler, an unknown author who wrote after the exile in Babylon. Many think it was Ezra, but this is not certain. He presents each king with his age, years of reign, and mother, as an official record. Then he evaluates his life: Jotham did what was right before God, although the people still continued in their wrong ways.

For today: our lives also leave a record, and what matters most is whether we walk with God. Jotham was faithful even when the people around him were not. We can ask God to help us live with integrity, even when others do not.
exp.26:6:
The rest of the acts of Jotham, his wars, and his conduct are recorded in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah, as the verse says. Here "ways" means his conduct and his decisions.

The one speaking is the Chronicler, the author of Chronicles, who closes his summary of Jotham's reign. He names that book as a source where the reader can find more details. We do not know for certain whether it is the same book we today call 1 and 2 Kings, or a different document that no longer survives; it has been understood in several ways.

For today: our lives also become a record. The verse before this one says that Jotham grew strong because he ordered his ways before the LORD. Today we can ask ourselves whether our daily decisions, though they may seem small, are made with God in mind.
exp.27:0:
Ahaz was twenty years old when he began to reign, and he ruled sixteen years in Jerusalem. He did not do what was right in the eyes of the Lord (Jehovah), as David, his ancestor, had done. Here "father" means an ancestor, not a direct father.

The author of Chronicles, whose name is not stated with certainty, sums up the life of this king of Judah. He compares him with David, the model of faithfulness. In this way he reminds the people, who were writing or reading after difficult times, that loyalty to God matters more than power.

Today we can ask ourselves whom we are imitating. Ahaz had a good example in David, but he followed other paths. Let us seek models who bring us closer to God, and let us ask him for help in deciding well, without being carried along by the current.
exp.27:3:
King Ahaz offered sacrifices and burned incense on the high places, which were raised places of worship, also on the hills and under every green tree. These were places where false gods were worshiped, not the God of Israel.

The one telling the story is the chronicler, who reviews the history of the kings of Judah. Ahaz is presented as a king who abandoned the LORD and copied the practices of the neighboring peoples. The text that follows shows the consequences: defeats and many deaths. The chronicler wants the reader to understand that turning away from God brings ruin.

For today: examine what or whom you are placing your trust and your time in. Ahaz sought help in many places, except from God. Today we can do something similar with money, success, or the approval of others. Return to God simply, and trust Him first.
exp.27:4:
It says that, because of the wickedness of King Ahaz, God allowed him to be defeated by his enemies. First he handed him over to the king of Syria, who beat him and carried away a great number of captives and plunder to Damascus. Afterward he handed him over to the king of Israel, who punished him with a great slaughter.

Context: the chronicler tells the story of the kings of Judah. Ahaz abandoned God: he practiced idolatry, offered incense on the high places, and even burned his children in the valley of Hinnom. The text presents these defeats as the consequence of having left the Lord. The verses that follow show how hard that blow was.

For today: God warns us out of love, because turning away from Him brings harm. If we notice that we have strayed, we can return today with humility, for He remains willing to forgive.
exp.27:5:
This verse tells that Pekah, son of Remaliah and king of Israel, killed one hundred and twenty thousand brave soldiers of Judah in a single day. The text gives the reason: they had forsaken the Lord God of their fathers. "Forsaken" means that they had turned away from God and no longer followed him.

The one speaking is the author of Chronicles, who explains the history from a spiritual point of view. He speaks of the reign of Ahaz in Judah, who practiced idolatry on the high places. The chronicler presents this defeat as a consequence of the people's unfaithfulness. The number is very high, and some scholars think it may be an expression of great magnitude, although the text does not make this clear.

For today: strength, preparation, or success do not replace God. If I turn away from him, I lose my true support. Today I can set aside a moment each day to pray and read his Word, so that I stay close to him.
exp.27:6:
Verse 7 tells how Zichri, a mighty warrior from the tribe of Ephraim, killed three important men of Judah: Maaseiah, the son of King Ahaz; Azrikam, the officer in charge of the palace; and Elkanah, the person with the most authority after the king.

The writer of the book describes the consequences of King Ahaz's unfaithfulness. According to the text, Judah had turned away from the Lord and therefore suffered defeats against Syria and Israel. This blow reached even the royal family and its leaders. Later on, the prophet Oded reminds Israel that their violence was excessive.

For today: turning away from God brings consequences that can affect many people. But we must also take care that our sense of justice does not become cruelty. Let us ask God for humility and faithfulness.
exp.27:7:
This verse tells that the army of Israel, the northern kingdom, took captive two hundred thousand people from Judah, the southern kingdom. They were women, boys, and girls, all of them their own relatives. Besides this, they carried off a great many goods, and they brought everything to Samaria, the capital of Israel. The spoil is what is taken from a defeated enemy, and the goods were taken by force.

The chronicler is the one telling the story, and he explains that Judah was suffering this punishment for having abandoned God under King Ahaz. But Israel went much further than was right: they killed in fury and wanted to enslave their own brothers. For this reason, the prophet Oded soon confronted them.

For today: God may allow someone to face consequences, but that does not give us permission to treat them with cruelty. Before judging another, let us examine our own hearts and deal with compassion toward someone who has fallen.
exp.27:8:
This verse tells how a prophet named Oded went out to meet the army of Israel as it was returning to Samaria. He told them that God had allowed them to win against Judah because God was angry with Judah. But they went too far: they killed with such fury that their violence reached up to heaven, meaning God saw it.

Oded speaks on God's behalf. Israel, the northern kingdom, had just defeated Judah, the southern kingdom, and was bringing back captives and plunder. They were brother peoples. God used that defeat to correct Judah, but that did not give Israel permission to treat them with cruelty.

For today: even when someone receives the consequences of their mistakes, we have no right to humiliate or mistreat them. God expects us to show compassion and to remember that we too need his forgiveness.
exp.27:14:
This verse tells how certain men of Samaria, the kingdom of Israel, rose up and cared for the captives from Judah. They gave them clothing and sandals from the plunder, gave them food and drink, and anointed them (they put oil on them, which was a common way to ease the body). They lifted the weakest ones onto donkeys and brought them to Jericho, the city of palm trees, near their brothers. Then they returned to Samaria.

Israel had defeated Judah and had brought back many prisoners. The prophet Obed and some leaders of Ephraim, the men named in the text, told them that taking those captives would be another sin against God. The army listened to them and set the prisoners free.

When we understand that something is wrong, we can change course and do good through concrete actions. Compassion is not just feeling sorry: it means giving food, clothing and real help to those who suffer, even if they were once our enemies.
exp.27:15:
The passage says that at that time King Ahaz sent to the kings of Assyria for help. Sending word to them to come to his aid is the same as asking them to rescue him.

The one speaking is the chronicler, who tells the history of Judah. Ahaz ruled over a kingdom that was struck hard: Israel had defeated him and taken captives, and the Edomites and the Philistines also attacked him. Instead of seeking God, Ahaz turned to Assyria. The text that follows shows that this help did not solve his problem; the chronicler presents it as a decision made out of little faith.

When pressure comes, we often reach first for the fastest human way out. Today we can ask ourselves: to whom do I turn first in my distress? Asking for advice and help is not wrong, but God should be our first refuge, not our last resort.
exp.27:17:
This verse tells us that the Philistines raided the towns of the foothills and the Negev of Judah. They captured Beth-shemesh, Aijalon, and Gederoth, along with Soco, Timnah, and Gimzo, and their villages, and they moved in and settled there.

Here the chronicler speaks, recounting the time of King Ahaz. Judah was weak, attacked by the Edomites and the Philistines. The text that follows gives the cause: God humbled Judah because of Ahaz's unfaithfulness. Ahaz sought help from Assyria, but that king only brought him more pressure.

For today: when everything seems to be falling apart, let us not first run to human solutions that draw us away from God. Let us return to Him with humility, for only He gives true security.
exp.27:22:
This verse says that King Ahaz offered sacrifices to the gods of Damascus, the city that had defeated him. He reasoned that if those gods helped the kings of Syria, they would also help him. But the text states that those gods were his ruin and the ruin of all Israel. The word for this kind of betrayal of faith is unfaithfulness, and being struck down refers to having been defeated.

The one speaking here is the Chronicler, who recounts the history of Judah. Ahaz was under military pressure, and even paying Assyria did not save him. Instead of turning to God, he sought help from false gods. Then he shut the temple and set up altars everywhere, so his idolatry grew ever deeper.

For today: when pressure comes, it is easy to look for solutions wherever they seem to work for others. Before deciding, ask yourself whom you are really trusting. God is faithful, and you can return to Him with your fears.
exp.27:23:
This verse tells how King Ahaz gathered up the articles of the temple and broke them into pieces. Then he shut the doors of the house of the Lord, that is, the temple. He also built altars to false gods in every corner of Jerusalem.

Here the chronicler speaks, recounting the history of Judah. Ahaz was under pressure from wars with neighboring peoples. Instead of seeking God, he turned to the gods of his enemies, believing they would give him help. The text says that this led him to ruin.

For today: when pressures come, it is easy to look for help in anything that seems strong. This passage invites us to return to God in difficult moments, not to shut the door on Him. We can pray and trust Him before looking for other ways out.
exp.28:0:
Hezekiah began to reign over Judah at the age of twenty-five, and he ruled for twenty-nine years from Jerusalem. The verse also names his mother, Abijah, the daughter of Zechariah. Older spellings such as "Jerusalem" were simply the spelling of their time; today we write the same name as it appears in the verse.

Here the speaker is not a character in the story; the narrator of the book of Chronicles introduces Hezekiah's reign. The verses that follow say that he did what was right before God and that, in his first year, he opened and repaired the temple. This had been neglected under his father Ahaz. Chronicles was written to encourage a people who were seeking to return to God, and for that reason it highlights the reigns that led them back.

For today: no one chooses their family or their past, but each person can decide how to begin again. Hezekiah did not wait; he took his first step early. Think about something you have neglected in your relationship with God, and take one concrete step toward it today.
exp.28:2:
It says that Hezekiah, as soon as he began to reign, in the first month of his first year, opened the doors of the temple of the Lord and repaired them. "House of the Lord" is the temple in Jerusalem. Those doors had been shut, and he restored them so that worship could return.

The one telling the story is the chronicler, who recounts the history of Judah. Hezekiah succeeds his father Ahaz, and the text suggests that the temple had been neglected in his time. That is why Hezekiah begins with what matters most: returning to God. Right away he calls the priests and Levites to purify the temple. The chronicler presents him as a king who did what was right, like David.

For today: do not wait until everything is resolved before returning to God. Think about which area of your spiritual life has been neglected, such as prayer or Bible reading, and begin to repair it this week.
exp.28:5:
It says that the ancestors of Judah rebelled against God and did what was evil in his sight. They abandoned him, stopped turning their faces toward the temple (here it refers to the temple, the house of God), and turned their backs on him, as one who deliberately rejects someone.

King Hezekiah of Judah speaks at the beginning of his reign. His father Ahaz had neglected and defiled the temple. Hezekiah gathers priests and Levites so that they may purify themselves and cleanse the house of God. He honestly acknowledges the sin of the previous generation and its consequences, in order to start again.

For today: honestly recognizing where we have drifted away from God is the first step to returning. It is not about blaming others, but about deciding today to turn our gaze back to him, to pray, and to put in order what we have neglected.
exp.28:6:
What the verse says: The verse describes how worship in the temple was abandoned. They shut the doors of the porch, the entrance to the temple. They put out the lamps that were meant to light the holy place. They did not burn incense, nor did they offer burnt offerings, which were sacrifices completely consumed on the altar, to the God of Israel.

Context: Hezekiah, king of Judah, is speaking at the beginning of his reign. He gathers the Levites and asks them to purify the temple. He reminds them that their ancestors, during the reign of Ahaz, stopped worshiping God, and that this brought painful consequences on the people.

For today: When we neglect our relationship with God, the light inside us gradually goes out. But Hezekiah shows that it is always possible to return. Today you can open the doors again with a daily moment of prayer and Bible reading, without waiting to feel perfect.
exp.28:7:
This verse says that God was angry with Judah and Jerusalem because of their disobedience. As a result, the people became a source of dread, of cursing or contempt, and of mockery. Moreover, the king says this is not a rumor: they see it with their own eyes.

King Hezekiah of Judah speaks at the beginning of his reign. He addresses the priests and Levites and asks them to cleanse the temple. His ancestors, during the reign of Ahaz, had abandoned the worship of God, shut the temple, and put out the lamps.
