Hezekiah recognizes that the people's troubles were connected to that abandonment, and he wants to return to God.

For today: when we see the consequences of drifting away from God, we should not stop at lamenting. We can, like Hezekiah, acknowledge the mistake with humility and make the concrete decision to return to Him.
exp.28:8:
It says that the people's ancestors died by the sword, and that their sons, daughters, and wives were taken away as prisoners. "Fallen by the sword" means they died in war, and "in captivity" means they were carried off as prisoners to another land. The text presents this as a consequence of having abandoned God.

King Hezekiah is speaking to the priests and Levites at the beginning of his reign. He reminds them that under his father Ahaz the temple was shut and the worship of God was abandoned. Hezekiah sees the defeats and the captivities as the result of that unfaithfulness. That is why he wants to restore the temple and make a covenant with God. The Bible does not detail each historical event here, but the idea is clear.

For today: do not minimize spiritual neglect. If anything has drawn you away from God, returning to Him with humility and sincerity is never too late. Start with one concrete step: pray and seek Him today.
exp.28:12:
This verse continues a list of Levites who stood up to answer the king's call. Here appear the descendants of Elizaphan (Shimri and Jeiel) and the descendants of Asaph (Zechariah and Mattaniah). The names are spelled as they appear in the verse you are reading: Asaph is the same man as in the verse, and Mattaniah is the same name as in the verse.

Hezekiah, king of Judah, had just asked the Levites to clean the temple, which had been neglected and defiled in earlier times. The writer of Chronicles lists the men by name, and so shows that the work was done by real people from different Levite families. Asaph was known for his service in the music of the temple.

God values people who respond with name and face. Today, your simple service in your church or family also counts. Do not wait to be famous: stand up and obey when God calls you.
exp.28:13:
This verse continues a list of Levites who answered the call of King Hezekiah. Here appear the last names: from the family of Heman, Jehiel and Shimei; and from the family of Jeduthun, Shemaiah and Uzziel. Heman and Jeduthun (also called Ethan) were musicians and worship leaders in the time of David.

The one telling the story is the chronicler, who reviews the history of Judah. King Hezekiah had just reopened the temple, which his father Ahaz had closed and filled with idolatry. The Levites rose up to cleanse it, and the chronicler records their names one by one, like a register of honor.

For today: God notices those who serve, even in silence and without fame. If He asks you to help with something, even if it is small or hardly visible, respond with willingness. Before serving, examine your own heart.
exp.28:14:
This verse tells how the Levites named in the previous list gathered their fellow Levites. First they made themselves holy, that is, they set themselves apart and purified themselves for God, and then they went into the temple to clean it. They did this in obedience to the king's command and to the words of the Lord.

The writer of the book describes the beginning of the reign of Hezekiah, king of Judah. The temple had been neglected and defiled in the days of his father Ahaz. Hezekiah ordered the Levites to restore worship, and they responded with obedience.

For today: before trying to clean up or repair something in the lives of others or in the church, it is good for us first to draw near to God with humility, confessing what we owe and seeking his forgiveness. God often begins the cleansing with the heart of the one who serves.
exp.28:16:
This verse tells how long it took to cleanse the temple. The Levites began to sanctify, that is, to set apart and clean, on the first day of the first month. On the eighth day they reached the porch, the entrance of the temple. Then they spent eight more days cleaning the house itself, and on the sixteenth day they finished. In total it was about sixteen days of work.

The account describes what the Levites did at the command of King Hezekiah. His father, Ahaz, had neglected and defiled the temple. Hezekiah wanted the people to worship God again, and so he began by cleaning the house of the Lord, first the outside and then the inside.

For today: renewing our relationship with God sometimes requires patient and steady work. We can ask him to show us what needs cleaning in our hearts or in our habits, and move forward step by step, without rushing but without giving up the task.
exp.28:18:
This verse says that the priests and Levites arranged and set apart for God all the temple utensils that King Ahaz had neglected and damaged. Now those objects are ready in front of the altar.

The ones speaking are the priests and Levites, and they report to King Hezekiah. He had just reopened the temple and wanted to restore the worship of God. According to 2 Chronicles 28, Ahaz had been unfaithful and had shut the doors of the temple. This report shows that the cleaning work was already finished.

For today: if something in your spiritual life has been neglected or damaged, such as prayer or Bible reading, God invites you to restore it. Begin with one concrete, simple step, and put it back into his service.
exp.28:20:
They brought seven young bulls, seven rams, seven lambs, and seven male goats as a sin offering, that is, to ask for forgiveness and to cleanse the guilt. It was for the kingdom, for the sanctuary, and for Judah. The king then commanded the priests, the descendants of Aaron, to offer them on the altar of the Lord.

This is the account of the reform of King Hezekiah. His father Ahaz had neglected the temple and mistreated its furnishings. Hezekiah reopens the house of God, purifies it, and gets up early to gather the leaders. He wants the people to return to worshiping God and to acknowledge their sins. The number seven usually points to something complete, though the text does not explain this.

For today: returning to God begins with humbly acknowledging what we have done wrong, without excuses. Christians believe that Christ offered the complete sacrifice for our sins, so we can come near with sincerity and confidence to receive forgiveness and start again.
exp.28:21:
They killed the bulls, and the priests caught the blood and splashed it on the altar. Then they killed the rams and splashed their blood on the altar as well, and they also killed the lambs and splashed their blood on the altar. The verse tells how each animal brought to the temple was put to death, and how its blood was handled in the same way: it was poured out on the altar, as the law of Moses required.

This is part of the account of how King Hezekiah restored worship in the temple, which had been neglected under earlier kings. The narrator explains that these sacrifices were for atonement, that is, to ask forgiveness for the kingdom, the sanctuary, and Judah. Hezekiah wanted the people to return to God with humility.

For today: Christians believe that Jesus is the final sacrifice for sin. So instead of hiding our faults, we can acknowledge them honestly before God and receive his forgiveness with gratitude, knowing that the cost has already been paid.
exp.28:23:
This verse tells how the priests killed the male goats and spread their blood on the altar as a sin offering. The king commanded that the burnt offering and the sin offering be made for all of Israel, not just for a few people.

This is part of the account of the cleansing of the temple under King Hezekiah. The text is narrative, not a speech. After years of neglect and disobedience, the people return to worshiping God and seek forgiveness. The chronicler emphasizes that the offering was made for the whole nation.

For today: forgiveness and restoration with God begin with honestly acknowledging our guilt. Many Christians see in these sacrifices a shadow of Christ, whose blood offers forgiveness. We can come before God without pretense, trusting in his mercy, and also pray for our families and communities.
exp.28:24:
He set the Levites in the house of the Lord with cymbals, harps and lyres, following what David, Gad and Nathan had commanded. Gad is called "seer," which means prophet. The text states that this command came from God himself, through his prophets.

Here the narrator of Chronicles speaks. Hezekiah is restoring worship in the temple, which had been neglected by his father Ahaz. After the sin offering, music accompanies the offering. The author emphasizes that Hezekiah invented nothing new, but returned to what God had already established.

For today: when we worship, what matters most is not the style, but that our hearts obey God and rest on his Word. Let us pray that our praise springs from gratitude for the forgiveness we have received.
exp.28:25:
This verse describes how the musicians were positioned in the temple. The Levites held the instruments that David had left for praise, such as harps, lyres and cymbals. The priests had the trumpets. Each group had its place according to its service.

The account tells how King Hezekiah restored worship in the temple after years of neglect. Before beginning, sacrifices were offered to ask forgiveness for all Israel. The text says the music followed a command given through David and the prophets Gad and Nathan, and that it came from God. For that reason the worship was carried out in an orderly way.

For today: praise to God is not something done without thought. We can worship him with order, with sincerity and with gratitude, and each person can serve with the gift they have, without competing with others.
exp.28:26:
This verse tells us that King Hezekiah commanded that the burnt offering be offered on the altar. A burnt offering was a sacrifice in which the offering was completely burned up for God. At the very moment the sacrifice began, the song to the Lord also began, accompanied by trumpets and by the instruments that David had left for worship.

The book of Chronicles recounts this after Hezekiah had reopened and purified the temple, which had been neglected under his father Ahaz. The text explains that the music followed the instructions given by David and by the prophets Gad and Nathan. In this way, the people were worshiping God as he had directed, and not according to custom or improvisation.

For today: when we draw near to God, worship is not just carrying out a ritual. It joins repentance with praise. We can prepare our hearts and sing with gratitude, remembering that God deserves our sincere and orderly devotion.
exp.28:27:
It says that while the burnt offering was being offered, the whole congregation worshipped, the singers sang, and the trumpeters played without stopping. All of this continued until the sacrifice was finished. A burnt offering was a sacrifice that was burned whole on the altar, given entirely to God.

It is part of the account of how King Hezekiah restored worship in the temple after years of neglect. The Chronicler describes how worship was restarted with the order associated with David: Levites with instruments, priests with trumpets. Music and sacrifice went together, as a sign that the people were returning to God.

Today we can learn that worship is not only listening, but taking part with the whole heart. Before singing on Sunday, think about what you want to give to God completely, and sing with that same devotion.
exp.28:28:
It says that when they had finished presenting the offerings, King Hezekiah and everyone who was with him bowed down and worshipped. "Bowed down" here means bending low or lying prostrate in humility before God. "Offering" refers to the burnt sacrifices offered on the altar, called burnt offerings.

The text is a narrative, so it does not speak of any particular person. Hezekiah had just reopened and cleansed the temple, which had been neglected by his father Ahaz. After everything was purified, worship was restored with sacrifices, music, and songs, as in the days of David. This moment of worship marks a new beginning for the people.

For today: after asking forgiveness, serving, or giving, pause for a moment to worship. Acknowledging God with humility and gratitude reminds us that everything we do is for Him and by His grace.
exp.28:29:
It says that King Hezekiah and the leaders asked the Levites, who were in charge of the service in the temple, to praise God with the songs of David and of Asaph. The word "seer" is someone to whom God gave understanding so that they could speak on his behalf. The Levites sang with great joy, bowed down, and worshipped.

Hezekiah had reopened and cleansed the temple, which had been neglected. They had just offered the burnt offering, a sacrifice that was burned whole before God. The worship was carried out with music and with ancient psalms. That shows they wanted to return to God according to what they had already been taught.

For today: when we worship, we should not depend only on our mood. We can use the words of the Bible, such as the psalms, to praise God. In this way our joy rests on the truth and not only on emotion.
exp.28:30:
King Hezekiah spoke, urging the people to come near to the temple with sacrifices and thanksgiving. He reminds them that they have already dedicated themselves to the Lord, that is, they have set themselves apart for him. The crowd responded by bringing their offerings, and those who were willing and open-handed, ready to give freely, brought burnt offerings, which were offerings burned completely on the altar.

King Hezekiah of Judah is the one speaking. The temple had been neglected and dirty, and the priests and Levites had just cleansed it. Now the worship of God was being restored, with sin offerings, music, and praise. After that cleansing, the king invites everyone to take part.

For today: God does not seek mere religious duty, but a willing heart. After returning to God, we can answer him with gratitude and generosity, giving him praise, time, and what we have, without being forced to.
exp.28:31:
This verse tells how many animals the people brought for the burnt offering: seventy bulls, one hundred rams, and two hundred lambs. A burnt offering was an offering that was burned whole on the altar, as a sign of complete surrender to God.

King Hezekiah had reopened and cleansed the temple, which his father Ahaz had neglected. Now worship was being restored. The account comes from the Chronicler, who emphasizes that the people gave willingly, with a generous and ready heart.

For today: God looks at the attitude with which we give and serve, not only at the amount. We can ask ourselves what we offer the Lord: our time, our talents, or our resources. Let it be with joy and sincerity, as a grateful response to Him, and not out of obligation or appearance.
exp.28:33:
This verse says that the priests were too few and could not skin all the burnt offerings. Then their brothers, the Levites, helped them until the work was finished and until the other priests had purified themselves. The Levites were more willing in heart to dedicate themselves than the priests were.

No one speaks directly here; this is the Chronicler's account. King Hezekiah had just reopened and cleansed the temple, which had been neglected. The people brought a great many animals for the offering. There were few priests, or not all of them were ready, so the Levites helped. The text does not explain why prepared priests were lacking; it only says the Levites were more willing.

For today: when God's work needs hands, do not wait for a title or an office before you serve. Offer yourself with a willing spirit and a sincere heart, and help wherever it is needed.
exp.28:34:
This verse says there was a very large number of burnt offerings, animals offered whole on the altar. The fat of the peace offerings was also presented, and the drink offerings, liquid offerings such as wine, were poured out alongside each burnt offering. In the end, the service of the temple was restored and put in order.

Here the speaker is not a character but the narrator of Chronicles. He tells how King Hezekiah reopened and cleansed the temple, after years of neglect under his father Ahaz. There were few priests for so many animals, and the Levites helped with a willing heart.

For today: when God calls us to return to Him, restoration is lived out through concrete obedience and teamwork. If you see that your church lacks help, serve with enthusiasm, even if it is not your official task.
exp.28:35:
Here is how the verse reads in plain English:

It says that King Hezekiah and all the people rejoiced because God had prepared the people to worship him again. Also, everything happened suddenly, that is, quickly and unexpectedly. The Hezekiah named in the verse is the same king described in the rest of this account.

The one telling the story is the chronicler of Israel. Hezekiah had reopened the temple, which had been neglected, and the priests and Levites purified it. Sacrifices were offered to ask for forgiveness and to renew the covenant with God. There were few priests, so the Levites helped. The text indicates that they were more willing in heart. The joy comes from seeing that God himself had been at work among the people.

Today we can learn that when we return to God, he can act faster than we expect. If you feel that your spiritual life has been neglected, take a simple first step: pray, ask for forgiveness, and seek the help of other believers. Then thank God for what he does.
exp.29:0:
Hezekiah, the king of Judah, sent messengers and letters to all the people, both of Judah and of Israel, including the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh. He invited them to come to the temple in Jerusalem to celebrate the Passover.

Hezekiah was king of Judah. The temple had been neglected and closed before his reign, and he had just cleansed it. Now he wanted the people to remember again how God had brought them out of Egypt. He even invited the northern tribes, who had been separated from the kingdom of Judah, which shows his desire to unite all the people before God.

Today, we can imitate Hezekiah by inviting others to draw near to God, regardless of differences or distance. A simple invitation, such as a phone call or a message, can help someone return to faith.
exp.29:1:
King Hezekiah did not decide on his own, the verse says. He spoke with his princes, that is, his officials and leaders, and with the whole assembly gathered in Jerusalem. Together they agreed to keep the Passover in the second month, not the first, which was the usual date.

The book of Chronicles tells us that Hezekiah wanted the people to worship God again. According to the verses that follow, they could not keep it in the first month because the priests had not yet made themselves holy, that is, prepared themselves for service, and the people had not yet gathered. The Law allowed in certain cases that it be kept in the second month (Numbers 9:10-11), and this explains the decision.

For today: before making important decisions, in the family, the church, or at work, seek wise counsel and listen to others. And if something cannot be done as expected, look for a way to obey God with humility.
exp.29:2:
This verse explains why the Passover had not been kept in the usual month, the first. There were two reasons: there were not enough priests who had sanctified themselves, that is, purified and set themselves apart to serve God, and the people had not yet gathered together in Jerusalem. Keeping the feast means carrying it out.

The writer of Chronicles tells how King Hezekiah, after cleansing the temple, wanted to restore worship. Since they were not ready in the first month, he and his leaders decided, with the agreement of the assembly, to keep the Passover one month later. The law of Moses allowed this in cases of uncleanness (Numbers 9:10-11).

For today: God values a prepared heart more than a perfect date. If you are not ready to draw near to Him, do not give up; prepare yourself with sincerity and return to Him without delay.
exp.29:5:
The verse tells how messengers went out with letters from King Hezekiah and his officials, carrying them throughout all Israel and Judah. The letters urged the people to turn back to the Lord, the God of Abraham, Isaac and Israel. They promised that God would return to those who were left, the ones who had escaped from the hands of the kings of Assyria.

King Hezekiah of Judah had restored the temple and wanted to celebrate the Passover in Jerusalem. The northern kingdom had been struck by Assyria, and many had been taken captive. With these letters, the king invites even the people of the north to return to God and worship him together.

For today: it is never too late to return to God, even if we are wounded or have failed. He welcomes whoever comes near with humility. And we can kindly invite others to return as well.
exp.29:8:
This verse says that if the people turn back to the LORD, God will show kindness to their relatives who are held captive, and they will be able to return to their land. The reason is that God is gracious (kind, patient) and merciful (compassionate). And "he will not turn his face away from you" means that he will not turn his back on them if they return to him. "Turn" here means to repent and come back wholeheartedly.

King Hezekiah sent letters throughout Israel, including to the northern kingdom, which had fallen to Assyria. He invited the people to come to Jerusalem to celebrate the Passover and to return to God. Some mocked the message, but others humbled themselves and went. Those who had been taken captive are the people of the northern tribes.

If you have drifted away from God, do not think it is too late. He gladly welcomes whoever comes back to him sincerely. Take one simple step today: pray and tell him honestly that you want to return.
exp.29:9:
So the messengers of King Hezekiah went from town to town through the land of Ephraim and Manasseh, even as far as Zebulun. They carried an invitation to return to God. The messengers were sent out with a call, and the verse tells us that many of the people treated them with contempt.

Hezekiah, king of Judah, wanted to celebrate the Passover in Jerusalem and to invite the tribes of the north as well. They had lived far from God, and many of their people were in captivity or under foreign rule. The message called for repentance and promised mercy. Still, not everyone accepted it, though some did humble themselves and came.

For today: do not be discouraged if, when you speak of God with love, someone mocks you. Your task is to be faithful and kind; God is the one who touches hearts. And if God invites you to return to Him, do not harden your heart.
exp.29:13:
The verse tells how the people rose up and removed the false altars from Jerusalem. They also took away all the altars where incense was burned, and threw them into the brook Kidron, a stream that ran alongside the city.

The book tells the story of the kingdom of Judah. King Hezekiah had invited the people to celebrate the Passover, and many people came to Jerusalem. Before celebrating it, they wanted to clean the city of what offended God. The text says that God himself gave them a heart ready to obey. The altars had probably been set up in the time of the previous king, although the passage does not detail this.

For today: before we approach God with sincerity, it is wise to remove from our lives whatever has taken His place. We can ask Him for a willing heart and take a concrete step, such as giving up a habit or a priority that pulls us away from Him.
exp.29:15:
They stood in their places, as was their custom and as the law of Moses commanded, the man of God. The Levites handed over the blood of the sacrifice, and the priests sprinkled it, that is, they splashed it on the altar.

Here the chronicler tells how King Hezekiah gathered the people to celebrate the Passover in Jerusalem, after removing the false altars. Although the celebration was held a month late and was imperfect, care was taken to follow the order that God had given.

For today: serving God with order and faithfulness to his Word is important, but he looks at the heart. Let us seek to obey him sincerely, and trust in his goodness when we lack something.
exp.29:20:
This verse tells that the Israelites who were in Jerusalem celebrated the Feast of Unleavened Bread for seven days, with great gladness. The Levites and the priests praised God every day, singing with loud instruments, which were probably instruments that made a powerful, strong sound.

The author of Chronicles recounts this during the reign of King Hezekiah. He invited the people to celebrate the Passover, which had been neglected. Many were not purified as required, but Hezekiah prayed for them, and God forgave them and healed the people. That is why the feast was filled with joy.

For today: God values a heart that truly seeks him, and his forgiveness leads us to joy. We can set aside a moment each day to praise him with gratitude, without waiting to feel perfect.
exp.29:23:
King Hezekiah gave the assembly a thousand bulls and seven thousand sheep for the offerings of the feast. The leaders of the kingdom, that is, its princes, gave another thousand bulls and ten thousand sheep. In addition, a great number of priests made themselves holy, that is, they set themselves apart and purified themselves to serve God as was fitting.

This is part of the account of the great Passover in Jerusalem. Hezekiah had restored the worship of the LORD and invited Judah and people from Israel to celebrate. The feast lasted seven days, and the people decided to continue for another seven. The writer of Chronicles explains how such a large number of offerings could be sustained: the leaders gave generously.

Today we can learn that those who lead, in the church or in the home, teach by example. Giving joyfully and preparing ourselves with a clean heart helps others to worship God as well.
exp.29:25:
It says there was enormous joy in Jerusalem. Since the days of King Solomon, son of David, there had not been a celebration like that.

The passage tells of the great Passover that King Hezekiah organized in Jerusalem, after cleansing the temple and returning to the worship of God. He also invited people from the northern kingdom of Israel, along with foreigners who lived among them. The narrator, whom tradition associates with the author of Chronicles, highlights that the people were united once again. The leaders gave animals generously, and the priests prepared themselves to serve.

For today: true joy often comes when we return to God wholeheartedly and join with others in generosity. Today you could give or serve in your church, and celebrate with gratitude.
exp.29:26:
The verse says that the priests and the Levites stood up and blessed the people. God heard their voice, and their prayer reached his holy dwelling place in heaven.

The writer of Chronicles tells how King Hezekiah gathered all the people in Jerusalem to celebrate the Passover, after years of spiritual neglect. They had continued the festival for seven more days, with joy and worship. This verse closes the celebration: the spiritual leaders bless the people, and God responds. It emphasizes that God accepted that worship.

For today: when we return to God with humility, he listens to us. We can pray for others and bless them with confidence, knowing that our prayers reach his presence, not because of our merit, but because he is good.
exp.30:0:
This verse tells what happened after the great Passover in Jerusalem. The Israelites who were there went out through Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim and Manasseh. They broke the statues (stones that were worshiped), tore down the sacred poles (wooden posts used to worship the goddess Asherah), and pulled down the high places and the false altars. They did this until they had finished, and then each one returned home.

No one speaks directly; it is the chronicler who narrates. Under King Hezekiah, the people had just turned back to God at the festival. According to this account, their renewed worship led them to remove everything that competed with God, even in the northern territories.

When we return to God from the heart, action is also needed. We can ask ourselves what thing in our lives has taken God's place, and take a concrete step to leave it behind, without waiting for someone else to do it.
exp.30:2:
This verse says that King Hezekiah set aside from his own possessions the animals for the burnt offerings, that is, the offerings that were burned whole in honor of God. They were for every morning and every evening, and also for the sabbaths, the new moons (the beginning of each month), and the appointed feasts, just as the law of the Lord commanded.

It is the writer of Chronicles who tells this. After clearing the land of idols, Hezekiah reorganized the temple service. Before asking anything of the people, he gave the example with what was his own. Then the people responded with generosity, as the following text shows.

For today: if we want others to serve God with devotion, let us start with ourselves. We can give of our time, money, and care to the church with consistency and joy, not only when we have something left over, but as a habit that honors God.
exp.30:5:
The verse tells how the people of the towns of Judah, including some Israelites who lived there, also brought the tithe of the herds, that is, of the oxen and the sheep. They also brought the tithes of the holy things, which were dedicated to the Lord their God, and they laid them in heaps, one pile after another, because of the abundance.

This is part of the account of King Hezekiah, who restored worship in the temple after years of neglect. He had commanded the people to give the portion for the priests and Levites, so that they could devote themselves to serving in the law of the Lord. The people responded with generosity.

For today: when we give joyfully and keep what we have promised to God, we support those who serve and show that He comes first. We can ask ourselves what promise I still have pending, and take one concrete step this month.
exp.30:7:
This verse says that King Hezekiah and his officials went to see the large piles of offerings that the people had brought. When they saw them, they praised God and also blessed Israel. "Blessed the Lord" means that they gave thanks to God and praised him. The officials were the leaders or authorities of the kingdom.

This is recounted by the Chronicler, who tells of Hezekiah's reform. The king had called the people to return to the temple and to support the priests and Levites with the tithes. The people responded with generosity, from the third month through the seventh. Seeing such abundance, the leaders did not become proud; they gave thanks to God and recognized the people.

For today: when you see the generosity of others or the blessings God gives you, give thanks to God first. And do not forget to encourage, with sincere words, those who served gladly.
exp.30:8:
This verse tells how King Hezekiah, seeing the large piles of offerings, wanted to know where they had come from and what would be done with them. He asks the priests and the Levites, who were in charge of the temple. The name "Hezekiah" is the same king, and the piles are the heaps of tithes and firstfruits that the people had brought in.

The people responded with generosity to Hezekiah's religious reform, which had restored the service in the temple and commanded that the priests and Levites be supported. The offerings piled up over several months. Hezekiah speaks as a grateful and responsible king: he does not only bless God, but he also wants to understand what is happening. The chief priest Azariah answers that there was enough for everyone and some was left over.

For today: when God blesses us, let us give him thanks and manage what we have received with order. Asking questions, planning, and sharing generously is a wise way to care for what God entrusts to us.
exp.30:11:
The verse says that the people brought into the temple, faithfully and honestly, the firstfruits (the first produce of the harvest), the tithes (the tenth part of what they earned) and the dedicated things (what was set apart for God). The king placed Conaniah the Levite in charge of everything, with his brother Shimei as second. The word "faithfully" means with integrity, without deceit.

The one who tells this is the author of Chronicles. Earlier, King Hezekiah had led the people back to God. The people responded with such generosity that there was a great surplus, as the high priest Azariah said. For this reason Hezekiah ordered that storerooms be prepared to keep everything in good order.

For today: when God gives us something, it is good to handle it with honesty and order. If you help in your church or manage resources belonging to others, do so with transparency, and give with gratitude, trusting that God cares for his people.
exp.30:13:
This verse says that a Levite named Kore, son of Imnah, was the gatekeeper at the east gate of the temple. He was put in charge of the freewill offerings, that is, the gifts people gave willingly, in addition to the offerings to the Lord and everything that had been set apart as holy.

Here the chronicler is describing the reform of King Hezekiah. The people had brought their first fruits and tithes with generosity, and these had to be managed with order and honesty. That is why trustworthy overseers were appointed to distribute what had been received among the priests and Levites, who lived from their service in the temple.

For today: generosity also needs faithfulness. If God entrusts you with something, whether money, time, or a service in the church, take care of it with honesty and order, even when your task seems small or little noticed.
exp.30:16:
This verse continues a list of those who received their portion from the people. It says that the priests were also given a share, recorded according to the houses of their fathers, and the Levites from twenty years old and upward. Each one received according to his charge and his course of service, the groups in which the work of the temple was organized.

No one speaks in the first person; it is the chronicler who recounts what happened under King Hezekiah. The people had brought abundant tithes and offerings, and Hezekiah organized their distribution. In this way the priests and Levites could devote themselves fully to service in the temple. Care was taken that the distribution be orderly and fair.

For today: God values order and faithfulness in caring for those who serve. Think about how you can support, with your time or your resources, those who serve in your church.
exp.30:17:
This verse says that the priests and Levites listed in the family records received their portion of food along with their little children, their wives, and their sons and daughters. In other words, the whole family was supported. The word "genealogy" here refers to the list of lineages. The reason given is that they devoted themselves faithfully to holy things, that is, to service in the temple.

The one who tells this is the chronicler, who recounts the reforms of King Hezekiah in Judah. The people had brought tithes and offerings in abundance, and Hezekiah organized their distribution so that those who served in the temple could devote themselves to that work without worrying about the provision for their households.

Today we can support with generosity and fairness those who serve in the church, thinking also of their families. And if we serve, let us do it with faithfulness.
exp.30:18:
This verse says that the priests, descendants of Aaron, who lived in the pasturelands around their cities, also received their share. Men named individually were in charge of distributing it to all the males of the priestly families and to all the Levites who were registered.

No one is speaking here; this is the account of the chronicler. King Hezekiah had restored worship in the temple, and the people brought tithes and offerings in abundance. So that those who served God would not be neglected, an orderly and fair distribution was arranged, including in the towns far from Jerusalem.

For today: supporting those who serve in the church is a task for everyone, and it is done best with order, honesty, and care for each person, including those who live far away or go unnoticed.
exp.30:20:
This verse says that Hezekiah, king of Judah, sought God in everything he undertook: in the service of the temple, in the law, and in the commandments. He acted with his whole heart, which means he committed himself sincerely and completely. The result is stated plainly: he prospered.

The author of Chronicles, who writes after the exile, gives a summary of Hezekiah's reign. Just before this, he describes how the king restored worship in the temple and organized the support of priests and Levites. This verse closes that account with an evaluation: his success was tied to seeking God sincerely. The Bible does not promise that this always happens; here it describes what happened with this king.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we put God at the beginning of our projects, great or small. Before starting something, pray, seek his guidance in Scripture, and work with sincerity, not halfheartedly.
exp.31:0:
After all the good that Hezekiah had done in turning back to God, King Sennacherib of Assyria invaded Judah. He camped in front of the fortified cities, intending to take them for himself.

Here the chronicler speaks, recounting the history of the kings of Judah. Hezekiah had just restored the temple and the worship of God (chapters 29 to 31). Even so, the threat came. The text does not say that God abandoned him; it simply shows that faithfulness does not always prevent trials. Some scholars see in this a test of the king's faith.

For today: if you do what is right and problems still come, do not conclude that God has left you. Prepare with wisdom, as Hezekiah did, and keep trusting in Him.
exp.31:2:
This verse tells us that King Hezekiah did not act alone. He gathered his officials and his mighty men to decide whether they would stop up the springs of water that were outside Jerusalem. To stop up means to block or hide them, so that the water could not be used. His advisers agreed and supported him.

Here the narrator, the Chronicler, recounts what Hezekiah did when the Assyrian king Sennacherib invaded Judah and threatened Jerusalem. The idea was that the enemy would not find water easily during the siege. The verses that follow show that the people also took part and that the king strengthened the walls.

For today: before making a difficult decision, seek the counsel of wise and trusted people. Preparing with care and asking others for help is not against faith, and it can be part of trusting God.
exp.31:3:
This verse tells how many people gathered together and stopped up all the springs and the stream that ran through the land. They did it with one clear purpose: so that the kings of Assyria would not find much water when they arrived. The word "stopped" here means blocked or closed off.

The one telling the story is the chronicler of Israel. King Hezekiah knew that the Assyrian army of Sennacherib was coming against Jerusalem. With the support of his officials and his brave men, he decided to take away the water from the invaders. Afterward he strengthened the walls and towers, and encouraged the people. Scholars often connect this with Jerusalem's water works, but the exact details are still debated.

For today: when faced with a great problem, God invites us to act wisely and to work together, without ever ceasing to trust in Him. Being well prepared and praying do not oppose each other.
exp.31:4:
This verse says that Hezekiah took courage and got to work. He repaired all the broken parts of Jerusalem's wall, raised towers, built another wall on the outside, and strengthened the Millo, which was an area of earthworks or fill in the City of David (some believe it was a fortification; this is not known for certain). He also had many swords and shields made.

Here the narrator of the book of Chronicles is speaking. Hezekiah was king of Judah, and the army of Assyria, under King Sennacherib, was coming against Jerusalem. He prepared wisely, with the help of his advisers, and then encouraged the people to trust in God.

For today: trusting in God does not remove our responsibility to prepare. Hezekiah did what he could do and left the rest in God's hands. When facing a problem, do diligently what is within your reach and pray with faith.
exp.31:5:
This verse says that King Hezekiah appointed military leaders over the people. He gathered them in the square beside the city gate and spoke to their hearts, that is, with sincere words meant to truly encourage them.

The one acting here is Hezekiah, king of Judah. The army of Sennacherib, king of Assyria, was approaching Jerusalem. Hezekiah had already strengthened the walls and cut off the water from the springs. Now he was also caring for the spirit of the people. What he tells them afterward, that God is with them, comes from his trust in the Lord.

For today: preparing what is within our reach is wise, but it is not enough. When someone is afraid, we can speak to them with kindness and remind them that God does not leave them alone.
exp.31:8:
This verse tells us that Sennacherib, king of Assyria, was attacking the city of Lachish with his whole army. From there he sent his servants (his messengers) to Jerusalem, to deliver a message to King Hezekiah and to all the people of Judah who were in the city.

The one speaking is the writer of Chronicles, telling what happened. Just before this, Hezekiah had encouraged the people to trust in God, and the people had grown firm in his words. Now Assyria responds with pressure and threats, trying to break that trust. Lachish was a fortified city of Judah, southwest of Jerusalem.

When we decide to trust in God, voices often come that try to weaken our faith. We do not have to listen to them in fear. We can remember God's promises, pray, and stand firm, as Hezekiah did.
exp.31:11:
Here the passage asks whether it was not Hezekiah who took away the high places and the altars, and commanded Judah and Jerusalem to worship before one altar, the altar of the temple, and to burn incense there.

Sennacherib, king of Assyria, speaks through his messengers while he threatens Jerusalem. He wants to discourage the people and make them believe that Hezekiah offended God by removing those places. What Sennacherib does not understand is that Hezekiah was obeying God's law, which called for worship in one place only. Some scholars think he may have confused the LORD with the gods of other peoples.

For today: sometimes those who oppose God twist obedience and present it as a mistake. Do not let those voices confuse you. Always compare what you hear with God's Word, and keep obeying, even when others criticize you.
exp.31:12:
Here the king of Assyria, Sennacherib, speaks and proudly asks whether the people of Judah do not know what he and his ancestors have done to other nations. He says that the gods of those peoples could not save them from his power. The word "nations" here refers to the peoples of other lands, and "hand" means his strength.

The Assyrian king attacks Judah and wants Jerusalem to surrender without a fight. So he tries to discourage the people and to cast doubt on King Hezekiah's trust in God. Sennacherib places the LORD on the same level as the idols of other peoples, and that is where his error lies. Later, the Bible tells how God did defend Jerusalem.

Today, when voices of fear or pride tell you that God cannot help you, do not measure God by the strength of your problems. Pray, remember his promises, and trust that he is greater.
exp.31:13:
Here it is said that none of the gods of the other nations were able to save their people from the Assyrian kings. For this reason the speaker asks, mockingly, how the God of Judah could deliver them now.

The speaker is Sennacherib, king of Assyria, speaking through his servants while his army threatens Jerusalem. He wants to frighten the people and make them lose their trust in King Hezekiah. He places the LORD on the same level as the idols of the conquered nations, which was a serious mistake.

For today: when threats or voices of fear seem stronger than God, do not measure God by the experiences of the world. Pray, remember his promises, and trust that he is different from everything else.
exp.31:14:
Here Sennacherib, king of Assyria, tells the people of Jerusalem not to be deceived by King Hezekiah. He argues that no god of the other nations was able to save its people from Assyria, so the God of Israel will not be able to either.

The speaker is Sennacherib, through his servants, at a time when Assyria had already conquered many cities of Judah. He wants the people to lose hope and surrender. The king's mistake is to place the LORD on the same level as the idols made by human hands, and for this reason the text says he spoke blasphemy.

For today: when threats or voices of fear tell you that God cannot help you, remember that He is not like the powers of this world. Pray with confidence, as Hezekiah did, and do not measure God by your circumstances.
exp.31:18:
This verse says that the messengers of the king of Assyria spoke of the God of Jerusalem as if he were just one more of the gods of the peoples of the earth. It calls those gods the work of human hands, that is, idols made by people. Speaking against God here means mocking Him and treating Him with contempt.

The one speaking is the chronicler, who summarizes what the messengers of Sennacherib, king of Assyria, said. He had conquered many nations and wanted to frighten the people of Jerusalem into surrendering. He compared the God of Israel with idols that had been unable to save their peoples. Hezekiah and Isaiah responded by praying, and God acted.

For today: when someone mocks your faith or makes you feel that God is small, do not argue out of fear. Do what Hezekiah and Isaiah did: pray with sincerity and trust that God is not an idol made by human hands, but the living God.
exp.31:20:
It says that God sent an angel who destroyed the mighty warriors, the leaders, and the captains of the army of Sennacherib, king of Assyria. He returned to his own land humiliated, shamed to the face. Later, when he entered the temple of his god, some of his own sons killed him with the sword.

The writer of Chronicles tells how God delivered Jerusalem. Sennacherib had threatened the city and mocked the God of Israel, comparing him to the idols made by human hands. In response, King Hezekiah and the prophet Isaiah prayed and cried out to heaven. This verse shows God's answer. The Bible does not explain in detail how it happened; it only says it was the work of an angel.

When you find yourself surrounded by problems bigger than you are, do what Hezekiah and Isaiah did: pray sincerely and trust in God. He listens, and his answer may come in ways you do not expect.
exp.31:23:
This verse says that King Hezekiah became so sick that he was close to death. Then he prayed to the Lord, and God answered him and gave him a sign. The word "sign" refers to a visible event that confirmed God had heard his prayer.

The writer of Chronicles gives a brief summary. It comes after telling how God rescued Jerusalem from the Assyrians, and Hezekiah was greatly honored. The fuller account of this illness appears in 2 Kings 20 and Isaiah 38. Here it is mentioned only in passing, because what follows is that Hezekiah became filled with pride and then humbled himself.

For today: when you are weak or afraid, pray with confidence, because God listens. And when He answers you, do not forget to thank Him with humility, so that success does not make you think you are more than you are.
exp.31:29:
This verse tells how King Hezekiah blocked the upper outlet of the spring of Gihon and channeled its water underground to the west side of the city of David, that is, Jerusalem. The verse also says that Hezekiah prospered in all that he did.

Here the narrator of Chronicles speaks. He tells how Hezekiah prepared for the threat of Assyria by caring for the city's water supply and its stores. But the following text shows that God also tested him, to reveal what was in his heart. Success did not make him perfect.

For today: planning wisely is good, and God does not despise orderly work. But when things go well, it is wise to guard the heart and stay humble, thankful, and dependent on God.
exp.32:0:
Manasseh was twelve years old when he became king of Judah, and he ruled for fifty-five years in Jerusalem. This is the longest reign of all the kings of Judah.

The book of Chronicles was written by an author who is not named in the text, to remind the people of their history after the exile. Here it is not a character speaking but the narrator. Manasseh was the son of the good king Hezekiah, and the verses that follow show that, even so, he did a great deal of evil. Later in the same book it is told that Manasseh humbled himself before God and was forgiven.

For today: no one is condemned by their past or their family. God can use and restore anyone who humbles himself before Him, and we can pray for young people who have great influence even while they are so young.
exp.32:1:
It says that Manasseh, king of Judah, did what was evil in the sight of the Lord. He copied the detestable practices of the peoples whom the Lord had driven out of the land when Israel entered it. The word "abominations" here refers to those detestable practices.

Context: Here the chronicler speaks, recounting the history of the kings of Judah. Manasseh came to the throne at the age of twelve, after his father Hezekiah, who was a faithful king. The chronicler highlights the contrast: the son undid what the father had done. The verses that follow show that he rebuilt pagan altars, even inside the temple.

For today: Having a good example at home does not guarantee following God; each person must decide. Let us be careful about which customs of our surroundings we accept, and let us seek God with a heart of our own.
exp.32:2:
It says that Manasseh rebuilt the high places, which were raised sites where worship was offered, often to idols. His father Hezekiah had torn them down. He also set up altars to the Baals (false gods of Canaan), made wooden poles (sacred posts linked to the goddess Asherah, as is commonly understood), and worshipped all the host of heaven, that is, the sun, the moon, and the stars.

The one telling the story is the chronicler, who recounts the history of the kings of Judah. Manasseh was twelve years old when he began to reign. The text stresses that he undid his father's reform and copied the practices of the peoples whom God had driven out of the land.

Today it reminds us that a generation's faith is not passed down automatically. It is wise to take care of the good we have received and to cultivate our own relationship with God, so that we do not return to what others have already left behind.
exp.32:3:
It says that King Manasseh built altars inside the temple in Jerusalem, the place where God had said his name would remain forever. The altars were for false gods, not for the Lord.

The writer of Chronicles tells the story of Judah. Manasseh, son of the good king Hezekiah, undid his father's reforms and copied the practices of the peoples whom God had driven out of Canaan. What made it so serious was not only the idolatry, but that he did it in the house God had set apart for himself. Later in the same chapter, the text tells how Manasseh humbled himself and turned back to God.

We can let other things take the place that belongs to God in our hearts. Today we can ask ourselves what has been gaining room in our lives, and humbly give God first place once again.
exp.32:5:
This verse tells what King Manasseh did. He made his children pass through the fire in the valley of Hinnom, that is, he offered them in pagan worship, probably burning them. The phrases about looking for signs and omens refer to seeking signs to foretell the future. The spirit-mediums and the sorcerers were people who practiced magic and claimed to contact the spirits of the dead. All of this provoked the anger of the Lord.

The author of the book of Chronicles recounts the history of Judah. Here he shows how far Manasseh went: he set up pagan altars even in the temple, where God had said his name would dwell. The text wants us to see how serious it is to abandon God.

For today: let us not seek direction in horoscopes, lots, or hidden powers. When we need guidance, let us turn to God in prayer and to his Word, because only in him is there a secure future.
exp.32:6:
He says that King Manasseh made a carved image of cast metal and put it inside the temple. It was the place where God had promised to put his name forever. "Carved image" refers to a figure made of melted and shaped metal, that is, an idol. "Jerusalem" is Jerusalem.

The narrator of Chronicles tells the story of Manasseh, a king of Judah who did a great deal of evil. He recalls the promise God made to David and to Solomon about the temple. In this way it is seen that Manasseh not only worshiped idols, but placed them right where God had said his name would dwell. This was a great offense. The text then adds that God demanded obedience to his law.

Today, we can ask ourselves what things are occupying the place that belongs to God alone in our hearts. God deserves first place, not a place shared with other things.
exp.32:9:
God spoke to Manasseh and to his people, but they would not listen. Then God allowed the commanders of the army of Assyria to come against them. They captured Manasseh, bound him with shackles (metal cuffs or rings for the feet or hands) and chains, and carried him off to Babylon.

The writer of Chronicles tells us that Manasseh, king of Judah, led the people into a wickedness worse than that of the nations around them. God had warned them, perhaps through prophets, but they paid no attention. It is striking that they took him to Babylon rather than Assyria; some think Babylon was then under Assyrian control. The text gives no further details.

God sometimes corrects us to awaken us, not to destroy us. If today you feel that God is speaking to you through his Word or through your conscience, do not harden your heart. Listen to him soon, and remember that, like Manasseh, you can always return to him with humility.
exp.32:13:
This verse says that King Manasseh, after repenting, removed from Judah what he had previously promoted. He took away the foreign gods and the idol he had placed in the temple. He also removed the altars he had built on the temple mount and in Jerusalem, and threw them outside the city.

The one speaking is the narrator of Chronicles. He tells how Manasseh was deeply given to idolatry, but God humbled him and brought him back to Jerusalem. By acknowledging that the LORD is God, his change shows up in concrete actions. The following verse makes clear that the people kept offering sacrifices at the high places, though to the LORD.

For today: true repentance does not stay in words; it seeks to remove what pulls us away from God. Ask Him to show you which altar you need to tear down, even if not everyone around you is doing it with you.
exp.32:14:
It says that King Manasseh repaired the altar of the Lord, which had been neglected or damaged. There he offered sacrifices of peace offerings (of fellowship and thanksgiving to God) and sacrifices of praise (of thankfulness). He also commanded Judah to serve the Lord, the God of Israel. Commanded Judah means that he gave the order to all the people.

The one telling the story is the chronicler, who recounts the history of Manasseh. This king had been very wicked and given to idolatry, but he humbled himself before God and changed. He removed idols and false altars, and then returned to true worship. However, the next verse shows that the people changed only halfway, since they still kept sacrificing at the high places.

For today: returning to God includes repairing what we have neglected, such as prayer, gratitude and obedience. And if we have influence in our family or at work, may our example invite others to serve God.
exp.32:20:
It says that Amón, son of Manasés, did what was evil in the eyes of God, just as his father had done at the beginning. He worshiped and offered sacrifices to all the idols that Manasés had made.

It is part of the account in the book of Chronicles, written to remind the people why the kingdom of Judah fell. Amón reigned only two years, beginning at twenty-two years of age. His father Manasés, although he did great evil, afterward humbled himself before God. Amón, on the other hand, followed his father's bad example at the start and never repented, according to the verse that follows.

For today: what we do in front of our children marks them. But each person answers for himself or herself. It is not enough to inherit the faith or the mistakes of others. We can humble ourselves before God, ask for forgiveness, and choose to follow him out of our own conviction, today.
exp.33:2:
It says that Josiah, when he had only eight years of reign (about sixteen years of age), began to seek the God of David, his ancestor. Four years later he began to purge Judah and Jerusalem of the high places (places of worship on the hills), the groves (poles or trees dedicated to idols), the carved images, and the molten images (figures of melted metal).

Here the narrator of Chronicles speaks. Josiah came to the throne as a child, after very wicked kings. The text shows that his reform began in the heart, by seeking God, and later became visible in public actions. The details of his age are worked out from the text.

For today: seek God first, even if you are young or the surroundings are difficult. Then, patiently, remove from your life whatever has taken the place of God.
exp.33:4:
This verse tells how King Josiah burned the bones of the pagan priests on the very altars where they had served the idols. In this way he cleansed Judah and Jerusalem, that is, he removed the defilement of idolatry from the land. Here, "cleansed" means purifying the worship of the true God.

The account is told by the Chronicler, who writes after the exile to remind the people how a young king returned to God. Josiah began to seek the Lord at the age of sixteen, and at twenty he began this reform. Burning bones was an act of desecration against the altars; in this way they were declared unclean and unfit for use. The same thing is mentioned in 1 Kings 13:2.

For today: if we truly seek God, there will be things we must remove from our lives, not merely decorate. Ask Him to show you what you need to leave behind and do it with determination, leaving nothing half-done.
exp.33:6:
This verse says that King Josiah completely destroyed the altars of false gods and the sacred poles, which were symbols of worship to the goddess Asherah. He also broke and ground up the carved images and tore down all the idols in the territory of Israel. When he had finished, he returned to Jerusalem.

The narrator of the book of Chronicles tells here of Josiah's reform, the king of Judah. He was young, but he wanted to return to the God of his ancestors. His cleansing reached even into areas of the former northern kingdom. After removing the idolatry, he began to repair the temple, and there the book of the law was found.

For today: before building something new with God, it is wise to remove whatever has taken His place in the heart. Ask Him to show you what weighs more than Him in your life, and set that thing aside with determination and humility.
exp.33:7:
This verse tells us that King Josiah, when he had been reigning for eighteen years, had already removed the idols from the land and cleansed the temple. Then he sent three men: Shaphan, Maaseiah (governor of the city), and Joah (the recorder, that is, an official in charge of the kingdom's records) to repair the house of the Lord. Here, to cleanse the land means to remove idolatry.

The one speaking is the narrator of Chronicles. Judah had lived for years in idolatry under earlier kings, and the temple had been neglected. Josiah, who had sought God since he was young, first removed what was false and then turned to repairing what had fallen into disrepair. Shortly afterward, the book of the law would be found.

For today: it is not enough to leave behind what pulls us away from God; we also need to rebuild. We can ask ourselves which habit of prayer, Bible reading, or fellowship needs repair in our lives, and take one concrete step this week.
exp.33:8:
This verse tells how the messengers of King Josiah came to the high priest Hilkiah and handed over the money that the people had brought into the temple. The Levite gatekeepers had collected it from people of the north (Manasseh, Ephraim, and the rest of Israel) and also from Judah, Benjamin, and Jerusalem. "High priest" means chief priest. The word "remnant" here refers to the survivors, or the rest of the people.

The one speaking is the narrator of Chronicles. Josiah had already removed the idols and wanted to repair the temple, which had been neglected and damaged. The money came from freewill offerings from many people, and it was gathered in an orderly and careful way.

For today: God's work moves forward when many give generously and when resources are handled with honesty. Think of one concrete way to support your church or someone in need, and do it sincerely.
exp.33:9:
This verse tells how the money for repairing the temple was handled. First it was placed in the hands of the men in charge of the work, who were supervisors. They then distributed it to the workers who were doing the labor in the house of the Lord. The word to repair means to restore the temple to good condition again.

The passage is a historical narrative, not a speech. It tells what King Josiah did in the eighteenth year of his reign, after cleansing the land of idolatry. The money came from offerings that the Levite gatekeepers had collected from all the people. After that, the text says the men worked faithfully.

For today: when it comes to what belongs to God, whether money or service in the church, order and honesty are needed. If you are entrusted with managing something, do it with clarity and faithfulness, as one who must give an account before God.
exp.33:10:
This verse says that the money collected was given to the workers, that is, to the master builders and masons, to buy dressed stone and timber. The timber was used for the beams that joined and held up the structure, and for the flooring of the buildings. Those houses, or structures of the temple, had been damaged by the kings of Judah who came before.

It is part of the account of King Josiah, who sought God and repaired the temple. The narrator tells us that the offerings from all Israel were managed with order and honesty. The ruin of the temple came from years of neglect and idolatry.

For today: what is neglected deteriorates. If something in your spiritual life, your family, or your church has been damaged, begin to repair it with concrete steps, with order and honesty, and ask God for his help.
exp.33:11:
This verse says that the workers repairing the temple did their job faithfully. There were overseers who directed the work: Jahath and Obadiah, Levites from the sons of Merari, and Zechariah and Meshullam, from the sons of the Kohathites. Their task was to set the work forward, that is, to oversee it and encourage it so that it would advance. There were also Levites who knew how to play musical instruments.

No one speaks here in the first person; it is the chronicler who narrates. He tells how King Josiah ordered the temple to be restored, since it had been neglected and damaged. The money was handed over to trusted men. The account highlights their faithfulness just before it tells of the finding of the book of the law. Why the musicians are mentioned is not entirely clear; perhaps they supported the spirit of the work, but the text does not explain it.

For today: serve God with integrity, even when no one is watching, and recognize that every gift, whether leading, working, or singing, has value in his work.
exp.33:15:
Shaphan, the king's secretary, is the one speaking here. He went to see King Josiah and gave him a report. He told him that the men in charge of the work had done everything they had been entrusted with. The phrase about explaining the matter is not used in the verse, so it is left out, and the phrase about being assigned responsibility is simply a way of saying they had been given the task.

Shaphan speaks as the king's secretary. Josiah had ordered the temple to be repaired, and Shaphan reports to him on the work and on the money. After this, he will mention the book of the law that Hilkiah had found. Some think it was Deuteronomy or part of it, though the text does not say so.

For today: Shaphan shows the importance of being faithful and doing what we are entrusted with, and of giving an honest account of it. Sometimes, in the middle of ordinary tasks done with integrity, God meets us with his Word. Let us do well what is in our hands.
exp.33:18:
This verse says that King Josiah, when he heard the words of the law that Shaphan read to him, tore his clothes. Tearing one's clothes was an ancient way of showing deep sorrow, grief, or repentance.

The book had been handed over by the priest Hilkiah while the temple was being repaired. Many believe it was the whole book of the law or a part of it, such as Deuteronomy, though the text does not specify. Josiah understood that the people had turned away from God, and so he asked that they inquire of the LORD, for he feared his judgment.

Today, when we read the Bible, it is good to do so with a willing heart. If a word from God confronts us, let us not avoid it or justify ourselves. We can respond as Josiah did: with humility, repentance, and a desire to obey.
exp.33:19:
This verse says that King Josiah gave an order to five trusted men: Hilkiah the priest, Ahikam, Abdon, Shaphan the scribe, and Asaiah, a servant of the king. The word "scribe" in this verse refers to the man who copied and kept official documents, and the "servant of the king" was an official who worked closely with him. The order itself is completed in the next verse.

After hearing the law read, Josiah tore his clothes, a sign of grief and repentance. He understood that his people had turned away from God. So he sent these men to inquire of God, and they went to the prophetess Huldah.

When God's Word confronts us, let us not ignore it or make excuses for ourselves. We can respond as Josiah did: with humility, seeking God, and acting without delay.
exp.33:20:
King Josiah tells his officials: "Go and inquire of the LORD for me and for those remaining in Israel and Judah concerning the words in the book that has been found." He recognizes that the wrath of the LORD is great, because their ancestors did not keep the word of the LORD by doing all that is written in this book.

Josiah, king of Judah, is the speaker. During repairs to the temple, the book was found. Many believe it was all or part of Deuteronomy, though the text does not say so. When he heard its words, the king tore his clothes as a sign of grief and repentance, and he wanted to know what God would do.

For today: when God's Word confronts us, let us not ignore it or make excuses for ourselves. Let us respond with humility, seek the Lord, and be willing to change.
exp.33:29:
King Josiah went up to the house of the Lord, accompanied by all the people: the men of Judah, the people of Jerusalem, the priests and the Levites, from the greatest to the least. There he read aloud, so that everyone could hear, the book of the covenant that had been found in the temple.

The chronicler tells us that as Josiah heard the words of that book of the law, he was moved. The prophetess Huldah had told him that judgment would come because of the people's disobedience, but that he would not see it, because of his humility. Even so, he gathered everyone so they could hear what God had said. Many think the book was the law of Moses, although the text does not specify exactly which part it was.

For today: God's Word is not only for leaders or specialists. Josiah shared it with everyone. We can read it carefully, listen to it with humility, and, if we have family or friends, read it together.
exp.33:30:
This verse says that King Josiah, standing in his place, made a solemn commitment before God. He promised to follow the Lord, to keep his commandments, his decrees and his statutes, with all his heart and all his soul. In addition, he committed himself to carry out what was written in the book of the covenant.

Here the Chronicles account speaks of Josiah. The book of the law had been found in the temple, and the king read it before all the people. When he heard it, he renewed the covenant between God and Judah. Afterward he removed the idols, and the people followed God as long as he lived.

For today: it is not enough to hear the Word of God; it must be obeyed. Choose one teaching from the Bible that you have read this week and decide today how to live it out in one concrete step, with sincerity and with all your heart.
exp.33:31:
It says that King Josiah made all who lived in Jerusalem and in the territory of Benjamin commit themselves to the covenant. The word "stand" in the verse means that they took on a formal commitment. And the people of Jerusalem lived according to that covenant with the God of their ancestors.

This is an account from the Chronicler, who tells the story of Judah. Josiah was a young king who sought God. The book of the law had been found in the temple, and he read it before all the people. Then he renewed the covenant with God and called everyone to follow him. After that he removed the idols from the land. Some think the people's obedience was mostly outward, but the text emphasizes that they did not turn away from God as long as Josiah lived.

When we discover what God says in his Word, it is not enough to admire it. We can decide today to obey one specific thing, and kindly invite our family to do so as well.
exp.33:32:
This verse says that King Josiah removed all the detestable things, that is, the idols and practices of false gods, from all the land of Israel. He also made everyone who lived there serve Jehovah, their God. As long as Josiah lived, the people did not stop following the God of their fathers.

The one speaking here is the narrator of Chronicles. He tells what happened after Josiah read the book of the law, which had been found in the temple, and renewed the covenant with God before everyone. His reform aimed to bring the people back to obeying God. The text says the people followed God while he lived, but it does not make clear how deep each person's faith was.

For today: if you want to follow God, remove from your life whatever competes with Him. And make sure your faith does not depend only on someone who guides you, but is your own.
exp.34:2:
Josiah speaks to the Levites, who were in charge of teaching all Israel and who were set apart for the Lord. He orders them to put the holy ark in the temple that Solomon built, so that they no longer have to carry it on their shoulders. He tells them that from now on their work will be to serve the Lord and his people.

The speaker is King Josiah, during the preparations for a great Passover in Jerusalem. It is not known with certainty why the ark was out of its place. Some think it had been moved during times of religious disorder, but the text does not explain it. What is clear is that Josiah wants everything done with order and reverence.

For today: serving God includes serving his people. Ask yourself what unnecessary burden you should set down, and how you can help someone in your community today.
exp.34:5:
This verse says the Levites must kill the Passover lamb, and that first they must sanctify themselves, that is, set themselves apart and purify themselves to serve God. Then they must prepare their brothers, that is, get them ready and help them, so that everything is done according to what the Lord commanded through Moses.

King Josiah speaks to the Levites, who served in the temple. He was restoring the worship of God in Judah and celebrating a great Passover, following the order that David and Solomon had left for the service of the sanctuary. The Levites were to help the people take part properly.

For today: before serving others in matters of God, it is good to prepare ourselves with humility and obedience to his word. And then, to help others follow God, with order and kindness, and without burdening them beyond what he asks.
exp.34:7:
This verse says that the leaders of the people also gave offerings willingly, just as King Josiah did. Among the leaders, the ones who are named are Hilkiah, Zechariah and Jehiel, who were in charge of the temple. They gave the priests 2,600 sheep and 300 oxen for the Passover celebration.

The passage tells how King Josiah restored the Passover in Jerusalem. The author of Chronicles, whose name is not known for certain, points out that the king gave many animals from his own possessions, and that the leaders followed his example. In this way the whole people could take part and worship God in the way that Moses had commanded.

For today: when those who lead give with joy and set a good example, they encourage others to do the same. We can ask ourselves what we can give to God and to others, whether time, help or resources, with a willing heart and without feeling forced.
exp.34:11:
It says that they set apart the part of the burnt offering, that is, the offering that was burned whole, to be given out among the families of the people. In this way each family group could present its offering to God, as the law of Moses commanded. They did the same with the oxen.

This takes place at the great Passover of King Josiah, as told by the chronicler. It is not a speaker; the author describes how priests and Levites worked in an orderly way, following the king's command and the written law. Some details of how the offerings were combined are not entirely clear to scholars.

For today: God is pleased when we serve him with order and obedience to his Word, and when each person takes part. Ask yourself what part you can play in your church or family, without leaving everything to a few people.
exp.34:14:
The verse says that the singers, descendants of Asaph, were in the place that belonged to them, following what David had ordained. It also mentions Heman and Jeduthun, called the king's seer, that is, someone who received messages from God. The gatekeepers guarded every gate and did not have to leave their work, because their fellow Levites, their brothers, prepared the food for them, that is, they made it ready for them.

The account is from the Chronicler, who tells of the great Passover that King Josiah celebrated in Jerusalem. It stresses that everything was done in good order, following the instructions given since the time of David.

Today we can learn that serving God is teamwork. Some sing, others keep watch, and others cook. If you have a place of service, stay faithful in it; and if you help in unseen ways, your labor also makes everyone's worship possible.
exp.34:15:
This verse says that everything needed for the worship of God was ready that day. The Passover was celebrated, and the burnt offerings (offerings that were burned up completely) were offered on the altar, just as King Josiah had commanded.

The one speaking is the author of Chronicles, who summarizes what happened during King Josiah's reform in Judah. The priests, Levites, singers and gatekeepers each carried out their own task, following what God had established through Moses and David. The text that follows says that no Passover like this had been kept since the days of Samuel.

For today: worshiping God truly requires preparation and teamwork. If you serve in your church, do your part faithfully and support others so that they can also fulfill theirs.
exp.34:16:
This verse says that the people of Israel who were present in Jerusalem kept the Passover at that time, and then the Feast of Unleavened Bread for seven days.

The writer of Chronicles tells of the great revival under King Josiah, who restored the worship of God according to the law. Everything was done with care: singers, gatekeepers, priests and Levites, each in their place. Shortly after, the text says that no Passover before this one could be compared to it. Scholars debate how many people from the north took part, but the text mentions people from Israel and from Judah.

For today: when we return to God, it is good to do so with order, gratitude and steadiness, valuing what He has done for us. We can set aside time to remember His work and serve Him with joy, each in the place that belongs to us.
exp.34:17:
It says that the Passover King Josiah celebrated was extraordinary. Since the days of the prophet Samuel, no one in Israel had kept one like it. The priests, the Levites, the people of Judah and Israel who were present, and the inhabitants of Jerusalem all took part.

The one speaking is the chronicler, who summarizes the history of Judah. He wants to highlight that Josiah, in his reform, put God back at the center of the people. This Passover recalled the deliverance from Egypt. The text does not make clear exactly in what sense it was unique, and it has been interpreted in several ways: by its order, its size, or its faithfulness to the law.

For today: faith does not sustain itself alone. We need to return with purpose to remember what God has done and to worship him with order and gratitude, together with other believers.
exp.34:18:
This verse says that this very special Passover was kept in the eighteenth year of the reign of Josiah. It is a date detail: it places the exact moment when the people once again celebrated this feast with order and with all their heart.

The writer of Chronicles, whose identity we do not know for certain, tells the story of the kings of Judah. Here the emphasis falls on how Josiah had sought God and had renewed worship in the temple. The verses before this one say that no Passover had been kept like this since the days of Samuel. The date highlights how important that revival was.

For today: God values sincere and steady obedience. We can ask ourselves which habit of faith, such as prayer, Bible reading, or gathering with others, we need to take up again with enthusiasm and order, without putting it off for later.
exp.34:20:
Here Necho, king of Egypt, sends messengers to Josiah, king of Judah. He tells him that he has no quarrel with him and is not coming to attack him, but is going to fight against another nation. He claims that God told him to hurry. He warns Josiah not to interfere with God, who is with him, so that God does not destroy him. The "messengers" here are official envoys.

Necho goes up toward Carchemish, by the river Euphrates, to fight. Josiah goes out to meet him, even though Necho was not going against Judah.
