The text then says his words came from God, but it does not explain how Necho received them. Josiah did not listen to him and died in the battle of Megiddo.

Even a good leader can make mistakes when he acts without seeking direction from God. Before entering a conflict that is not ours, it is wise to pray, to listen to wise counsel, and to examine whether God truly calls us into that fight.
exp.34:22:
This verse tells how the archers of the Egyptian army shot arrows at King Josiah, and how he, badly wounded, asked his servants to take him out of the battle.

King Josiah was a king of Judah who had sought God and carried out reforms. Earlier, Pharaoh Necho warned him not to fight against him, saying that God had sent him. The text says that Josiah did not listen and disguised himself to enter the battle at Megiddo. Scholars discuss how this warning should be understood, but here the account presents it as serious.

Today we can learn to be humble enough to listen to advice, even when it comes from an unexpected place. Before acting with determination, it is wise to pray, to wait, and to examine whether we are hearing the voice of God.
exp.34:23:
He says that Josiah's servants took him out of the chariot where he had been wounded and put him in another of his chariots. They brought him to Jerusalem, where he died, and they buried him in the tomb of his ancestors. All the people of Judah and Jerusalem mourned his death. The phrase about mourning means that they were in grief.

The narrator of Chronicles tells of the end of the good king Josiah. He had been struck by arrows at Megiddo, after confronting Pharaoh Neco. The text says that Josiah did not heed the words of Neco, which are presented as coming from God. Some scholars debate exactly how this should be understood, but the account shows that his decision came at a very high cost.

Today we can learn to listen with humility, even when counsel comes from an unexpected place, and to seek wisdom before we act. We also see that a faithful life leaves a memory that others honor with gratitude.
exp.34:24:
The verse says that Jeremiah composed a funeral song for the death of King Josiah. To lament means to sing or recite mournful verses for someone who has died. The singing men and singing women of Israel repeated those laments year after year, down to the author's own day, and they became a custom for mourning the dead. The verse says they are written in the lamentations, although it is not clear whether this refers to the biblical book of Lamentations or to another collection that we do not have today.

The chronicler tells the end of Josiah, a king who sought God and died wounded in battle. All the people mourned him, and Jeremiah, the prophet, expressed that grief in a song.

For today: when loss comes, there is no need to keep silent about the pain. The Bible makes room for weeping and for the sad song. Mourning together, remembering the one who has gone, is also a way of honoring them and of healing.
exp.34:26:
This verse closes the account of King Josiah. It says that everything he did, from the beginning to the end of his reign, was written down in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah. The book of the kings of Israel and Judah is not the same as our books of Kings; it is thought to have been an official record, but this cannot be known for certain.

The writer of Chronicles, who writes after the exile, ends the account of Josiah as he usually does with other kings. Earlier he spoke of the mourning at Josiah's death and of Jeremiah composing a lament. Here he refers the reader to another record for more detail, and makes clear that his life was remembered with care.

For today: our lives also leave their marks, from beginning to end. We can ask ourselves what will be remembered of us. Living faithfully before God each day, in small things and in great ones, is what truly endures.
exp.35:2:
This verse tells how the king of Egypt, Necho, removed Jehoahaz from the throne in Jerusalem. He also forced the land to pay a tribute: one hundred talents of silver and one talent of gold. The phrase about the land being fined means that it was made to pay a forced payment or penalty. A talent was a unit of weight; some estimate that the total came to about three and a half tons of silver and thirty-three kilograms of gold, although the exact value is debated.

It is part of the account of the last kings of Judah. The people had made Jehoahaz king, but Egypt, the dominant power of the time, took control. The writer of Chronicles shows that Judah was already losing its freedom and depending on other nations.

For today: when we place our security in people, power, or money, sooner or later we lose it. Let us seek God first and trust in Him, for He alone truly sustains our lives.
exp.35:5:
Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, marched against Jehoiakim, king of Judah. "Came up" means that he advanced with his army toward Jerusalem. The verse says that he bound the king in fetters to carry him to Babylon. Other biblical accounts do not fully clarify whether Jehoiakim actually arrived there or what happened afterward, so some scholars debate this.

The author of Chronicles writes after the exile, for a people who remembered their fall. Shortly before, the text says that Jehoiakim did what was evil in the eyes of God. The account shows that the disobedience of the king and the people had real consequences, and that no human power stood above God.

For today: our choices, especially the choice to ignore God, have consequences. We can humbly examine the areas where we have stopped obeying Him, and return to Him before the consequences grow.
exp.35:11:
This verse speaks of Zedekiah, the last king of Judah. It says that he did what was evil in the sight of God and did not humble himself before the prophet Jeremiah, who spoke to him on God's behalf. Here, to humble oneself means to recognize one's error and be willing to obey.

The writer of Chronicles recounts the final days of the kingdom of Judah. Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, had placed Zedekiah on the throne after taking his nephew Jehoiachin captive. Although God sent Jeremiah to him with warnings, Zedekiah hardened his heart and rebelled. The account shows that the fall of Jerusalem was not for lack of warnings, but because he did not want to listen.

Today, when God speaks to us through his Word or through someone who advises us sincerely, pride can close our ears. Let us ask for a humble heart that knows how to listen and to correct its course in time.
exp.35:12:
He says that King Zedekiah rebelled against Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, to whom he had sworn loyalty in the name of God. "Stiffened his neck" means he was stubborn, like someone who refuses to bow his head. "Hardened his heart" means he set his mind not to change. In this way he refused to turn to the Lord, the God of Israel.

The writer of Chronicles recounts the last days of the kingdom of Judah, shortly before the fall of Jerusalem. Zedekiah was a king placed under Babylonian rule, and his rebellion broke an oath made before God. Moreover, he did not listen to the prophet Jeremiah, who spoke to him on behalf of the Lord. The text emphasizes that the underlying problem was not only political, but a heart closed to God.

For today: when God speaks to us through his Word or through wise counsel, it is good to respond with humility. We should also keep what we promise, because stubbornness leads us to harms that could have been avoided.
exp.35:15:
This verse says that the people of Judah mocked God's messengers. To mock is to laugh at someone with contempt, and to despise is to treat something as if it had no worth. In this way they rejected the words of the prophets again and again. In the end, God's anger rose to a point where, as the verse says, there was no way out left to them.

The writer of Chronicles, looking back on the history of Judah, explains why the exile to Babylon came. Before this verse, God had sent warnings again and again, a way of saying that he did so with persistence and compassion. The problem was not a lack of warning, but repeated refusal.

For today: when a sincere correction makes us uncomfortable, we should not dismiss it right away. Let us ask God for humility to listen to it, compare it with the Bible, and respond in time.
exp.35:16:
This verse tells how God allowed the king of the Chaldeans (the Babylonians) to attack Judah. They killed the young men with the sword, even within the temple, and showed no pity to anyone: not to young men, not to young women, not to the elderly or the frail.

The writer of Chronicles recounts the fall of Jerusalem, which took place in 586 B.C. according to most scholars. Before this, God had sent prophets with patience and compassion, but the people mocked them and rejected their words. The text presents the judgment as the consequence of that prolonged rejection.

For today: when God speaks to us, whether through his Word or through wise counsel, let us not harden our hearts. His patience is real, but listening to him in time spares us much pain.
exp.35:22:
Cyrus, king of Persia, declares that the God of heaven has given him all the kingdoms of the earth and has charged him to build his house in Jerusalem. He invites anyone among God's people to go up there, and he wishes that the Lord be with them.

Speaking is Cyrus, a foreign king, in a public decree near the end of the seventy years of Judah's exile. The text says that God himself stirred his spirit, fulfilling what Jeremiah had announced. How Cyrus understood the Lord is a matter of debate, but the book presents him as an instrument of God.

For today: God keeps his promises in his own time, even by using unexpected people. If you are waiting for an answer today, trust and stay ready to take the step when he opens the door.
exp.22:15:
Jehoiada the priest made a covenant, that is, a solemn commitment, between himself and the king and the people. That covenant declared that they would be the LORD's people, meaning that they would belong to Him and remain faithful to Him. The verse shows Jehoiada himself included in the commitment, together with the people and the king.

The one speaking is the narrator of Chronicles. Athaliah, the queen, had just been removed and put to death, and Joash, still a child, had been crowned king. During Athaliah's reign, Judah had turned away from God and worshiped Baal. Jehoiada wanted to reorder the nation, and that is why he renewed the covenant with God before tearing down the temple of Baal and restoring true worship.

For today: genuine change begins with a commitment to God, not merely with removing what is wrong. We can renew our devotion to Him sincerely and together with other believers who encourage us to persevere.
exp.22:10:
What it says: Jehoiada and his sons brought out the king's son Joash, put the crown on him, and presented him with the Testimony. They proclaimed him king, anointed him, and the people shouted, "Long live the king!"

Context: The account is told by the Chronicler. Athaliah, the queen mother, had seized the throne and killed the royal family, but Joash was saved by being hidden in the temple. Jehoiada, after years of waiting, organized the coronation with courage and wisdom to protect the line of David.

For today: God keeps His promises even when everything seems lost. We can trust Him, act with courage and obedience, and place His Word at the center of our decisions, just as the Testimony was given to the new king.
exp.13:8:
Zerah, a king or leader from Cush (Ethiopia), came against Judah with a huge army of 1,000,000 men and 300 chariots, and advanced as far as Mareshah, a city to the southwest of Judah. Some scholars think the number may be exaggerated or symbolic, but the text is meant to show that this was an overwhelming force.

The writer is the chronicler, who is writing to a people returning from exile. King Asa had led Judah to seek God, had built fortified cities, and enjoyed peace. Now that peace was put to the test by a threat far greater than his army.

For today: the peace God gives does not always last without trials. When a problem comes that is greater than we are, we can do what Asa did: cry out to God and trust in his help, not only in our own strength.
exp.5:6:
This verse says that David, the father of Solomon, had a sincere desire to build a temple to honor the LORD, the God of Israel. The phrase "in the heart" means that he carried it in his mind and in his longings, so the verse itself puts it in those terms. The phrase "a house for the Name" means a place set apart for the presence and honor of God.

The one speaking is Solomon, during the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem. He explains to the people that God chose Jerusalem and chose David, but that the temple would be built by the son, not the father. Even so, God recognized David's good desire and said that he had done well to have it.

For today: God looks at the heart, not only at the results. If you desire to serve Him and cannot carry it out as you imagined, your intention is still valuable to Him. Offer Him your plans, and trust that others can continue what you began.
exp.34:13:
After the Passover meal had been prepared for the people, the Levites also prepared their own meal and the meal of the priests. The phrase "made preparations" here means to get something ready or set up. The fat portions of the animals, which were burned on the altar, are the parts the priests offered. The priests, the descendants of Aaron, were busy offering burnt offerings and fat until nightfall, so they could not prepare their own food.

This is part of the account of the great Passover that King Josiah celebrated in Jerusalem. The writer of Chronicles, whose identity is not known for certain, describes in detail how everything was done in order, according to the law of Moses. The Levites served everyone, and that included the priests.

Today we can learn to serve without being seen. Perhaps someone in your church or family is so busy caring for others that no one is caring for them. Today you can prepare something for them, help them, or encourage them.
exp.33:28:
This verse says that King Josiah summoned all the leading elders of Judah and Jerusalem. The "elders" are the older men of greatest authority, who guided the families and cities. The word "summoned" means that he sent out messengers to call them to come.

The one acting is King Josiah. The book of the law had been found in the temple, and he was frightened when he heard what it said. God answered him, through the prophetess Huldah, that judgment would come upon the people, but that He had listened to Josiah because of his humility. After receiving that answer, he did not keep his own relief to himself, but gathered the leaders so that the law could be read to everyone and the covenant with God renewed.

When God speaks to us through His Word and touches our hearts, it is not meant to be kept only in private. We can share it with our family or with our church, and encourage one another together to obey.
exp.3:1:
It says that Solomon made a large basin of cast metal, called "the Sea." It was circular and measured ten cubits from rim to rim. It was five cubits high, and thirty cubits in circumference. A cubit was roughly half a meter. "Cast" means metal melted and poured into a mold.

Here the chronicler speaks, telling how Solomon furnished the temple in Jerusalem. The sea was there so that the priests could wash themselves, according to 2 Chronicles 4:6. Some note that thirty divided by ten is not exact, since it would come out a little more. Scholars explain this in several ways, such as a rounded measurement, and there is no single certain answer.

God made sure that those who served him were cleansed before they drew near. Today we can take a moment each day to ask his forgiveness and renew our hearts before serving him.
exp.13:3:
This verse says that King Asa commanded the people of Judah to seek the LORD, the God of their fathers, and to observe his law and his commandments. "Seek" here means drawing near to God with sincerity, and "observe" means putting into practice what God commands, not merely hearing it.

The one who acts is Asa, king of Judah. After removing the altars and the images of false gods, he leads the people back to the true God. The text tells that afterward there was peace and the kingdom was quiet. It says that it was God who gave him rest.

Today we can learn that removing what is wrong is not enough; we must also seek God with our whole heart and obey him in our everyday lives. You might ask yourself this week: what specific thing from God's Word can I put into practice today?
exp.32:15:
The verse says that after King Manasseh removed the foreign idols, he restored the altar of the LORD and offered peace offerings and thank offerings on it, and he told Judah to serve the LORD, the God of Israel. Even so, the people still offered sacrifices on the high places, which were raised places where worship was held. The difference now was that they did this for the LORD, their God, and not for false gods. The word "but" in this passage is a plain word, and it marks the contrast between the good change and what remained.

Context: the narrator is the chronicler, who reviews the history of the kings of Judah. Manasseh had done much evil, but he humbled himself before God and changed. The chronicler shows that the reform was real, though not complete. The Bible does not explain everything here, but in other passages it becomes clear that worshiping on the high places was not what God had commanded.

For today: we can obey God in the great things and still keep customs that do not fully honor him. Today we might ask him to show us which habits we should correct, so that we worship him as he wants and not only as is convenient for us.
exp.12:21:
It says that the rest of Abijah's life, that is, his actions, his ways, and his words, was recorded in a writing called "the Treatise of the Prophet Iddo." That book is not available to us today, and it is not known for certain whether it was a separate work or part of another record from that time.

Here the chronicler summarizes the reign of Abijah, king of Judah, after his victory over Jeroboam of Israel. It was customary to close the account of each king by pointing to other written sources. The text shows Abijah as strengthened, although other passages in the Bible present him with both light and shadow.

For today: our lives also leave a record, whether in the memory of others or in what God sees. It is worth asking ourselves what our ways and our words will say. Let us live with integrity and trust in God, rather than in our victories or achievements.
exp.16:14:
This verse is part of a list of the military commanders of King Jehoshaphat. It says that next to him was Jehohanan the commander, and that he led 280,000 men. "Commander" here means a leader of troops.

The writer of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition identifies with Ezra (though this is not certain), tells how God strengthened the kingdom of Judah under Jehoshaphat, a king who sought the LORD. Armies are listed by tribes and family houses to show their strength and organization. The numbers are very high, and some scholars think they may have a symbolic meaning, or that the word for a thousand refers to a military unit, but there is no full agreement.

For today: the text shows that an orderly life and a well-organized community can be a blessing. Serve God with your abilities, but remember that true security comes from trusting Him, not only from your own resources.
exp.14:17:
This verse says that King Asa brought into the house of God the silver, the gold, and the articles that he and his father Abijah had dedicated. "Dedicate" means to set something apart for the service of the Lord. "Articles" are the objects and furnishings used in worship.

Here the narrator of the book of Chronicles is summarizing Asa's reign. Earlier it is told that Asa removed his grandmother Maachah from her position for making an idol, and he destroyed it. Although the high places did not disappear completely, his heart was wholly devoted to God. This act shows that his reform was not only about removing what was wrong, but also about giving the best to God.

For today: it is not enough to simply leave behind what displeases God; it is also wise to offer him generously our time, talents, and resources, fulfilling what we have promised.
exp.18:8:
He tells us that King Jehoshaphat gave a charge to the judges he had appointed: they were to serve in the fear of the Lord, that is, with respect and reverence toward God. They were also to serve faithfully and wholeheartedly, which means with reliability, sincerity, and full commitment.

Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, is organizing justice in the kingdom. He placed judges in the cities and also a group of Levites, priests, and heads of families in Jerusalem to settle the most difficult cases. He reminded them that God is not unjust, does not show favoritism, and does not accept bribes. For that reason, they too were not to do these things. Many understand this as part of a spiritual renewal in his government.

For today: in your work, your family, or your church, before deciding something that affects others, ask yourself whether you are being honest and whether you would do the same with someone you do not like or who cannot give you anything in return.
exp.16:7:
This verse gives the names of those who went with King Jehoshaphat's officials to teach the law in Judah. There were nine Levites (Shemaiah, Nethaniah, Zebadiah, Asahel, Shemiramoth, Jehonathan, Adonijah, Tobijah and Tob-adonijah) and two priests (Elishama and Jehoram). The phrase "accompanied by" means that they went along with the officials mentioned before.

The one telling the story is the chronicler, who describes how Jehoshaphat ruled in Judah. The king removed the altars used for idol worship and wanted the people to know God's law. For this reason he sent leaders, Levites and priests with the book of the law to travel through the cities. The text that follows says that the people were taught and that Judah lived in peace with its neighbors.

For today: God uses many people, even some we hardly know by name, to teach his Word. We can serve faithfully by sharing what we learn from the Bible with our family, friends or church.
exp.27:9:
This verse says that the people of Israel, the northern kingdom, planned to reduce to slavery the men and women of Judah and Jerusalem, their own brothers. The prophet asks them a question that confronts them: are you not also guilty before the LORD your God?

The prophet Obed speaks as the army of Israel goes out to meet them on its return to Samaria with about two hundred thousand captives from Judah. God had allowed that defeat of Judah because of its sin, but Israel acted with excessive anger. Obed reminds them that they too stand in need of God's forgiveness.

For today: before we judge or take advantage of someone who has failed, let us remember our own faults. God calls us to treat others with compassion, not with harshness or pride.
exp.32:24:
1) What it says: The verse itself did not come through in the text you sent, so this explanation uses the context that was provided, which contains that idea. Some of King Amon's servants secretly agreed together and killed him in his house. Then the people of the land, meaning the common people of Judah, punished the conspirators and made Amon's son Josiah king.

Context: The narrator is the author of Chronicles, who tells the story of the kings of Judah. Amon followed the wicked ways of his father Manasseh and reigned only two years. According to the next chapter, Josiah was eight years old when he began to reign.

For today: God can bring something good even after dark times. If today you live in the midst of mistakes or a bad environment, trust that God can raise up a new season, and decide to be part of the solution.
exp.9:14:
So the king did not listen to the people, and the Bible says this turn of events was from God, so that the LORD might fulfill the word He had spoken through Ahijah the Shilonite to Jeroboam son of Nebat. The people were asking Rehoboam for fairer treatment, and he refused them. The verse presents this as part of God's plan, which He had already announced through the prophet Ahijah from Shiloh.

The narrator recounts how the kingdom was divided. Rehoboam rejected the advice of the elders and followed that of the young men, and he answered harshly. God had announced beforehand that the kingdom would be divided (1 Kings 11:29-39). The Bible presents Rehoboam's decision as his own, and at the same time says that God used it to fulfill His word.

For today: listening with humility and seeking wise counsel prevents many wounds. Even when others fail, we can trust that God keeps His word and can work even through our mistakes.
exp.17:10:
All of King Ahab's prophets urged him to go to war. They said, "Go up to Ramoth-gilead," meaning attack that city. They also said he would triumph, for the LORD would deliver the city into the hand of the king.

These prophets spoke before Ahab, king of Israel, and Jehoshaphat, king of Judah. Jehoshaphat wanted to know God's will before going into battle. These prophets all repeated the same pleasing message. But then Micaiah is called, and he will be the only one to say what God actually tells him. Many spokesmen agreed, though their message was not true.

That many people say the same thing does not prove it is true. Before deciding something important, seek God's voice in his Word and in prayer, even when what you hear is not the most comfortable.
exp.7:0:
This verse marks a moment in time. It says that twenty years had passed since Solomon finished two great works: the temple of the LORD and his own palace. The phrase "at the end of the twenty years" simply points to the close of that period. "His own palace" refers to his royal residence.

It is part of the account of Solomon's reign, written by the chronicler, who tells the history of Israel to remind the people of their identity and of their life with God. According to 1 Kings 6 and 7, the temple took seven years and the palace thirteen, and that is where the twenty years come from. What follows shows that Solomon kept building and strengthening the kingdom.

For today: great works are accomplished through steady effort, year after year. And after finishing something important, God invites us to keep going faithfully, without staying stuck in the past.
exp.31:30:
But in the matter of the envoys of the rulers of Babylon, who were sent to him to inquire about the wonder that had happened in the land, God left him alone to test him, so that He might know all that was in Hezekiah's heart.

The writer of Chronicles recounts the life of Hezekiah, a king who was greatly blessed and prosperous. Here he pauses to show that even a faithful king had a moment of testing. The text does not detail here what went wrong; the parallel account in 2 Kings 20 and Isaiah 39 indicates that he showed his treasures to the visitors. Some see pride in this, others a lack of caution.

For today: God allows us to be tested, not because He does not know what is in us, but so that we can see it for ourselves. When all goes well, let us ask for humility and place our trust in Him, not in our achievements.
exp.2:4:
The verse says that Solomon paneled the main room of the temple, the holy place, with cypress wood. He then overlaid that wood with fine gold and decorated it with carved palm trees and chains. Some readers today take the phrase "decorated with" to mean the figures stood out from the surface. The exact kind of wood is hard to pin down with certainty, so the identification of cypress should be held as a likely reading rather than a settled fact.

This is the account from the book of Chronicles, written for the people who were returning from exile. It describes in detail how Solomon built the temple in Jerusalem, to remind them that God deserves the best and that his house was raised with order and care.

For today: God deserves the best of us, not our leftovers. We can give him the best of our time, talent, and affection, not out of obligation, but with gratitude, doing well what he entrusts to us.
exp.31:24:
It says that Hezekiah did not respond with gratitude for the favor God had shown him. "Because his heart was proud" means that he became arrogant. For this reason, God's anger came upon him and upon Judah and Jerusalem, meaning his displeasure and discipline fell on him and on the people.

The one narrating is the chronicler, who reviews the history of the kings of Judah. Hezekiah had just recovered from a deadly illness, had received a sign from God, and was admired by the surrounding nations. The text does not spell out what his pride consisted of, and some connect it with what he showed the envoys from Babylon. The following verses say that he humbled himself, and the anger did not come in his days.

For today: when God blesses us or heals us, it is easy to take the credit for ourselves. A good practice is to give thanks openly and to serve others. If we notice pride in our hearts, we can humble ourselves quickly, as Hezekiah did.
exp.33:22:
What it says: Huldah, the prophetess, answers the men sent by King Josiah. Before giving the message, she makes clear that she does not speak on her own, but that the LORD, the God of Israel, is the one speaking. She asks them to tell the man who sent them, that is, the king, what God has said. The words "This is what the LORD says" introduce the message as coming directly from God.

Context: The book of the law had been found in the temple, and when Josiah heard it, he was shaken to see how far the people had turned away from God. He sent his men to inquire of God, and they went to Huldah, who lived in Jerusalem. She speaks in God's name and is not afraid to say hard things.

For today: Before making important decisions, let us seek God's voice in his Word and listen with humility, even when it confronts us.
exp.6:16:
What it says: God speaks to Solomon and sets a condition. If Solomon lives with awareness that God sees him and guides him, as David did, doing everything God has commanded, the promise will remain in place. The "statutes" are God's laws and rules, and the "ordinances" are his just decisions. The opening phrase "as for you" simply turns God's attention directly to Solomon.

Context: God answers Solomon after Solomon dedicated the temple. He assures him that he will hear the prayers offered in that place. Then he reminds him that his kingdom will depend on his faithfulness. The following verses also warn of the consequences if the people abandon God.

For today: God values a faithful life more than a beautiful building. Today we can ask ourselves: does my daily life show that I live in God's presence? Choose one concrete act of obedience and practice it this week.
exp.23:16:
After the death of the priest Jehoiada, the officials or leaders of Judah came to present themselves before King Joash and paid homage to him. The Berean wording says they paid homage, and the idea is that they showed him respect and bowed before him. They may also have been flattering him. Then the king listened to them, that is, he gave heed to what they said.

The writer of Chronicles tells the story of Judah. Jehoiada had guided Joash since he was a child and kept him faithful to God. With his death, the king lost that influence. The verses that follow show that the officials led him to abandon the temple and serve idols. The text does not say what words they used, but it makes clear that their influence was harmful.

For today: faith borrowed from others is not enough. Make sure your relationship with God is your own, and choose carefully whom you listen to, especially when they flatter you.
exp.16:4:
God made Jehoshaphat's kingdom secure and kept it steady under his rule. All of Judah brought him tribute, a way of honoring him and showing loyalty. Because of this he had great wealth and honor. "Tribute" means payments or gifts given to a ruler, and "honor" here refers to respect and a good reputation.

Context: The writer of Chronicles, who wrote for the people of Israel after the exile, tells how God blessed Jehoshaphat. The verse before explains the reason: he sought the God of his father, obeyed his commandments, and did not follow the idols or the practices of the northern kingdom. Afterward we see that he taught the law to the people.

For today: God's blessings are not a prize to boast about, but come with a call to serve. Seek God first and obey him in everyday life. If he gives you stability or resources, use them to help others come to know him.
exp.33:0:
It says that Josiah was eight years old when he became king of Judah, and that he reigned thirty-one years in Jerusalem. The phrase "became king" means that he took the throne. He was only a child, so others surely helped him govern at first, although the text gives no details about who they were.

This is the narrator of Chronicles, who summarizes the history of the kings of Judah for a people who were returning from exile. He wants to show that a king, even while very young, can please God. Josiah came to the throne after very wicked kings, such as his father Amon. The verses that follow tell how he sought God and cleansed the land of idolatry.

For today: your age or your family's past does not limit what God can do with you. You can begin seeking him today, without waiting to be older or to have everything settled.
exp.17:14:
Here King Ahab asks Micaiah that, when he speaks in God's name, he tell only the truth. The word "swear" in the verse means to make someone promise solemnly, and the king's words "How many times?" show his irritation: he had already asked him before.

Ahab, king of Israel, wanted to go to war against Ramoth-gilead together with Jehoshaphat, king of Judah. Four hundred prophets had promised him victory. Micaiah gave the same answer, but apparently in a mocking or ironic tone, and Ahab noticed that he was not speaking seriously. That is why he demands the truth from him, even though he later rejects what he hears. We see this in the context that follows.

Asking for the truth is easy; receiving it is harder. Today we can ask ourselves whether we truly want to hear what God says, even when it contradicts our plans. Let us pray with humility and be ready to obey before we listen.
exp.11:13:
It says that King Rehoboam did evil. The reason is that he did not set his heart to seek the LORD. To set one's heart to seek God means turning to him with sincerity and depending on him.

The speaker is the author of Chronicles, who summarizes the reign of Rehoboam. Earlier he had humbled himself before God and was spared from total destruction. But the text shows that this repentance did not become a steady way of life. Some understand that his humility was real but temporary; the text gives no further detail. His reign ended with constant war against Jeroboam.

For today: seeking God does not happen only in a crisis. It is good to set the heart every day through prayer, Bible reading and obedience, so that a good moment of repentance becomes a steady path.
exp.5:7:
God did not overlook David's desire to build a temple for him. Although David would not be the one to build it, God told him that he had done well to have this in his heart. The verse's comments on the old wording are not carried over here, since they refer to words that do not appear in the verse you are reading. The phrase "to have this in your heart" means to have a sincere intention or desire.

Here Solomon is speaking during the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem. He is telling the people what the LORD had said to his father David. Solomon explains that although God did not allow David to build the house, God did recognize his good intention, and then fulfilled his promise through Solomon.

For today: God sees and values the good desires of our hearts, even when we cannot carry them out as we had imagined. If your plan to serve him does not happen just as you pictured it, do not think it was in vain. Offer him your desire with sincerity, and trust that God can use others, or another time, to bring it about.
exp.11:15:
This verse says that King Rehoboam died. The phrase "rested with his fathers" is a gentle way of saying he died, like someone lying down to rest in the same way his ancestors did. They buried him in the City of David, which is Jerusalem, and his son Abijah, also called Abijam in the book of Kings, took the throne.

The speaker is the Chronicler, the author of Chronicles, who summarizes Rehoboam's reign. Shortly before this, he says Rehoboam did evil because he did not set his heart on seeking God. His reign was marked by conflicts with Jeroboam and by the invasion of Egypt. This ending closes his story with a serious assessment.

For today: our lives will also have an ending. It is wise to decide now to seek God with a willing heart, and not to leave it for later, because that is what truly gives meaning to what we leave behind for others.
exp.15:4:
This verse tells how Baasha, king of Israel, learned that Ben-hadad of Syria was attacking his cities, and so he stopped fortifying Ramah and abandoned that work. "Fortifying" here means strengthening the city's walls and defenses, and "stopped" means he halted the work.

The chronicler then recounts what happened after King Asa of Judah sent silver and gold to Ben-hadad to break his alliance with Baasha. Baasha was fortifying Ramah to block the way to Judah. Asa's strategy worked in the short term, but the seer Hanani rebuked him, because Asa trusted a foreign king and not the LORD.

For today: sometimes a quick fix solves the problem, but it does not honor God. Before acting, it is wise to pray and ask ourselves whom we are truly trusting.
exp.22:7:
This verse says that the Levites and all the people of Judah did everything the priest Jehoiada had ordered. Each leader gathered his men, both those coming on duty on the Sabbath and those going off duty. Jehoiada had not released any of the divisions, so on that day there were twice as many people available. The word "divisions" refers to the groups or shifts of service.

The author tells how Jehoiada prepared the moment to crown Joash, the young heir, after Athaliah had seized the throne. Jehoiada used the temple's system of shifts to gather a large guard without drawing attention. His purpose was to protect the rightful king and remove Athaliah from power.

For today: good work is accomplished when there is good leadership and people who obey with order and unity. Serve wherever God has placed you, and offer more than the minimum when the cause is just.
exp.11:5:
The passage tells us that the leaders of Judah and King Rehoboam humbled themselves before God. They admitted that God was in the right. The verse's statement "The LORD is righteous" is worded here as "The LORD is righteous," and the word "leaders" refers to the heads of the people. The name "Israel" is used here for Judah, the southern kingdom.

The prophet Shemaiah had told them that, because they had abandoned God, God was now leaving them in the hands of Shishak, king of Egypt, who was invading the land. Faced with that message, the king and the leaders did not defend themselves or grow angry, but accepted their wrong. God saw their humility and held back their destruction, although they remained under Shishak's control.

For today: when we face the consequences of our failures, instead of blaming others, we can humbly acknowledge that God is righteous and ask for his mercy.
exp.7:17:
It says that Hiram, king of Tyre, sent ships captained by his own servants, along with crews of experienced sailors. They sailed together with Solomon's servants to Ophir and brought back 450 talents of gold for King Solomon. "Experienced" means capable and knowledgeable at sea. A talent was an ancient unit of weight; its exact modern equivalent is not known, but it was a very large amount.

The speaker is the chronicler, who summarizes the reign of Solomon. After finishing the temple, Solomon developed trade from the ports of Ezion-geber and Eloth, on the coast of Edom. Israel had little seafaring experience, so Hiram contributed his knowledge. Where Ophir was is not known for certain; scholars hold different opinions.

For today: no one achieves everything alone. Solomon accepted the help of those who knew more in one area. We can be humble, recognize what we do not master, and work as a team, thanking God for the people he places beside us.
exp.0:1:
Then Solomon spoke to all Israel: to the commanders of thousands and of hundreds, to the judges, and to every leader in all Israel, the heads of the families. The commanders of thousands led a thousand soldiers each, and the commanders of hundreds led a hundred. The heads of the families were the leaders of the households or clans.

The book of Chronicles tells the story of Israel with its attention fixed on God and his temple. Here the narrator has just said that God was with Solomon and made him very great. Solomon gathers the leaders before going to Gibeon to worship. He wants the whole nation, and not only himself, to draw near to God at the beginning of his reign.

Today, whoever has some responsibility, in the family, at work, or in the church, can follow this example: before making important decisions, seek God together with the people you lead, and not do it alone.
exp.10:9:
This verse ends a list of cities that King Rehoboam fortified. Zorah, Aijalon and Hebron were in the territories of Judah and Benjamin. The fortified cities were places he protected with defenses, such as walls and military posts. Stocking them with food and supplies is also part of what the list describes.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, telling the story of Judah. After the kingdom was divided, Rehoboam remained as king of the south. He strengthened these cities to protect his territory, especially facing the northern kingdom. The text only reports what he did; it does not explain all his motives.

For today: caring well for what God has entrusted to us is good wisdom. We can prepare our home, our finances and our spiritual life with order and prayer, without forgetting that our final trust is in God.
exp.3:12:
This verse describes the decoration of the two great columns of the temple. On top of each column was a bowl-shaped head, and each head was covered by a network of small interlaced chains. Hanging from each network were pomegranates made of metal: one hundred for each network, arranged in two rows, for a total of four hundred. The "network" here is a small mesh, and the "bowl-shaped capital" is the upper part of a column.

The author of Chronicles, writing after the exile, reviews the building of Solomon's temple. He mentions that Hiram, the craftsman from Tyre, completed the work. He wants the people to remember the beauty and order with which God's house was made. The pomegranate was often a symbol of abundance, though the text does not explain its meaning here.

For today: God cares about details and about work done well. Doing with care what falls to us, even when no one notices, can be a way of worshiping him.
exp.3:19:
It says that Solomon made the lampstands and their lamps of pure gold. The lampstands were the stands that held the lamps, and the lamps were the small bowls that burned oil. They were set to burn in front of the inner sanctuary, that is, the most holy place, as had been prescribed. Here "inner sanctuary" refers to the place of God's presence, not to a modern chapel.

This is part of the account by the writer of Chronicles (tradition associates him with Ezra, though this is not known for certain) about building the temple. He wrote for a people returning from exile, to remind them of the beauty of worship and that God should be honored with the best. The phrase "as prescribed" shows continuity with what God had already commanded.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we give God the best of our time, attention and affection, and not merely what is left over. Doing so faithfully and simply is also a form of worship.
exp.5:11:
Solomon stands before the altar of the LORD, in front of the whole assembly of Israel, and spreads out his hands to pray. "Assembly" means the people gathered together. Spreading out the hands was a posture of prayer and petition.

This happens on the day the temple that Solomon built is dedicated. He has just recalled that God kept his promise to David. The next verse explains that he went up onto a bronze platform in the courtyard, knelt down, and began to pray in view of everyone. In this way, the king leads the people in prayer.

For today: when God fulfills what he has promised, the best response is to stop, give thanks to him, and pray with humility. We can do this in public too, in church or in the family, to encourage others to trust in him.
exp.26:4:
Here is what the verse says: King Jotham of Judah went to war against the Ammonites and defeated them. As a result, they had to pay him tribute: one hundred talents of silver (roughly three and a half tons, approximately), ten thousand cors of wheat and ten thousand cors of barley. A cor was a large measure of grain, and its exact quantity is debated. They paid this for three years in a row. Defeated means that he won the war.

Here the chronicler is speaking, recounting the reign of Jotham. There is no dialogue, just a historical summary. He wants to show that Jotham was a faithful king and that God strengthened him. The verse that follows says so: he "prepared his ways before the Lord his God." His success is presented as the fruit of that faithfulness.

For today: true strength comes from a life well directed before God. Before seeking achievements, we can ask ourselves whether we are preparing our ways through prayer, honesty and obedience. God does not always promise material success, but he does honor those who seek him with a sincere heart.
exp.31:15:
The verse says that the servants of Sennacherib spoke further against the LORD God and against His servant Hezekiah. "Servants" here refers to the officials and messengers of King Sennacherib. The phrase "spoke against" means that they insulted God and treated Hezekiah with contempt.

These are the messengers of Sennacherib, king of Assyria, who had invaded Judah with his army. They wanted the people of Jerusalem to lose their trust in Hezekiah and in God, so that they would surrender without fighting. They mocked God by placing him on the same level as the idols of other nations.

When someone mocks our faith or tells us that God will not help us, let us remember that such words do not change who God is. Instead of arguing out of fear, we can pray and keep trusting, as Hezekiah did.
exp.20:1:
This verse gives the list of Jehoram's brothers, who were all sons of Jehoshaphat: Azariah, Jehiel, Zechariah, Azariah, Michael, and Shephatiah. The verse calls Jehoshaphat "king of Israel," although he reigned over Judah. Here "Israel" is used as a name for God's people in general.

The one speaking is the narrator of Chronicles, who tells the history of the kings of Judah. After Jehoshaphat's death, his son Jehoram takes the throne. The author names his brothers one by one because in the next verse he will tell that Jehoram killed them. The names make that violence more painful, since they were real people with their own identity.

For today: value your family and do not let power, money, or ambition damage those relationships. Ask God for a humble heart that cares for your brothers and sisters instead of seeing them as a threat.
exp.31:7:
This verse compares two kinds of strength. The king of Assyria has "only the arm of flesh," that is, human power: soldiers, weapons, and his own strength. Judah has the LORD their God, who helps them and fights their battles. When the people heard this, they were strengthened and regained their confidence in the words of their king.

Hezekiah, king of Judah, speaks in a moment of great danger. Sennacherib, king of Assyria, had invaded Judah and threatened Jerusalem. Hezekiah had already organized the defense, and now he encourages the people not to be afraid, reminding them that their true help is God.

For today: when problems seem bigger than you, do what is yours to do with responsibility, but do not place your trust only in your own resources. Pray and rest in the knowledge that God walks with you and sustains you.
exp.11:11:
Rehoboam humbled himself before God, and so God's anger turned away from him and did not completely destroy him and his people. The BSB names God as "the LORD," and that is the wording the verse uses. The anger "turned away" means it withdrew. "Completely" means fully. The verse also says that conditions were good in Judah, meaning there were still good things there.

The one speaking is the narrator of Chronicles. Earlier, Egypt invaded Judah because of the unfaithfulness of Rehoboam and his people. The leaders humbled themselves when they heard the word of the prophet Shemaiah. God did not deliver them from everything, since they lost the gold shields, but he saved them from destruction. Then the text says that Rehoboam "did evil," so his humility was not lasting.

For today: when we fail, admitting it with humility opens the door to God's mercy. But a moment of repentance is not enough; we must keep seeking him wholeheartedly every day.
exp.10:18:
This verse says that Abihail, one of King Rehoboam's wives, bore him three sons: Jeush, Shemariah, and Zaham. The phrase "she bore sons to him" simply means that she gave birth to them. It is part of a family list, like the ones that sometimes appear in the Bible.

The writer of Chronicles tells how Rehoboam, son of Solomon, ruled Judah. For three years the kingdom grew strong because the people followed the way of David and Solomon. Then the text mentions the king's wives and children. It is a historical detail that shows his power, though it also foreshadows that his family life would be filled with many wives, something the Law of Moses warned kings to avoid (Deuteronomy 17:17).

For today: even when a family grows and everything seems to be going well, true strength comes from following God faithfully, and not from what we have or how much we have accomplished.
exp.35:10:
This verse says that Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he became king and that he reigned in Jerusalem for eleven years. The verse gives simple facts, such as his age and how long his reign lasted.

The author of Chronicles, whom many believe was Ezra, though this is not certain, tells of the last years of Judah before the exile. Nebuchadnezzar placed Zedekiah on the throne. Here he is called the "brother" of Jehoiachin, but other passages indicate that he was his uncle, and the word may have been used for a close relative. The verses that follow explain why the kingdom fell.

For today: having a position is not enough; one must have a humble heart. Zedekiah did not heed God's warning. Today we can ask God for a heart willing to listen and to correct course in time.
exp.19:1:
Some messengers warned King Jehoshaphat that a vast army was coming against him. They said it was coming from Edom, from beyond the sea, and they reported that the enemy was already at Hazazon-tamar, also called En-gedi, an oasis on the shore of the Dead Sea.

Jehoshaphat was king of Judah. The news was alarming: the enemy was already very close, only a few kilometers from his territory. That is why, in the verses that follow, the king feels fear, but decides to seek God and calls the whole people to fast and pray.

When you receive news that frightens you, you may feel fear, as Jehoshaphat did. What matters is what you do next: instead of freezing in place, bring the problem to God in prayer, and seek to do it together with other believers.
exp.31:32:
Here the verse says that King Hezekiah died. "Rested with his fathers" is a gentle way of saying that he passed away. They buried him in the upper tombs of David's descendants. Some scholars think this could refer to the highest part of the tombs, and the text does not allow us to be certain. All Judah and the people of Jerusalem paid him honor, and his son Manasseh became king in his place.

The one speaking is the Chronicler, the author of the book, who closes the account of Hezekiah's reign. He sums up that Hezekiah was a king who was remembered and respected, though he was also tested by God and showed what was in his heart.

For today: living with faith and faithfulness leaves a mark that others recognize. But a person's faith is not inherited on its own. Teach your children and those around you to follow God with purpose and through your example.
exp.26:7:
This verse says that Jotham was twenty-five years old when he became king over Judah, and that he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. The verse gives these details plainly, almost like a closing note on the account of his reign.

The one speaking is the chronicler, the author of Chronicles, who repeats this same information about Jotham in 27:1. Earlier he explained that Jotham grew strong because he lived uprightly before God. Right after this, he tells of Jotham's death and that his son Ahaz reigned in his place. The author wants to show that a reign, even a short one, is judged by its faithfulness to God.

For today: what matters most is not how much time we have, but how we live. We can ask ourselves each day, "Am I living uprightly before God?" A faithful life, even a brief one, leaves a lasting mark.
exp.5:3:
This verse says that Solomon praises the Lord, the God of Israel, because God carried out with his own hand what he had promised with his mouth to Solomon's father David. "With his own hand" means with God's power and action. "With his mouth" refers to what God spoke. "Blessed be the LORD" means that God deserves to be praised and acknowledged. At the end, the colon introduces the promise that Solomon is about to recall.

The one speaking is King Solomon, just after finishing the building of the temple in Jerusalem. He turns toward all the people, who are standing, and blesses the assembly. Before praying to God, he reminds them that the temple is the fulfillment of a promise made to David, who wanted to build it.

Today we can imitate Solomon: stopping to remember the times when God was faithful and giving him thanks out loud. Remembering his fulfilled promises strengthens our confidence when we wait for other answers.
exp.10:10:
This verse tells that Rehoboam strengthened the fortified cities of Judah. He placed officers in them and stocked them with supplies of food, oil, and wine. The idea behind these supplies is provisions for holding out through a hard time, and the oil and wine were part of that basic reserve.

The narrator is the chronicler, who reviews the history of the kings of Judah. After the kingdom divided, Rehoboam ruled the south and feared an attack from the north. So he prepared his cities. The text does not say this was a fault; it simply shows how he looked after his territory at that time. Later, the same account shows that his fortresses were not enough once he stopped seeking God.

For today: it is wise to prepare with order and foresight, such as saving money or caring for health and family. But human preparation does not replace trust in God. Do your part, and pray with humility.
exp.0:10:
God answers Solomon and tells him that what was in his heart pleases him. Solomon did not ask for riches or wealth, for honor, or for the death of his enemies. He did not even ask for a long life. He asked for wisdom and knowledge, that is, understanding and insight, to govern God's people well. The word "judge" in this context includes guiding and ruling with justice.

God speaks in Gibeon, where Solomon had gone to offer sacrifices at the beginning of his reign. Solomon had just acknowledged that the people were enormous in number and that he could not lead them by his own strength. God responds to that humility and to that desire to serve others.

For today: before asking for things for ourselves, we can ask God for wisdom to carry out well what He has entrusted to us, in the family, at work, or in the church. He is pleased with a heart that seeks to serve well.
exp.8:8:
This verse says that the queen of Sheba gave King Solomon 120 talents of gold, a great quantity of spices, and precious stones. A "great quantity" means a very large amount, and the spices were perfumes or aromatic substances. It says there had never been spices like those she gave. A talent was a very large unit of weight; its exact equivalent in kilograms is debated, but it was an enormous amount.

The queen of Sheba visited Solomon because she had heard of his fame and wanted to test his wisdom. The text tells us she was greatly impressed. Her earlier words praise Solomon and bless God, who had set him as king to execute judgment and justice. These gifts were a sign of honor and gratitude.

For today: when we truly value something good, such as the wisdom of God, we show it with generosity. Think about what you can give today, with your time or your resources, to honor God.
exp.33:27:
God says he will gather Josiah to his fathers, meaning that he will die and be buried. He will be gathered to his grave in peace, and he will not see the calamity that God is bringing on this place and on its people. The words about being gathered to the grave are a way of speaking about death. In the end, the messengers carry the answer back to the king.

God speaks through the prophetess Huldah. The book of the law was found in the temple, and Josiah was frightened to see how much the people had disobeyed God. He humbled himself, tore his clothes, and wept. God announces judgment on the people, but he responds with mercy to the king's repentance. Some think that "in peace" refers to his not seeing the destruction; the Bible tells that Josiah died in battle, so the expression does not necessarily mean a calm death.

For today: when the Word of God confronts us, we can respond with humility and not with excuses. God sees a tender heart and listens to it.
exp.12:10:
This verse says that in Judah the priests offer to God the burnt offerings every morning and every evening, together with the incense. They also set the bread out in rows on the clean table and light the lamps on the golden lampstand every evening. The lamps are the lamps on the lampstand. The phrase "we are carrying out the requirements of the LORD our God" means that they are doing what God has required of them. Abijah says that they obey him, but Israel has forsaken him.

King Abijah of Judah is speaking. He is on Mount Zemaraim, facing the army of Jeroboam, king of the northern tribes. Before the battle he reminds them that Israel drove out the priests descended from Aaron and appointed other priests. Abijah wants to show that Judah keeps the worship that God commanded.

For today: following God is not only saying it, but keeping a steady life of prayer and obedience. We can set aside a fixed moment each morning or evening to seek him, without letting routine make us grow cold.
exp.32:21:
This verse says that Amon never humbled himself before God, as his father Manasseh did. Humbling oneself here means acknowledging one's own sin, repenting, and turning back to God. Instead, Amon kept sinning more and more, and his guilt grew.

It is part of the chronicler's account of the kings of Judah. The narrator speaks here, not a character, and he compares father and son. Earlier, 2 Chronicles 33 tells how Manasseh was very wicked, but later humbled himself before God in his affliction. Amon copied his father's idols, but not his repentance. He reigned only two years and was killed by his servants.

For today: it is not enough to inherit the faith or the mistakes of our family. If we have failed, we can humble ourselves before God today, ask for forgiveness, and change, without waiting until it is too late.
exp.34:9:
When everything was ready for the Passover celebration, the priests took the places that belonged to them, and the Levites did too, each group in its own division. The word "prepared" in the verse you're reading points to the work of getting everything in order, and "divisions" refers to the groups of Levites who took turns in service. Everything was done according to what the king had commanded.

The book of Chronicles tells here of the great Passover of King Josiah in Jerusalem. The writer recounts that the leaders had given animals generously. Now the account shows how the worship was organized: each person had their task, following what the law of Moses established and what the king had commanded.

For today: serve God and others with order and humility. Learn what your place is in your church or community, do your part faithfully and respect the work of others, so that everything is done with reverence.
exp.33:5:
King Josiah did not stop at cleansing Judah and Jerusalem of idols. He carried that cleansing into other regions to the north: Manasseh, Ephraim, Simeon, and as far as Naphtali. He also dealt with the ruins that lay around these places.

Here no character is speaking; it is the chronicler who is narrating. He writes for a people returning from exile, and he wants to show that Josiah sought God with his whole heart. This takes place before the temple was repaired, as the following context says.

For today: faithfulness to God does not stay in what is visible or nearby. We can ask ourselves what "idols" exist in every corner of our lives, not only in public, and ask God for help to clear them out before we build anything new.
exp.11:8:
This verse tells that King Shishak of Egypt attacked Jerusalem and seized the treasures of the temple and of the royal palace. He took everything, including the gold shields that Solomon had made. The phrase "attacked Jerusalem" reflects a military campaign against the city.

The one telling the story is the chronicler, who explains what happened in the time of King Rehoboam. Before this, the people had abandoned God, but they humbled themselves, and God did not allow their total destruction. Even so, they remained under the power of Egypt, so that they would understand the difference between serving God and serving human kings. Afterward, Rehoboam made bronze shields to replace the gold ones.

For today: turning away from God often costs us things of great value. But if we humble ourselves, God is merciful and gives us the opportunity to begin again.
exp.35:8:
This verse tells us that Jehoiachin, also called Jeconiah, became king in Jerusalem while still very young. He reigned only three months and ten days, and the text says he did evil in the sight of the Lord. A word to note: "Jerusalem" is spelled with an old form, but it is the city we call Jerusalem today. One detail: the book of 2 Kings gives his age as eighteen, so the figure in this verse is different there. Some think it is a copying error, and others offer other explanations.

The author of Chronicles recounts the final days of the kingdom of Judah before the exile. His father Jehoiakim had already been taken to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar, and the people still remained far from God. The account shows how that collapse came to an end.

For today: what we inherit does not decide what we do. Each person answers before God for their own choices, so we can choose to walk differently from the bad examples we have seen.
exp.7:13:
Solomon set up the temple service. He divided the priests into groups that took turns on duty, gave the Levites the job of leading praise and helping the priests each day as needed, and appointed gatekeepers in their own groups to watch over each gate. The words "divisions" (meaning groups or shifts) and "ordinances" (the arrangements that had already been set up) are explained here, and the gatekeepers were those who watched over the entrances.

This is told by the Chronicler, who wrote after the exile to remind the people how worship ought to be done. Solomon had just finished the temple and wanted to follow the arrangement left by his father David, here called "the man of God." This shows that worship was not improvised but ordered and faithful to what had been received.

For today: God values both heartfelt praise and orderly service. If you are given a task that seems small in your church, such as opening the door, doing it faithfully is also worship.
exp.7:16:
This verse tells that King Solomon went to Ezion-geber and to Eloth, two ports on the coast of Edom. The older form of the place name appears in the sea-side details, and these were probably in the area of the Red Sea, at the Gulf of Aqaba, though their exact location is debated.

The account comes from the Chronicler, who summarizes Solomon's reign. He has just said that the building of the temple was finished in good order and without flaws. Now he shows how Solomon promoted maritime trade, with the help of Hiram, king of Tyre, to bring gold from Ophir.

For today: when God allows us to finish a task well, we can take the next step with the same discipline and gratitude. Planning with order and working alongside others is a wise way to manage what God has entrusted to us.
exp.13:0:
Abijah rested with his fathers, which means he died, and he was buried in the City of David, that is, Jerusalem. His son Asa then became king in his place. During Asa's reign the land had peace for ten years.

The speaker here is not a character in the story but the narrator of the book of Chronicles. He reports the change of king in Judah and prepares the reader for what follows: Asa did what was good in the eyes of the Lord and removed the worship of other gods. The text links that time of peace with his faithfulness, though it does not explain every detail of how the peace came about.

For today: peace often grows when we put God first. If something in your life has taken his place, ask him for help to remove it and return to him.
exp.35:0:
According to the verse, after the death of King Josiah, "the people of the land" took his son Jehoahaz and made him king in Jerusalem, in place of his father. Jehoahaz also appears under the name Shallum in other texts.

Here the chronicler speaks as he tells the story of Judah. Josiah had been a faithful king, and his death left a gap. The expression "the people of the land" is usually understood to mean the citizens or landowners of Judah, though some interpret it in other ways. The verses that follow show that their choice did not last long: Egypt removed him after three months and imposed a tribute.

For today: before we choose the one who will guide us, whether in the church, at work, or in the country, it is wise to pray and to think beyond what is immediate. A hasty decision can have painful consequences.
exp.17:12:
Micaiah swears by the name of the Lord, the living God, that he will say only what God tells him. He will not speak what others want to hear. "As surely as the LORD lives" is a solemn way of making a vow. After saying this, he goes to appear before the king.

Micaiah is a prophet of the Lord. King Ahab of Israel, together with Jehoshaphat of Judah, wants to attack Ramoth Gilead. Four hundred prophets promise him victory, and the messenger presses Micaiah to say the same thing. But he answers that he will speak whatever God tells him. Later, his ironic answer to the king shows that he does not mean it seriously, and the king notices.

For today: before we speak, advise, or give our opinion, let us seek to be faithful to what God says, even when it is unpopular. Speaking the truth in love is worth more than pleasing everyone.
exp.27:11:
These verses tell us that four important men from the tribe of Ephraim stood up to confront the soldiers who were coming back from the war. "Some of the leaders of the Ephraimites" means respected leaders. The phrase "stood in opposition" shows that they took a brave step and resisted what was happening.

Here the northern kingdom, Israel, had defeated Judah and was bringing back many prisoners, women and children included. Before this verse, the prophet Oded had already rebuked the army. Now these leaders back up his message and ask that the captives be returned, because they are brothers and God is angry.

For today: when we see injustice, it is sometimes easier to stay silent. These men encourage us to speak up with courage and to defend those who suffer, even when the crowd is going in another direction.
exp.13:10:
Asa prays to God before the battle. He says that for God it does not matter whether a person is strong or weak: God can help anyone. The phrase "there is no one besides You to help the powerless against the mighty" means that for God it makes no difference whether the one needing help is strong or has no strength at all. The phrase "we rely on You" means "we put our trust in You." The request "Do not let a mere mortal prevail against You" is asking that no human being be able to stand stronger than God.

King Asa of Judah speaks in a moment of great danger. Zerah the Cushite came with an enormous army, a force so large that some understand the number literally and others take it as an expression of vastness. Asa was clearly outnumbered, so he did not place his trust in his own army but prayed. Afterward, the text tells us that God gave them the victory.

When you feel small before a problem, do not wait until everything is resolved before you pray. Bring your weakness honestly before God and trust that He can help you.
exp.19:34:
After this, Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, made an alliance with Ahaziah, king of Israel, a man who acted wickedly. The verse describes Ahaziah as someone who lived in wickedness, far from God and from what was right. The word "alliance" means Jehoshaphat formed a partnership with him.

The author is the Chronicler, who reviews the life of Jehoshaphat. He presents him as a king who sought God, but with flaws. Just before this, he says that the high places were not taken away and that the people had not yet fully turned their hearts to God. The verses that follow show that this alliance displeased God: a prophet rebuked him, and the ships were broken.

For today: even someone who follows God can go wrong by partnering with someone who does not respect Him. Before entering into partnerships or business dealings, ask yourself whether that union brings you closer to God or pulls you away, and seek wise counsel.
exp.32:22:
Some of King Amon's servants secretly made a plan together against him and killed him inside his own house. The word "conspired" means they made a secret plan to harm him. The verse's word "Matáronlo" means "they killed him." The "servants" were his close attendants in the palace.

Here the chronicler speaks, telling the story of the kings of Judah. Amon followed the idols that his father Manasseh had served, but he did not humble himself before the LORD as his father had done. Instead, his guilt kept increasing. For this reason the account presents his death as the end of a path of evil that kept growing. The Bible does not explain why his servants killed him. Afterward, the people punished the conspirators and made his son Josiah king.

For today: it is not good to put off humbling ourselves before God. If we recognize our wrong today and return to Him, we keep sin from growing and destroying us.
exp.27:13:
This verse tells that the soldiers of Israel, returning from the war against Judah, left the captives and the plunder before the leaders and all the people gathered. The word "plunder" means what was taken in battle, and "leaders" means the chiefs or those in authority.

Here it is not a character speaking; it is the account of the chronicler. Earlier, the prophet Oded and some leaders of Ephraim, among them Azariah, warned that bringing in those captives, who were brothers of Judah, would be another sin against God. The soldiers, on hearing them, handed everything over and let the assembly decide.

For today: when someone humbly points out to us that we are going the wrong way, we can listen, stop, and correct course. Recognizing a mistake in time and doing good, as they did when they clothed and cared for the captives, shows a heart that is sensitive to God.
exp.20:9:
This verse says that Edom broke free from Judah's rule and has stayed independent. The writer adds "to this day," meaning up until the time when the book was written. At that same time Libnah, a city of Judah, also rebelled against Judah's king. "Rebelled" means it rose up against authority, and "forsaken" means abandoned.

The speaker is the Chronicler, who explains why the reign of Jehoram, son of Jehoshaphat, was so weak. Jehoram had forsaken the LORD, the God of his fathers. The Chronicler presents these revolts as a sign of the consequences of that abandonment, though he does not detail how God acted in each case.

For today: when we turn away from God, sooner or later the areas that sustain our lives grow weak. Today you can return to Him with humility, pray, and give priority to His Word.
exp.10:19:
This verse says that King Rehoboam married Maacah, the daughter of Absalom, and that she bore him four sons: Abijah, Attai, Ziza, and Shelomith.

The one who tells this is the Chronicler, who goes over the history of the kings of Judah. Here he shows how the family of Rehoboam, the son of Solomon, grew. It is clear that Maacah was his favorite and that her son Abijah would become the heir. Some think that "daughter" here means "granddaughter" of Absalom, but the text does not make this clear.

For today: let us care for our home with wisdom and without favoritism. Family decisions leave a mark, and God invites us to guide our loved ones with justice and love.
exp.17:1:
After some years, Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, went down to visit Ahab in Samaria, the capital of Israel. Ahab welcomed him with a lavish feast: he sacrificed many sheep and cattle for him and for the people who came with him. He used this generous hospitality to urge him to march with him to fight at Ramoth-gilead.

The narrator of Chronicles shows how Jehoshaphat, a godly king, ended up allied with Ahab, a king who had turned away from God. Earlier the text says that, because of his wealth, Jehoshaphat became related by marriage to Ahab, joined to Ahab's family through a marriage. That closeness led to this pressure.

For today: alliances and favors can lead us further than we expect. Before committing ourselves to someone, it is wise to ask, as Jehoshaphat should have done, what God says.
exp.26:3:
This verse says that King Jotham continued building in his kingdom. He built cities in the hill country of Judah, and in the forests he built fortresses and towers. The word "fortresses" here can be understood as strongholds or sturdy buildings; scholars do not fully agree on the exact detail. The verb "built" means that he built, or worked hard at building.

Here the chronicler, the author of Chronicles, tells the life of Jotham, king of Judah. Earlier it is said that he did what was right before God, although the people still followed corrupt practices. Then the reason for his success is explained: he made his ways firm before the LORD. These constructions show an orderly life, with protection and growth for the people.

For today: God values steady, well-done work. If you are called to build something, such as a home, a business, or a friendship, do it with diligence, and place your ways before God, not relying only on your own strength.
exp.6:15:
God says that he has chosen this temple and set it apart for himself. "Consecrated" means dedicated, set apart for a holy purpose. There his name will be, that is, his presence and his authority. His eyes and his heart will be there: he will watch over that place with care and affection. "Forever" here is understood within the promise, which later depends on the faithfulness of the people.

God speaks to Solomon at night, after the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem. He answers with a promise: he will hear the prayer of his people and forgive if they humble themselves and turn back to him. But he also warns him that he must walk in obedience, as David did. Some interpreters debate how to understand "forever" in light of the later destruction of the temple.

Today we can come near to God with confidence, knowing that he cares about us. But that closeness calls for a humble heart: today, acknowledge a fault before him and return to his way.
exp.27:24:
This verse says that King Ahaz built high places in every city of Judah. In these places incense was offered to other gods. In doing this he provoked the LORD, the God of his fathers.

The one speaking here is the chronicler, who sums up the life of Ahaz as an unfaithful king. Ahaz had been defeated by Syria and thought that the gods of that people would help him. For that reason he abandoned God, damaged the objects of the temple, and shut its doors. The text shows that this decision was a mistake that brought ruin.

For today: when difficulties come, let us not run after other things that promise help, such as money, power, or superstitions. Let us return to God, who is faithful, and seek our security in Him.
exp.32:18:
This verse says that Manasseh died and was buried in his house, and that his son Amon became the new king. "He slept with his fathers" is a gentle way of saying that he died. "They buried him" means "they laid him to rest." It is a simple close to a very long life as king.

The writer of Chronicles is summarizing the reign of Manasseh, who was very given to idolatry but later humbled himself before God and prayed. The text says they buried him "in his house," and it is not certain whether this refers to the palace or to his garden (2 Kings 21:18 speaks of the garden of his house). Right after this, Amon appears, who will repeat his father's sins but not his repentance.

Today we can learn that repentance is important, but we also must care for the example we leave to those who come after us. If we have failed, God forgives, and it is good for us to speak honestly with our children and show them a better way.
exp.32:10:
It says that when Manasseh was in trouble, that is, in great suffering and distress, he turned to the Lord, his God, in prayer. He humbled himself deeply, that is, he gave up his pride, before the God of his fathers. The words "but when" point to the turn in the story here, and "was heard" means that God listened to him.

The writer of Chronicles tells the story of Manasseh, a king of Judah who had done much evil and led the people down the wrong path. God spoke to them, but they would not listen. Then the commanders of the Assyrian king captured Manasseh, bound him in bronze shackles, and took him to Babylon. There, in his captivity, he returned to God, and God restored him to his kingdom.

No one is so far away that they cannot return to God. If you recognize your mistakes and humble yourself sincerely, you can pray today. God does not despise a repentant heart, and often hardship helps us wake up and seek him.
exp.12:5:
This verse says that Jeroboam, son of Nebat, was a servant of King Solomon, but he rose up and rebelled against his master. The phrase "rose up" means that he took a step of open opposition, and "his master" refers to Solomon, to whom he owed loyalty.

The one speaking is Abijah, king of Judah, who is on a mountain before the battle against Israel.
