He wants to persuade Jeroboam and his people that the kingdom of David was given by God through a covenant of salt, an expression that speaks of a firm and lasting pact. This is a speech by Abijah, and the Bible presents it as his point of view; other parts of the account give more detail about the division of the kingdom.

For today: loyalty and respect for authority matter, but above all faithfulness to God. Before opposing someone or following a leader, it is wise to ask whether our decisions come from proud ambition or from obedience to God.
exp.16:11:
This verse says that Jehoshaphat grew stronger and stronger, becoming more and more powerful. He built fortresses, which were strongly defended places to protect the kingdom, and store cities, that is, cities where supplies and resources such as food and weapons were kept.

Here the narrator of the book of Chronicles speaks, telling the story of the kings of Judah. Earlier it is said that God caused the neighboring peoples to fear him, and some of them brought him gifts and tribute. The author shows that Jehoshaphat's growth was tied to God's support. Then his army and his works are described.

For today: trusting God does not remove the responsibility to plan wisely. Jehoshaphat received blessing, but he also built and organized. We can pray and, at the same time, save, prepare, and take care of what God has entrusted to us.
exp.12:2:
This verse tells how Abijah, king of Judah, went into battle with an army of 400,000 chosen men. Jeroboam, king of Israel, came against him with 800,000 chosen and mighty men of valor. The phrase "drew up in formation" means that Jeroboam lined up his troops in order for the fight. The numbers are very large, and some scholars think they may have a more symbolic meaning, but the text stresses that Judah had half as many soldiers.

The one telling the story is the chronicler, who writes to help the people remember their history. The kingdom had split: Judah, with the descendants of David, was in the south, and Israel, under Jeroboam, was in the north. That is why there was war between them. Soon after, Abijah reminds Jeroboam that God had promised the kingdom to David.

For today: sometimes we feel at a disadvantage, with fewer resources or less strength. Before we put our trust in numbers, let us remember God's promises and pray for his help.
exp.20:13:
It says that God is going to send a serious blow on the people of Joram, the king of Judah. That disaster would reach his sons, his wives, and all his possessions. The word "possessions" refers to his property, and the phrase "the LORD is about to strike" means that God himself would bring judgment upon him.

The one speaking is the prophet Elijah, through a letter addressed to Joram. The king had turned away from the path of his father Jehoshaphat, had promoted idolatry in Judah, and had killed his brothers. Some scholars note that this letter is a curious detail, because it is believed that Elijah had already been taken up into heaven; the Bible does not explain how he came to write it, and there are several opinions on the matter.

For today: our decisions never affect only ourselves. Whoever has influence over others, at home or at work, should take care of their example and seek God with humility, because He is just and also merciful to those who repent.
exp.27:16:
The Edomites had again come and attacked Judah, and they carried away captives. The word "again" shows that this attack came on top of other troubles Judah was already suffering.

The one speaking is the narrator of Chronicles, who tells the story of King Ahaz of Judah. Ahaz turned away from God, and the text explains that the Lord brought Judah low because of this. First came defeats against Israel, then the Edomites, and after that the Philistines. Even so, Ahaz asked Assyria for help instead of returning to the Lord.

For today: when difficulties pile up, it is worth stopping to ask ourselves humbly whether God is calling us back to Himself. Not every trial is a punishment, but seeking God first is always the better path, before rushing to human solutions.
exp.31:27:
This verse tells how Hezekiah built storehouses to keep the harvest of grain, the new wine, and the oil. He also made stalls for all kinds of livestock and pens for the flocks.

Here the chronicler, the author of Chronicles, who recounts the history of the kings of Judah, is speaking. It comes right after Hezekiah humbled himself for his pride, and God did not pour out his anger. The author shows that the king's prosperity was a blessing from God, as the context says: "God had given him very much substance."

For today: when God gives us blessings, it is wise to manage them with order and foresight, without pride. Caring well for what we receive is a way of thanking him and of being ready to help others.
exp.13:1:
The verse says that Asa, king of Judah, did what was good and right in God's sight. The words "good and right" describe a life that pleases God, not only people. "In the eyes of the LORD" means "according to God's view." "LORD" is the name of God in this translation.

This is told by the Chronicler, an author who is not identified with certainty. He writes after the exile to remind the people that obeying God brings blessing. Asa succeeds his father Abijah, and the text shows that his obedience was concrete: he removed idols and encouraged the people to seek God. Furthermore, the land had peace.

For today: it is not enough to say that we believe in God. We can ask ourselves what specific thing we should leave behind or change in order to live in a way that pleases him. Truly obeying usually begins with a practical and visible step.
exp.32:4:
It says that King Manasseh built altars to worship "all the host of heaven," meaning the sun, the moon, and the stars. He placed them in both courtyards of the temple of the LORD. It was an act of idolatry inside the holiest place in Israel.

The writer of Chronicles tells the story of the kings of Judah. Manasseh, son of the godly Hezekiah, undid the reforms of his father. The serious thing was not only worshiping other gods, but doing it in the house where God had placed his name. The passage shows how far the people had turned away. Later in the same chapter, it tells how Manasseh humbled himself and God heard him.

Today we can ask ourselves what things occupy in our hearts the place that belongs to God. He wants to be the only Lord of our lives, and he always offers forgiveness to anyone who returns to him with humility.
exp.7:3:
Solomon built the city of Tadmor in a desert region, and he also built store cities in the area of Hamath. The Berean Standard Bible describes these as cities he had built in Hamath, in addition to Tadmor. The cities were used to store supplies and provisions, not weapons. Many believe Tadmor is the ancient city later known as Palmyra, but this is not completely certain.

The writer of Chronicles, who writes long after these events, summarizes Solomon's achievements. These cities helped protect the kingdom, keep the trade routes open, and maintain reserves. For a people returning from exile, it was a reminder that God had given Israel stability in times of peace.

Today we can learn that planning and preparing is also part of living with faith. Saving, organizing, and caring for what God entrusts to us are acts of responsibility, always depending on Him.
exp.33:14:
What it says: The priest Hilkiah tells Shaphan the scribe that he has found the Book of the Law in the temple, and he hands it over to him. "Said" means that he spoke and gave the report. A "scribe" was a secretary who knew how to read and write documents. "The house of the LORD" is the temple in Jerusalem.

Context: Hilkiah speaks during the repairs of the temple that King Josiah had ordered. While they were taking out the money that had been brought as offerings, he found the book. It is not known for certain which exact part of Scripture it was; many think it was Deuteronomy or the whole Pentateuch. Hilkiah gives it to Shaphan, who will take it to the king.

For today: God's Word can be forgotten, even close to us. Shake the dust off your Bible, read it carefully, and let it correct and guide your life, as it did for Josiah.
exp.27:25:
As for the rest of the acts of Ahaz and all his ways, from beginning to end, they are indeed written in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel. It means that everything about his reign, from start to finish, was recorded. "Acts" refers to what he did, and "ways" refers to how he lived.

This is the chronicler's usual closing note when speaking of a king. Ahaz had just shut the temple, broken its vessels, and set up altars to other gods. The Book of the Kings is an official record that we no longer have as a separate book today, and it is not known with certainty exactly what it was. What follows shows that he was not buried among the kings.

For today: our lives also leave a record, and God knows it completely. It is worth asking ourselves what direction we are taking and, if needed, turning back to God today.
exp.7:11:
This verse says that Solomon offered burnt offerings to the LORD on the altar of the LORD that he himself had built in front of the portico, the entrance of the temple. A "burnt offering" was an animal offering that was burned completely as a sign of total surrender to God. "To the LORD" refers to God by his personal name.

Here the chronicler speaks, narrating Solomon's life after he finished the temple. His interest is to show that worship in Israel was organized with order and according to the Law of Moses and the instructions of David. Solomon took care that what was holy was respected, which is also why he kept his wife, the daughter of Pharaoh, away from the place where the ark had been.

For today: before filling your agenda with pending tasks, give God a fixed and constant place, such as daily prayer, with reverence and order.
exp.23:8:
He says that King Joash ordered a public announcement throughout Judah and Jerusalem, calling the people to bring to the Lord the tax that Moses, the servant of God, had imposed on Israel while they were in the wilderness. The announcement was to be made loudly, so that everyone would know. The word "imposed" here means ordered or established.

King Joash wanted to repair the temple, which Athaliah and her sons had damaged, and they had used holy things for idols. To pay for the work, a tax was called for that came from the law of Moses. The people rejoiced and gave.

For today: when a need is clear and is communicated honestly, people often respond with joy. We can give generously to our church and to the work of God, and take care that everything is handled with order and transparency.
exp.19:19:
This verse tells how Judah got up early in the morning and went out into the Wilderness of Tekoa. As they set out, King Jehoshaphat stood up and asked the people of Judah and Jerusalem to listen to him. He told them to believe in the LORD their God so that they would be upheld, and to believe in his prophets so that they would succeed.

King Jehoshaphat is the one speaking. An enemy army made up of Ammon, Moab, and the people of Mount Seir was coming against Judah, and the people had prayed and worshiped God. Jehoshaphat encourages them to trust before the battle. Then he places singers at the front, and the text says that God acted against the enemies while the people were praising him.

Today, when you face a big problem, before you act out of fear, place your trust in God and in what he says in his Word. You can pray and praise him, and take the next step with faith.
exp.24:1:
He did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, but not wholeheartedly. The phrase "what was right in the eyes of the LORD" means what God regarded as correct. "Wholeheartedly" speaks of total and sincere devotion, without an inner division.

Here the narrator of Chronicles speaks, summarizing the reign of Amaziah. His purpose is to evaluate the king according to his faithfulness to God. The verses that follow show his obedience to the law of Moses in not punishing the children of the murderers. Later in the chapter, however, Amaziah turns to idols, and so we see what that divided devotion meant.

For today: it is not enough to do good things on the outside. God looks at the heart. Ask him to help you obey him with sincerity and out of love, not merely out of habit or convenience.
exp.2:16:
Solomon set up the two great bronze pillars in front of the temple, one on the south and one on the north. He named the pillar on the south Jachin, and the pillar on the north Boaz. The Hebrew names are commonly understood to mean something like "he establishes" (Jachin) and "in him is strength" (Boaz), though there is no complete certainty about their exact meaning.

Here the chronicler speaks, recounting the building of the temple in Jerusalem. He writes for a people who had returned from exile and needed to remember that God dwelt among them. The pillars stood at the entrance as a reminder that God holds up and steadies his people.

For today: before you come into God's presence, remember that it is He who sustains you. When you feel weak or unsure, begin your prayer by recalling that your steadiness does not depend on yourself, but on Him.
exp.3:3:
This verse describes the "Sea," a great bronze basin for water in the temple. It rested on twelve bronze oxen, in groups of three, facing north, west, south, and east. The oxen's hindquarters were turned toward the center, so the bases were hidden from view inside the circle.

The chronicler tells how Solomon built and furnished the temple in Jerusalem. According to the text that follows, the Sea was used so that the priests could wash before serving. Some see in the twelve oxen a reference to the twelve tribes, but the text does not say this, so it is only one possible interpretation.

For today: drawing near to God with reverence matters. We can ask him to cleanse our hearts before we pray or serve, trusting that Christ has already made us clean.
exp.22:5:
No one was allowed to enter the house of the LORD except the priests and the Levites who were serving at that time. They could go in because they were consecrated, set apart for God. Everyone else was required to obey the LORD's instructions, which meant staying in their assigned places and guarding what had been entrusted to them.

The one speaking is the priest Jehoiada. Athaliah was ruling Judah unjustly, and Jehoiada planned to make the young Joash king, since Joash was the rightful heir. To protect him, Jehoiada arranged watches in the temple and made sure only authorized people went in.

For today: God values order and reverence in what is sacred. We can ask ourselves whether we take care in how we draw near to Him. We also see that each person has a useful place: not everyone does the same task, but everyone is called to look after what God loves.
exp.35:4:
Jehoiakim was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for eleven years. The verse also says that he did evil in the sight of the LORD his God, meaning that he did what God saw as wrong.

The book of Chronicles was written by an author whom tradition often identifies with Ezra, though this is not certain. It tells the story of Judah to remind the people why the nation fell. Jehoiakim was placed on the throne by Egypt, which changed his name from Eliakim. Later, Babylon came against him. His reign shows a country under the control of foreign powers and far from God.

For today: having a position or a title is not enough. What matters is how we live before God. Today you can ask him, "Lord, what do you see in my decisions?" and correct whatever he shows you.
exp.17:16:
Here King Ahab of Israel complains to Jehoshaphat, king of Judah. He reminds him that he had already warned him that the prophet Micaiah never prophesies good for him, but only bad. To prophesy means to speak on behalf of God. Jehoshaphat is the king of Judah, and Ahab is the king of Israel.

Ahab and Jehoshaphat were about to go to war against Ramoth-gilead. Four hundred prophets had promised victory. Jehoshaphat wanted to hear a prophet of the LORD as well, so they sent for Micaiah. He had told the truth: Israel would be left without a shepherd, that is, without its king. Ahab was angry because the truth did not please him.

Many times we prefer voices that tell us what we want to hear. But an honest word, even when it hurts, can save us from a serious mistake. Let us seek counselors who speak with truth and love, and let us listen with humility.
exp.32:11:
The passage says that Manasseh prayed to God in his distress, and God heard him and brought him back to Jerusalem, to his kingdom. Some key words: "sought the favor" means that he asked God for mercy; "earnestly humbled himself" means that he bowed low and sincerely. Seeing this, Manasseh recognized that the Lord alone is God.

The narrator of Chronicles tells us that Manasseh was a very wicked king in Judah. God spoke to him, but he paid no attention, and the Assyrians took him captive to Babylon. There, in his distress, he sought the Lord. The text does not explain every detail of his captivity, but it emphasizes that God answered and that Manasseh changed, as his later actions show.

For today: it is never too late to return to God. If you have wandered away or done a great deal of harm, you can come near with humility and sincerity. God receives the one who repents, and a changed heart shows itself in concrete actions.
exp.30:19:
This verse sums up the work of King Hezekiah throughout the whole kingdom of Judah. "Did" here means that he carried it out, that he put it into practice. He is said to have done what was good, right, and true "before the LORD," that is, with the awareness that God was watching him.

The author of Chronicles, whose exact identity is not known for certain (Jewish tradition often names Ezra), closes here the account of Hezekiah's reforms. He restored the temple, the Passover, and the service of the priests and Levites. The people brought their offerings and tithes, and a system was organized for distributing provisions to those who served in the temple. The next verse adds that he did this with all his heart.

Doing what is right is not only about fulfilling what others can see, but about living with integrity before God. We might ask ourselves: "Would what I do at home, at work, or at church be the same if only God knew about it?" Let us ask him for help to act with sincerity.
exp.11:1:
This verse tells us that in the fifth year of Rehoboam's reign, Shishak, king of Egypt, attacked Jerusalem. The text gives the reason: the people had been unfaithful to the Lord. The phrase "attacked Jerusalem" fits the city's location high in the hills.

The writer of Chronicles, looking back over the history of Israel, explains why this attack happened. The verse before says that Rehoboam, as soon as he was firmly established on the throne, abandoned the law of God, and all the people followed him. For the chronicler, the attack was not a matter of chance but a consequence of that abandonment. Some scholars point out that there were also political reasons, but the text emphasizes the spiritual reason.

When we feel strong and secure, it is easy to neglect God. Today we might ask ourselves: am I seeking God in my times of stability as well, or only in times of crisis? Keeping prayer and the Word daily protects us from drifting away without noticing.
exp.35:17:
This verse says that the king of Babylon carried away everything of value: the articles of the house of God, both large and small, the treasures of the house of the LORD, and the treasures of the king and his officials. The "articles" are the sacred items used in worship, such as cups and containers. "Carried off" here means they were taken by force.

The chronicler tells of the fall of Jerusalem, around 586 B.C. He explains that the people mocked the prophets and despised God's words, and that is why judgment came. This verse shows that the punishment reached both the religious and the political spheres. Nothing was left untouched.

For today: God speaks to us with patience, often through other people. Today you can listen humbly to a correction, without mocking or hardening your heart, and return to God before the consequences grow.
exp.12:3:
Abijah stood on Mount Zemaraim in the hill country of Ephraim and spoke out loud to Jeroboam and the whole army of Israel. The words "Hear me" mean "listen to me." He wanted them to listen before the fighting began.

Abijah was king of Judah. After the kingdom had split, Jeroboam ruled the northern tribes. Both armies were already drawn up, and Jeroboam's was twice as large. Before the battle, Abijah gives a speech to remind them that God had given the kingdom to David. No one knows exactly where that mountain was, but it was in northern territory.

Before acting, it is worth pausing to speak truthfully and to look for the deeper reason. Even in a conflict, we can appeal to what God has said, and not only to our own strength. It is also good to remember that Abijah was not a perfect king.
exp.34:6:
Josiah gave the people animals from his own flocks and herds for the Passover offerings. He contributed thirty thousand lambs and young goats, along with three thousand bulls, for all the people who were present. "Possessions" here means his wealth or property, and "the common people" refers to ordinary people.

The chronicler tells how Josiah restored the Passover in Jerusalem, in keeping with what God commanded. Many people would not have had enough animals to offer, so the king provided them. The leaders also gave generously. The numbers are very large, and the text does not explain further details about them.

For today: worship is strengthened when those who have more resources or influence use them so that others can take part. We can ask ourselves what we have, whether time, money or help, that can serve so that someone else may draw near to God.
exp.5:0:
Here the verse says that Solomon begins to speak before the people and recalls that God had said he would dwell in the thick cloud. The word "cloud" here means a dense cloud, a kind of mist that covered the presence of God. "Dwell" means to live or remain in that place.

Solomon is the king of Israel, and he has just finished building the temple. The priests have set the ark in its place, and a cloud filled the house (2 Chronicles 5:13-14). That is why Solomon recalls that God had already made known that he would reveal himself wrapped in a cloud, and in this way he presents the temple as the place where God dwells among his people.

Today we can learn that God is near, yet he is greater than we can understand. We do not always see clearly what he is doing, and even so we can trust his presence. When there are dark or confusing things in your life, draw near to him with humility and reverence.
exp.14:7:
When King Asa heard the words of the prophet Oded, he was encouraged. The verse says he "took courage," meaning he felt strong and ready to act. With that courage, he removed the detestable idols from all of Judah and Benjamin, and also from the cities he had captured in the hill country of Ephraim. He also restored the altar of the Lord, which stood in front of the portico of the temple.

The prophet's message, which the verse connects to Azariah son of Oded, had reminded Asa that God is with those who seek him and that faithful work would be rewarded. That is why Asa was moved to carry out a spiritual reform throughout the kingdom.

For today: when God speaks to us through his Word, it is not enough to feel encouraged. We must act, removing what pulls us away from him and restoring what has been neglected in our spiritual lives.
exp.8:19:
All of King Solomon's drinking cups were gold, and all the utensils of the House of the Forest of Lebanon were pure gold. It says that there was no silver, because silver was considered as nothing in the days of Solomon. The drinking cups, plates and utensils refer to the vessels and containers used for eating and drinking. "Pure gold" speaks of gold of very high quality. Silver, which is valuable today, was hardly considered in those days, because there was so much gold.

The chronicler describes the greatness of Solomon's kingdom, right after describing his throne. It is not God speaking here, but the narrator, who wants to show how God blessed Solomon with wealth and wisdom. The ships' voyages to Tarshish brought in those riches. Scholars are not sure where Tarshish was located.

For today: Solomon's wealth was a gift from God, but it was not lasting. Remember that everything you have comes from God, so use it with gratitude and generosity, without setting your heart on it.
exp.33:25:
This verse begins a special message for King Josiah. God tells the messengers: "Tell the king of Judah, who sent you to inquire of the LORD, that this is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says." The phrase "to inquire" means "to ask" or "to seek an answer."

The words "the words that you heard" refer to what the king had listened to, namely the words of the book that had been read to him, and the message continues in the next verse.

God speaks through the prophetess Huldah. King Josiah had heard the reading of the book, which was probably a part of the Law of Moses. He was alarmed to see how far the people had drifted away from God, and so he sent to ask what would happen.

For today: when the Word of God confronts us, He looks with favor on a heart that listens with humility. We can read the Bible without defending ourselves, let it correct us, and respond to Him with sincerity, knowing that God hears the one who draws near to Him.
exp.13:11:
This verse tells how God defeated the army of the Cushites before King Asa and the people of Judah. The word "defeated" here means that he overcame them completely, and the Cushites ended up fleeing.

The narrator of Chronicles describes this battle in the valley of Zephathah, near Mareshah. Asa faced an enormous army, and before fighting he prayed, acknowledging that for God it makes no difference whether someone is strong or weak. The verses that follow say that Judah pursued the enemy and took a great deal of plunder. The text presents the victory as the work of God, an answer to that humble prayer.

For today: when you face something that is beyond you, do what Asa did. Pray sincerely, admit that you cannot do it alone, and trust God. This does not replace effort or responsibility, but it places your trust in the right place.
exp.28:4:
Hezekiah calls the Levites to listen. He asks them to consecrate themselves, that is, to set themselves apart for God and make themselves clean according to God's law. Only then could they cleanse the house of the LORD. He also commands them to remove every impurity from the Holy Place, everything that had built up there and was contrary to God.

This is Hezekiah, king of Judah, speaking at the beginning of his reign. His father, Ahaz, had neglected the worship of God, and the doors of the temple had been shut. Hezekiah gathers the Levites because they were responsible for the temple service. First he wants them to be clean themselves, and then to cleanse the house of God.

Before trying to fix what is wrong around us, it is good to examine our own hearts and ask God to cleanse us. A life close to God is the best foundation for serving him well.
exp.34:12:
It says they roasted the Passover animals over the fire, as the regulation required. But the other holy offerings, which were set apart as holy, they boiled in pots, kettles, and bowls, and quickly brought them to all the people. "Quickly" means they were brought out without delay.

The one telling this is the chronicler, who recounts the great Passover of King Josiah in Jerusalem. Here he describes the order of the service: the priests and the Levites worked together so that all the people could take part. The Law called for the Passover animal to be roasted (Exodus 12:8-9), and the text notes that the other sacrifices were prepared in a different way.

Today we can learn that serving God is teamwork. Each person has their own task, and doing it with order and promptness helps everyone to receive and enjoy what God offers.
exp.9:8:
Rehoboam, the new king, asks his advisers what he should say in reply to the people. They had asked him to lighten the load that his father Solomon had placed on them. The word "yoke" refers to the wooden frame fitted over oxen so they could pull heavy loads, and here it stands for heavy labor and taxes.

Rehoboam, son of Solomon, is speaking shortly after being crowned in Shechem. The people ask for fairer treatment. He had already heard from the elders, who advised him to serve the people with kindness, and now he turns to the young men he grew up with. The text shows that this decision would have serious consequences for the kingdom.

For today: before deciding, listen humbly to wise people with experience. Do not choose only the advice that flatters your pride or that is most comfortable for you.
exp.5:15:
Solomon asks God to keep the promise he made to David: there would always be a man from David's line sitting on the throne of Israel. But that promise came with a condition: David's descendants had to guard their way and walk in God's law, as David himself had walked before him. Here "keep" means "fulfill," and the phrase "if only" means "provided that."

Solomon speaks at the dedication of the temple, in front of all the people. He has just acknowledged that God has fulfilled what he promised David, since the temple is already built. Now he prays that God will remain faithful to that promise in the future.

For today: God is faithful to his word, and we can trust his promises. But he also calls us to respond with obedience. We can ask him each day to help us walk with him sincerely, not only to receive his blessings.
exp.31:26:
He says that King Hezekiah came to have very great riches and honor. He made treasuries for his silver, gold, precious stones, spices, shields, and all kinds of valuable articles.

The writer of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition does not always identify with certainty, tells this after showing Hezekiah's pride and his humbling. The earlier verses explain that God did not take away the blessing when he repented. In this way, the wealth is presented as a gift from God, and the next verse says it clearly: "God had given him very much wealth."

For today: if God gives you possessions, success or recognition, receive everything with gratitude and humility. If you notice that pride is creeping in, do as Hezekiah did: acknowledge it quickly and return to God.
exp.8:30:
It says that Solomon died and was buried in Jerusalem, the city of his father David. "Rested with his fathers" is a gentle way of saying that he died. The sentence that follows describes the burial itself. Afterward, his son Rehoboam became king in his place.

The author of Chronicles, whose identity tradition usually attributes to Ezra, though this is not certain, summarizes here the end of Solomon's reign, which lasted forty years. He mentions books of the prophets where more details were kept. The book was written for a people returning from exile who needed to remember their history, their royal line, and the faithfulness of God. This verse closes one chapter and prepares the next.

Even great leaders finish their time, but God's work continues. We can ask ourselves what we will leave to those who come after us: faith, a good example, and words that encourage them to follow God. Let us live today with that in mind.
exp.34:0:
This verse says that King Josiah kept the Passover to honor the Lord in Jerusalem. The Passover lamb was slaughtered on the fourteenth day of the first month. The phrase "kept the Passover" means that he organized and led the feast.

The one telling the story is the chronicler, who recounts the history of the kings of Judah. Josiah was a king who wanted to return to proper worship. The Passover remembered Israel's deliverance from Egypt. The verses that follow show that he arranged the service of the priests and Levites, so that everything was done in good order and as it had been commanded.

For today: remembering with gratitude what God has done for us is not optional. We can set aside specific times to thank him, and do so with order and sincerity, not out of mere habit.
exp.31:19:
And in response, King Hezekiah and the prophet Isaiah, the son of Amoz, prayed together about this situation. "Cried out to heaven" means they called on God for help with a strong and sincere voice, fully aware of their need for him.

The army of Assyria, sent by King Sennacherib, threatened Jerusalem. His messengers shouted in Hebrew to the people on the walls to frighten them, and they mocked God as if he were an idol made by human hands. Faced with this, the king and the prophet stopped trusting in their own strength and sought God. Afterward, the text tells how God sent an angel and delivered Jerusalem.

When a threat overwhelms you, do not face it alone. Pray honestly, and if you can, pray together with someone of faith. God hears the sincere cry of his children.
exp.29:3:
This verse says that the plan to celebrate the Passover in the second month pleased King Hezekiah and the whole assembly of people gathered together. "Pleased" means that it seemed good to them. "Assembly" refers to the gathering that was with him.

The account in Chronicles tells that Hezekiah consulted with his leaders and with the assembly in Jerusalem. It could not be celebrated on the usual date because there were not enough priests who had been made ready and the people had not gathered. So they decided to postpone it by one month. Afterward they sent letters throughout Israel inviting them to return to God.

For today: when an important decision has to be made, it is wise to seek counsel and seek agreement, without imposing. Hezekiah wanted to honor God, and listening to others helped many to join in with joy.
exp.9:3:
Here the people of Israel ask the new king, Rehoboam, to be gentler than his father, Solomon. A "yoke" is the wooden frame placed on oxen to make them work. Here it stands for a crushing burden. They describe the hard service laid on them as a heavy weight. They tell him: if you lighten the load, we will serve you.

Jeroboam speaks together with all Israel, gathered in Shechem to make Rehoboam king. Jeroboam had fled to Egypt out of fear of Solomon. The Bible shows that Solomon imposed hard labor and heavy burdens. The people do not rebel yet: first they make a respectful request and offer loyalty in exchange for relief.

For today: whoever has authority in the home, the workplace, or the church should listen humbly to those under their care. A wise leader does not ignore a fair complaint; he listens and seeks to ease unnecessary burdens.
exp.34:3:
This verse says that the Levites were to prepare themselves and organize themselves by their families and their turns of service. The phrase "prepare yourselves" in the verse expresses what this means.

The "instructions written by David king of Israel and Solomon his son" refer to the written directions that David and Solomon left about how the service in the temple was to be arranged.

King Josiah is speaking, renewing worship in Judah and preparing a great celebration of the Passover. He reminds the Levites that they no longer have to carry the ark, because it has a fixed place in the temple. Now their task is to serve God and the people. Josiah wants everything done in order and following what God had already established.

For today: serving God is best when we prepare ourselves and work in order. Before serving in the church or in the family, we can pray, organize ourselves, and faithfully carry out the part that belongs to us.
exp.9:4:
Rehoboam tells the people to come back to him in three days, and the people leave. The wording is easy to follow: "Come back to me in three days" means they should return to him within that time. The people wait for his answer.

King Rehoboam, son of Solomon, is the speaker. Jeroboam and all Israel have just asked him to lighten the heavy burdens his father left them, and they promise to serve him if he does. Rehoboam does not answer right away, but takes time to think and to seek counsel. Afterward he consults the elders and, as the account goes on, others as well.

For today: when someone brings you a serious complaint, do not respond in haste or in pride. Taking time to pray and to seek wise counsel is a good idea. But pay close attention to whom you listen to, because not all advice leads to peace.
exp.8:0:
Now the queen of Sheba heard about the fame of Solomon, so she traveled to Jerusalem to test him with difficult questions. She arrived with a very large caravan, including camels carrying spices, a great amount of gold, and precious stones. When she came to Solomon, she spoke with him about everything on her mind.

The account comes from the chronicler, who describes the greatness of Solomon's reign. Sheba was a distant kingdom, and scholars do not agree on its exact location; it is often linked with southern Arabia, though some propose other regions. She was drawn to what she had heard about his wisdom.

Today we can learn from her attitude: she did not settle for rumors, but sought the truth with humility and effort. Bring your most sincere questions to God and to his Word, without fear, for he is able to answer them.
exp.20:15:
This verse says that God caused the Philistines and the Arabs who lived near the Cushites to feel a desire to attack Jehoram, king of Judah. "Stirred against" means that God moved or impelled their spirit against him. "Spirit" here refers to their disposition or eagerness to fight.

Jehoram was a king who turned away from God, and according to this chapter, he killed his brothers and promoted idolatry in Judah. Before this verse, the prophet Elijah had sent him a letter with a warning of judgment. Here that warning begins to be fulfilled: enemies invade the land and carry off riches and family. Some scholars see this passage as God's discipline for his sin.

For today: God takes wickedness seriously, but he also warns before he acts. If we sense that God is speaking to us through his Word or through someone wise, it is good to listen and correct our course in time.
exp.6:3:
This verse says that King Solomon and all the people offered sacrifices to God. The "offerings" were the animals presented on the altar as gifts. They did this "before the LORD," that is, acknowledging that God was present.

The chronicler tells of the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem. God had just shown his presence with fire and a glory so great that the priests could not enter. The people bowed down and praised God for his mercy. The sacrifices were the natural response to what they had just seen: gratitude and worship, not just a ceremony.

For today: when we recognize what God has done for us, our response should be to give him something real. Today we do not offer animals, but we can offer our time, gratitude, obedience, and praise with a sincere heart.
exp.31:22:
After God delivered Jerusalem, many people brought offerings to the Lord in Jerusalem and valuable gifts to King Hezekiah. From then on, he was exalted in the eyes of all the nations, meaning the surrounding nations looked up to him and respected him.

This is the account of the chronicler, who tells the story of Judah. He has just described how an angel destroyed the army of Sennacherib, king of Assyria, who had been threatening Jerusalem. Hezekiah had prayed, and God answered. The honor he received came as a result of that deliverance. But the text that follows shows that his heart became filled with pride, which brought consequences.

When God helps us and things get better, it is easy to feel important. We can remember that every good moment is a gift from God, and respond with gratitude and humility, as someone who still depends on Him.
exp.21:6:
Ahaziah's downfall came from God, and the verse says so plainly. Ahaziah, king of Judah, went to visit Joram, king of Israel. When Ahaziah arrived, he went out with Joram to meet Jehu son of Nimshi, the man the LORD had anointed to destroy the house of Ahab. "Destroy" here means to sweep away completely.

The chronicler is telling the story of Judah's history. Ahaziah had close ties to the family of Ahab and followed their poor advice. Because of that, he was caught up in the judgment God had decreed against that house. Readers and scholars differ in how they understand the way God directs events like these, but the text shows that He rules over history even when wicked people act.

For today: the friendships and the advice we choose lead us down a path. Let us seek wise counsel and trust that God is just and in control, even when we do not understand everything.
exp.31:16:
This verse says that Sennacherib, king of Assyria, also wrote letters mocking the LORD, the God of Israel, and speaking against him. He wrote that, just as the gods of other nations did not deliver their people from his hand, the God of Hezekiah would not deliver his people from his hand either.

Sennacherib had invaded Judah and was threatening Jerusalem. His messengers had already spoken to discourage the people, and now he was also using letters. He placed the LORD on the same level as the idols made by human hands, without understanding who God really is. The account that follows shows that Hezekiah and the prophet Isaiah prayed, and God answered.

For today: when someone mocks your faith or tells you that God will not help you, do not stay alone with your fears. Do as Hezekiah did: bring that pressure to God in prayer and trust that he is far greater than any threat.
exp.5:34:
It says God hears, from heaven where he dwells, the prayer and the plea of his people when they go out to war. And the request that God "uphold their cause" means that he will defend them and do justice to their cause. A "plea" is a petition made with insistence.

Solomon speaks at the dedication of the temple he built in Jerusalem. He is asking God to attend to the prayers made toward that place. In this case, he prays for the people who go out to fight on the path that God himself had shown them. Some scholars note that the request depends on the war being sent by God, not on pride or ambition.

Today we can pray with confidence in the middle of struggles or injustice, knowing that God hears. But it is also worth asking ourselves whether we are walking the path He approves, and asking Him to guide us before asking Him to defend us.
exp.29:24:
This verse says there was great joy in the whole gathering of the people. The word "assembly" here means the group of people gathered together. Those who rejoiced were the people of Judah, the priests and Levites (the ones in charge of service in the temple), the crowd that came from the north, and also the foreigners, both those who had come from Israel and those who lived in Judah.

The writer of Chronicles tells of the Passover that King Hezekiah celebrated in Jerusalem, after cleansing the temple and turning back to God. He even invited people from the northern kingdom. The feast was so good that they decided to continue for seven more days. It stands out that people who were very different from one another were gathered in one shared joy.

Today we can learn that the joy of worshiping God is best lived in community, and that there is room for everyone. This week, greet or invite someone who feels new or set apart in your church, and share with them the joy of standing before God.
exp.22:17:
This verse tells how the priest Jehoiada put the temple service back in order. He placed the duties in the hands of the Levitical priests, the same arrangement David had set up for the house of the LORD. They were to offer the burnt offerings (sacrifices that were burned completely) to the LORD, as the Law of Moses required, with rejoicing and song. "Oversight" here means the care and management of the work.

The writer of Chronicles tells this after Jehoiada protected the young king Joash and ended the reign of Athaliah. Jehoiada renewed the covenant with the LORD, and the people tore down the temple of Baal. Now worship is restored according to what God had commanded through Moses and David.

For today: when a community turns away from God, it helps to return to what His Word teaches and to serve Him with order. Let us do our service with joy and gratitude, not out of mere obligation.
exp.17:25:
Here King Ahab orders the prophet Micaiah to be put in prison. He tells them to feed him only bread and water as punishment, which means the bare minimum needed to survive. This will last until the king returns safely from the battle.

Ahab speaks to his officers. Micaiah had announced that the war against Ramoth-gilead would end badly, while four hundred prophets had promised him victory. The king was troubled to hear the truth, so he punished the messenger instead of weighing the message. Micaiah answers that if Ahab returns safely, God has not spoken through him.

For today: let us not reject a warning just because it hurts. Good advice, even when uncomfortable, can save us. Let us ask God for humility to listen to the truth and not only to what pleases us.
exp.16:17:
It says that after Amasiah came Jehozabad, another commander in King Jehoshaphat's army, and with him were 180,000 men armed for battle.

The author of Chronicles is listing the military leaders of Judah during Jehoshaphat's reign. Earlier he mentions Amasiah, who offered himself willingly to the Lord, and Eliada, of Benjamin. The author most likely wants to show that God blessed Jehoshaphat with strength and security because the king sought the Lord. The numbers are very large, and scholars do not always agree on how to understand them, but the central message is clear.

For today: preparation is valuable, but the most important thing is to serve God wholeheartedly. Prepare diligently for whatever God entrusts to you, and trust in Him more than in your own resources.
exp.9:15:
When all Israel saw that the king had refused to listen to them, they answered him with anger. They asked what share they had in David, and what inheritance they had in the son of Jesse. In other words, they no longer felt tied to his royal family. Their words "To your tents, O Israel!" told everyone to go back to their own homes, and "Look now to your own house, O David!" meant that Rehoboam should take care of his own affairs and his own family. Then all the Israelites went home.

The speakers are the people of the northern tribes, gathered at Shechem. They had asked Rehoboam to lighten the heavy burdens that his father Solomon had placed on them. He followed the advice of the young men and answered them harshly. The text says that God allowed this to happen to fulfill what he had announced through the prophet Ahijah. So the kingdom was divided.

For today: whoever has authority must listen with humility. A harsh word can break what years of unity built. Before we answer, let us ask God for wisdom and seek wise counsel.
exp.29:12:
Many people gathered in Jerusalem to celebrate the Feast of Unleavened Bread in the second month. The verse describes them as "a very great assembly," meaning a very large gathering.

This is the chronicler's account of King Hezekiah's reform. Because of problems with purification, the Passover was celebrated one month later than usual, which the law allowed in certain cases (Numbers 9). Hezekiah also invited people from the north. Some humbled themselves and came, and the text says that God himself gave Judah a heart ready to obey.

For today: when God calls you to return to him, do not wait until everything is perfect. Humble yourself, take the first step, and draw near, also alongside other believers. He can give you a willing heart.
exp.29:17:
This verse tells that a large number of people, many from the northern tribes of Ephraim, Manasseh, Issachar and Zebulun, ate the Passover without having purified themselves as the law required, and so they ate it contrary to what was written. The verse describes them as not yet prepared for the feast, and it names this group as a large part of the crowd.

Hezekiah, king of Judah, had invited all Israel to celebrate the Passover in Jerusalem after cleansing the temple. Many came from far away and were not able to prepare themselves according to the law. The king, as the one responsible for the people, prayed on their behalf. The following text says that God heard him and healed the people.

For today: God values a sincere heart that seeks him, and invites us to pray for one another with mercy. That does not make obeying him unimportant, but it reminds us that his goodness reaches us where our own strength falls short.
exp.35:7:
This verse closes the account of the reign of Jehoiakim, king of Judah. The chronicler says that the rest of his deeds, the abominations he committed, and all that was found against him are written in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah. Then he notes that his son Jehoiachin reigned in his place.

The author of Chronicles writes for a people who returned from exile, and he reviews the history of their kings to explain why Jerusalem fell. He says little about Jehoiakim because his story was already recorded in another source. Some scholars think he means an official document that is now lost; it is not known for certain.

Our choices leave a mark, and at the end of life a record remains of what we were. It is worth asking ourselves what our life will leave written behind, and asking God to guide us to live in a way that honors his name.
exp.1:4:
Solomon says that the temple he is going to build must be great, and he gives the reason: his God is greater than all gods. "House" here means temple. The name of God in the Old Testament is "Jehovah."

Solomon writes to Hiram, king of Tyre, to ask for timber and craftsmen. He wants to build a place to worship God, offer sacrifices, and set out the holy bread. Although he says the temple will be great, in the verses that follow he admits that no building can contain God. His greatness is a way of honoring him, not of limiting him.

Today we might ask whether what we give to God reflects how much we value him. Perhaps it is not a building, but our time, our best effort, and our heart, offered with humility.
exp.30:14:
These six men served under Kore, the man in charge. They worked in the cities where the priests lived. Their job was to hand out faithfully to their fellow priests the portions that belonged to them from the offerings, according to their divisions. They treated old and young alike.

This comes from the account of King Hezekiah's revival in Judah. The people had brought offerings and tithes in great abundance for the temple. Then the king ordered that the distribution be organized. The writer wants to show that everything was handled with order and honesty, so that the temple servants could give themselves fully to their work.

For today: if you handle money or resources that belong to others, whether in the church or anywhere else, do so with honesty and fairness, without looking at who is important and who is not.
exp.15:8:
The LORD watches over the whole earth, roaming back and forth to find those whose hearts are fully devoted to Him, so that He can show His strength on their behalf. Here, the phrase "show Himself strong" means He displays His power to support and protect them. "Fully devoted" means a sincere heart given wholly to God, not one that is free of all faults. Then the prophet tells the king that he has acted foolishly in this matter, and that from now on he will be at war.

The one speaking is Hanani, a seer, meaning a prophet. He speaks to King Asa of Judah. Asa had paid the king of Syria to help him against Israel, instead of trusting in God, as he had done before with the Ethiopians. Asa responded with anger and imprisoned the prophet.

Today, when you face a problem, before looking for human solutions, pray and trust in God. He sees you and wants to hold you up. And if someone corrects you, listen with humility.
exp.0:6:
That same night God appeared to Solomon and said, "Ask, and I will give it to you!" It was a wide-open invitation, and Solomon had come to it through worship.

Solomon had just gone up to the bronze altar at Gibeon and offered a thousand burnt offerings, sacrifices that were burned up completely as an offering to God. He had gathered the leaders of the people there. The one speaking is God, who answers the worship of a young king who is just beginning to rule and who needs help for an enormous task.

For today: when we seek God sincerely, he invites us to ask him. Before asking, it is good to consider what we truly need most, and to bring it to him with humility and confidence.
exp.35:19:
This verse says that the survivors of the destruction of Jerusalem, those who escaped the sword, were carried by Nebuchadnezzar into exile in Babylon. There they became servants to him and his sons until the kingdom of Persia came to power.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition identifies with Ezra although there is no certainty, tells of the fall of Judah before Nebuchadnezzar. He presents it as a consequence of the people's disobedience, but also as part of what God had announced through Jeremiah. The text marks a painful ending, yet already points toward hope: Cyrus, king of Persia, would allow the return.

For today: even when we live with the consequences of serious mistakes, God does not abandon us. We can recognize our faults, accept his correction, and trust that he knows when and how to open a new path.
exp.6:13:
If God's people humble themselves, pray, seek his face (that is, long to be close to him), and turn from their wicked ways, then God will hear them from heaven, forgive their sin, and heal their land. The phrase "called by my name" means that they belong to God and carry his name. Turning back means returning to God.

God speaks, appearing to Solomon at night after the dedication of the temple. He warns that if drought, plagues, or sickness come as a consequence of the sin of the people of Israel, the way back is repentance. It is a promise addressed to Israel under the covenant.

For today: when something in your life or your family is wrong, do not start by blaming others. Pray with humility, acknowledge your faults before God, and take a concrete step of change. He remains merciful to whoever returns to him.
exp.28:1:
It says that Hezekiah did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, just as his ancestor David had done. The phrase "in the eyes of the LORD" means according to God's judgment, the view of what is right. And "his father" here refers to his ancestor, since David lived centuries before him. The phrase "just as his father David had done" means following David's example.

The book of Chronicles tells this as a historical account, probably written to encourage the people to return to God after the exile. Hezekiah was a young king of Judah, twenty-five years old. Before him, his father Ahaz had led the people into idolatry. That is why this verse summarizes his reign with a positive evaluation, and right afterward the text shows how it began: by opening and repairing the temple.

For today: no matter what those who came before us did, we can choose a different path, one that is right before God. Today you can start with one concrete step: repairing something neglected in your spiritual life, such as prayer or Bible reading.
exp.10:4:
Rehoboam settled down to live in Jerusalem, and he built up several cities to protect the land of Judah. The verse says he lived in Jerusalem, and that he built up cities for defense, meaning he made them stronger and safer against possible attacks.

The writer of Chronicles tells what happened after the kingdom was divided. God had commanded through a prophet that they not fight against their brothers in the north, and Rehoboam obeyed. After that obedience, he began to prepare himself with wisdom. The cities mentioned next were to the south and west of Jerusalem. Scholars often think they formed a line of defense.

For today: obeying God does not remove our responsibility to be prudent and to work with good sense. We can trust him and, at the same time, diligently do what is ours to do to care for our family and our home.
exp.24:13:
When King Amaziah returned from defeating the Edomites, he brought back the gods of that people, the Seirites, who were the Edomites. He set them up as his own gods, bowed down before them, and burned sacrifices to them.

The one speaking is the narrator of Chronicles. Amaziah had won the battle because God gave him the victory. Even so, he worshiped the gods of the defeated people. This is shocking, since those gods had not been able to save their own people. That is why God was angry and sent him a prophet, but the king refused to listen.

For today: when God gives us a blessing, it is easy to set our hearts on other things, such as success or money. Let us remember who helped us and give Him the gratitude and first place.
exp.35:1:
This verse says that Jehoahaz was twenty-three years old when he became king, and that he ruled in Jerusalem for only three months. "Became king" means that he took the throne. In other passages he is also called Shallum.

The writer of Chronicles tells the story of Judah after the death of the good king Josiah. The people chose Jehoahaz even though he was not the eldest son, since he had an older brother, Eliakim. His reign was very brief because Pharaoh Necho of Egypt removed him, imposed a tribute on the land, and carried him away as a prisoner. This shows that Judah was already weakened and under the control of foreign powers.

For today: holding a position or power does not guarantee that it will last. What matters is placing our trust in God and acting with humility and wisdom in the time we are given.
exp.3:18:
This verse says that Solomon had all the furnishings made for the temple: the golden altar and the tables on which the bread was placed, that is, loaves set out before God as an offering. The phrase "furnishings" here refers to the objects used in the house of God, and the bread is called "the Bread of the Presence."

The author of Chronicles recounts the building of the temple in Jerusalem for a people who were returning from exile. He wanted to remind them that the worship of God was carried out with order, care and generosity. Ancient texts speak of so much metal being used that it could not be weighed. Some details about the materials are interpreted in different ways.

For today: what we do for God deserves our best effort. We can serve him with dedication and joy in small things, such as preparing a meeting, helping in the church or praying sincerely, because he sees the heart.
exp.30:10:
Hezekiah gave orders to prepare storerooms in the house of the LORD, and this was carried out. The storerooms were rooms set aside to keep the offerings safe.

Hezekiah had restored worship in Judah, and the people responded by generously bringing their firstfruits and tenth parts. When the king asked about the great piles of offerings, the chief priest Azariah explained that the priests had eaten their fill and much remained, because the LORD had blessed his people. Faced with such abundance, the king ordered that everything be stored in an orderly way.

When God blesses us, we also need to manage well what we receive. We can prepare room for generosity by planning, getting our finances in order, and caring for what God entrusts to us, so that nothing is wasted and it continues to serve others.
exp.10:6:
This verse is part of a list of cities that King Rehoboam fortified. Three are named here: Beth-zur, Soco, and Adullam. "Fortified" here means that he rebuilt or strengthened them with walls and defenses, not that he founded them from scratch.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Chronicles, who tells the story of Judah. After the kingdom was divided, Rehoboam was in charge of the south and sought to protect his territory. These cities were located in areas of Judah, and the list shows a plan of defense. The text does not explain every military detail, so it is best not to add more than it says.

For today: a stronghold is built with time and care. Just as Rehoboam reinforced specific places, we can strengthen, with prayer, healthy habits, and good relationships, the areas of life where we are most vulnerable, before pressure arrives.
exp.34:25:
This verse sums up the life of King Josiah. It says that the rest of his deeds and his acts of loving devotion were in line with what is written in the Law of the LORD. "Acts of loving devotion" refers to deeds of kindness and faithfulness to God. "The LORD" is the name of God.

The speaker is the author of Chronicles, who tells the story of the kings of Judah. It comes right after Josiah's death and the great mourning of the people. Before closing his account, the chronicler wants to remember that this king was valued for obeying God's Word, and not only for his battles or his power.

For today: our lives are remembered more for what we do than for what we say. We can ask ourselves whether our daily decisions, at home, at work, and with others, are in line with what the Bible teaches.
exp.17:15:
Here Micaiah says he saw all Israel scattered over the hills, like sheep without a shepherd. Then he reports that the LORD said this people has no master, meaning they have no one to lead them, and that each person should return home in peace.

Micaiah, a prophet of God, speaks before Ahab, king of Israel, and Jehoshaphat, king of Judah. At first Micaiah repeated, with irony, what the false prophets were saying: "Go up, and you will prosper." Ahab, suspicious, demanded the truth from him. Then Micaiah announced that Ahab would die in the battle and the army would be left without its leader. Many understand that "these people have no master" points to the death of the king.

For today: God prefers a painful truth to a pleasing lie. Let us seek honest counselors, and above all let us listen to God, the Good Shepherd, before making important decisions.
exp.4:2:
This verse says that all the men of Israel came together before King Solomon at the feast held in the seventh month. "Came together" means they gathered as one group. The men here are the adult males. The feast is an important religious celebration. Many understand that this is the Feast of Tabernacles, though the text does not name it.

It is a historical account, not a sermon. The writer of Chronicles tells how Solomon finished the temple and called the leaders of the people together to bring the ark of the covenant to its new place. He made use of a feast when the people were already gathering, so that the whole nation could take part in this very important moment.

For today: the important moments of faith are best lived in community. Make an effort to meet with other believers to worship, give thanks, and celebrate what God is doing.
exp.12:11:
It says that God himself stands with Judah as their head, or leader, and that the priests sound their trumpets to call them into battle. The phrase about the trumpets refers to a clear signal that calls the people to fight. The verse then warns the Israelites of the north not to fight against the LORD, the God of their fathers, because they will not succeed.

Abijah, king of Judah, speaks from a mountain before facing the army of Jeroboam, king of Israel. He reminds them that Judah keeps the worship that God commanded in the temple, while Israel has turned away from Him. Even so, the account shows that Judah was surrounded and had to cry out to God.

For today: it is not enough to speak well of God; one must truly depend on Him. When you face pressure, do as Judah did: pray with sincerity and trust that God is guiding you.
exp.17:29:
This verse tells that the king of Aram had given an order to his chariot commanders: they must not fight with anyone, whether high or low, except the king of Israel. The chariot commanders were the officers in charge of the battle chariots. Anyone at all, regardless of rank, is what is meant by "anyone, small or great."

Ahab, the king of Israel, had invited Jehoshaphat, the king of Judah, to attack Ramoth-gilead. Ahab disguised himself so that no one would recognize him, but he had Jehoshaphat keep his royal robes. In this way, Jehoshaphat was left very exposed. The one giving the order here is the king of Aram, who wanted to finish off Ahab and bring the war to a quick end.

For today: we cannot hide our decisions from God. Ahab trusted his disguise, but Jehoshaphat, when he cried out to God, received help. In dangers, it is better to seek God than to trust our own tricks.
exp.25:18:
King Uzziah, also called Azariah, became enraged while he was holding a censer to offer incense. As he raged against the priests in the house of the LORD, right before the altar of incense, leprosy broke out on his forehead. The incense is the sweet-smelling smoke burned on the altar.

The Chronicles account tells us that Uzziah, already strong and successful, went into the temple to do what only the priests were allowed to do. The priest Azariah and eighty other priests confronted him. Instead of listening, the king grew furious, and the text presents the leprosy as a judgment from God.

For today: when someone correctly corrects us, it is wise to stop and listen instead of defending ourselves in anger. Success can make us proud, but humility keeps us open to correction.
exp.9:9:
This verse says that the young men who grew up alongside Rehoboam gave him harsh advice. They suggested he tell the people that his father had made their burden heavy, but that he would make it even heavier. The young men are the friends who had grown up with him. A "yoke" is the wooden frame placed on oxen; here it stands for a heavy burden or hard labor. The phrase "My little finger is thicker than my father's waist" is a way of saying: "My little finger is stronger than my father's waist."

Rehoboam had just become king after Solomon. The people asked for relief from the labor and the taxes. Rehoboam set aside the counsel of the elders and preferred that of his young friends, who spoke with pride.

For today: seek wise counsel, not only voices that please you. Before deciding, ask yourself whether the one advising you has experience, humility, and the fear of God.
exp.24:18:
Joash, king of Israel, speaks frankly to Amaziah. He tells him that, having defeated Edom, his heart has become proud and boastful, and he now wants more glory. The phrase "your heart has become proud and boastful" means he has puffed himself up with arrogance. "Boastful" means he talks loudly about his victories. "Stir up trouble" means he is getting himself into a dangerous situation. Joash advises him to stay at home, because if he fights, he will fall, and Judah with him.

Amaziah had defeated Edom and then challenged Joash to a battle. Joash answered with a parable of the thistle and the cedar, mocking his arrogance. The text says that Amaziah did not listen, because God allowed that outcome, since the king had sought out the gods of Edom.

Today it reminds us that success can become a trap if it fills us with pride. Before we get into unnecessary conflicts, it is wise to stop, listen to wise counsel, and seek God's direction.
exp.20:8:
Jehoram, king of Judah, went out with his officers and all his chariots. Edom had surrounded him, but he rose up at night and attacked, striking down the Edomites who had surrounded him, along with the commanders of his chariots. The verse describes him rising up and attacking by night, and "Edomites" refers to the people of Edom.

The chronicler tells the story; no one speaks. Edom had rebelled against Judah, and Jehoram, who had turned away from God, was left in danger. The text does not make clear whether it was a complete victory. It seems he managed to break through, but Edom remained independent. Even so, God did not destroy the house of David because of his promise.

For today: God is faithful even when we fail, but we should not take advantage of his patience. If today you feel surrounded by problems that come from your own bad decisions, return to God with humility. He listens to you and provides a way out.
exp.20:4:
This verse says that Jehoram was thirty-two years old when he became king over Judah, and that he reigned for eight years in Jerusalem. "Became king" means that he took the throne. Jerusalem is the capital of the kingdom of Judah.

Here the writer of Chronicles is recalling the history of the kings of Judah. Jehoram received the throne because he was the firstborn son, but then he killed his brothers to secure his power. After that the text says that he married the daughter of Ahab and followed the evil ways of the house of Ahab. Even so, God did not destroy the house of David, because of the promise he had made to David.

For today: having power or a good position does not guarantee good character. What matters is how we use what God entrusts to us. We can also trust that God is faithful to his promises, even when others fail.
exp.17:11:
This verse tells how the messenger sent to bring Micaiah spoke to him, saying that the prophets, all in one accord, were speaking favorably to the king. So he asked Micaiah to let his words be like theirs and to speak favorably. This verse says that "with one accord" means "all together, in agreement," and that "favorable" means "good news for the king."

King Ahab of Israel wanted to go to war against Ramoth Gilead, together with King Jehoshaphat of Judah. Four hundred prophets were promising him victory. Jehoshaphat asked to hear another prophet of the Lord, so they called for Micaiah. The messenger wanted to spare him trouble, but he pressed him to join the majority.

Today, the majority or the pressure of the group does not decide what is true. Before we speak or decide, let us seek what God says in his Word, even when it is hard to say or hear, and even when we are left standing alone.
exp.5:12:
This verse tells that Solomon had a bronze platform made, about two and a quarter meters long and wide, and about a meter and a half high. A cubit was roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the fingers. He placed it in the middle of the courtyard of the temple. There he stood on it, knelt down before the whole assembly of Israel, and spread out his hands toward heaven to pray.

The one speaking is the writer of Chronicles, describing Solomon. The temple was already finished and the ark of the covenant was inside. Solomon builds this platform so that all the people can see and hear him as he dedicates the temple to God.

For today: Solomon, though a king, knelt in humility. We can draw near to God by recognizing that He is great, no matter who we are or what we have.
exp.31:17:
This verse says that the Assyrians shouted loudly in Hebrew to the people of Jerusalem who were on the wall. They wanted to frighten them and fill them with fear so they could capture the city. Here "to frighten and terrify" points to the same goal: to break the people's courage.

The servants of Sennacherib, king of Assyria, were surrounding Jerusalem. They spoke in the language of the people, not in a diplomatic one, so that everyone would understand. Their plan was to discourage the people and turn them away from their king, Hezekiah, mocking the God of Israel. It was psychological warfare. Afterward, Hezekiah and Isaiah responded with prayer.

Today we too may hear voices that want to cause us fear and make us doubt God. When they come, let us not argue with them until we are exhausted. Let us do as Hezekiah did: bring that anguish to God in prayer, and ask, together with other believers, that He sustain us.
exp.29:22:
The whole assembly that gathered in Jerusalem agreed together to observe seven more days. So in total there were fourteen days of celebration. They observed those extra days with joy.

This takes place during the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah, who called the people to keep the Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread after years of spiritual neglect. The verse does not single out one speaker; it tells how the crowd itself reached the decision. People came from Judah, from Israel, and from among the foreigners, and the renewal had brought repentance, worship, and great generosity.

For today: when God renews us, we do not have to rush back into routine. We can give ourselves time to give thanks, worship, and enjoy his presence, and to do so together with others, with a joyful and generous heart.
exp.1:1:
It says that Solomon organized a large workforce to build the temple. Seventy thousand would be porters who carried loads, eighty thousand would cut stone in the mountains, and three thousand six hundred would be supervisors who directed the work. The phrase "supervisors" means that they oversaw the workers and kept the work moving in order.

Here the narrator of Chronicles speaks, telling how Solomon, son of David, decided to build a house for the name of the LORD. Before asking for help from King Hiram of Tyre, Solomon had already organized the labor force. Scholars understand in different ways where these workers came from, but the text shows that the project was planned with order and effort.

For today: serving God deserves good organization and teamwork. If you have a task for his work, plan it carefully and share out responsibilities, valuing the role of each person, whether great or small.
exp.12:14:
This verse says that the men of Judah raised the battle cry together, and that when they raised it, God routed Jeroboam and all Israel before Abijah and Judah. The phrase "routed" means that God broke and scattered the enemy army. A battle cry is a loud shout raised at the start of a fight.

The account in Chronicles tells of the war between Abijah, king of Judah, and Jeroboam, king of Israel. Judah was surrounded, with enemies in front and behind. Then they cried out to the Lord, and the priests blew the trumpets. The chronicler stresses that the victory came from God, not from military strength. The figures for the casualties are explained in different ways by scholars, but the emphasis of the text is on trust in God.

For today: when you feel cornered, do not wait until everything is resolved. Cry out to God, keep doing what is yours to do with faith, and remember that the final victory depends on Him, not only on your own strength.
exp.24:25:
This verse is the closing formula the chronicler uses at the end of the account of Amaziah. It says that the rest of his deeds, from beginning to end, are written in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel. It is like saying: "If you want more details, look for them there." That book is not the one we have today under that exact name, and it is not known with certainty what it was; some believe it was an archival work that the author consulted.

The one speaking is the author of Chronicles, who repeats this formula with several kings. He has just told how Amaziah defeated Edom, but then worshiped their gods, was defeated by Israel, and lost the treasures of the temple. After that would come his death.

For today: our lives also leave a record. How we finish matters more than how we begin, so it is wise to remain faithful to God every day.
exp.9:2:
The verse tells us that the people sent for Jeroboam, who was living in exile in Egypt. He came along with all Israel, and together they went to Rehoboam to speak with him. The words "sent for him" describe the summons, and the phrase "came to Rehoboam and said" means that they came before him and spoke.

The narrator describes how the gathering began at Shechem, where Israel had assembled to make Rehoboam, son of Solomon, king. Jeroboam had fled from Solomon and was now returning. What follows shows that the people had come to ask for relief from the heavy labor they had endured. This request was the beginning of a decision that ended up dividing the kingdom.

For today: when someone in authority receives a complaint, it is wise to listen with humility and patience before responding. A well-handled conversation can heal a relationship or prevent a great division.
exp.16:12:
He says that King Jehoshaphat kept large supplies in the cities of Judah. He also kept fighting men of great courage in Jerusalem. The word "supplies" refers to stored goods, such as the provisions kept in the fortresses and supply cities mentioned earlier.

Here the writer of Chronicles speaks, telling the history of the kings of Judah. He wants to show that Jehoshaphat prospered because he sought God and followed faithful ways (see the earlier verses of the chapter). Neighboring peoples brought him gifts, and the kingdom grew strong. The verses that follow list the commanders and their troops.

For today: God often blesses those who are faithful to Him, but He also expects us to be responsible and far-sighted. We can trust Him and, at the same time, work with order and effort in our family, our job and our church, never forgetting that true strength comes from God.
exp.23:22:
This verse says that in the spring, the army of Aram went to war against Joash. They entered Judah and Jerusalem, killed the leaders of the people, and sent all the plunder to their king in Damascus. The plunder was the goods they took from the land in the war.

Here the chronicler speaks, telling the story of Judah. Joash, the king, had killed Zechariah, son of the priest Jehoiada who had protected him, and he had also turned away from God. The text that follows explains that the defeat of a large army by a small enemy was a judgment for having forsaken the LORD.

For today: ingratitude and turning away from God bring consequences. Today we can remember with gratitude those who helped us in the faith, and return to God with humility before our mistakes grow.
exp.32:16:
The verse in your Bible says that the people still sacrificed at the high places, but only to the LORD their God. This is part of the wider account of King Manasseh, whose later years and repentance are recorded in other writings. These writings, the records of the prophets and seers, show what he did, how he prayed to God, and the messages they spoke to him for the LORD, the God of Israel. The "records of the kings of Israel" mentioned in the text are ancient sources that we cannot identify precisely, and it is not known whether any of them survives as a book today.

The chronicler, who wrote this history, closes his account of Manasseh here. Manasseh did much evil, yet he humbled himself before God and was heard. The chronicler wants his readers to remember that God listens to repentance and that his prophets spoke with clarity.

For today: do not think your past is too dark for God. If you humble yourself and pray with sincerity, he hears you. And pay close attention to those who speak his Word to you with truth.
exp.30:9:
Azariah, the chief priest, answers King Hezekiah. He tells him that since the people began to bring their contributions to the temple, the priests have had enough to eat, and there is plenty left over. He explains that the reason is that the Lord has blessed his people. The word "enough" describes having all you need, and "great abundance" refers to this large amount of food left over.
