Hezekiah had restored worship in Judah and asked the people to give their share to the priests and Levites. The people responded with generosity, and large piles of contributions were formed. The king asked about them, and Azariah, of the household of Zadok, explains where such abundance comes from. He credits everything to God, not only to human generosity.

For today: when we give with joy for the work of God and the good of others, we can trust that he cares for everyone. And when we see abundance, let us give thanks to him.
exp.22:18:
Joiada, the priest, stationed guards at the gates of God's temple. Their job was to keep out anyone who was unclean, that is, someone who, according to the law of Moses, was impure for worship. The guards at the gates kept watch, and the words "in any way" mean "not at all."

The account is told by the chronicler of Israel. Joiada had just renewed the covenant with God, after the reign of Athaliah and the worship of Baal. Now he was restoring the order of the temple according to the law and the instructions of David. Watching the gates protected the holiness of the place.

For today: God deserves a carefully kept heart. We can set guards over our lives, such as habits of prayer, good friendships, and healthy boundaries, so that whatever pulls us away from God does not enter without permission.
exp.31:28:
This verse tells us that King Hezekiah built cities for himself and gathered very large flocks of sheep and herds of cattle. The reader will notice that the wording here is about flocks of sheep and cattle, and about great wealth in general. The text makes clear that all of this came because God gave him very great wealth.

The one telling the story is the chronicler, who writes about the kings of Judah. Here he explains that Hezekiah's riches came from God's blessing, after the king sought the Lord and the Lord delivered him from Assyria. But the account continues with a warning: God left him to be tested through the envoys of Babylon, to show what was in his heart.

For today: if God gives us possessions, we receive them with gratitude and humility. What we have is a gift, not a reason for pride. It is worth asking ourselves whether prosperity draws us closer to God or makes us trust in ourselves.
exp.4:8:
This verse says that the poles used to carry the ark were long enough that their ends could be seen from in front of the inner sanctuary, but could not be seen from outside the Holy Place. The inner sanctuary is the innermost room of the temple. The phrase "and they are there to this day" means that when this account was written, the poles were still there.

It is part of the account of the dedication of Solomon's temple. The author, traditionally identified with the chronicler, tells that the ark was placed under the wings of the cherubim. This detail about the poles also appears in 1 Kings 8:8. When "to this day" was written and exactly what time it refers to is not known for certain.

For today: God cares about the details, and his presence deserves reverence. We can draw near to him with respect and gratitude, knowing that through Christ we today have access to his presence.
exp.28:10:
This verse says that King Hezekiah speaks to the Levites with affection and asks them not to be negligent or careless. Here the phrase "do not be negligent" means "do not be careless" or "do not be complacent." God chose them to stand before him, to serve him, to minister before him, and to burn incense, which was the incense used in worship in the temple.

Hezekiah, king of Judah, speaks at the beginning of his reign. The temple had been neglected and closed because of the unfaithfulness of earlier kings. He recognizes that this disobedience brought suffering and captivity, and he wants to renew the covenant with God. That is why he calls the Levites to carry out their service.

For today: God calls us to serve him, and we should not put it off for later. Ask yourself what responsibility he has given you, and carry it out today with reverence and steadiness.
exp.15:9:
King Asa became so angry with the prophet who corrected him that he had him put in prison. A "seer" is another word for a prophet, someone who receives messages from God. The verse says Asa was enraged over this matter, meaning his anger had taken over. Asa also oppressed some of the people at the same time.

The prophet Hanani had rebuked Asa because, instead of trusting God, the king asked the king of Syria for help to face Israel. Hanani reminded him that God had earlier given him victory over a huge army because he trusted in Him. Asa did not accept the correction and responded with harshness.

For today: when someone corrects us sincerely, let us not respond with anger or pride. Let us ask God for humility to listen, to think, and, if necessary, to change course.
exp.33:16:
They say that the money found in the Lord's house was paid out and put into the hands of the supervisors and the workers who were carrying out the repairs. The "supervisors" are the men appointed to oversee the work. "Put it into their hands" simply means the money was handed directly to them.

The one speaking is Shaphan, the scribe, who reports to King Josiah. The temple was being repaired, and in the middle of that work the priest Hilkiah found the book of the law. Shaphan first gives an account of the money and the work, and right after this he will read the book to the king. This orderly report prepares the moment when Josiah will hear the Word and respond with humility.

For today: serve God with order and honesty, even in simple tasks such as managing money or carrying out an assignment. And while you work on practical things, leave room to hear the Word of God, because it can guide your life more than any project.
exp.3:15:
This verse lists several utensils of the temple: large pots (kettles for cooking the offerings), shovels (for gathering the ashes from the altar), and meat forks (large forks for handling the meat of the sacrifice). Huram-abi, the craftsman from Tyre, made them for Solomon, and they were made of polished bronze. The phrase "Huram-abi" names the craftsman directly, so the question of how his name should be understood does not arise in this wording.

The narrator of the book, who writes after the exile, describes the building of the temple in detail. He wanted to remind the people returning from exile of the beauty and order of worship to God. Each utensil, even the most humble, had a purpose in the sacred service.

For today: God values work done well, even in small and common things. A shovel or a pot does not draw attention, yet they were necessary. Serve God with excellence in your daily tasks, without despising the ordinary.
exp.12:18:
After defeating Jeroboam, King Abijah pursued him and captured some cities from the northern kingdom: Bethel, Jeshanah, and Ephron, along with their villages, meaning the smaller towns that depended on them. "Pursued" here means he went after Jeroboam and chased him. Some scholars believe that the name in this verse may refer to a city and not the whole region.

The book of Chronicles tells the history of Judah to encourage the people who were returning from exile. Before the battle, Abijah told Israel that God was with Judah. The text explains that Judah won because they trusted in the LORD. Bethel was a very important place, since Jeroboam had set up one of his golden calves there.

For today: the victory did not come from having more strength, but from relying on God. When you face something that is beyond you, trust in Him first and then take the steps that are yours to take.
exp.13:12:
The verse tells how Asa and his army chased the Cushite army as far as Gerar, a city to the southwest of Judah. The enemy fell in such numbers that none of them was left standing, meaning they had no strength left to regroup. Their defeat was complete. Afterward, the people of Judah carried off a great amount of plunder.

This is the account of the battle, told by the chronicler. Asa, king of Judah, faced a huge army, probably led by Zerah, who is called a Cushite (the text does not make clear exactly where he came from). Before fighting, Asa prayed, acknowledging that for the LORD it makes no difference whether one is powerful or weak in giving help. The credit for the victory is given to the LORD, not to the strength of Judah.

Before facing a problem that is bigger than you, pray first, acknowledge your need, and rely on God. Then act with courage, and when victory comes, give Him the glory.
exp.28:11:
This verse begins a list of Levites who responded to the call of King Hezekiah. Leaders from the families of Kohath, Merari, and Gershon are named, since these were the three main branches of the Levites. The Levites set to work, ready to act.

Hezekiah speaks to the Levites after years of neglect of the temple under his father Ahaz. The king wants to renew the covenant with God and asks them to cleanse the house of the Lord. These men are the first to answer. The Bible gives us no further details about them, so we know little of their lives, but their names were written down.

For today: when God calls us to renew something in our own lives or in the church, it does not take fame. It takes only rising up and obeying. God remembers those who serve faithfully, even when others do not notice them.
exp.25:12:
This verse says that under the command of those leaders there was an army of 307,500 trained soldiers. Their job was to support King Uzziah (or Uzzah) and defend him against his enemies. The description of them as a powerful force points to men who were capable and well prepared for battle.

The author of Chronicles, who writes after the exile, tells how King Uzziah organized Judah. The verses before this one name the officials in charge of the army and the heads of families. The verses that follow show that he gave them weapons and built defensive machines. Some scholars think the numbers are literal, while others think they might be approximate. The text wants to show that God helped him wonderfully.

Today we can learn that preparation and order are good, but they are not enough. Planning, working together, and making good use of what we have is wise. Still, it is worth remembering that true strength comes from God's help, and that success should not make us proud, as it later did with Uzziah.
exp.34:8:
This verse tells us that the leaders of the Levites contributed to the Levites 5,000 Passover offerings and 500 bulls. The names listed are Conaniah, Shemaiah, Nethanel, Hashabiah, Jeiel, and Jozabad. The word "officers" here refers to leaders or those in charge among the Levites, and "contributed" means they gave from their own resources, as a generous gift for the Levites who would help with the sacrifices.

The passage is part of the account of the great Passover of King Josiah in Jerusalem. First the king gave, then his officials, and then the officers of the Levites. In this way the feast could be celebrated for all the people, and the Levites were provided for so they could serve. The passage highlights a spirit of cooperation and generosity.

For today: when there is a need in the church or the community, leaders can encourage others by example, giving first and giving with joy. All of us can ask ourselves: what can I contribute, according to what God has given me, so that others may worship and serve well?
exp.5:35:
If the people sin against God, and God becomes angry and hands them over to their enemies, who take them captive to a land far away or near, there is still hope. The words "for there is no one who does not sin" acknowledge that everyone fails. When God becomes angry, he allows them to fall into the hands of their enemies.

Solomon speaks in the prayer at the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem. He asks God to listen to his people in various difficult situations. Here he considers the worst case: losing the land because of sin. What follows shows that if they repent and pray, God can hear them.

For today: you do not have to hide your failures or believe it is already too late. No matter how far you may feel from God, you can return to him sincerely, acknowledge your sin, and pray. He welcomes the one who comes back with a whole heart.
exp.28:15:
The priests went into the inside of the temple of the LORD to clean it, and they carried all the unclean things they found out into the courtyard. There the Levites picked them up and carried them outside the city to the Kidron Valley. The "unclean things" were objects and remains that were not fit for worshiping God.

This took place under King Hezekiah, who ordered the work. His father, Ahaz, had neglected the temple and allowed idol worship there. Hezekiah wanted the people to worship the LORD properly once again. The priests cleaned the inside, and the Levites handled the removal of what was taken out. The passage does not say more about what the objects were.

For today: before we can renew our relationship with God, we sometimes have to remove what stands in the way. We can ask him to show us which habits or attitudes we need to leave behind, and we can do this patiently, with the help of others, just as the priests and Levites worked together as a team.
exp.9:6:
The elders tell Rehoboam that if he is kind to the people, pleases them, and speaks kind words to them, they will serve him forever. Being kind means treating the people with goodness and understanding. Pleasing them means doing them good and meeting their needs.

The ones speaking are the older counselors, who had served Solomon. Rehoboam had just become king, and the people asked him to ease the heavy burdens that his father had placed on them. The elders, drawing on their experience, advise him to win the people over with kindness. But Rehoboam did not heed them, and that led to the kingdom being divided.

For today: whoever holds authority, whether in the home, the workplace, or the church, wins more loyalty by serving with kindness than by pressing their will on others with harshness. Listening to wise people and treating others well builds lasting trust.
exp.24:10:
Amaziah, king of Judah, gathered his courage and decided to act. He led his troops to the Valley of Salt and struck down ten thousand men of Seir, that is, the Edomites. "Summoned his strength" means that he rallied himself and found the resolve to fight. "Struck down" means that he defeated them in battle.

Here the narrator of Chronicles speaks. Amaziah had hired soldiers from Israel, but a man of God warned him not to take them into battle. He was worried about the money he had already paid, and the prophet answered that God could give him much more. Amaziah obeyed, and then this victory came.

Obeying God may cost us something, but he can care for us and give us more than we lost. When God asks us to let go of something, we can trust that he knows what he is doing and act with courage.
exp.31:10:
Sennacherib, king of Assyria, asks the people of Jerusalem whether Hezekiah is not misleading them. In his view, Hezekiah is leading them toward death by famine and thirst by telling them that the Lord will rescue them from the king of Assyria. The phrase "give you over to death" means letting yourselves fall into death, and "misleading" means making them believe something false.

The speaker is Sennacherib, speaking through his servants, while his army is at Lachish. Jerusalem is under threat of siege. He wants to discourage the people and turn them away from their king, mocking their trust in God. He presents their faith as a dangerous deception.

Today too there are voices that ridicule trust in God and say that waiting on Him only brings loss. When pressure comes, do not measure God by the size of the problem or by the mockery of others. Pray, remember His promises, and seek counsel in Scripture before letting yourself be intimidated.
exp.29:10:
Here the verse says that, although many mocked the call, some men from the tribes of Asher, Manasseh and Zebulun decided to humble themselves. That is, they set aside pride, acknowledged their need for God, and traveled to Jerusalem. The verse reads, "Nevertheless, some from Asher, Manasseh, and Zebulun humbled themselves and came to Jerusalem."

King Hezekiah sent messengers throughout northern Israel, inviting everyone to keep the Passover in Jerusalem and to return to God. Many laughed and rejected the invitation. But some responded. The text also says that in Judah God gave them one heart to obey, which shows that obedience is both God's work and a human decision.

When God calls you, do not lose heart if others mock or ignore his voice. Humble yourself and take the step, even if you are among the few. God receives those who return to him with sincerity.
exp.19:20:
This verse tells how King Jehoshaphat, after talking things over with the people, chose some of them to sing to the Lord and praise the splendor of His holiness. They went out in front of the army, singing: "Give thanks to the Lord, for His loving devotion endures forever." The word "consulted" simply means he asked the people for their advice.

Judah faced the threat of a great army from Ammon, Moab, and Seir. Jehoshaphat had already sought God in prayer, and a prophet had said that the battle belonged to God. So the king encouraged the people to trust. Afterward, the text says God caused the enemies to turn against one another and destroy each other.

For today: when you face a big problem, make praise part of your trust. Thank God for His faithfulness before you see the solution.
exp.17:24:
Here the king of Israel, Ahab, orders his men to seize the prophet Micaiah and return him to Amon, the governor of the city, and to Joash, the king's son. The phrase "return him" means the order is to have him put in prison.

Micaiah had just announced that the battle against Ramoth-gilead would end in defeat, while about 400 prophets were promising the king victory. Ahab did not want to hear the truth and became angry. First Zedekiah struck Micaiah, and now the king responds with punishment. The texts do not explain in detail who Amon and Joash were, but they seem to be officials in charge of holding him.

For today: it is easy to surround ourselves only with voices that tell us what we want to hear. Let us ask God for humility to listen to the truth, even when it is uncomfortable, and let us weigh advice in the light of his Word.
exp.25:21:
This verse says that the rest of the story of King Uzziah, from beginning to end, was recorded by the prophet Isaiah, the son of Amoz. Uzziah is the same king, and the phrase "from beginning to end" means the whole of his reign, from start to finish.

The Chronicler closes the life of Uzziah here. He was a successful king, but he ended up with leprosy because he entered the temple in pride. Isaiah is mentioned because he prophesied in those years, though we do not know for certain which writing this refers to. Some think of a document that has been lost; others think it may be part of the book of Isaiah. It is hard to say for sure.

For today: our lives will also be remembered as a whole, not only by their good beginnings. Let us guard our hearts in the days of success, ask God for humility, and finish well, serving him with gratitude and without thinking of ourselves as more than we are.
exp.14:4:
This verse describes a time of great insecurity. No one could travel safely: neither the one who went out nor the one who came in. "Residents" means the people who live in a place, and "conflicts" means fighting and disputes. The people of those lands were caught up in many conflicts.

The prophet Azariah speaks to King Asa of Judah after a military victory. He reminds them of an earlier time, probably the era of the judges, when the people lived without God, without teaching, and without law. Some scholars think it could also refer to other periods of disorder. His purpose is to encourage Asa to seek God, for when the people sought Him in their trouble, God let Himself be found.

For today: when God is absent from life, peace is lost. But if we are in trouble, we can return to Him in prayer and in His Word, trusting that He responds to those who seek Him sincerely.
exp.33:3:
King Josiah ordered that everything tied to idol worship be destroyed. His servants tore down the altars of the Baals, the false gods, in his presence. They cut down the incense altars that stood above them. They smashed the Asherah poles, the carved idols, and the cast images, crushed them to dust, and scattered the dust over the graves of those who had sacrificed to them.

The one telling the story is the chronicler, who reviews the history of Judah. Josiah began to seek God while still young, in the eighth year of his reign, and in his twelfth year he began to cleanse the land. The people had fallen into idolatry for generations, and the king wanted to return to the covenant with the God of David.

For today: if something holds in your heart the place that belongs to God, it is not enough to ignore it. Josiah destroyed it completely. Ask God to show you what you should remove, and act with resolve.
exp.19:11:
This verse says the people ask God to act as judge against their enemies. They admit they are powerless before this vast army that is coming against them, and that they do not know what to do. Because of this, they fix their eyes on God. To look to God in this way means to wait for his help. In this context, to judge means to act justly and to defend them.

The one speaking is King Jehoshaphat, in public prayer before all Judah, in the temple in Jerusalem. The Ammonites, the Moabites, and the people of Mount Seir were attacking them. Jehoshaphat reminds God that Israel had spared these peoples when they came out of Egypt, and now they wanted to drive them from the land God had given them. After this prayer, God answers through Jahaziel.

When you feel powerless or without answers, you can pray honestly: "Our God, we do not know what to do, but our eyes are upon You." Admitting your limit is not a lack of faith; it is the first step toward looking to God and waiting for his help.
exp.31:1:
King Hezekiah saw that Sennacherib, king of Assyria, had arrived and that he intended to make war against Jerusalem. The phrase "had come to make war" tells us that the enemy's plans were clear. The word "saw" shows that Hezekiah did not ignore the danger; he recognized it and prepared to respond.

The one telling this account is the chronicler, who writes about the kings of Judah. Hezekiah had just carried out spiritual reforms in the land, and yet the threat came anyway. That shows that faithfulness to God does not always spare us from trials. The text does not say that Hezekiah doubted God; it only tells us that he saw the danger and began to act wisely.

When a great problem comes, we should not pretend it does not exist. We can look at it honestly, ask advice from sensible people, do what is within our reach, and at the same time trust in God.
exp.28:9:
Here the verse says that King Hezekiah has made a firm decision: to make a covenant, that is, a solemn commitment, with the LORD, the God of Israel. His aim is that God's fierce anger turn away from them. The word "fierce" in the verse means intense and burning.

Hezekiah, king of Judah, speaks at the beginning of his reign. He gathers the priests and Levites to cleanse the temple, which had been neglected and shut during the reign of his father Ahaz. He reminds them that the people's unfaithfulness brought defeats, deaths and captivity. His covenant is a returning of the heart to God, and that is why it begins with restoring worship.

For today: when you see that something in your life has fallen into disorder because you drifted away from God, do not wait any longer. Decide to return to Him sincerely, beginning with one concrete step, such as praying, asking forgiveness, and resuming your time with Him.
exp.35:13:
This verse says that the leaders of the priests and all the people kept multiplying their unfaithful deeds, their rebellion against God and their refusal to obey him. They followed the detestable practices of the surrounding nations. In this way they defiled the house of the LORD, the temple that God had set apart as holy in Jerusalem.

The book of Chronicles does not name its author in the text. It looks back to explain why Judah fell before Babylon. Earlier, King Zedekiah had stubbornly refused to listen to the prophet Jeremiah. Here the guilt is shown to belong to everyone: leaders, priests, and people alike. Even so, God kept sending messengers out of compassion.

For today: it is not enough to be near what is sacred; the heart must be cared for. If we notice that we are growing used to what God rejects, let us listen quickly to his correction and return to him before our hearts become hard.
exp.1:10:
Hiram, king of Tyre, replies to Solomon with a letter. He says that the LORD loves his people Israel and for that reason has placed Solomon on the throne over them. "Wrote a letter in reply" means that Hiram answered in writing. "LORD" is the name of God.

Solomon was getting ready to build the temple, and he had asked Hiram for timber and workers in exchange for wheat, barley, wine, and oil. Hiram, who was a foreign king and had been a friend of David, accepts the arrangement. He recognizes that Solomon's reign was no accident, but something that comes from God's love for his people. We do not know how far Hiram's personal faith went; his language may also be diplomatic courtesy.

For today: Recognize that the responsibilities and opportunities you have come from God's care. In this way you can serve with humility and gratitude, without boasting about what you do.
exp.12:15:
This verse tells how the army of the northern kingdom, called Israel, fled before the army of Judah. It says that God himself delivered them into the hands of Judah, that is, he gave them the victory. The phrase "delivered them into their hands" means giving them triumph over the enemy.

The writer of Chronicles recounts the war between King Abijah of Judah and Jeroboam, king of Israel. Judah was surrounded, with enemies in front and behind. Then they cried out to the LORD, the priests blew the trumpets, and the people shouted. The text emphasizes that they trusted in the God of their fathers. The numbers of the dead are very large, and some scholars believe they may be symbolic or greatly exaggerated.

For today: when you feel there is no way out, surrounded by problems, cry out to God. He can act in ways you do not expect. Trusting in him is firmer than trusting in your own strength.
exp.35:6:
King Nebuchadnezzar took some of the sacred objects from the temple in Jerusalem, such as cups, trays, and other articles used in worship, and carried them off to Babylon. There he put them in his temple.

Here the chronicler, who tells the story of Judah, speaks. Jehoiakim did what was evil in the sight of God, and Babylon began to dominate the kingdom. Carrying off the temple articles showed that Judah was losing its strength and its protection. Some believe it was also a sign that God was judging his people for their disobedience. The Bible does not give more detail about which articles were taken.

For today: what belongs to God should not be treated lightly. We can ask ourselves whether we are caring with respect for our life, our church, and our relationship with God, or whether we let them be lost through carelessness.
exp.3:8:
It says that Solomon, in addition to the temple building, built the courtyard of the priests and the large court, with its doors. He overlaid the doors with bronze. The opening words of this sentence in the source are not repeated here; in plain terms they mean "in addition to this." The courtyard is an open yard around the temple.

The writer of Chronicles, who writes after the exile, tells how Solomon prepared the temple with great care. It is not God or a character speaking; it is a description. The furnishings and spaces are described so that the people would remember that worship had order and designated places: one for the priests and another for the people. Scholars explain the symbolism of the bronze in various ways, so it is wise not to claim more than the text says.

For today: God cares about things done with diligence. You can offer Him even simple and unseen tasks with care, such as preparing the meeting place of your church or serving in small things, knowing that nothing done for Him is insignificant.
exp.17:22:
Zedekiah, one of the king's prophets, went up to Micaiah, struck him in the face, and demanded, "Which way did the Spirit of the Lord go when He departed from me to speak with you?" By this he meant that Micaiah could not have a message from God different from that of the other prophets.

Micaiah had just told them that God had allowed a lying spirit to enter the mouths of King Ahab's prophets, and that disaster was coming. Zedekiah, who had prophesied victory, was offended and reacted with violence instead of examining the message. Afterward Ahab ordered Micaiah to be imprisoned.

For today: when someone tells us an uncomfortable truth, let us not respond with anger or mockery. Truth does not depend on how many support it, so it is wise to listen with humility and test everything in the light of God's Word.
exp.0:9:
Solomon asks God for wisdom and knowledge, that is, good judgment and understanding. "Lead this people" describes his task of directing the daily life of the nation and governing all that this involves. He recognizes that the people is very great and that he cannot govern it by his own strength.

Solomon, newly made king, speaks at Gibeon, where he offers sacrifices to God. Before this, he remembers God's faithfulness to his father David. Instead of asking for riches, fame, or a long life, he asks for help to serve well. God is pleased with this attitude and grants what he asked for, and besides that gives him what he did not ask for.

Today, if you have a responsibility, in the home, at work, or in the church, ask God for wisdom before success. Recognizing that you need help is a good beginning.
exp.3:20:
This verse says that the flower-shaped ornaments, the lamps, and the tongs of the temple were made of gold, of purest gold. The "tongs" were pincers used to trim the wicks of the lamps and keep the flame clean and steady. The lamps were small lamps or bowls for the oil.

The writer of Chronicles describes how Solomon finished the temple in Jerusalem. It is not a character who speaks but the chronicler, who lists the objects of worship in careful detail. He probably wanted to remind the people, who were returning from exile, of the importance of worshiping God with order and devotion. Scholars debate why he insists so much on gold, but he clearly highlights giving God what is best.

Today we can ask ourselves: do we give God our best, even in the small things? Praying with attention, serving with care, and looking after the details can be a way of worshiping him.
exp.16:2:
This verse says that the LORD was with Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, because he walked in the earlier ways of his father David. "The LORD" is the name of God. "The Baals" were the false gods of the neighboring peoples, and "did not seek" means that he did not turn to them or worship them.

The book of Chronicles tells the story as a narrator who reviews the history of the kings of Judah. Jehoshaphat reigned after his father Asa, strengthened his country and remained faithful to God. Some scholars note that David also failed later on, so "the earlier ways" probably highlights his period of greatest faithfulness.

Today we can ask ourselves what things take the place of God in our hearts. Like Jehoshaphat, we can choose to seek God first, and follow the example of faithful people who inspire us to trust Him more.
exp.5:8:
God tells David that he will not be the one to build the temple, but that his son, your own offspring, will build the house for God's name. The phrase "house for my name" refers to a temple set apart to honor God, and the wording in your Bible makes clear that the son is David's own child.

Solomon is speaking at the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem. He reminds the people that David wanted to build it. God recognized that David's desire was good, even though the task would not fall to him. Solomon explains that God's promise has been fulfilled, since he now sits on the throne and the temple is finished.

We can serve God sincerely even when we do not see the final result. God values the desire of the heart, and sometimes our part is to prepare the way so that others can carry on the work. Trusting in his timing frees us from the need to do everything ourselves.
exp.23:10:
This verse describes how the money given to repair the temple was handled. Whenever the chest was brought by the Levites to the king's overseers and they saw that it held a large amount of money, the royal scribe and an officer of the high priest would come and empty the chest, then carry it back to its place. They did this daily, and gathered the money in abundance.

The account is told by the chronicler, not by a character speaking. Under King Joash and the priest Jehoiada, the temple had fallen into disrepair. The people responded joyfully to the offering that Moses had established, and the money was counted by two authorities, one civil and one religious.

For today: when money is handled for the work of God, it is wise to do so with order, openness, and more than one person keeping watch. This protects trust and honors God.
exp.4:0:
It says that when Solomon finished all the building of the temple, he brought in what his father David had set apart for God. This included the silver, the gold and all the furnishings, which he placed in the treasuries of the house of God. "Dedicated" means set apart for God's exclusive use.

The one who tells the story is the chronicler, who writes to a people who were rebuilding their life of faith. He reports that the temple was finished and that Solomon fulfilled David's desire, since David had gathered the materials but was not able to build it. Next comes the bringing of the ark of the covenant, the central moment of the dedication.

For today: what we give to God is sometimes prepared by others before us, and it falls to us to complete it faithfully. Think about what legacy of faith you have received and how you can honor it today, by faithfully carrying forward what others began.
exp.19:12:
This verse says that all the men of Judah, together with their wives and children and little ones, were gathered before God, waiting in his presence. It was not only the leaders or the warriors: the whole household was there too.

The phrase "standing before the LORD" means that they came together in humility to seek God.

The name "the LORD" refers to God.

King Jehoshaphat had received word that a great army was coming against Judah. He called the people to fast and pray in the temple at Jerusalem. Shortly before, he had prayed, saying that they had no strength and did not know what to do, but that their eyes were on God. This verse shows the whole people quiet and attentive, and soon God answers through Jahaziel.

For today: when you face a crisis, do not carry it alone. Seek God together with your family and your church, acknowledge your weakness, and wait with confidence for his answer.
exp.24:23:
It says that Joash, king of Israel, took all the gold and silver and all the articles found in the house of God with Obed-edom, and the treasures of the royal palace. He also took some hostages. Then he went back to Samaria.

This is part of the account of the reign of Amaziah, king of Judah. He challenged Israel to war and lost. The text is not a speech but a narrative. A few verses earlier, the chronicler explains that Amaziah had adopted the gods of Edom, and so this defeat is presented as a consequence of his turning away from God.

For today: what seems secure, such as success or resources, can be lost quickly if the heart turns away from God. It is worth examining whom we are truly following, and returning to Him with humility before losses force us to.
exp.8:5:
She says the queen did not believe what she had been told about Solomon. But when she arrived and saw it with her own eyes, she understood that not even half of his wisdom had been told to her. The phrase "you have far exceeded the report I heard" means that Solomon was far greater than the reputation she had heard about him.

The queen of Sheba speaks here, having traveled from very far away to Jerusalem to test Solomon with hard questions. She had seen his table, his servants, his clothing, and the way up to the house of the LORD, and she was left breathless. Afterward she blesses God, who set Solomon as king to rule with justice.

For today: do not rely only on what others say about God. Come close, pray, read the Bible, and see for yourself. And when you see his wisdom, as she did, give the glory to him.
exp.12:6:
It says that worthless and wicked men gathered around Jeroboam to resist Rehoboam, and they became stronger than him. "Worthless" means empty of value, without worth or honor. "Wicked" describes people who are given to doing evil. "Young, inexperienced, and unable to resist" describes someone young, lacking experience and firmness, who was not able to stand against them.

Abijah, king of Judah, speaks before the battle against Jeroboam, king of Israel. He wants to persuade Israel not to fight, because God gave the kingdom to David. His account places the blame on Jeroboam and on Rehoboam. Scholars note that Rehoboam was about 41 years old when he began to reign, so "young" probably refers to a lack of maturity and not only to his age.

For today: weakness of character opens the door to bad influences. Ask God for wisdom and firmness, and surround yourself with people who draw you closer to Him.
exp.32:17:
This verse says that Manasseh's prayer to God, the way God heard him, and all his sins and rebellion were recorded. It also mentions the places where he built altars on the high places and set up images of Asherah and other idols, before he humbled himself before God. Unfaithfulness or betrayal of God is what the verse is pointing to. All of this is written in the words of the seers, that is, the prophets.

The chronicler, who writes for the people after the exile, sums up the life of Manasseh, one of the most wicked kings of Judah. Even so, he stresses that Manasseh turned back and God heard his prayer. He points readers to where the details can be found: the records of the prophets.

For today: no one is so far away that God does not hear their sincere prayer. Humbling ourselves and returning to Him is always possible.
exp.34:1:
This verse says that King Josiah appointed the priests to their duties and encouraged them in the service of the house of the LORD. The point is that the priests were given clear responsibilities and were motivated to carry out the work in the temple with commitment.

This passage from the Chronicles account tells of Josiah, a king who sought to restore the worship of God. Before celebrating the Passover, he wanted everything to be in order. Each priest was to know his place, as established by David and Solomon. In this way, the feast would not be improvised but carried out with reverence.

For today: serving God includes doing it with order and commitment. Ask yourself what your responsibility is in your church or family, and fulfill it faithfully, encouraging others to do the same.
exp.17:21:
Here the prophet Micaiah tells the king that the LORD has put a lying spirit in the mouths of the king's prophets. Those prophets promised him victory, but the LORD had already pronounced disaster against him. The word "pronounced" here means that God declared it, settling what would happen.

Micaiah speaks before Ahab, king of Israel, and Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, before they go to war against Ramoth-gilead. Four hundred prophets were saying what the king wanted to hear, but Micaiah told him the truth, though it was harsh. It is a difficult scene: scholars understand it in different ways, but they all agree that God is sovereign and that Ahab had already rejected the truth.

Today, this invites us not to look only for voices that flatter us. Let us ask God for the humility to listen to the truth, even when it is uncomfortable, and to measure every piece of advice against Scripture.
exp.5:16:
Solomon asks God to keep the promise he gave to his father David. The phrase "please confirm" in the verse means God should make good on what he said. In other words: "Lord, make true what you promised."

Solomon is praying at the dedication of the temple, in front of all Israel. He has just recalled that God has already kept part of his promise, since the temple is built. Now he prays for the rest: that David's descendants will continue to reign. God had set a condition: that David's sons be faithful to his law. Solomon relies on what God has already said.

When you pray, you can rest on the promises God has already given in his Word. Ask him with confidence, and also with a willingness to obey him.
exp.29:6:
This verse is a loving warning: "Do not be like your fathers and brothers who were unfaithful to the LORD, the God of their fathers." They turned away from God, and for that reason He made them an object of horror, as you can see. To be unfaithful here means to abandon your loyalty to God on purpose.

King Hezekiah sent messengers with letters throughout Israel and Judah, inviting the people to keep the Passover in Jerusalem. It had been a long time since they had kept it as God commanded. The northern kingdom had suffered at the hands of Assyria, and Hezekiah offers them a way out: to return to God, who is gracious and merciful.

For today: the mistakes of the past, our own or those of our family, do not have to decide our future. If today we see the consequences of drifting away from God, we can turn back to Him sincerely. He receives with mercy the one who returns.
exp.14:6:
This verse says the people should be encouraged and not give up. The words "But as for you, be strong" mean to be brave and steadfast. "do not be discouraged" means not to lose heart or grow tired in the work. "for your work will be rewarded" means that God promises their labor will not be in vain.

The prophet Azariah, son of Oded, speaks to King Asa and to Judah. He reminds them that God is with those who seek Him, and that in times without God there was chaos. He encouraged them to return to Him. Asa took courage, removed the idols, and repaired the altar.

For today: when you grow tired of doing good or of being faithful to God, do not give up. Take one concrete step today, such as praying or serving, trusting that God sees your effort and does not forget it. The final reward is in His hands.
exp.29:11:
It says that God's power was at work among the people of Judah, giving them one heart, that is, a sincere willingness to obey the command of King Hezekiah and his officials. That command agreed with what the LORD had already commanded.

King Hezekiah had invited all Israel to celebrate the Passover in Jerusalem, after the temple had been purified. In the north, many mocked the messengers, but some humbled themselves and went. In Judah, the writer of Chronicles explains that God himself moved their hearts. The Scriptures do not say how exactly he did it.

Obeying God is our decision, but it is also his gift. We can pray like this: "Lord, give me a willing heart." When you feel the desire to draw near to God, respond promptly, without mockery or excuses.
exp.35:3:
The king of Egypt, Necho, placed Eliakim, brother of Jehoahaz, on the throne over Judah and changed his name to Jehoiakim. The phrase "placed on the throne" in the verse means put into office, and "changed his name" is the name change the verse describes. Necho seized Jehoahaz, Eliakim's brother, and carried him off to Egypt.

The writer of Chronicles tells the story of Judah in a time of decline. Judah was no longer free: Egypt decided who would rule. Changing the name showed that Necho had authority over Jehoiakim, who was left as his subordinate. Afterward, the text says that Jehoiakim did evil in the eyes of God.

For today: human powers can seem to be the ones who decide everything, but they do not have the last word. Trust God more than leaders or systems, and remember that everyone who holds authority will answer to Him.
exp.9:11:
After three days, Jeroboam and all the people returned to Rehoboam, just as the king had told them to. "Since" here means "because," and the king had asked them to come back on the third day.

After Solomon's death, the people asked Rehoboam to lighten the burden of labor and taxes. Rehoboam asked for three days to think it over. He consulted the elders and the young men he had grown up with. Now the time has come to answer, and he will respond harshly, following the young men. This mistake divided the kingdom. The biblical text also sees in this the hand of God fulfilling what he had said.

Taking time to decide is wise, but it does little good if we then ignore good advice. Before we answer others, let us seek out mature people and ask God for the humility to listen.
exp.35:20:
This verse says that the exile fulfilled what God had said through Jeremiah. While the land lay in ruin, it finally got the rest it had been denied. "Enjoyed its Sabbath rest" means that the land received the rest that had been withheld from it before. "Desolation" means ruin or devastation. All of this lasted seventy years.

The writer of Chronicles writes after the exile. He wants the people to understand that the fall of Jerusalem was no accident. He connects the words of Jeremiah with the law of Moses about the land's rest (Leviticus 26:34-35). Scholars count the seventy years in different ways, so the exact dates are not certain.

For today: God keeps his word, both his warnings and his promises. He also designed rest as something good. This week, set aside real time to rest and trust that God sustains your life.
exp.16:18:
This verse closes the list of Jehoshaphat's armies. It says that all those fighting men were in the direct service of the king. In addition, there were other soldiers whom the king had stationed in the fortified cities, spread throughout Judah. That is, the kingdom had troops in the capital and also defense in every region.

Here the writer of Chronicles speaks, recounting the history of Judah. Jehoshaphat was a king who sought God and strengthened his kingdom (2 Chronicles 17:3-6). The list of commanders and soldiers shows how much he prospered under his rule. The numbers are very large, and some scholars debate how to understand them, but the central idea is clear: the kingdom was well protected.

For today: God values responsible preparation. Jehoshaphat trusted the Lord, but he also organized and took care of what was entrusted to him. We can pray and trust God, and at the same time work wisely in our family, our work, and our church.
exp.33:1:
This verse says that Josiah did what was right in the eyes of the LORD. The phrase "in the eyes of the LORD" means "in God's judgment." He walked in the ways of his father David, whom the verse calls his ancestor. The phrase "he did not turn aside to the right or to the left" means he did not wander from the right path in either direction, staying firm in what was good.

The author of Chronicles is unknown, although Jewish tradition often points to Ezra. He writes for a people who returned from exile. He wants to show them what faithfulness to God looks like in daily life. Josiah was a boy king who came to the throne in the midst of much idolatry. The verses that follow show that his faith became visible in concrete actions.

For today: faithfulness does not depend on age or surroundings. We can begin seeking God while young and remain firm, leaving behind whatever draws us away from Him.
exp.25:22:
He says that King Uzziah died and was buried with his ancestors, but not inside the royal tombs. He was laid in the field next to them, for the people said, "He was a leper." "Rested with his fathers" is a gentle way of saying he died. Afterward his son Jotham reigned in his place, though he was already governing in practice.

This is part of the chronicler's account of the kings of Judah. Uzziah had a long and prosperous reign, but his pride led him to enter the temple to burn incense, something reserved for the priests (vv. 16-21). Then leprosy broke out on him. His separate burial shows that this consequence marked him to the end. The ones who say "He was a leper" are not identified; they seem to be the people or those in charge of the burial.

For today: success does not free us from humility. If we have received blessings or responsibilities, let us guard our hearts and serve God on his terms, never thinking ourselves above his word.
exp.13:14:
It says that Asa's army also attacked the tents of the herdsmen, that is, the places where those who looked after the animals lived. They carried off many sheep and camels, and afterward they went back to Jerusalem. The word "returned" here means "went back."

Here the narrator of the book of Chronicles speaks. He tells how God gave Judah the victory over the Ethiopians, who had come with a huge army. Before the battle, Asa had cried out to God asking for help (14:11). The text stresses that the victory came before the LORD, not by human strength. Camels and sheep were an important source of wealth in that time.

For today: when God helps us through a difficulty, let us not forget to give him the credit. Returning home thankful rather than proud reminds us that every good thing comes from his hand.
exp.28:22:
Then they brought the goats for the sin offering before the king and the assembly, and the king and the people laid their hands on them. The verse describes this ritual act as part of the sin offering. Atonement means covering or wiping away guilt so that peace with God can be restored.

The narrator of the book tells how Hezekiah cleansed the temple and restored worship after years of neglect under his father Ahaz. The sacrifices were for the kingdom, the sanctuary, and Judah. Laying hands on the animal is usually understood as a way of identifying oneself with it and acknowledging that the sin was theirs. Scholars debate the exact details of its meaning.

For today: returning to God begins with honestly acknowledging our guilt, without excuses. Christians believe that Christ offered the definitive sacrifice, so we can approach God with humility and confidence, asking for forgiveness and starting again.
exp.35:18:
This verse describes the destruction of Jerusalem. The Chaldeans set fire to the temple, broke down the city's walls, burned the palaces, and destroyed every valuable article. The "articles of value" are the precious objects kept in the temple and the palaces.

Here the author of Chronicles speaks, telling the history of Judah. He explains that this happened because the people and their leaders turned away from God and did not listen to his prophets. Even so, the account continues and reminds us that the exile had a set time limit, according to the word of Jeremiah: seventy years.

For today: the consequences of ignoring God can be painful, but his word never ends in pure ruin. If you are living through a loss today, return to God with humility. He can bring rest and a new beginning.
exp.8:28:
It says that everything else Solomon did, from beginning to end, was recorded in three writings: the records of the prophet Nathan, the prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite (the name means "from Shiloh"), and the visions of Iddo the seer, which also spoke about Jeroboam son of Nebat. The word "seer" is another word for prophet.

The one speaking is the author of Chronicles, whose identity we cannot know for certain; Jewish tradition connects him with Ezra, but this is not certain. The account of Solomon ends with the custom of citing sources, so that the reader knows there is more information and that what has been said is reliable. Those writings are not preserved today.

For today: our life is also being recorded, and what matters is not only the brilliance of what we achieve, such as silver and cedars, but how we live from beginning to end. Live today in such a way that your whole story could be read honestly before God.
exp.8:6:
It says that those who serve Solomon and are always with him are very blessed, because they hear his wisdom every day. "How blessed" and "how blessed" mean fortunate, greatly favored. "Servants" are those who work in the service of the king.

The queen of Sheba speaks. She traveled from a distant country to meet Solomon. She had heard of his fame, but did not believe it. Seeing him with her own eyes, she acknowledges that the reality surpassed what she had been told. Then she praises God, who placed Solomon as king to rule with justice.

For today: it reminds us how valuable it is to stay close to wisdom. We can seek it every day in the Bible, in prayer, and in the advice of sensible people. And if we have access to that wisdom, let us not let it pass by, but value it.
exp.34:21:
He says that King Josiah did not turn away from Necho, king of Egypt. Instead, he disguised himself in order to fight against him, and he did not listen to Necho's words, which the text says came from the mouth of God. So he went out to fight on the Plain of Megiddo. "Disguised himself" means that he put on a disguise, and "did not listen" means that he did not pay attention to what Necho said.

The writer of Chronicles records this end of Josiah's reign, a king who had sought God and restored the temple. Necho was on his way to fight at Carchemish and asked Josiah not to get involved. Some wonder how God could speak through a foreign king, but the text only says that Josiah did not listen, and it does not explain further. Shortly afterward, Josiah died of his wounds.

For today: even someone who has walked well with God needs humility to listen. Before making risky decisions, it is wise to pray, to seek wise counsel, and to examine whether we are acting out of pride or out of obedience.
exp.22:14:
This verse tells of the end of Athaliah, the queen who had seized the throne of Judah. The soldiers seized her as she reached the entrance of the Horse Gate on the palace grounds, and there they put her to death. The word "seized" means to take hold of her and stop her.

Jehoiada, the priest, gave the order not to kill her inside the house of the LORD, so as not to defile the holy place. Athaliah had ruled with violence and had promoted the worship of Baal. Now the young Joash was presented as the rightful king, and the people rejoiced. The Bible presents this as the end of an unjust rule.

For today: God wants us to take care of what is holy, and also to seek justice with respect and order. Ask yourself what things you should protect in your life so that they remain clean before God.
exp.14:10:
That same day, during the great assembly in Jerusalem, the people sacrificed to the LORD seven hundred oxen and seven thousand sheep. The animals came from the plunder they had brought back from an earlier battle.

The account is told by the chronicler, and it concerns King Asa of Judah. After a spiritual reform, Asa gathered the people, together with people from the north who had joined him when they saw that the LORD was with him. They made this sacrifice as an expression of thanks and as the beginning of a renewed commitment to God, which the following passage describes as a covenant.

For today: what God has given us, we can return with gratitude. Before promising anything to God, it is good to thank Him generously and sincerely, acknowledging that every good thing comes from Him.
exp.27:10:
Now hear me, the prophet Obed tells the army of Israel, and send back the captives you have taken from your kinsmen, because the fierce anger of the LORD is upon you. The people in question are their kinsmen, members of the same nation.

Obed, a prophet of God, speaks when the army of the northern kingdom of Israel is returning to Samaria with prisoners from Judah, the southern kingdom. God had allowed that defeat because of Judah's sin, but Israel was too cruel and wanted to enslave its own kinsmen. Obed reminds them that they, too, have sinned against God.

For today: when we have an advantage over someone, even if that person is at fault, we should not take advantage with pride or harshness. Remembering our own failings helps us act with mercy.
exp.0:13:
It says that Solomon built up a large force of war chariots and horses. He had one thousand four hundred chariots and twelve thousand horses. He stationed them in two places: some in the chariot cities, which were towns set up to house them, and others with him in Jerusalem. The phrase "chariot cities" refers to those towns set up to house the chariots, and "horses" refers to the animals that carried the soldiers into battle.

The one telling this is the author of Chronicles, who recounts Solomon's reign after God had granted him wisdom and riches. This verse shows the power and security of his kingdom. Later, the Bible warns that the king should not multiply horses (Deuteronomy 17:16), so some readers see here a warning sign, although the text itself does not comment on it.

Today we can be thankful for what God gives us, but without placing our trust in resources, savings, or our own strength. May our security be in God.
exp.23:21:
Joash, the king, failed to remember the kindness that Jehoiada the priest, Zechariah's father, had shown him. Instead of being grateful, he had Jehoiada's son killed. Here "kindness" means goodness and loyalty. To "call to account" means to call for an accounting, to bring about justice. As Zechariah lay dying, he asked that the LORD would see what had happened and hold the king to account for it.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book, who closes the account by quoting Zechariah's last words. Jehoiada had protected Joash as a child and had made him king. After Jehoiada died, the king and the people turned away from God. Zechariah called them back, but they stoned him. The account shows that, according to the chronicler, turning away from God brought consequences, such as the invasion of Syria.

For today: let us not forget those who have helped and cared for us. And when someone corrects us with truth, let us listen with humility instead of responding with resentment.
exp.33:24:
God says he will punish Judah because the people abandoned him and burned incense to other gods, provoking him to anger with everything they did. "Other gods" here means false gods belonging to other nations. The phrase "poured out" describes a judgment that falls steadily, like water that keeps coming and does not stop. The "wrath" mentioned is his righteous anger. "Will not be quenched" means the judgment would not be stopped.

The speaker is the prophetess Huldah, sent by God. King Josiah had found the book of the law in the temple, heard it read, and was grieved to see how much the people had disobeyed. He sent to inquire of God, and Huldah answered with this announcement of judgment. Later, God promises mercy to Josiah because of his humility.

For today: God takes seriously that we give our hearts to him alone. But he also listens to those who humble themselves. We can ask ourselves what things today have taken his place in our lives, and turn back to him sincerely.
exp.31:25:
It says that Hezekiah became proud (to be "conceited" means thinking more highly of oneself than one should), but afterward he humbled the pride of his heart, and the people of Jerusalem did the same. Because of this, the wrath of the LORD did not come upon them while Hezekiah lived. Here the name of God is the LORD, and wrath refers to his judgment.

It is the narrator of Chronicles who speaks, and he writes to remind the people that God responds to repentance. Hezekiah had been healed by God, but he did not respond with gratitude; he responded with pride. That brought a warning of judgment upon Judah. The text does not detail here what his pride looked like, and other passages suggest it had to do with showing off his treasures. Even so, his humility held back the punishment.

For today: when God blesses us, let us give thanks and not become self-sufficient. And if we notice pride in ourselves, humbling ourselves promptly brings us back to the favor and peace of God.
exp.27:19:
Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria, came to Ahaz. Instead of helping him, he afflicted him and brought him more trouble. "Afflicted him" means that he oppressed and troubled him. Rather than giving him strength, he gave him no real help or support.

The chronicler tells the story of Judah and explains why these things happened. Ahaz had turned away from the LORD, and the text says that God humbled Judah because of it. Ahaz sought help from Assyria, but that king did not come to his aid, even though Ahaz paid him with treasures from the temple and the palace.

Today we can learn that human solutions, when we set God aside, can cost us a great deal and not give us peace. In trouble, it is wise to seek God first with humility, without failing to act with wisdom.
exp.10:8:
This verse continues a list of cities. It says that Rehoboam also fortified Adoraim, Lachish and Azekah. The names in this Bible appear as Adoraim, Lachish and Azekah in the verse itself. Words in the verses nearby, such as "provisions," mean supplies or food kept in storage.

The text comes from the narrator of Chronicles, who tells how Rehoboam, son of Solomon, strengthened the kingdom of Judah after the kingdom had divided. He built or fortified cities as a defense, especially in the south and west. The passage does not state the exact reason for each project, but the context shows that he was seeking to protect Judah.

For today: preparing with wisdom is not a lack of faith. We can care for our family, finances, health and spiritual life with order and foresight, while trusting that God is our true strength.
exp.24:17:
Joash, king of Israel, answers Amaziah with a short fable. A thistle, a prickly plant of little value, sends a message to a cedar, a large and noble tree, asking that his daughter be given in marriage to his son. But a wild beast from Lebanon comes along and tramples the thistle. "Trampled" means stepped on and crushed.

Amaziah had just defeated Edom and, full of pride, challenged Joash to battle. He ignored the prophet who warned him, because he had worshiped the gods of Edom. Joash uses the fable to tell him not to think more of himself than he is. The text says God allowed this as a consequence of his idolatry.

A victory can swell our hearts and lead us into trouble we don't need. When a wise person warns us, it is good to listen with humility and not let pride make our decisions for us.
exp.6:9:
On the twenty-third day of the seventh month, Solomon sent the people home, joyful and glad at heart for the good things the LORD had done for David, for Solomon, and for His people Israel. The people went back to their own homes, which is where the verse says they returned. They left happy and thankful because of what God had done for the king and the nation.

The writer of Chronicles tells how the dedication of the temple came to an end. The people had celebrated the dedication of the altar for seven days and then kept the feast for seven more days, which was probably the Feast of Tabernacles. Afterward God answered Solomon and confirmed that he had chosen that place. It was a moment of national thanksgiving.

For today: when God blesses us, it is good to pause and remember his kindnesses and to thank him with joy. A life of gratitude sends us back to our daily routine with a renewed heart, and not merely with good memories.
exp.5:17:
Solomon asks in amazement whether God can truly dwell with people on the earth. He recognizes that the heavens, even the highest heavens, cannot contain God. If the whole sky is too small for Him, how much less a temple built by human hands. The phrase "the highest heavens" describes the greatest heaven one can imagine.

Solomon speaks during the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem. He has just asked God to keep His promise to David. Before asking that God hear the prayers of His people in that place, he humbly confesses that God is far greater than any building.

For today: we can draw near to God with confidence, but also with humility. He is immensely great, and yet He hears our prayers. We do not need a special place to meet with Him.
exp.25:11:
This verse says that the family leaders of the strong and brave men numbered 2,600. The "family leaders" were the heads of the clans, or family groups, of Judah. The word "valor" here means courage and determination.

The writer of Chronicles recounts the reign of Uzziah, king of Judah. Earlier, his towers, cisterns, livestock and crops are mentioned. Afterward it is explained that these 2,600 leaders were in charge of an army of about 307,500 soldiers, equipped by the king. The text shows how strong and well organized the kingdom was at that time. How exactly these numbers relate to one another is something some scholars debate, but the central idea is preparation.

Today we can learn that God often blesses orderly work and good organization. Let us care responsibly for what has been entrusted to us, but without forgetting that true strength comes from God and not from our own resources.
exp.23:2:
This verse says that the priest Jehoiada took two wives for Joash, the young king, and that Joash had sons and daughters. The phrase "took for him" means that he got wives for him. The text does not make clear whether "him" refers to Jehoiada or to Joash; many understand it to mean the king, and others think it refers to Jehoiada himself.

The writer of Chronicles tells here the story of King Joash. Joash began to reign as a child, and Jehoiada was his guide. While the priest lived, the king did what was right. This detail about the family shows that Jehoiada cared for the future of the kingdom and of the line of David. Then comes the project of repairing the temple.

For today: God uses people who guide with wisdom, but our faith must have roots of its own. Give thanks to those who guide you, and seek God personally so that you may stay firm.
exp.3:16:
It says that King Solomon had the bronze objects for the temple made in the plain of the Jordan, where the ground was clay, between two places called Succoth and Zeredah (Zaretán in the parallel text of 1 Kings 7:46). The verse describes the objects as being made in clay molds. The "plain" refers to the flat lands of the valley.

The writer of Chronicles describes the preparations and the furnishings of the temple. Hiram, the craftsman from Tyre, made the pieces, and Solomon oversaw the work. It is thought that the clay was used to make the molds, though the text does not explain this further. The exact location of those places is uncertain.

For today: God is concerned even with the details of work done well. Whatever you do with effort and care, whether at home, at your job, or in the church, can be an offering to Him. Do your task today with diligence, as for the Lord.
exp.32:23:
The verse describes what happened after some of King Amon's servants conspired against him and killed him in his palace. The people of the land then put to death all those who had plotted against the king, and they made Josiah, Amon's son, king in his place. Here "struck down" means that the conspirators were killed or punished with violence.

The chronicler includes this to show how the reign of a king who would not humble himself before God came to an end, unlike his father Manasseh. The phrase "the people of the land" usually refers to the free inhabitants of Judah, and scholars debate exactly who they were. What is certain is that they defended David's line and placed Josiah on the throne, who would later become a reforming king.

For today: even when a person's mistakes have serious consequences, God can raise up something new and good in the next generation. Do not define yourself by your family's failures; seek to humble yourself before God and follow a different path.
exp.33:23:
It says that God himself is going to bring calamity on Jerusalem and on the people who live there. That calamity matches the curses, that is, the consequences of disobedience, which were written in the book that was read before King Josiah. "I am about to bring calamity" means God is going to send disaster.

The prophetess Huldah speaks on God's behalf. King Josiah had sent for a word from God after the book was found in the temple and read to him. He was distressed when he saw how far the people had turned away. Huldah confirms that the warnings in the book are real and that the people deserve them because of their idolatry.

For today: God speaks in earnest, and his Word can be trusted, both in its warnings and in its promises. Let us read the Bible with humility, let it correct us in time, and return to God without delay.
exp.22:13:
Jehoiada the priest, the chief priest, gives an order to the commanders of the army: bring Athaliah out between the ranks. Anyone who follows her would be put to the sword. The reason is that he did not want her killed inside the house of the LORD, so that the holy place would not be defiled.

Athaliah was the queen who had seized the throne of Judah. Jehoiada had secretly protected the young Joash, the rightful heir, and now he was crowning him as king. When Athaliah cried out "Treason!", Jehoiada acted firmly, but he took care that the temple remained clean. Some see justice here; others note that it was a very violent moment.

For today: even when we must make difficult decisions, let us try to act with respect for what is sacred and to seek justice with order, not with revenge.
exp.3:21:
This verse says that the objects of the temple that Solomon made were of pure gold: the wick trimmers, the sprinkling bowls, the ladles, and the censers (where incense was burned). The gold doors are also mentioned: the inner doors leading into the Most Holy Place, and the doors of the main hall of the temple.

Here the chronicler speaks, recounting the building of Solomon's temple. He probably wrote after the exile in Babylon, and he wanted to remind the people of the importance of worshiping God with order and reverence. We do not know with certainty all the details of these objects, and some scholars understand "of gold" to mean a covering of gold.

For today: God deserves our best. We can ask ourselves what we offer him: time, attention, talents. Today it is not a matter of golden objects, but of a devoted and sincere heart.
exp.19:23:
The verse says that when the men of Judah came to a place overlooking the wilderness, they looked for the vast army they had been expecting. But they found only corpses lying on the ground, and no one had escaped. The description of the place is clear as it stands, so there is nothing to add there.

This passage is part of the historical account in Chronicles. King Jehoshaphat and his people had cried out to God when they learned that three armies were coming against them. They went out singing praises, and God caused the enemies to turn against one another. Judah never had to fight.

For today: when you face a problem that is bigger than you are, you can pray and praise God before you see the solution. Trusting Him does not remove your responsibility to move forward, but it reminds you that He can work where you cannot.
exp.34:4:
He says that the Levites were to take their place in the Holy Place, arranged by the divisions of the families of their kinsmen, the lay people. Each group of Levites would serve alongside one group of families. The words "divisions" and "families" refer to that order, set out by turns and by groups.

King Josiah speaks, preparing a great celebration of the Passover in Jerusalem. He asks the Levites to stop carrying the ark, to set it in the temple, and to organize themselves as David and Solomon had commanded. In this way the people would be well attended as they offered their sacrifices, and everything would be done in accordance with the word given through Moses.

For today: serving God includes order and care for others. If you have a place of service in your church, do your part with responsibility, thinking about how to help others draw near to God.
exp.27:2:
It says that King Ahaz burned incense in the Valley of Ben-hinnom and sacrificed his sons in the fire. In doing this he followed the detestable practices of the nations that the LORD had driven out before the Israelites. "Burned incense" here means incense offered to false gods. "Abominations" are customs that God hates.

The book of Chronicles tells the history of the kings of Judah to show the people, after the exile, why the nation fell into disgrace. Ahaz was twenty years old when he began to reign, and he turned away from the way of David. Some scholars debate whether "sacrificed his sons" describes a royal sacrifice or a dedication ceremony, but the text presents it as a very grave sin. The verses that follow narrate the defeats he suffered.

For today: let us not sacrifice what is most precious, such as family, peace, or faith, to modern idols like success or money. Let us put God first and care for those He has entrusted to us.
exp.9:5:
This verse tells that Rehoboam, the new king, asked the advice of the elders, who had served his father Solomon during his lifetime. He asked them how he should answer the people. "Consulted with" means that he sought their guidance, and "asked" shows that he put the question directly to them.

The people of Israel, gathered at Shechem, asked him to lighten the hard labor and heavy burdens that Solomon had laid on them. Rehoboam asked for three days to think it over. The elders had experience in governing, so their opinion was valuable. What follows shows that he did not take it into account.

For today: asking for counsel is a good beginning, but it is not enough; we must be willing to listen to and obey wise words, even when they are not the ones we would like to hear. Let us seek mature and godly people, and ask God for humility.
exp.5:13:
Solomon praises the Lord, declaring that there is no God like him, either in heaven or on earth. God keeps his covenant, his solemn promise, and shows loving devotion to those who serve him. "Walk before you" means to live in his presence, and "with all their hearts" means with complete sincerity.

The king speaks on the day the temple in Jerusalem is dedicated. He is on his knees, with his hands spread out, in front of all the people. Before he asks for anything, he remembers who God is and how he has kept what he promised to David, Solomon's father.

For today: before bringing your requests to God, take a moment to remember how faithful he has been to you. That strengthens trust. And ask him for help to serve him with a sincere heart, not just out of habit.
exp.18:2:
Although Jehoshaphat made a mistake, God still recognizes the good in him. "However" signals a contrast, and "some good" points to real, if partial, faithfulness. Your verse names two good things: he removed the Asherah poles from the land, and he has set his heart on seeking God. The Asherah poles were likely objects of worship linked to Asherah, a pagan goddess, though the exact meaning of the word is debated among scholars.

The one speaking is Jehu, a prophet. Jehoshaphat had just returned safely from the war where he allied himself with Ahab, the wicked king of Israel. Jehu rebukes him for that alliance, but right away he reminds him of the good he had done. After this, Jehoshaphat traveled through the kingdom and called the people to return to God.

For today: God corrects with truth, but he also sees our sincere efforts. If you are corrected, do not sink into guilt; acknowledge the mistake, be thankful for the good God has planted in you, and keep seeking him with your whole heart.
exp.27:1:
This verse says that Ahaz did not follow the example of David, his ancestor, but instead copied the kings of the northern kingdom, Israel. On top of that, he had cast images made, that is, idols formed from melted and molded metal, to worship the Baals. The word "instead" here marks a sharp contrast, and the Baals were the false gods of Canaan, linked to rain and harvests.

The speaker is the chronicler, who reviews the history of Judah. He wants to show why the kingdom suffered so much under Ahaz: he abandoned the God of his fathers and embraced idolatry. The verses that follow describe even more serious practices, including sacrificing his own children.

For today: let us be careful about whom we learn from. Ahaz copied bad examples and ended up far from God. Let us seek models who truly love God, and put only Him first in our hearts.
exp.30:1:
This verse says that King Hezekiah reestablished the divisions of the priests and the Levites, so that each group served in its turn. Each one had a set task: offering the sacrifices (the burnt offering was burned whole on the altar, and the peace offerings were fellowship offerings), serving, giving thanks, and singing praises. The phrase "at the gates of the LORD's dwelling" refers to the entrances of the temple area.

Here the narrator of Chronicles speaks. After the great Passover and the destruction of the idols throughout the land, Hezekiah wanted worship in the temple to run with order and consistency. This follows the pattern that is attributed to David.

For today: serving God is not only enthusiasm, it is also order and responsibility. Ask yourself what concrete task falls to you in your church or in your family, and carry it out with joy and steadiness.
exp.29:21:
King Hezekiah encouraged the Levites and spoke kindly to them, because they served the LORD skillfully. He was genuinely appreciative of their work. Then, for seven days, the people ate their portion of what had been sacrificed during the feast. They offered peace offerings, which expressed fellowship with God, and they gave thanks to the LORD, the God of their fathers.

The narrator describes the great Passover in the days of King Hezekiah, after years of spiritual neglect. The people had returned to Jerusalem, and God had heard the king's prayer and healed the people. Hezekiah recognizes the Levites, who kept the worship going, and encourages them to continue faithfully.

For today: Encourage, with sincere words, those who serve in your church or community. A timely word of thanks strengthens someone who works without being seen. And remember that serving God includes rejoicing and giving thanks together.
exp.28:3:
This verse says that King Hezekiah brought in the priests and Levites, who were the ones who served in the temple, and gathered them in the square on the east side. The verse about "gathered" meaning "brought them together" is not needed here, since the verse reads "gathered them." The square on the east side was an open area near the temple; its exact location is not known.

The speaker is the chronicler, who tells how Hezekiah began his reign. His father Ahaz had neglected the worship of God, and the temple had been left in neglect. Hezekiah had already opened and repaired the doors. Now he gathers the spiritual leaders to call them to purify themselves and to cleanse the house of God.
