For today: when something spiritual has been neglected, the first step is to stop and come together in humility to listen. We can set aside a specific time this week to pray and ask God to show us what we need to cleanse or restore in our lives and in our community.
exp.20:0:
It says that King Jehoshaphat died. The phrase "rested with his fathers" is a gentle way of saying he died. He was buried with them in the City of David, which is Jerusalem, where other kings of Judah were also buried. His son Jehoram took the throne in his place.

It is the narrator of Chronicles who speaks. This book reviews the history of the kings of Judah, and here it marks a change of reign. The verses that follow explain that Jehoshaphat gave gifts and cities to his other sons, but the kingdom passed to Jehoram as the firstborn. The text does not say here what kind of king Jehoram would be; that is told later.

Today it reminds us that we all pass away and that what we leave behind matters. We can ask ourselves what inheritance of faith, character and example we are leaving to those who come after us.
exp.19:33:
This verse closes the account of Jehoshaphat's reign. It says that the rest of his deeds, from beginning to end, are written in the Chronicles of Jehu son of Hanani. Those records are recorded in the Book of the Kings of Israel. The phrase "from beginning to end" tells us the record covers his whole reign, not just part of it.

Here the chronicler, the author of Chronicles, who writes after the exile, speaks. He wants his readers to know that his account rests on real records. Jehu was a prophet who had earlier rebuked Jehoshaphat (2 Chronicles 19:2). That work by Jehu is not preserved today, so we know nothing more about it.

For today: our lives are also recorded, with both successes and failures. Jehoshaphat did much good, but he left some things uncorrected. Let us ask God to show us which areas of our heart we have not yet fully surrendered to him.
exp.23:14:
This verse says that the priest Jehoiada lived many years and died at the age of 130. The phrase "full of years" means that he had a long and full life, and that he came to the end of it at peace, with nothing left he still needed to live for.

Here the chronicler speaks, telling the history of Judah. Jehoiada was the priest who guided the young king Joash and helped restore the temple. His long life is mentioned with respect, and the following text says that they buried him among the kings because of the good he had done. But after his death, the officials influenced the king, and things began to go wrong. Some scholars note that an age of 130 years is very uncommon; the text simply states it.

For today: a faithful person can support others, but we should not depend on them alone. Let us seek God for ourselves and give thanks to those who guide us well.
exp.27:26:
He says that King Ahaz died, that he was buried in Jerusalem, but not in the tombs of the kings of Israel. Then his son Hezekiah became the new king. "Rested with his fathers" is a gentle way of saying he died. The "tombs" were the burial places.

It is the chronicler who tells the story of the kings of Judah. Ahaz had led the people into idolatry, and the account closes his life with a note of dishonor: he was not placed among the tombs of the kings of Israel. Some understand "kings of Israel" to mean the kings of Judah in general; the text does not fully make this clear. Even so, the contrast is that Hezekiah follows, a king who would seek God.

For today: our decisions leave a mark on those who come after us. We can choose to live in a way that leaves a good example, and trust that God can raise up new faith, even after dark times.
exp.6:7:
This verse tells us that Solomon held a feast lasting seven days, together with all Israel. It was a very great gathering, a huge crowd that came from every part of the land. "Lebo-hamath" marked the northern border, and "the Brook of Egypt" marked the southern border of the land.

This happened after Solomon had dedicated the temple. The account is told by the chronicler, who wants to show the people how important it is to worship God together. The feast was held with praise, sacrifices, and music. It probably coincided with the Feast of Tabernacles, though the text does not give the details.

For today: God rejoices when his people gather to celebrate with thankfulness. Today we can seek fellowship with other believers and give thanks together, and not let routine dampen the joy of worship.
exp.3:4:
This verse continues describing the "sea," a huge bronze basin that Solomon made for the temple. It says its wall was a handbreadth thick, or about eight to ten centimeters. Its rim was fashioned like the brim of a cup, like a lily blossom. It could hold three thousand baths, a measure of liquid, though its exact equivalent is debated.

Here the narrator of Chronicles speaks, writing long after Solomon. He wants to remind the people what the temple was like and how God was served in it. This basin was for the priests to wash themselves before ministering, as the following text says.

For today: God cares about the details of his service. Before we draw near to him, we need cleansing. Today we can ask him for forgiveness sincerely, trusting that Christ cleanses us completely.
exp.8:4:
Here the queen of Sheba speaks to King Solomon and confirms that the report she had heard about him in her own country is true. "Words" refers to what he said and taught, and "wisdom" to his wise way of thinking and governing.

The queen came from a distant land, drawn by Solomon's fame. She had seen his palace, his table, his servants, and his going up to the house of the LORD, and she was left amazed and overwhelmed with wonder. The Bible does not say precisely where she came from, and scholars debate the location of Sheba. She begins by humbly acknowledging that the report was true.

For today: do not rest only on what others say about God or his Word. Draw near, seek for yourself, and test it. And when you see something good and true, acknowledge it with humility and gratitude, as she did.
exp.19:9:
They say that the people of Ammon, Moab, and Mount Seir, that is, the Edomites, are now coming against Judah. Jehoshaphat recalls that when Israel came out of Egypt, God did not let Israel invade their lands. Israel turned away from them and did not destroy them.

The phrase "whom You did not let Israel invade" means that God did not allow Israel to enter their territory.

King Jehoshaphat speaks in public prayer in the temple in Jerusalem. A great enemy army was approaching, and the people were afraid. Jehoshaphat brings his complaint before God: Israel was obedient and respected those peoples, and now they respond with an attack. He appeals to God's justice and to God's promises.

When you face injustice, do as Jehoshaphat did: speak to God honestly, remind Him of what He has said, and leave the outcome in His hands instead of taking revenge.
exp.11:0:
This verse says that after Rehoboam had established his sovereignty and royal power, he and all Israel with him forsook the Law of the LORD. In other words, when he felt secure as king, he stopped obeying what God had commanded, and the people followed him in this. The phrase "established his sovereignty and royal power" means that he had firmly secured his rule.

Here the writer of Chronicles speaks, recounting the history of the kings of Judah. Rehoboam was the son of Solomon. After the kingdom was divided, his rule grew stronger, but his heart turned away from God. The verses that follow show the consequence: Shishak, king of Egypt, invaded Jerusalem. The text presents this as the result of having rebelled against God.

For today: moments of success and comfort can also be dangerous. When everything goes well, it is easy to neglect God. Let us seek his Word with the same steadiness in abundance as we do in need.
exp.24:27:
It says that the body of King Amaziah was carried back on horses, from Lachish to Jerusalem, and that they buried him beside his ancestors. The phrase "the City of Judah" here refers to Jerusalem, which is also called "the City of David."

The one telling the story is the chronicler, who summarizes the end of Amaziah's life. He had begun well, but he turned away from the LORD and ended up the victim of a conspiracy. He fled to Lachish, and there he was killed. Even so, he received an honorable burial in the land of his fathers. Scholars give no further detail about why he was buried in this way.

For today: it is not enough to start well; what matters is persevering in God to the end. Amaziah left his faith halfway along the road, and his end was sad. Let us ask God to keep us faithful each day, not only in good beginnings.
exp.33:13:
This verse tells that, while the workers were bringing out the money that had been brought into the temple, the priest Hilkiah found the book of the law that God gave through Moses.

The one telling the story is the author of Chronicles. He describes the repair of the temple under King Josiah. The workers carried out their task faithfully, and the Levites supervised them. It is not known with certainty which book it was: many think it was the whole Pentateuch or a part of it, especially Deuteronomy, but it is understood in several different ways.

For today: sometimes God speaks to us anew when we return to places we had neglected. Open your Bible with humility, even if it has been a long time since you set it down, and let it correct and guide your life.
exp.28:19:
Early the next morning, King Hezekiah of Judah gathered the city officials and went up to the house of the LORD. Here "the house of the LORD" refers to the temple. The "city officials" were the leaders and those in authority in Jerusalem. "Early the next morning" means very early.

The priests and Levites had just reported that they had cleaned the temple, which had been neglected and defiled under King Ahaz, Hezekiah's father. Now the king did not wait: at once he took the leaders to worship and to offer sacrifices for the sin of the people. The account presents this as a new beginning for the nation.

When God shows us that something must change, it is wise to act soon and not put it off. Hezekiah did not only clean the temple; he also sought God together with others. We can begin the day, or an important decision, by drawing near to God with sincerity and, if possible, inviting others to do the same.
exp.13:9:
This verse tells us that King Asa went out to face the enemy army. The two armies lined up in battle formation in the Valley of Zephathah, near Mareshah. The idea is that both sides drew up their ranks and got ready to fight.

The account is told by the writer of Chronicles. Asa, king of Judah, had a large army, but Zerah the Ethiopian came with a much greater force. The text speaks of "a thousand thousand," a figure that some understand literally and others as an expression of a very great number. What matters is that Judah was at a disadvantage, and for that reason Asa will soon cry out to God.

For today: prepare yourself and give your best effort, as Asa did by taking his place. But when the problem is greater than you, do not rely on your own strength alone. Pray sincerely, leaning on God, who can help both the strong and the weak.
exp.33:12:
This verse describes how the work of repairing the temple was organized. The laborers were the workers who carried materials and did the heavy lifting. The supervisors watched over everyone doing the work, task by task. Some of the Levites served as secretaries (those who kept accounts and records), officers (those who gave direction), and gatekeepers (those who guarded the entrances).

The book of Chronicles tells this story without any character speaking at this point. King Josiah ordered the house of the LORD to be restored, since the kings before him had let it fall into disrepair. The text stresses that there was order, faithfulness, and a division of tasks. Shortly after, in this same work, the book of the law was found.

For today: God values the one who leads as much as the one who carries, and the one who guards the door as much as the one who keeps the accounts. Ask yourself what simple task you can do faithfully in your church or community, without seeking applause.
exp.22:4:
The plan of protection divides the guard into three groups: one third will be stationed at the royal palace, another third at the Foundation Gate, while the rest will remain in the courtyards of the house of the LORD.

The Foundation Gate was an entrance to Jerusalem; it is not known for certain exactly where it stood.

Speaking is the priest Jehoiada, who gathers the leaders of Judah to protect the young Joash, the king's son, from the rule of Queen Athaliah. He wants to restore the heir of David, according to God's promise. For this reason he organizes shifts of priests, Levites, and guards, so that everyone has a clear task and the temple remains a holy place.

For today: God often works when each person faithfully does their part, even when it seems small. Ask yourself what specific task God has placed before you in your family or your church, and do it with steadiness and trust.
exp.10:11:
It says that Rehoboam, king of Judah, put shields and spears in all the cities, that is, weapons to defend them. The verse also says he strengthened the cities greatly. In this way he made them very secure. At the end it is explained that Judah and Benjamin remained loyal to him.

The author of Chronicles, who writes long after these events, tells what happened when the kingdom was divided. Rehoboam ruled the southern kingdom and was preparing for the threat from the north, led by Jeroboam. The verses that follow show that faithful Levites came to Judah. Some understand that these fortified cities also provided a safe place for them.

Today we can wisely prepare our home, our work, and our spiritual life. It is good to plan and to take care of what God has entrusted to us, but without forgetting that our true security is in obeying Him and trusting in Him.
exp.10:12:
This verse says that the priests and the Levites who lived throughout the northern kingdom of Israel went over to side with Rehoboam, king of Judah. They came from all their districts. The verse's wording, "stood with Rehoboam," shows that they took his side and aligned themselves with him.

Here the narrator of Chronicles is telling the story after the kingdom had divided. Jeroboam, king of Israel, had set up his own altars and had driven the Levites away from serving God. Because of this, they left their lands and homes and went to Judah and to Jerusalem, where the temple stood. For them, being faithful to God came at a great cost.

For today: faithfulness to God sometimes requires giving up valuable things, such as comfort or the place where we live. Let us ask Him for the courage to put God first, even when it costs us.
exp.29:4:
They decided that King Hezekiah and his officials would send a public announcement throughout the country, from one end to the other, "from Beersheba to Dan," which were the outer limits of the land. The invitation was to come to Jerusalem and keep the Passover of the LORD.

To "circulate a proclamation" means to announce something widely, and "prescribed" means according to what the Law of Moses required. The people had not kept it in great numbers for a long time.

Context: Hezekiah had just restored the temple. That year they could not celebrate the Passover on its usual date, because there were not enough purified priests and the people were not gathered together. So they agreed to hold it one month later. They even invited the northern tribes, which had suffered attacks from Assyria.

For today: Returning to God is never too late. If we have neglected prayer or life in community, we can take a concrete step today, and invite others to join us.
exp.29:16:
Since many in the assembly had not consecrated themselves, the Levites took charge of slaughtering the Passover lambs for everyone who was unclean, so that the lambs could be offered to the LORD on their behalf. This means that many people were not ready to take part in the Passover on their own. The Levites stepped in to make the offering for them. "Consecrate" here means to set apart or prepare someone for God. The "assembly" is the gathering of the people.

The account describes King Hezekiah's great Passover, celebrated a month late, in the second month. Many came from the north (Ephraim, Manasseh, Issachar, Zebulun) and were not ready in the way the law required. The Levites helped as best they could, but then Hezekiah prayed asking forgiveness for those who sought God with their whole heart. The text does not explain all the details of this arrangement.

Today we can learn that God looks at the heart that seeks him sincerely. And we can imitate the Levites: patiently help those who come to God in weakness, instead of turning them away.
exp.20:6:
This verse says that God was unwilling to bring an end to the family of King David, even though King Joram was doing evil. The reason was the promise God had made to David. A covenant is a binding agreement or solemn commitment. The lamp stands for a flame that keeps burning, that is, a descendant who would always rule. "Forever" means without end.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Chronicles. He tells that Joram, king of Judah, married the daughter of Ahab and followed the wicked ways of the kingdom of Israel. Even so, God kept David's line going out of faithfulness to his word, not because of any merit in Joram. Christians see in this promise a path leading to Jesus, a descendant of David.

For today: God is faithful even when we fail. That is no excuse for sin, but a reason to turn back to Him with confidence, knowing that his love does not depend on our performance.
exp.3:6:
He says that Solomon had ten gold lampstands made, following their specifications, that is, the design already set out. He placed them in the temple: five on the south side and five on the north. A lampstand is a stand for lamps that gave light to the holy place.

Here the chronicler speaks, recounting how Solomon finished the furnishings of the temple. It was written for the people who returned from exile, to remind them that worship of God was carried out with order and care. Some think the pattern came from the instructions given earlier for the tabernacle, but the text only says "according to their specifications."

For today: God values what is done with order and dedication. We can offer him, with care, the simple tasks of each day, knowing that he is pleased with service done carefully and from the heart.
exp.31:21:
This verse says that the LORD rescued Hezekiah and the people of Jerusalem from King Sennacherib of Assyria and from all their other enemies. The phrase "gave them rest on every side" means that God gave them peace and security on every side, so they no longer had to live under threat.

The writer of Chronicles summarizes what happened when Assyria surrounded Jerusalem. Hezekiah and the prophet Isaiah prayed asking for help, and God sent an angel who defeated the Assyrian army. Sennacherib returned in disgrace to his land and, some time later, was murdered in the temple of his god. The author wants to show that the deliverance came from God, not from the military strength of Judah.

For today: when you face a problem that is bigger than you are, do what Hezekiah and Isaiah did: pray with sincerity and trust in God. He can care for you and give you peace, even though his answer does not always come the way you expect.
exp.35:9:
He says that in the spring, King Nebuchadnezzar summoned Jehoiachin and took him to Babylon as a prisoner, along with valuable articles from the temple. Then he made Jehoiachin's relative Zedekiah king over Judah and Jerusalem.

The phrase "in the spring" marks the time of year when the king's campaigns and decisions were typically carried out. "Relative" here is the wording of the verse, and 2 Kings 24:17 identifies him as Jehoiachin's uncle.

The speaker is the chronicler, who writes after the exile. He wants to explain why Judah fell: its kings and its people turned away from God. Babylon held the throne, but the text shows that all of this happened under God's judgment for disobedience.

For today: do not wait until the consequences force you to change. When God speaks to you through his Word or through a wise person, listen with humility and correct your course in time.
exp.32:12:
This verse picks up the story of King Manasseh after he was brought back to Jerusalem. The verse before tells how he prayed to the LORD, and the LORD received his plea and heard his petition. Now the writer of Chronicles describes what Manasseh did next: he built an outer wall for the city of David, running west of Gihon in the valley as far as the entrance of the Fish Gate. He also built a wall around Ophel and made it very high. In addition, he put military commanders in all the fortified cities of Judah.

The writer tells this as part of the larger story of Manasseh. Earlier he had been a very wicked king, but when he was in distress he humbled himself, and the LORD restored him. Now, back in his kingdom, he takes up the work of protecting the city. Some of the exact locations are hard to pin down today.

For today: when God restores us, He also gives us the chance to rebuild well. We can care for what God has given back to us, being wise and thankful for it.
exp.25:9:
This verse tells that King Uzziah built towers in the desert and dug many cisterns, which are reservoirs for keeping water. He did this because he had much livestock in the foothills and in the plain. He also had farmers and vinedressers in the hill country and in the fertile fields. And the text gives the reason: he was a lover of the soil.

The author is the Chronicler, who recounts the reign of Uzziah in Judah. Earlier he speaks of his power and his defenses in Jerusalem, and afterward of his army. This verse shows that his strength also came from caring for the land and the people's provisions. The towers served to watch over and protect the flocks and the crops.

For today: God blesses work that is well planned and steady. Ask yourself what "cistern" you can dig today, that is, what habit or savings will prepare your future. Do your work with love and responsibility.
exp.30:12:
This verse gives a list of ten men who were overseers, meaning people in charge of supervising. They worked under the authority of Conaniah and his brother Shimei, and everything was done by appointment of King Hezekiah and Azariah, the chief official of the house of God.

The text is a narrative; it is not speaking about one particular person. The people had brought so many firstfruits and tithes that Hezekiah commanded that storerooms be prepared to keep them. These men were appointed to take care of and distribute those offerings with order and faithfulness, so that the priests and Levites would be provided for.

For today: God values orderly and faithful service, even when it is not very visible. If you are given the job of caring for resources in your church or for others, do it with honesty, and recognize that this simple work also serves God.
exp.29:19:
This verse says that God heard the prayer of King Hezekiah and "healed the people." "Heard" means that God paid attention and answered. "Healed" can be understood as meaning that he delivered them from the punishment or harm that could have come from eating the Passover without being purified. The text does not explain exactly how it happened.

The one telling the story is the chronicler of Israel. Hezekiah was king of Judah and had invited people from the north to celebrate the Passover in Jerusalem. Many came without meeting the requirements of purification. Hezekiah asked God to forgive those who sought God with their whole heart, even though they had not followed the ritual well.

For today: God values a sincere heart that seeks him. That does not make obeying him unimportant, but it encourages us to pray with confidence for others who want to draw near to God, even when they still have much to learn.
exp.6:17:
God promises Solomon that he will establish his royal throne, just as he made a promise to his father David. In the verse, God says he covenanted with David, meaning he made a firm agreement with him, and that David would never fail to have a man to rule over Israel.

God speaks after Solomon finished building the temple and prayed at its dedication. God answers with a promise, but he ties it to a condition: walking in obedience, as David did. The verses that follow warn that if the people turn away to serve other gods, there will be serious consequences. The promise is firm, but it calls for a faithful response.

For today: God's promises are sure, but he invites us to live in obedience and closeness with him. Today you might ask yourself, "What concrete step of obedience can I take, trusting that God is faithful?"
exp.17:7:
This verse says that the king of Israel, Ahab, called for one of his officials, a member of his palace staff, and told him to bring Micaiah, son of Imlah, right away. "At once" here means immediately. Micaiah was the prophet of the LORD whom Ahab did not want to listen to.

Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, had asked to consult a prophet of the LORD before going to war against the Syrians. Ahab already had four hundred prophets who told him what he wanted to hear. Ahab admitted that Micaiah bothered him because he always announced bad things. Even so, he gave in to Jehoshaphat's insistence and sent for him.

For today: sometimes we prefer the voices that flatter us and avoid the ones that correct us. God can speak to us through sincere people who tell us what we do not want to hear. Let us ask for humility to listen to the truth, even when it is uncomfortable, and always to measure it against the Word of God.
exp.1:15:
He says that Hiram's workers will cut all the logs from Lebanon that Solomon needs. Then they will float them to him by sea as rafts (logs tied together so they stay afloat), bringing them to Joppa, the port on the coast. "As many as you need" means exactly what it says: whatever amount Solomon requires. From Joppa, Solomon will have to take the logs up to Jerusalem.

The one speaking is Hiram, king of Tyre, in his reply to Solomon. Solomon had asked for help building the temple and had offered wheat, barley, oil and wine in exchange. Hiram agrees and divides the work: he takes charge of the cutting and the transport by sea, and Solomon takes charge of what follows.

For today: great works are accomplished through cooperation and good organization. Recognize what others can contribute, agree clearly on who does what, and work with gratitude and commitment in your part.
exp.5:18:
He asks God to pay attention to his prayer and his plea. "Regard" means that God would notice carefully and not ignore it. A "plea" is a request made with humility. "Hear the cry" means to listen to a sincere and urgent call. Solomon calls himself "servant" because he places himself under God's authority.

Solomon speaks at the dedication of the temple he built in Jerusalem. He has just acknowledged that God is so great that even the heavens cannot contain him, much less a building. Even so, he asks God to listen to the prayers offered in that place, because God had promised to set his name there.

For today: you can pray without fear, even though God is so great. He is inclined to listen to those who come to him with humility. Speak with him sincerely, without complicated formulas.
exp.6:21:
This verse says that when people ask why God allowed so much ruin in the land and in the temple, the answer will be clear: the people abandoned the Lord, the God who brought their ancestors out of Egypt, and attached themselves to other gods. The verse does not use the words "embraced" or "foreign," so the meaning is stated directly: they took up these other gods, giving them devotion and loyalty as though they belonged to them. "Serve" here means worshipping them.

God is speaking to Solomon after the dedication of the temple. It is a warning: if the people turn away from Him, consequences will come. God wants everyone to understand that the punishment would not be a matter of chance, but the result of leaving the God who had set them free.

For today: examine what you give your heart and your time to. Remember what God has done for you and put Him first again, before other things take His place.
exp.35:14:
It says that the Lord, the God of Israel's ancestors, sent word to his people again and again through his messengers, the prophets. The phrase "again and again" shows that he kept at it persistently and from the very start, never giving up on them. The reason was that he had compassion on his people and on his dwelling place, the temple, where he dwelt among them.

The writer of Chronicles sums up the fall of Judah. Earlier, he speaks of the rebellion of King Zedekiah and of the corruption of the people and the priests. This verse shows that the judgment did not come without warning: God warned them patiently, and what follows tells how they rejected it.

For today: God is still patient and speaks to us persistently, for example through his Word or through people who advise us. Let us not harden our hearts; let us listen promptly and turn back to him.
exp.5:38:
This verse asks that God hear from heaven, where he dwells, the prayer and the pleas of his people. It also asks that he uphold their cause and forgive his people for having sinned against him. "Uphold their cause" means that God would look after them and do them justice. A "plea" is a sincere appeal.

King Solomon is speaking during the prayer he offered when he dedicated the temple in Jerusalem. He imagines that, because of their sin, the people could end up captive in a foreign land. Then he asks that, if they repent with all their heart and pray, God would hear them and forgive them.

For today: when you fail, do not turn away from God out of shame. Return to him sincerely, acknowledge your mistake, and trust that he hears and forgives those who repent.
exp.19:25:
On the fourth day the people of Judah gathered in a valley and there praised God. For this reason the place came to be called the Valley of Beracah, which in Hebrew means "blessing." The words "to this day" show that the name was still in use when the book was written. "Place" refers to a location, and "blessed the LORD" means that they gave thanks and praised him.

This is part of the historical account in Chronicles. King Jehoshaphat and Judah were surrounded by a very large enemy army, and they had cried out to God. He delivered them without their having to fight: the enemies destroyed one another. After gathering the spoil for three days, the people stopped to give thanks.

For today: it is not enough to receive God's help, we must also stop and give him thanks. Today you can remember a prayer that was answered, and set aside a moment to thank him in a concrete way. In this way your "valley" of difficulty can become a place of blessing.
exp.1:0:
It says that Solomon made a firm decision: to build a house for the Name of the LORD, a place set apart to honor God, and also a royal palace for himself to rule from. "Purposed" means that he set his mind and resolved to do it. "A house for the Name of the LORD" refers to a place dedicated to God, where his name would be honored. "A royal palace for himself" refers to his own residence as king.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, the one who tells the story of Israel. Solomon was the son of David, and David had gathered materials for the temple, but it was Solomon who built it. The text that follows shows the scale of the project: thousands of workers and help from the king of Tyre. The author places the house of God first in the description.

Today we can ask ourselves what place God holds in our plans. Before building our work, home, or future, it is wise to resolve firmly to give God first place, and to do so with steadfastness and commitment.
exp.1:12:
Here King Hiram of Tyre tells Solomon that he has sent him a man with great skill and creativity. "Skillful" means that he is good at his craft, and "endowed with creativity" means that he has a gift for making fine things. The verse names him Huram-abi and says that Hiram is sending him. Some take the phrase about "my father" to mean that this man was a close servant or adviser to Hiram, but this is not certain.

Hiram is answering a letter from Solomon, who asked him for materials and a skilled worker to build the temple. Hiram acknowledges that the God of Israel made the heavens and the earth, and sends this craftsman, the son of a woman from the tribe of Dan and a Tyrian father, to help with the work.

For today: God uses the talents of people, even those who come from other places, to do his work. Put your skills at the service of God and of others, and value what others contribute.
exp.12:7:
This verse says that the people of the north, Israel, believe they can resist the kingdom of the Lord, which is in the hands of David's descendants. They trust that they are a vast army and that they have the golden calves Jeroboam made for them as gods.

Abijah, king of Judah, speaks before the battle against Jeroboam. From a mountain he reproaches them for rebelling, changing the priesthood, and worshiping images. Abijah affirms that Judah remains faithful to the Lord. The text records his speech; it does not tell us everything that was in his heart.

For today: it is not enough to be the majority or to have resources. We should ask ourselves what we truly trust in, and place our security in God and not in things we ourselves make.
exp.29:18:
This verse completes King Hezekiah's prayer. He asks that the LORD, the God of their fathers, pardon the one who sets his heart on seeking God, even if that person is not cleansed according to the purification rules of the sanctuary. The phrase "sets his heart" means he has made up his mind and turned his whole inner self toward God.

Hezekiah was king of Judah and was holding a great Passover in Jerusalem. Many from the north, from Ephraim, Manasseh, Issachar and Zebulun, came without carrying out the purification rules and ate the Passover in an irregular way. The king prayed for them, and God heard him and healed the people. For this reason the feast ended with great joy.

For today: God cares about the rules, but above all he looks at the heart that seeks him with sincerity. Come near to him with humility, trust in his goodness, and also pray for others who struggle to draw near to him.
exp.30:15:
This verse says that, in addition, portions were distributed to the males registered by family lines who were three years old or older, and to everyone who would enter the house of the LORD to carry out their daily duties and the responsibilities of their divisions. The phrase "registered by family lines" means enrolled in the records of their households. The word "divisions" refers to their rotating groups of service.

Here no single character speaks; it is the chronicler who recounts what happened in the days of King Hezekiah. The people had brought abundant tithes and offerings, and faithful men were appointed to distribute them fairly among priests and Levites, the great and the small, so that they could devote themselves to the service of the temple.

For today: God cares for those who serve, and we can support with generosity and fairness those who work in ministry. Whoever distributes what belongs to God must do it with faithfulness.
exp.0:8:
Solomon asks God to keep the promise he made to his father David. "Let Your promise be fulfilled" means that it should come true and be carried out completely. Solomon acknowledges that God has made him king over a people as numerous as the dust of the earth, that is, too many to count.

Solomon speaks at night, after offering sacrifices at Gibeon. God appears to him and tells him to ask for whatever he wants. Before asking, Solomon remembers God's faithfulness to David. He feels small before an enormous task: governing Israel. That is why he will soon ask for wisdom and not for riches.

For today: when a responsibility feels too big for us, we can begin by remembering that God has been faithful before. Then, instead of trusting only in our own strength, we can humbly ask him for his help and his guidance.
exp.32:7:
God promises that he will no longer force Israel out of the land he gave to their ancestors, on one condition: that the people carefully do everything he commanded them through Moses. "Cause the feet to leave" means to drive out or banish. "Your fathers" refers to the patriarchs and the generations before them. The laws, the statutes and the judgments are the commandments, moral standards and rules for living that God gave.

God is speaking, and the text recalls this during the reign of Manasseh, who practiced idolatry and sorcery and even set an idol in the temple. God had given them a promise of staying in the land, but tied to their obedience. The verses that follow show that the people did not listen, and Manasseh ended up captive in Babylon.

For today: God's blessings are a gift, but he invites us to respond to him with faithfulness. Ask yourself what things compete with God in your heart, and surrender them to him today.
exp.20:11:
This verse says that a letter came to King Jehoram of Judah from the prophet Elijah. In it, the LORD presents himself as "the God of your father David" and rebukes Jehoram for not walking in the ways of his father Jehoshaphat or of Asa, king of Judah, two kings who for the most part sought God.

God speaks through Elijah. Jehoram had abandoned the LORD, set up high places for idol worship, and drawn the people into that unfaithfulness. In addition, according to the text that follows, he had killed his brothers. There is a historical difficulty: some believe Elijah had already been taken up to heaven, and the Bible does not explain how this letter arrived. Several answers have been proposed, but there is no certainty.

Today, this passage invites us not to live on inherited faith, but to decide to follow God personally. God also speaks to us with clarity and calls us to return to him before the consequences grow.
exp.7:2:
It says that Solomon went to a region called Hamath-zobah and captured it. Hamath is an area north of Israel, in what is today Syria. The phrase "captured it" here means that he took control of the place by force.

This book was written by an unknown author who looked back at the history of Israel to encourage a people who were returning from exile. It recounts Solomon's achievements after building the temple. Scholars are not sure of the details of this campaign, since the Bible says little. Even so, it shows that the kingdom was strong and secure, and that Solomon took care of its borders.

For today: after a great task, do not be left with nothing to do. Solomon continued to look after what God had entrusted to him. Ask yourself what responsibility needs your constant attention, such as your family, your faith, or your work, and care for it faithfully.
exp.17:0:
This verse says that Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, had a great deal of wealth and respect. Yet he allied himself with Ahab, king of Israel, through a family marriage. The reader's wording "allied himself with Ahab by marriage" makes clear that the alliance was formed by marriage, so this is the connection to keep in view. Other passages of the Bible explain that Jehoshaphat's son Jehoram married Athaliah, daughter of Ahab.

The writer of Chronicles tells this as an introduction to the story of the war at Ramoth-gilead. Jehoshaphat had been a king faithful to God, but here he joins himself to a king who worshiped other gods. The account shows how that closeness led him into a dangerous situation, and later a prophet rebuked him for it.

For today: when God blesses us with success or money, we should be careful about whom we join ourselves to. Alliances can bring advantages, but they can also drag us into decisions that do not please God.
exp.7:9:
It says that Solomon had two hundred and fifty supervisors, placed over the people doing the work. These men directed and oversaw the laborers.

The phrase "chief officers" refers to the officers of highest rank among the overseers.

The phrase "supervisors" means that they had authority over the workers.

The one speaking is the chronicler, who is reviewing the reign of Solomon. He has just been describing the king's great building projects. The Israelites were not made into servants; that labor fell instead on the peoples who remained in the land. This verse shows a well-organized administration.

For today: God values order and good organization. If you lead something in your home, church, or work, do it with responsibility and treat people with justice, remembering that you too are accountable to God.
exp.11:7:
God says that Judah will become a servant of Shishak, king of Egypt, but the nation will not be destroyed. The opening word of the verse marks a turn from judgment toward mercy, and the goal stated in the verse is that the people would learn the difference between serving God and serving the kings of other lands.

The Lord speaks, through the prophet Shemaiah, to Rehoboam and the leaders. They had turned away from God, and Egypt invaded them. When they humbled themselves, God did not destroy them, but He allowed them to live with a consequence: becoming Egypt's servants and losing their treasures. Some understand this as a lesson and not only as a punishment.

For today: God can forgive us and rescue us from the worst, and still allow us to see the cost of having walked away from Him. That experience can teach us to value His care and to serve Him with gratitude, not with carelessness.
exp.30:4:
As soon as the order went out, the Israelites were generous. They brought the firstfruits, that is, the first and best of the harvest: grain, new wine, oil, and honey, and everything else the fields produced. They brought in an abundance, a tithe of everything, meaning a tenth of all they had. The phrase "the order went out" means it was announced publicly.

The one giving the order is King Hezekiah, after cleansing the temple and restoring worship in Jerusalem. He himself set the example with his offerings. He wanted the priests and Levites to be able to devote themselves fully to serving God, supported by what the people gave according to the law.

Giving joyfully and from the first of what we receive shows that we trust God. When leadership sets an example and the people respond wholeheartedly, the service of God is sustained and the whole community is blessed.
exp.23:18:
God sent prophets to his people to bring them back to himself. The prophets "testified against them," meaning they warned them plainly and bore witness against their sin. But the people would not listen to them.

The account concerns the kingdom of Judah after the death of the priest Jehoiada, who had been a good influence on King Joash. Without that guidance, the officials persuaded the king, and the people turned away from the temple and served idols. Even so, God did not abandon them at once: out of mercy, he sent them prophets. Later, Zechariah, son of Jehoiada, spoke and was stoned.

Today, God still calls us to return to him, sometimes through people who tell us uncomfortable truths. We can ask ourselves: do I listen with humility when someone corrects me according to the Bible?
exp.15:3:
This verse tells that Ben-hadad, king of Syria, listened to King Asa and agreed to his request. He then sent the commanders of his army against several cities of Israel, and they conquered them: Ijon, Dan, Abel-maim, and all the store cities of Naphtali. "Listened" means that he went along with the plan, and "conquering" means that his forces captured these cities and took control of them.

Here the narrator of Chronicles is speaking. Baasha, king of Israel, was building Ramah to pressure Judah. Asa, instead of trusting in God, took silver and gold from the temple and the palace to buy Syria's help. It worked in the short term, but the text goes on to show that God rebuked him for not relying on Him.

For today: when pressure comes, before reaching for a human shortcut, let us pray and seek God's counsel. A quick solution may solve today's problem, but it can also cost us our trust in the Lord.
exp.26:1:
Jotham did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, just as his father Uzziah had done. However, he did not enter the temple of the LORD. Yet the people still behaved corruptly, even with a good king on the throne.

The one telling the story is the chronicler of Judah, who summarizes Jotham's reign. By noting that he did not enter the temple, the chronicler is likely contrasting him with Uzziah, who went in to burn incense, a task reserved for the priests, and was punished with leprosy (2 Chronicles 26). Jotham did not repeat that mistake.

For today: learn from the mistakes of those who came before you, without repeating them. And remember that being faithful to God does not depend on what the majority does. Even when the people around you are behaving badly, you can keep doing what is right.
exp.31:6:
The verse tells the people of Judah to be strong and courageous, and not to be afraid or discouraged because of the king of Assyria and his vast army. The reason given is that there is a greater One on their side than on the side of the Assyrians. "Be strong and courageous" means: be brave and make yourselves strong.

King Hezekiah speaks to the officers and the people at the city gate of Jerusalem. The Assyrians, led by Sennacherib, were threatening the city. Hezekiah had already repaired the walls and prepared weapons, but now he speaks to their hearts. In the verses that follow he explains that the Assyrians rely only on human strength, while Judah has the LORD to help them.

For today: do what is yours to do with responsibility, as Hezekiah did, but do not let fear rule you. When you face a great problem, remember that God is with you and trust in his help.
exp.5:1:
Solomon tells God that he has built him an exalted house, the temple, as a place for God to dwell forever. The house is set apart for God's presence.

The one speaking is Solomon, the king of Israel, just after finishing the temple in Jerusalem and bringing the ark into the holy place. Earlier he recalled that God had said he would dwell in thick darkness, like the cloud of his glory. Here he speaks to God in prayer before the people. Later in his prayer he acknowledges that God cannot be contained in any building (2 Chronicles 6:18).

For today: God desires to be near his people. We can prepare a place, and also a time, to seek him with reverence, remembering that he is greater than any space.
exp.24:16:
Amaziah, king of Judah, took counsel and then sent word to Joash, king of Israel. He said, "Come, let us meet face to face." That invitation was a challenge: he wanted to confront him in battle. The words "took counsel" mean that he had already consulted his advisers.

Shortly before this, Amaziah had worshiped the gods of Edom, and God sent him a prophet to correct him. Amaziah not only rejected the prophet but threatened him. After this, the text shows that he decided to go to war against Israel. However, the account does not give all his reasons in detail; some think that pride moved him after defeating Edom.

Today, good advice is not enough if we stop listening to God. Before making important decisions, it is wise to pray, to receive correction with humility, and to guard against pride after success.
exp.23:3:
After some time, King Joash set his heart on repairing the temple. "Set his heart on" means that he made up his mind to do it and felt a strong desire to see it through. "The house of the LORD" is the temple in Jerusalem, which had fallen into disrepair.

Here the narrator of the book of Chronicles is speaking. Joash was a young king who had been protected and guided by the priest Jehoiada. While Jehoiada lived, Joash did what was right. The text shows that the king took the initiative to restore the temple, although later the Levites were slow to respond and the king had to insist.

For today: when you feel the desire to do something good for God or for your church, do not let it remain only an intention. Make a simple plan, ask for help, and be steady, even when others are slow to respond.
exp.33:17:
This verse tells us that Shaphan, the scribe, informed King Josiah that the priest Hilkiah had handed him a book. Then Shaphan read it aloud in the presence of the king. A "scribe" was the secretary who wrote and looked after documents.

The speaker is Shaphan, an official of the king. He had just reported on the money gathered to repair the temple. Then he mentions the book found in the house of the LORD. Many understand it to be the book of the law, or part of it, though the text here does not say more. When he heard it, the king tore his clothes, a sign of grief and repentance.

For today: it is not enough to have the Bible nearby; we must listen to it with attention. Josiah did not let it pass as just one more piece of information, but allowed it to speak to his heart. Today you can read a passage calmly and ask yourself: what is God asking me to change?
exp.20:19:
It says that Jehoram was thirty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for eight years. He died, and no one was sorry to see him go. They buried him in the City of David, but not in the tombs of the kings, so he did not receive the honor that other kings of Judah had.

The writer of Chronicles, who writes after the exile, tells the story of Jehoram, king of Judah. He married into a family that turned people away from the Lord, killed his brothers, and led the people into idolatry (2 Chron. 21:4-13). The chronicler shows how his life ended: sick, without honor, and without mourning from the people.

For today: what matters most is not position or fame, but how we live before God and how we treat others. Let us ask him for help to leave a legacy of faith, kindness, and faithfulness.
exp.17:2:
Here King Ahab asks Jehoshaphat whether he will go with him against Ramoth-gilead. Jehoshaphat says yes, and he does so without reservation: "I am as you are, and my people are your people; we will join you in the war." The phrase means that he places himself completely at Ahab's disposal.

Ahab was king of Israel in the north and Jehoshaphat was king of Judah in the south. They were already related through a family alliance, and Ahab had just received him with a great feast to win him over. Jehoshaphat gave his answer before seeking God's direction; only afterward does he ask to consult the LORD. Many readers see a hasty decision here.

For today: before we commit ourselves to a person or a project, even when we like them or they have treated us generously, it is wise to pray and ask God for guidance first, not afterward.
exp.8:3:
This verse lists what the queen of Sheba saw in Solomon's court: the food at his table, the seating of his servants, the service and attire of his attendants, the attire of his cupbearers, and the burnt offerings he presented at the house of the LORD. At the end it says "it took her breath away," that is, she was overwhelmed and left breathless.

The one who tells the story is the chronicler. The queen of Sheba came from far away to test Solomon with hard questions. Seeing the king's wisdom, his house, and his order, she was deeply impressed. She herself will say so in the following verse.

For today: excellence and order in what we do can move others to admire God. May our work and our lives, done with integrity, point to the Lord and not to ourselves.
exp.27:12:
What it says: Some leaders from Ephraim tell the army of Israel not to bring the captives from Judah into Samaria. If they do, they will bring more guilt on themselves before the LORD. They admit that their guilt is already great and that the LORD's fierce anger is upon Israel.

Context: The speakers are Azariah, Berechiah, Jehizkiah and Amasa, leaders of Ephraim. The northern kingdom, Israel, had defeated Judah and had taken many prisoners, who were their own brothers. The prophet Oded had already confronted them. These leaders supported and protected the captives.

For today: It takes courage to say "this is wrong" even when everyone is celebrating a victory. It is also wise to recognize our own failures before adding another. If we have hurt someone, God gives us the opportunity to correct course and make amends through concrete acts of compassion.
exp.5:36:
It says that if the people of Israel are taken away into captivity because of their sins, and there they come to their senses, meaning they recognize their error and change direction, they can pray to God. "Turning back" here means turning toward God. The words "wicked" and "wrong" refer to doing wrong and failing to honor God. The prayer is simple: "We have sinned and done wrong; we have acted wickedly."

King Solomon is speaking in his prayer at the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem. He asks that if the people fail and suffer the consequences, God will hear them when they repent. Solomon knows that no one stops sinning, and so he appeals to God's mercy. It is not a guaranteed prophecy but a request.

For today: no matter how far you feel from God, you can always return. Begin with honesty: acknowledge your wrongdoing without excuses, and pray. The Bible shows a God who is willing to listen to a repentant heart.
exp.26:5:
It says that Jotham grew powerful, that is, that he became strong and stable. The reason it gives is that he "ordered his ways" before the LORD his God. To order one's ways means to carefully arrange and direct one's own conduct. The word for "grew powerful" in the verse carries the same idea of strength.

The speaker is the chronicler, an inspired author who summarizes the history of the kings of Judah. Before this verse he mentions Jotham's works and his victory over the Ammonites. Here he explains the reason: his strength did not come only from cities, towers, or victories, but from living deliberately before God.

For today: before seeking success, stability, or achievements, it is wise to order our lives with God. You can begin each day by calmly thinking about your decisions, your work, and your relationships, and asking yourself whether you are living them honestly before Him.
exp.20:14:
It says that God announces to Joram a serious and long-lasting illness in his bowels, that is, in his intestines. Day after day he will suffer from it, and it will be so severe that, over time, his bowels would come out of his body.

The one speaking is the prophet Elijah, who sends Joram a letter on behalf of Jehovah. Joram, king of Judah, had killed his brothers, had imitated the idolatry of the kings of Israel, and had led the people astray with him. It is a judgment for his wickedness. Afterward, the account tells that he died of a painful sickness (21:18-19). Some scholars debate the exact timing of the letter, since it is believed that Elijah had already been taken up into heaven.

For today: God sees how we use our influence over others. Examine whether your decisions lead those around you toward God or away from Him, and seek his forgiveness and his way.
exp.26:8:
This verse says that King Jotham died and was buried in the City of David, that is, Jerusalem. The verse's phrase "rested with his fathers" is a gentle way of saying he died. Afterward his son Ahaz reigned in his place.

The one who speaks is the chronicler, who sums up the end of Jotham's reign, a king who, according to this chapter, was faithful to God and grew strong because he walked before Him. Here he closes Jotham's story with a brief note and passes the throne to his son. The text does not explain why Ahaz was so different from his father; it only announces the change. Later, the book presents him as an unfaithful king.

For today: even when a faithful life ends, we cannot guarantee how those who come after us will live. That is why it is good for us to teach and show our faith with love and steadiness, and to pray for our children, since each one will answer to God personally.
exp.25:5:
Uzziah went out to wage war against the Philistines, his neighbors to the west. He tore down the walls of three cities: Gath, Jabneh (also called Jabneel), and Ashdod. Then he built cities of his own in the area of Ashdod and among the Philistines, to establish his control. "Wage war" and "tore down" are plain words; "walls" means the defensive walls of a city.

The one speaking is the chronicler, who reviews the history of Judah. Uzziah reigned well because he sought God, guided by Zechariah, a man instructed in the things of God. The text makes clear that God helped him and prospered him while he sought him. Later, the same account shows that Uzziah grew proud and fell.

For today: our greatest achievements depend on staying close to God. If something in your life is going well, thank God for it and keep seeking him with humility, without trusting in your own strength.
exp.21:5:
This verse says that Joram of Israel returned to Jezreel to recover from the wounds the Arameans had inflicted on him at Ramah, when he fought against Hazael, king of Aram. Then Ahaziah, son of Jehoram, king of Judah, went down to Jezreel to visit Joram, because Joram had been wounded. "To recover" means to get well again, and "went down" points to his journey to Jezreel.

Here the writer of Chronicles tells the story with a spiritual perspective. He explains that Ahaziah did evil because he followed the counsel of the house of Ahab. He went along with Joram into this alliance, and that partnership led him into a dangerous place. The next verse says that God used this for his downfall, while Jehu carried out judgment.

For today: our friendships and the advice we receive shape us over time. It is wise to ask ourselves who advises us and where they are leading us, and to seek voices that draw us closer to God.
exp.32:19:
Amon was twenty-two years old when he became king of Judah, and he ruled for only two years in Jerusalem. The detail is brief, but it shows how short his reign was. The phrase "began to reign" means that he was crowned king.

The writer of Chronicles tells the history of Judah's kings to teach the people who had returned from exile. Earlier, he records that Amon's father Manasseh sinned greatly, but humbled himself before God and was forgiven. Amon had that example before him, but the verses that follow say he did not humble himself, and his sin grew worse. That is why his reign was so short.

Today, we can learn that the faith of our parents is not passed down automatically. Each person must humble himself before God for himself. If we have seen someone repent and be restored, let us not leave it as a simple memory. Let us make our own decision to turn back to God today.
exp.10:20:
Rehoboam, king of Judah, loved Maacah more than all his other wives and concubines. Concubines were wives of a lower rank. The text says he had eighteen wives and sixty concubines, and he was the father of twenty-eight sons and sixty daughters.

The one speaking is the chronicler, who tells how Rehoboam's reign went after the kingdom was divided. Maacah was the daughter of Absalom, though the word for "daughter" can sometimes mean granddaughter, so her exact relationship is not entirely clear. The passage does not criticize Rehoboam here, but the Law warned kings not to take many wives (Deuteronomy 17:17).

Today: favoritism and a divided heart hurt families. Let us seek God first and treat all of our own with justice and affection.
exp.31:9:
Sennacherib, king of Assyria, sends a message to the people of Jerusalem. He asks them, "What is the basis of your confidence," because the city was surrounded by the enemy army, unable to leave or receive help.

King Hezekiah of Judah had just encouraged the people, saying that with Assyria there was only a man of flesh, but with them was the LORD their God. Sennacherib, while at Lachish, sends his servants to sow fear and doubt, so that the people would stop trusting in their king and in God.

For today: when circumstances surround you and the voices of fear ask what you are relying on, do not lean only on what you can see. Stop, pray, and remember that God is still greater than any threat.
exp.19:22:
This verse tells how the armies of Ammon and Moab turned against the people living on Mount Seir, the Edomites, and set out to destroy them completely. Once they had finished off the people of Seir, they turned on one another and began to destroy each other.

The narrator of Chronicles describes how God rescued Judah under King Jehoshaphat. These three peoples were coming to attack Judah, but Jehoshaphat prayed, and the people sent singers out in front, praising God. As they praised, God caused the enemies to become confused and destroy one another. Judah did not even have to fight.

For today: when you face a problem that is greater than you, do not stop praying and praising God. He can act in ways you do not expect, and trusting Him is a way of facing your battles with faith.
exp.0:16:
Solomon's merchants bought chariots and horses in Egypt and paid a set price for them: six hundred pieces of silver for each chariot and one hundred and fifty for each horse. Then those same chariots and horses were sold on to the kings of the Hittites and the kings of Aram.

This is part of the Chronicler's account of Solomon's wealth and power. It shows that his kingdom was prosperous and had a large trade. However, the Law of Moses warned kings not to acquire many horses or to go back to Egypt for them (Deuteronomy 17:16). For that reason some readers see a warning sign here as well.

We can be thankful for what God gives us, but we should take care that our security does not rest on money or resources. Let us trust God first.
exp.16:6:
In the third year of his reign, King Jehoshaphat sent five of his officials to the cities of Judah. Their names were Ben-hail, Obadiah, Zechariah, Nethanel, and Micaiah. Their task was to teach. The word "officials" here means leaders or officers of the kingdom, not necessarily the king's sons.

The writer of Chronicles tells how Jehoshaphat strengthened his kingdom by following God. He had removed the places of idolatry and wanted the people to know the law of the Lord. The verses that follow explain that Levites and priests accompanied him, carrying the book of the law. Thus the king not only ordered changes, but also sought to instruct the people.

For today: a good change lasts longer when it is accompanied by teaching. In the family, the church, or the workplace, it is not enough to correct what is wrong; it is also wise to help others come to know God's Word with patience and clarity.
exp.0:3:
David had already brought the ark of God up from Kiriath-jearim to Jerusalem, to a place he had prepared for it. There he pitched a tent to keep it in. The verse opens with "Now," which links this fact to what came before it.

The writer of Chronicles points out something unusual: Solomon went to worship at Gibeon, where the tabernacle of Moses was, while the ark was in Jerusalem. So the people had two separate holy places. This happened before the temple was built. The text does not say why they were not brought together, and that question is left unexplained.

For today: God deserves a prepared place in our lives. David made an effort to give the ark a place. We can set aside a moment and a space each day to seek him, and not let routine crowd him out.
exp.19:15:
He says that the people of Judah were to go out to meet the enemy the next day. Jahaziel gives them the exact location: the enemy would come up the Ascent of Ziz, and Judah would find them at the end of the valley facing the Wilderness of Jeruel. Marching down means they would move from the high ground of Judah toward the wilderness. The exact location of these places is not known with certainty today.

Speaking is Jahaziel, a Levite of the sons of Asaph, on whom the Spirit of the LORD came. A great enemy crowd was threatening Judah, and King Jehoshaphat had gathered the people to pray. God answers through this prophet with encouragement and clear direction.

For today: God does not only tell us "do not be afraid," he can also give us clear steps. Pray, wait for his guidance, and move forward in obedience, trusting that he goes with you.
exp.15:12:
It says that King Asa died in the forty-first year of his reign. "Rested with his fathers" is a way of saying that he died and was joined to his ancestors, as is said of other kings of Judah.

The one speaking is the author of Chronicles, who summarizes the life of Asa. Shortly before, he tells that Asa became sick in his feet and did not seek the LORD, but sought the physicians. The author does not condemn the physicians; he points out that Asa no longer trusted in God, as also happened when he trusted in a foreign king (earlier verses). How exactly his illness should be understood is uncertain. The text goes on to describe an honorable burial.

For today: seeking medical help is wise, but we can do it while praying and trusting in God. It is not one or the other. Let us seek God in health and in sickness, until the end of life.
exp.30:3:
It says that King Hezekiah ordered the people of Jerusalem to make a contribution for the priests and Levites. The "contribution" refers to what the people were to give for their support. The aim was that the priests and Levites could devote themselves to the Law of the LORD, that is, give their full attention to serving God.

The passage speaks of King Hezekiah, who is restoring worship in the temple after years of neglect. The priests and Levites depended on the offerings of the people, since they had no land like the other tribes. By ordering this, the king fulfills what the law taught. The people responded with great generosity.

Today we can support with generosity those who serve in teaching the Word, so that they can devote themselves to it without excessive burdens. Giving with joy sustains the service to God.
exp.19:5:
Jehoshaphat begins his prayer by remembering who God is. He asks whether God is not the God who is in heaven, and whether he does not rule over all the kingdoms of the nations. The word "rule" here means having authority over others and governing them. Notice that the verse speaks of "the nations," meaning all the peoples of the earth, not just Israel. He declares that power and might are in God's hand, and that no one can stand against him.

Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, speaks here. A large enemy army was coming against his people, and he was afraid. So he gathered all the people in the temple to seek God's help. Before asking for anything, he starts by declaring who God is.

When you face a problem that is greater than you, do not begin only by talking about how big the problem is. First remember how great God is. Speak with him about his power and his faithfulness, and that will strengthen your trust before you present your request.
exp.26:2:
This verse says that King Jotham rebuilt the Upper Gate of the house of the LORD, which is the gate leading to the temple area. He also worked extensively on the wall at the hill of Ophel, the section of the city wall in Jerusalem that protected that area. The verse says he "worked extensively" on that wall, so the reference is to his large-scale repair and extension of that section of the wall.

The one telling the story is the chronicler, who reviews the history of the kings of Judah. Jotham ruled well, following the example of his father Uzziah, and avoided his mistake of entering the temple out of pride. Nevertheless, the people continued on their wrong path. The text highlights that his strength came from seeking to do what is right before God.

For today: take care of what sustains your spiritual life, like the care of the temple and the wall. Devote steady time to prayer, the Word, and community, and strengthen your home and your work with order and honesty.
exp.23:1:
This verse says that Joash did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, that is, what pleased God. He did this during all the days that the priest Jehoiada lived. The phrase "in the eyes of the LORD" means "according to God's judgment." Notice the limitation: his good conduct lasted as long as Jehoiada was alive.

Here the narrator of the book of Chronicles speaks, summarizing the reign of Joash. Joash came to the throne as a child of seven, and Jehoiada was his guide and counselor. The author makes clear that the king's faithfulness depended greatly on that influence. Later the account shows that, when Jehoiada died, Joash changed course.

For today: it is good to have wise counselors, but our faith must become personal. Make sure your relationship with God does not depend only on another person, but on your own trust in Him.
exp.25:8:
It says that King Uzziah built towers in Jerusalem in three places: at the Corner Gate, at the Valley Gate, and at the angle in the wall. He also fortified them, that is, he made them strong to defend the city.

The one speaking is the chronicler, who reviews the history of the kings of Judah. This account shows Uzziah's success: God gave him help against his enemies, and his fame grew. The towers were part of his preparation to protect the people. The text also says he prospered while he sought God, though later in his story it ends in pride.

For today: It is good to prepare ourselves and to care wisely for what God has entrusted to us, such as family, work, and faith. But we should not trust in our "towers," but in God, and stay humble when things go well for us.
exp.9:17:
Verse 18 tells us that King Rehoboam sent out Hadoram, the official in charge of the forced labor, to deal with the people. But the Israelites stoned him to death. When Rehoboam saw this, he mounted his chariot in haste and escaped to Jerusalem.

The people were already angry because Rehoboam had refused to lighten their heavy burdens and had threatened to be even harsher with them. That is why ten tribes broke away from the house of David. Sending the very official in charge of the forced labor may have stirred up their anger further. The text does not explain why he chose Hadoram.

When someone holds authority, listening with humility is worth more than asserting oneself. Harsh words and proud decisions can break relationships that are very hard to repair afterward.
exp.19:7:
This verse says that the people of Israel lived in the land God had given them, and that they built a holy place there for worshiping God. The word "sanctuary" means a set-apart place for worshiping God. The phrase "for your name" refers to honoring God himself. The verse ends with "saying," and what follows is the prayer they made there.

The one speaking is King Jehoshaphat of Judah. An enemy army was coming against his people, and he gathered everyone in Jerusalem to pray. He reminds God that he gave them the land and that the temple was built so the people could come to him in difficult times.

For today: when you face a large problem, don't start with fear, but with remembering what God has already done. Bringing to mind his faithfulness in the past strengthens the confidence to pray today.
exp.7:1:
Solomon rebuilt and strengthened the cities that King Hiram of Tyre had given him, and he settled Israelite families there to live. The phrase "settled Israelites there" in the verse above means that he placed them in those cities so that they would make their homes there.

The book does not name its author; tradition attributes it to Ezra, but this is not certain. The account takes place after twenty years of building the temple and the palace. In 1 Kings 9 it seems that Solomon was the one who gave cities to Hiram. Some think Hiram gave them back, but this is not known for certain.

For today: what we receive from God or from others is not meant to be left neglected. Ask for wisdom to care for it, improve it, and use it for the good of the people who live near you.
exp.10:14:
This verse says that Jeroboam appointed his own priests to serve in the high places, which were places of worship on the hills, and to worship the goat demons and the calf idols that he himself had made. The Berean wording names these as goat demons, so the verse follows that wording rather than the older term "devils."

The book of Chronicles tells this from a narrator who looks back, after the exile. Jeroboam ruled the northern kingdom and did not want his people to go up to Jerusalem to worship. For that reason he set up a worship of his own and drove out the Levites, who went to Judah. Faithful people from other tribes followed them.

For today: when religion bends to convenience or to fear, it ends up pulling us away from God. Let us seek the Lord sincerely, even when it costs us, and not a worship made to fit our own measure.
exp.7:7:
This verse says that Solomon made the descendants of the peoples who had stayed in the land, those whom Israel had not destroyed, into forced laborers. "Forced laborers" are people required to work for others against their will. "As they are to this day" means that this situation was still the case when the book was written.

Here the narrator of Chronicles speaks, recounting the works of Solomon. The peoples mentioned (Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites and Jebusites) were earlier inhabitants of Canaan. It is made clear that the Israelites themselves were not made into servants, but held military and command posts. Today this is hard to read, since it describes forced labor. The Bible records it, but does not say that we should imitate it.

For today: use whatever authority you have with humility and justice, without taking advantage of those who have less power.
exp.34:10:
The verse says that the Passover lambs were slaughtered. The priests splattered the blood that was handed to them, and the Levites skinned the animals, removing their hides so they could be prepared.

This takes place at the great Passover of King Josiah, in Judah. The chronicler, who tells the story, does not speak in the first person, but describes how everything was arranged "according to the command of the king." Each group had its place: the priests handled the blood, which was the most sacred part, and the Levites helped with the heavy work. In this way the people could celebrate the Passover according to the Law of Moses.

For today: God cares about order and values each person serving in their own place. In the church and in the family, both visible tasks and simple ones, such as skinning the animals, matter. Serve with joy wherever you are needed, without envying others.
exp.33:21:
It says that Hilkiah, the high priest, and the men the king had chosen went to see Huldah, a prophetess. She was the wife of Shallum, who was in charge of the wardrobe (the garments), and she lived in Jerusalem, in the Second District, which was probably a district or quarter of the city (the exact meaning is uncertain). They spoke with her about what the king had said.

The narrator tells what happened after they found the book of the law in the temple. When he heard it, Josiah was distressed because his people had disobeyed God. So he sent his men to ask God what would happen. Huldah would answer them with the word of the Lord.

When God speaks in his Word, it is good to listen with humility and to seek his direction without delay. We can also value the people God uses to encourage and correct us, no matter what their position is.
exp.28:17:
The priests report to King Hezekiah that they have finished cleansing the temple. They cleaned the entire house of the LORD, the altar of burnt offering (where the sacrifices were offered) along with all its utensils, and the table of the showbread (where the consecrated bread was placed before God) along with all its utensils.

The phrase "they went in to King Hezekiah" means they went to speak with him, and "reported" means they gave him an account of their work.

Hezekiah had just begun to reign, and he wanted to restore the worship of God. His father Ahaz had neglected the temple and mistreated its vessels. The priests worked about sixteen days and then gave an account to the king. This marks a new beginning for the people.

Before seeking God wholeheartedly, sometimes what gets in the way must be removed. We can ask ourselves what habit, resentment, or neglect needs cleansing in our lives. Let us do it with patience, step by step, and ask God for his help to start again.
exp.21:7:
This verse says that Jehu was carrying out God's punishment against the family of King Ahab. While doing so, he came upon the officials of Judah and the sons of Ahaziah's brothers, who were serving Ahaziah, and he killed them. The phrase "carrying out judgment" means carrying out God's sentence, and "killed them" is the plain meaning of the verse.

The chronicler explains why people from Judah also fell. God had anointed Jehu to bring an end to the house of Ahab. But Judah had joined itself to that family through marriages and alliances, and Ahaziah followed their evil ways. Some believe this account resembles the one in 2 Kings 10:12-14, although it is not certain that it refers to the same event.

Today it reminds us that our alliances and companions matter. If we join ourselves to what God rejects, sooner or later we pay the consequences. Let us seek friendships and decisions that bring us closer to Him.
exp.6:10:
This verse says that Solomon finished building the house of the Lord and the royal palace. He carried out everything he had planned to do for both the Lord's house and his own palace, and he succeeded in all of it. The phrase "what was in his heart" means what he had set his mind on and wanted to accomplish, and the idea of success means that his work went well.

The narrator of the book tells what happened after the great festival of the temple's dedication. The people had gone home joyful, and Solomon's building work, which had taken many years, was complete. Soon after, God appears to him at night to answer his prayer and to give him an important warning about faithfulness.

For today: success is a gift from God, not a guaranteed permanent state. If God allows you to finish something, thank him and use it to honor him. Keep your heart faithful to him, because what comes after an achievement is often the test of obedience.
exp.24:6:
A man of God, meaning a prophet, comes to King Amaziah and tells him not to let the army of Israel that he had hired go with him. The reason given is that the LORD is not with Israel, not with any of the Ephraimites, who were the main tribe of the northern kingdom. The instruction is that he should not take those soldiers with him into battle.

Amaziah, king of Judah, was preparing to fight against Edom. He already had three hundred thousand soldiers of his own, but he paid a hundred talents of silver for a hundred thousand extra soldiers from Israel. The prophet speaks for God because that northern kingdom had turned away from Him. Amaziah was relying on human strength more than on God.

For today: before we lean on resources, connections, or alliances, let us ask whether God is in that path. Sometimes obeying costs something, like the money Amaziah lost, but God can give far more than what is lost.
exp.34:19:
