After all the reforms Josiah had carried out to set the temple in order and to celebrate the great Passover, Neco, king of Egypt, marched north to fight at Carchemish by the Euphrates River. Josiah went out to confront him. The phrase "set the temple in order" refers to the temple itself, and "marched up" indicates that Neco was heading north.

The chronicler tells this episode after Josiah's spiritual revival. It is striking that, after so much faithfulness, he decides to enter a battle that was not his. The verses that follow say that Neco warned him not to get involved, but Josiah did not listen. Some scholars debate whether Neco truly spoke on God's behalf; the text presents it that way.

Having been faithful in the past does not keep us from making bad decisions today. Before entering a conflict, it is wise to stop, pray, and listen to counsel, even when it comes from where we least expect it.
exp.17:6:
Here the king of Israel (Ahab, according to the parallel account in 1 Kings 22) admits that there is a man through whom they can ask the Lord, Micaiah son of Imlah. But he says he hates him because he never prophesies anything good for him, only bad. Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, answers him respectfully: "The king should not say that!" "Hate" here means to despise deeply, and "prophesy" means to speak on behalf of God.

Ahab and Jehoshaphat are preparing to attack Ramoth Gilead. Four hundred prophets had already promised them victory, but Jehoshaphat is suspicious of so much agreement and asks to hear a prophet of the Lord. Ahab responds with irritation, because he prefers to hear what pleases him.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are seeking the truth of God or only words that comfort us. Sometimes God uses uncomfortable advice to protect us. It is wise to listen with humility, even when it hurts, and to compare everything with Scripture.
exp.2:13:
Solomon had the temple veil made with colored yarns: blue, purple, and crimson, along with fine linen. Cherubim, angelic beings who guard the presence of God, were woven into the fabric. "Woven into it" means their figures were worked into the cloth so that they could be seen clearly.

This is part of the Chronicler's account of building the temple in Jerusalem. The veil separated the Most Holy Place, where the ark was, from the rest of the temple. The cherubim had already appeared in the previous verse, inside the Most Holy Place. Scholars agree that the veil signaled that approaching God was not an ordinary thing, though not everyone explains every detail of the colors in the same way.

For today: God deserves respect and reverence. Today, thanks to Christ, we can draw near with confidence, but without forgetting his holiness.
exp.6:20:
The verse describes the temple, once famous and admired, being reduced to a heap of rubble so completely that everyone who passes by will be appalled. The word "appalled" carries both the sense of amazement and of horror. Those who see it will ask why the LORD has done such a thing to this land and to this temple.

God Himself is speaking, addressing Solomon after he finished building and dedicating the temple. God answers him with a promise and also with a warning: if the people turn away from Him and worship other gods, they will lose the land and the temple. The verse in the next sentence makes clear that the cause of the disaster was abandoning God.

For today: whatever God gives us, whether a blessing, a job, or a church, must not take the place of God. Today you can ask yourself what tends to draw you away from Him, and put Him first in your life again.
exp.4:10:
This verse tells that the priests came out of the holy place of the temple after setting the ark of the covenant in its place. It makes clear that all the priests present had consecrated themselves, that is, they had set themselves apart and purified themselves to serve God. Also, the phrase "regardless of their divisions" means that they did not follow their usual rotation of service; that day they all took part together.

The writer of Chronicles recounts the dedication of the temple that Solomon built. The ark was already inside, and soon the praise would fill the place and the cloud of God's presence would come. The writer emphasizes the unity and preparation of the whole people for that moment.

For today: when we gather to worship, it is good to prepare ourselves with a clean and humble heart. God is pleased when his people unite, regardless of rank or schedule, to honor him.
exp.22:9:
This verse says that Jehoiada stationed all the troops, each man with his weapon in his hand. They stood in a ring around the young king, close to the altar and the temple. The BSB describes their position as running from the south side of the temple to the north side, so the men formed a protective circle on every side of the king. The phrase "stationed" here means that he placed them in their assigned positions.

The account tells how the priest Jehoiada protected the young Joash, the king's son, and presented him as the rightful king of David's line. Before this, Athaliah had taken the throne by force. This passage is not a word of God addressed to anyone, but a narrative. Jehoiada acts with care and organization, using the weapons kept in God's house, to guard the king within the temple.

Today we can learn that serving God includes order, care, and teamwork. When there is something valuable to protect, such as a family, a church, or the truth, it is good for each person to take up his place with responsibility and without disorder.
exp.5:37:
This verse says that if the people of Israel are taken captive into the land of their enemies because of their sins, and there they return to God with all their heart and all their soul, and pray facing the land God gave their fathers, toward the city He has chosen and the house built for His Name, then God will hear them. The phrase "return to God" means turning back to Him, and "with all their soul" speaks of a sincere repentance.

The one speaking is King Solomon, in the prayer he offered when he dedicated the temple. He knows the people can fail, and he asks that God always leave open the door of forgiveness. Praying in the direction of the temple showed trust in God's promises, and the Bible does not say that the temple was the only place where God could hear.

For today: if you have drifted away from God, it does not matter how far away you feel. Return to Him sincerely, acknowledge your wrong, and pray. God still welcomes whoever comes back with a whole heart.
exp.4:6:
This verse says that the priests set the ark of the covenant of the LORD in its permanent place inside the temple: the Most Holy Place, the innermost room. There it rested beneath the wings of the cherubim, angelic beings shown in gold. This most sacred part of the temple was where worship of God was carried out.

The account tells how Solomon dedicated the temple in Jerusalem. The narrator, traditionally identified with the author of Chronicles, emphasizes that the ark, a symbol of God's presence and of his covenant with Israel, finally had a permanent home after centuries of being moved from place to place.

For today: God deserves the central place in our lives. Just as the ark was placed at the center of the temple, we can ask ourselves what real space we give God in our decisions and in our daily time.
exp.20:12:
Jehoram, king of Judah, did not follow the good example of his father. Instead, he walked in the ways of the kings of Israel. The verse says he caused Judah and the people of Jerusalem to prostitute themselves, that is, to turn away from God and worship idols, just as the house of Ahab had done. He also killed his brothers, members of his father's family, who were better men than he was.

God speaks through a letter from the prophet Elijah. Jehoram had married a daughter of Ahab, and that led him to imitate her wickedness. Some scholars debate the exact date of this letter, but its message is clear: God makes the accusation before He announces the punishment.

For today: the people around us influence our path, and our decisions also influence others. It is worth asking ourselves whom we are imitating and whom we are leading. God calls us to return to Him before we keep dragging others along.
exp.18:10:
It says that King Jehoshaphat left two leaders in charge: Amariah, the chief priest, for matters that pertain to the Lord, and Zebadiah, the son of Ishmael and ruler of the house of Judah, for matters that pertain to the king. The Levites would serve as officers or assistants. "Act resolutely" means: be courageous and get to work. It ends with a promise: the Lord will be with the upright.

Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, speaks to the judges he had just placed in the cities. After asking them to judge with the fear of God, he explains who would lead the most important cases and how the responsibilities were divided. In this way there was order, and no one was left alone with a difficult task.

For today: do good with courage, without expecting everything to be easy. If we work with honesty, as a team, and with respect for God, we can trust that He walks with us.
exp.3:9:
He set the great basin, a huge bronze bowl full of water, on the south side of the temple, at the southeast corner. "South side" means the side toward the south, "southeast corner" means the corner where south and east meet, and the bowl's position is described in plain terms.

The writer of Chronicles tells how Solomon built and furnished the temple in Jerusalem. He wrote for a people who were returning from exile and needed to remember the importance of worshiping God with order. Earlier, the bronze sea was described, which the priests used for washing. Scholars believe this reminded the people of the need for cleansing in order to serve God, although the text does not explain this in detail.

God cares about order and about the details of our worship. Just as there was a place to wash before serving, we can set aside time to cleanse the heart, confess our failings, and draw near to God with sincerity.
exp.15:10:
The verse says that everything King Asa did, from beginning to end, is written in the book of the kings of Judah and Israel. The phrase "from beginning to end" refers to the whole course of his reign. It was an official record of his life, with both the good and the bad.

The one who tells this is the Chronicler. Earlier he had recounted that Asa trusted the king of Syria and not God. When the prophet Hanani rebuked him, Asa became angry, had him put in prison, and mistreated some of the people. The Chronicler closes his account by showing that Asa started well but ended up turning away from God.

For today: our lives also lie open before God, from beginning to end. For that reason it is good to keep a humble heart, to receive correction, and to keep trusting God until the last day.
exp.25:1:
It says that Uzziah (also called Azariah or Uzzia) rebuilt Eloth, a city in the south, and brought it back under the control of Judah. This happened after King Amaziah rested with his fathers, which is a gentle way of saying he died. The idea behind "restored" is giving something back to its former owner.

The one speaking is the narrator of Chronicles, who reviews the history of the kings of Judah. Uzziah was a young man of sixteen who had just come to the throne. Eloth lay beside the Red Sea, and it is mentioned because it supported trade and the southern routes. The exact details of how he recovered it are not explained here.

For today: when we receive a task that others left unfinished, we can carry it on with diligence. Rebuilding what was lost, with patience and faith, is a way of serving God and others.
exp.19:0:
After the events just before, the Moabites and Ammonites, together with some of the Meunites, came to make war against Jehoshaphat, king of Judah. "After this" simply means what happened next.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Chronicles. He tells how Jehoshaphat, a king who had sought God and strengthened his kingdom, suddenly faces a great threat. The verses that follow show his response: he feels fear, but he seeks the LORD and calls the whole people to fast.

For today: problems can arrive even when we have done what is right. Feeling afraid is not a sin; what matters is where we take that fear. When a great difficulty comes, before doing anything else, we can stop, pray, and seek the support of other believers.
exp.1:3:
Solomon says he is about to build a house for the name of the Lord, his God. The house will be set apart for worship, and in it incense will be burned before God, the bread of the presence will be displayed continually, and burnt offerings (sacrifices that were burned completely) will be made every morning and evening, on the Sabbaths, on the New Moons, and at the appointed feasts. All of this was to continue forever in Israel.

Solomon, king of Israel, speaks. He writes to Hiram, king of Tyre, to ask for cedar wood, as he had done with his father David. He explains that the temple is not a whim, but a place to worship God in a constant way.

For today: God deserves constant worship, not only in special moments.
exp.18:7:
This verse tells that King Jehoshaphat appointed some of the Levites, priests, and heads of Israelite families in Jerusalem. Their task was to judge on behalf of the LORD and to settle disputes, both matters of religion and conflicts between people. The phrase "to judge on behalf of the LORD" refers to God's law, and "disputes" are lawsuits or conflicts. The verse adds that these men lived in Jerusalem.

Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, had already placed judges in the cities. Now he also organized a central court in Jerusalem. He reminded them that they judged in place of God, who does not accept bribes or favoritism. He wanted a land with justice and respect for God.

Today, if you have authority, even in your home, work, or church, decide with honesty, without favoritism. Remember that God sees your decisions.
exp.13:7:
This verse tells that King Asa had a large, well-prepared army. The men of Judah carried large shields and spears, and the men of Benjamin carried small shields and drew the bow. There were 300,000 from Judah and 280,000 from Benjamin. The "mighty men of valor" in the verse are men who are skilled and brave. Some scholars think the numbers can be understood in other ways, but the text emphasizes that it was a considerable force.

The Chronicler tells this after saying that Asa used the time of peace to strengthen cities and seek God. It was not an army prepared out of fear, but during a time of rest. Soon the invasion of Zerah would come, with a much larger army, and Asa would have to trust in God.

For today: use quiet times to prepare, pray, and strengthen your faith and your responsibilities. Even so, remember that preparation is good, but final trust must be placed in God.
exp.16:3:
It says that Jehoshaphat sought the God of his father Asa, meaning he set out to know him and to obey him. He walked by God's commandments, which means he lived according to what God had commanded. And he did not follow the practices of Israel, the northern kingdom, which had turned away from God through idolatry. Here, to seek means to turn to God with the whole heart, not merely to keep a religion.

The one speaking is the narrator of Chronicles, writing for a people who were returning from exile. He wants to show why God was with Jehoshaphat, king of Judah. The text contrasts two paths: that of God and that of Israel. Afterward it says that God established his kingdom and that Jehoshaphat removed the high places, places of worship, although other texts indicate that not all of them disappeared.

Today we can ask ourselves whom we imitate when we make decisions. It is good to learn from the faith of our fathers, but each person must seek God personally, read his Word, and not be carried along only by what most people do.
exp.5:33:
It says that if the people of Israel go out to fight against their enemies, wherever God sends them, and pray to him facing toward Jerusalem, the city he has chosen, and toward the temple built for his Name, God will hear them. "Go out to war" means go out to war, "pray to you" means pray to God, and "send them" means send them. The phrase "for your Name" means for the honor of God's name.

King Solomon is speaking. He is dedicating the temple and asking God to hear the prayers of his people in different situations. This is one of several requests. Notice that the war is legitimate only if God sends them; Solomon does not ask for help in just any fight.

Today we do not pray facing a building, because God hears us anywhere. But we can learn to ask for his help in our struggles only when we seek to follow his way. Before facing a conflict, ask him: "Lord, am I going where you send me?" Then pray with confidence.
exp.8:27:
This verse says that horses were imported into Israel for Solomon from Egypt and from all the surrounding lands. They were brought in from abroad and carried into the country. This shows how great his wealth and trade were.

The book of Chronicles was written by an author we do not know for certain, probably after the exile in Babylon. He wants to remind the people of the glory of Solomon's reign. This detail appears alongside the abundant silver and his rule over other kings. However, the law of Moses warned kings not to multiply horses or return to Egypt (Deuteronomy 17:16). Some see here a subtle sign that Solomon was moving away from that command.

For today: prosperity is not wrong, but it can lead us to trust more in what we have than in God. Examine where you place your security and return to trusting in Him.
exp.4:7:
It says that in the most holy place of the temple there were two large cherubim with their wings spread out. Their wings stretched over the place of the ark and overshadowed the ark and its poles, which were the long bars the priests used to carry it.

This is the account from the book of Chronicles, written for the people of Israel after the exile. It tells how Solomon and the priests brought the ark into the newly built temple. The cherubim, figures of heavenly beings, guarded and surrounded the place where God was understood to be present. The author wants to show that worship in the temple was carried out with order and reverence.

For today: God deserves that we seek him with respect and care. We can set aside a quiet moment to pray, remembering that he covers us with his care and that we can draw near to him with trust and humility.
exp.0:15:
This verse says that Solomon's horses came from Egypt and from Kue, and the royal merchants bought them from Kue. The king's merchants made these purchases through an agreed deal, that is, a fixed purchase arrangement. Some scholars think the name Kue may refer to a place, but this is not known with complete certainty.

The author of Chronicles, who writes long after these events, describes Solomon's wealth and power. But the Law said that the king must not multiply horses or go back to Egypt to get them (Deuteronomy 17:16). The account shows his greatness, and perhaps also a warning sign.

Today we can ask ourselves what we trust most: what we have, or God. Provisions and plans are useful, but true security comes from obeying Him and resting in Him.
exp.6:6:
Solomon set apart for God the middle part of the courtyard in front of the temple. There he offered the burnt offerings and the fat of the peace offerings, because the bronze altar he had made could not hold all of these offerings. The word "consecrated" means he set that space apart for sacred use. The "fat" is the fat of the animals.

The one speaking is the narrator of Chronicles, who recounts the dedication of the temple. It had reached a huge moment: thousands of animals, music, trumpets, and all the people standing. The altar was not enough, so Solomon adapted the space so he could keep worshiping God.

For today: when your heart wants to give or serve God and your means seem small, do not stop. Look simply for how to enlarge your space, your time, or your generosity in order to honor him.
exp.27:18:
This verse explains why Judah suffered so many defeats: the LORD himself had humbled it. The cause was Ahaz, whom the text calls "king of Israel," even though he ruled over Judah. In the Berean wording, Ahaz had thrown off restraint in Judah and had been deeply unfaithful to the LORD, which is the reason the verse gives for the nation's humbling.

The one speaking is the chronicler, who writes long after the events to remind the people why Judah suffered. The verses nearby describe attacks by Edomites, Philistines, and Assyrians. The chronicler does not see these defeats as mere political bad luck, but as the consequence of the king's unfaithfulness. It should be said that the text presents this reading from faith, not as the analysis of historians.

For today: when things become difficult, it is worth examining with humility whether we have stopped trusting God. Not every hardship is punishment, but returning to Him is always a good path.
exp.14:15:
King Asa removed his grandmother Maacah from her position as queen mother because she had made a detestable Asherah pole. Asa chopped the pole down, crushed it, and burned it in the Kidron Valley, near Jerusalem.

The Chronicler tells this as part of Asa's reform. The people had just committed themselves to seek God with all their heart. Asa shows that this commitment was serious, even when it reached into his own family. The Berean wording calls Maacah his grandmother, and it is a reminder that the family ties here were close.

For today: being faithful to God sometimes costs us in what is closest to us. Ask him to show you what thing or custom has taken God's place in your life, and remove it with courage and love.
exp.30:6:
The verse says that in the third month the people began building up the heaps, and they finished in the seventh month. "Building up" here means starting to pile the heaps, the way one begins stacking grain. The third month coincided with the wheat harvest and the seventh with the fruit harvest, so the offerings arrived over several months.

The one telling the story is the writer of Chronicles, who recounts how King Hezekiah renewed worship in the temple. He commanded the people to support the priests and Levites with their firstfruits and tithes. The people responded with such generosity that the offerings piled up in great heaps. Then Hezekiah saw them and blessed God.

For today: steady generosity is worth more than a passing impulse. We can decide to give to God and his work consistently, month after month, and thank him for what he allows us to give.
exp.8:22:
This verse says that kings from across the known world wanted to meet with Solomon to hear his wisdom. The phrase "sought an audience with" means they were trying to meet him in person. "To hear the wisdom" shows that what made him worth coming to was not only his riches, but the wisdom God had put in his heart.

It is part of the chronicler's account of Solomon's reign. It is not Solomon who speaks, but the writer, who probably wrote after the exile to encourage the people to remember the glory of the kingdom and that his wisdom came from God. The text stresses that it was a gift, not a personal achievement.

For today: true wisdom is a gift we can ask God for. Seek it in his Word and in prayer, and use it to serve and bless others, not to show off.
exp.17:30:
This verse says that the chariot commanders of the Syrian army saw Jehoshaphat wearing royal clothing and thought he was the king of Israel. They turned to fight against him, but Jehoshaphat cried out for help, and the LORD helped him and drew the commanders away from him. The phrase "cried out" means that he called loudly for help.

The king of Syria had ordered an attack only on the king of Israel, Ahab. Ahab disguised himself to hide, and left Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, in his royal robes. Jehoshaphat had allied himself with Ahab, which was a very dangerous thing to do. When the commanders realized it was not Ahab, they stopped pursuing him.

For today: when we get into dangerous situations, even through unwise decisions, we can call out to God. He is merciful and hears us. Even so, we should be careful about the company we keep and seek his guidance before we act.
exp.21:11:
This verse says that young Joash was hidden for six years in the temple, which the text calls "the house of God." During that time, Athaliah ruled over the land of Judah. The words "with them" refer to Jehosheba and her husband Jehoiada, the priest, who cared for him in secret.

The book of Chronicles tells the story of Judah. After King Ahaziah died, his mother Athaliah wanted to destroy the entire royal family so she could keep the throne. Jehosheba, Joash's aunt, rescued him and kept him hidden. The text does not say that God spoke directly here, but it shows how the promise to the house of David was still alive, even in dark times.

Today we can remember that God keeps working even when we cannot see it. Perhaps you are going through a season of waiting or silence. Like Jehosheba and Jehoiada, we can be faithful in the small and hidden things, caring for what God has entrusted to us, with patience and confidence that He carries out His plans in His time.
exp.27:20:
This verse tells how Ahaz, king of Judah, took treasures from the house of the LORD, from the royal palace, and from the princes, and gave them to the king of Assyria. Taking a portion here means that he stripped away as much as he could. Even so, the verse says that it did not help him. He paid a high price for help that never came.

The writer of Chronicles explains that the LORD brought Judah low because of Ahaz's unfaithfulness. Assyria, instead of being an ally, pressed him hard. Then, instead of turning back to God, Ahaz worshiped the gods of Damascus.

When we are in trouble, it is easy to look for powerful but empty solutions and spend what is most valuable on them. Today you might ask yourself: what am I trusting in more than God? Returning to Him, with humility, is the best way forward.
exp.19:13:
This verse introduces a man named Jahaziel, a Levite from the descendants of Asaph, that is, from the family of musicians who served in the temple. His list of ancestors is given to identify him clearly. The important point is that the Spirit of the LORD came upon him as he stood in the midst of the assembly. The word "assembly" refers to all the people gathered together.

King Jehoshaphat and all of Judah were gathered in Jerusalem, with their families, because a huge army was coming to attack them. They had prayed, acknowledging that they had no strength and did not know what to do. God answers by sending a message through Jahaziel. The text does not say he was an important leader, only that God used him at that moment.

For today: when you feel without strength and without answers, pray sincerely and keep your eyes on God. He can speak to you through his Word or through simple people in your community. Listen with attention and with humility.
exp.6:5:
This verse describes how the dedication of the temple took place. The priests stood at their posts, and the Levites played the musical instruments that King David had made for giving thanks to the LORD. David had used these instruments to offer praise, saying, "For His loving devotion endures forever." Across from the Levites, the priests sounded trumpets, and all the Israelites were standing. Here "for giving thanks" means giving praise and thanks. The Levites played the instruments while the trumpets sounded, and all the people remained standing.

The author of Chronicles, whom Jewish tradition often says was Ezra (this is not certain), recounts the inauguration of the temple that Solomon built. He recalls that worship was carried out as David had organized it, and with this he encourages the people to return to God and to his temple.

For today: faith is also expressed through orderly and constant gratitude. Before asking, we can stop and give thanks, remembering that God's loving devotion never ends.
exp.22:16:
Then all the people went to the temple of Baal and tore it down. They pulled down the building, smashed its altars and idols, and killed Mattan, the priest of Baal, in front of the altars.

This is a narrative, not a speech. Athaliah had ruled Judah and promoted the worship of Baal. Jehoiada, the priest, placed the young king Joash on the throne and renewed the covenant that Judah would be a people of the LORD. Removing the worship of Baal was the sign that this covenant was taken seriously. The violence here is recounted as part of that time and of Israel's law; it is not a model to imitate today.

For today: if we say we belong to God, it is worth examining what things have taken His place in our hearts, such as money, pride, or addictions, and removing them decisively, not keeping them just in case.
exp.7:15:
This verse says that all of Solomon's work was carried out carefully and completed. From the day the foundation of the Lord's house was laid until the work was finished, nothing was left half done. The word "carried out" here means that the work was put into action step by step, and "completed" means that the whole task was brought to its end.

The author of Chronicles, whose name the Bible does not state with certainty, summarizes here the building of the temple. Earlier, the text described how Solomon organized the priests, the Levites, and the gatekeepers as David had commanded. The passage aims to show that worship in the temple ran with order and that Solomon carried out what his father had left in place.

For today: God values what is done with order, perseverance, and faithfulness. Think of a responsibility you have, in your home, your work, or your church, and ask God for the strength to finish it well, one step at a time.
exp.4:5:
This verse tells us that King Solomon and all the people of Israel gathered before the ark of the covenant and offered so many sheep and oxen in sacrifice that no one could count them. The word "congregation" refers to the large crowd that had come together with the king, and the phrase "who had assembled with him" describes how they had gathered to join him in the act of worship.

The speaker is the author of Chronicles, who recounts the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem. The offerings were an act of worship and thanksgiving while the ark, a sign of God's presence, was being brought to its place in the temple. We do not know the exact number; the text only emphasizes that it was an enormous offering.

For today: when God is at the center, it is natural to respond with generosity and joy. Today we do not offer animals, but we can gladly give our time, care, and resources, not out of obligation, but as a response of gratitude to God.
exp.5:39:
Here Solomon asks God to have his eyes open and his ears attentive to the prayer offered in the temple. The words "may Your eyes be open" express his request, and "attentive" means listening closely.

Solomon speaks at the end of his long prayer at the dedication of the temple. He has just asked that God hear the people, even if they are held captive far away and pray facing toward Jerusalem, turning back to God with all their heart. His request rests on God's promise to be present among his people. Scholars do not agree on how much Solomon knew about the future, but the text shows his confidence in God's forgiveness.

Today we can pray with the assurance that God hears us when we return to him sincerely. No special place is needed; what matters is a humble and repentant heart.
exp.16:15:
This verse mentions another commander in King Jehoshaphat's army: Amasiah, the son of Zichri. He is described as a volunteer for the LORD, meaning he gave himself freely to serve God. With him were 200,000 mighty men of valor. The phrase "mighty men of valor" speaks of strong men capable of war.

The writer of Chronicles lists the commanders of Judah during the reign of Jehoshaphat. Earlier, Adnah and Johanan were mentioned, and after this the list continues with the leaders from Benjamin. The text shows that Jehoshaphat had a strong kingdom, and the chapter before says that the LORD was with him because he sought God. The numbers are very large, and some scholars debate how they should be understood, but the point is clear: there was great strength.

For today: Amasiah is remembered not only for his position but for his willing devotion to God. We can serve God in what we do each day, not out of obligation, but gladly and from the heart.
exp.5:23:
The verse says that if the people of Israel are defeated by an enemy because they have sinned against God, and then they return to Him, confess His name, and pray and plead with Him in this temple, God will hear them. The phrase "defeated before an enemy" describes being beaten in battle, and "return to You" means turning back to God.

The speaker is King Solomon, in his prayer at the dedication of the temple in Jerusalem. He is asking God to listen to His people when they fail Him. The prayer takes for granted that Israel would sin, but it also shows that God makes a way back through repentance.

For today: when you feel that your mistakes have brought painful consequences, do not pull away from God out of shame. Return to Him sincerely, acknowledge what you did, and ask for forgiveness. The Bible shows that God receives those who come back to Him with humility.
exp.18:0:
Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, arrived back at his home in Jerusalem safely. "Jehoshaphat" is the usual spelling of his name, and "safely" means he returned unharmed and out of danger.

At this point the narrator is telling the story. Jehoshaphat had just been in a battle alongside King Ahab of Israel, a wicked king (chapter 18). Ahab died in that war, but Jehoshaphat survived. However, the next verse shows that returning safely did not mean everything was right: the prophet Jehu rebukes him for helping someone who did not love God. Jehu also acknowledges the good Jehoshaphat had done.

For today: that God rescues us from a danger does not mean we have made the right choices. We can thank him for his care and, at the same time, listen humbly when he corrects us about our alliances and decisions.
exp.22:11:
This verse tells how Athaliah, the queen who ruled Judah, heard the noise of the people running and cheering for the new king. Then she went out to them in the house of the Lord. "Noise" means a very loud sound. "Cheering the king" means they were celebrating him with joy.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. The priest Jehoiada had just secretly crowned Joash, David's rightful heir, and Athaliah had seized the throne by force. She hears the commotion and comes, not knowing what awaits her.

For today: plans that rise up against God do not last forever. If you find yourself facing injustice today, trust that God works with patience and in his own time. In the meantime, remain faithful and serve with courage.
exp.13:13:
It says that the army of Judah, led by King Asa, attacked all the cities around Gerar. "Attacked" here means they struck these cities and defeated them. "Plunder" refers to the goods taken from a defeated enemy. The text explains that they were able to do this because the terror of the LORD had fallen upon those cities, that is, a fear that God placed on their people. In this way they were able to plunder them with little resistance, since there was much plunder to be taken.

Here the narrator of the book of Chronicles is speaking. He recounts what happened after Asa prayed and God gave victory over the Ethiopians, who had invaded Judah. The cities near Gerar were probably allies of that army or were under its influence, although the text does not say so in detail.

For today: the victory came when Asa trusted in God, not in his own strength. When you face something that is beyond you, pray first and trust that God works even where you cannot see.
exp.6:14:
God says that now his eyes will be open and his ears attentive to the prayers offered in this place. It is a way of saying that God watches carefully and listens closely. The phrase "will be open" means that he will not ignore the cry of his people.

God himself speaks, answering Solomon after Solomon dedicated the temple in Jerusalem. God promises that if his people humble themselves, pray, seek him, and turn from their evil ways, he will hear them, forgive them, and heal their land. The temple, which would serve as a sign that God attended to his people, is what the phrase "this place" refers to.

Today no special building is needed to pray. You can come to God with humility and sincerity, knowing that he hears you. Tell him honestly where you have failed and ask him for help to change.
exp.31:31:
This verse says that the rest of what King Hezekiah did, including his deeds of loving devotion and his faithfulness to God, was written down. It names the vision of the prophet Isaiah, son of Amoz, and also the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel. The word "indeed" stresses that the record is certain, and the idea that everything is written down shows that nothing was left unrecorded.

The speaker is the author of Chronicles, who closes the account of Hezekiah's reign as he does with other kings: he points the reader to where more can be read. We do not know with certainty whether that Book of the Kings is the same one we have today in the Bible or a different work. Earlier, the account spoke of his achievements and of his fall before the envoys of Babylon.

For today: our lives also leave a mark. It is worth living with faith and goodness, knowing that God sees everything, both our successes and our weaknesses, and that we can trust in his mercy.
exp.6:2:
They saw the fire come down from heaven and the glory of the LORD above the temple. Then they bowed down with their faces to the ground, on the stone pavement, and worshiped and gave thanks. They declared that the LORD is good and that his loving devotion endures forever.

The narrator tells what happened when Solomon finished praying at the dedication of the temple. The fire consumed the sacrifices, and this showed that God accepted the house and was present. The people responded with reverent awe and thankfulness. Then the sacrifices and the feast followed.

For today: when you sense the nearness of God, or remember what he has done for you, do not pass by. Stop, bow down in your heart, and give thanks, saying with sincerity: "You are good, and your loving devotion never ends."
exp.29:7:
Today's verse tells the people not to stiffen their necks like their ancestors did. Stiffening the neck means refusing to obey, like an ox that will not let itself be placed under the yoke. Submit to the LORD means giving yourselves over to Him and committing yourselves to Him. The sanctuary is the temple in Jerusalem, which He has set apart forever. If they return to God and serve Him, His fierce anger will turn away from them.

King Hezekiah sent messengers with letters to all of Israel and Judah. The northern kingdom had already suffered the invasion of Assyria, and only remnants of the people were left. Hezekiah invited them to celebrate the Passover in Jerusalem and to return to God. Some mocked the message, as the following context shows.

For today: if God is calling you to return to Him, do not harden your heart out of pride or habit. Respond today with humility, because He is gracious and merciful and receives whoever turns back to Him.
exp.8:13:
This verse says that Solomon received gold and silver on top of the revenue that already came to him each year. The merchants and traders brought their profits, and the Arabian kings and the governors of the land also brought him precious metals. The phrase "governors of the land" refers to local rulers.

Here the speaker is the author of Chronicles, who tells the story with an admiring view of Solomon's reign. It comes right after the visit of the queen of Sheba and the figure of the yearly gold. The text wants to show how great and prosperous his kingdom was, and how God kept his promise to give him wealth and honor.

For today: prosperity can be a gift from God, but it is not the most important thing. If God gives you resources, use them with wisdom, gratitude, and generosity, without trusting in them more than in Him.
exp.14:5:
This verse describes a time of great disorder. One nation was crushing another nation, and one city was attacking another city. It says that God "afflicted" them, which means that he brought them every kind of hardship and distress.

The one speaking is the prophet Azariah, son of Oded, who addresses King Asa and his people. He reminds them of hard times in the past, probably the era of the judges, although not all scholars agree on which period it was. His message: when the people turned away from God, there was chaos; when they sought him, they found him. With this he encouraged Asa to carry out reforms.

For today: when there is confusion or conflict in your life, do not wait until everything falls apart before seeking God. Draw near to him now, because he promises to be found.
exp.5:2:
This verse says that King Solomon turned around, faced the people, and blessed them. At the same time, the whole assembly of Israel was standing there. The phrase "the whole assembly" refers to the large crowd gathered together. The phrase "turned around" means that he turned to face the people.

Solomon has just finished the temple in Jerusalem. Before praying to God, he first speaks to the people gathered to dedicate the temple. His blessing is a word of gratitude and good wishes spoken on behalf of God. That the people were standing shows respect and attention in a solemn moment. Afterward, Solomon recalls how God kept the promise made to his father David.

For today: before asking things of God, we can pause to bless and encourage those around us, whether in the family, the church, or at work. A kind word, spoken with respect and gratitude, also honors the Lord.
exp.3:5:
It says that Solomon made ten basins, or large bronze washing basins, and placed five on the south side and five on the north. In them the parts of the burnt offering were rinsed: the pieces of the animal that were burned on the altar. The "Sea," a huge bronze basin, was used by the priests for washing.

The book of Chronicles recounts the building of the temple in the time of Solomon. Its author is not named with certainty, and he writes after the exile to remind the people how the worship of God was to be carried out. It emphasizes order and cleanliness, because approaching God was a serious matter.

For today: God values our seeking him with a clean heart. We can begin the day by asking him for forgiveness and renewal, knowing that in Christ there is always purification.
exp.33:26:
God tells the king that his heart was tender, that it softened and did not harden. When he heard what God had spoken against Jerusalem, the king humbled himself, tore his clothes as a sign of grief, and wept. For this reason God declares: "I have heard you."

God speaks, through the prophetess Huldah, to King Josiah. The book of the law had been found, and when Josiah heard it, he understood how far the people of God had drifted away. God announces that judgment will come, but that Josiah will not see it in his lifetime, because his heart responded with humility.

For today: when God's Word confronts you, do not become defensive. Respond with humility and sincerity, and remember that God hears the repentant heart.
exp.25:4:
This verse says that King Uzziah kept seeking God throughout the days of Zechariah, a man who instructed him in the fear of God, that is, someone who taught him to live with reverence toward God. The phrase "throughout the days" means he did not stop, and the phrase "God gave him success" means God granted him good results while he sought the LORD.

The author of Chronicles, writing after the exile, summarizes the reign of Uzziah. He began to reign at sixteen years old, so he needed guidance. Zechariah appears as a spiritual counselor, and we know nothing more about him. The following verses show the success: victories over the Philistines and other peoples.

For today: seek God consistently and surround yourself with people wise in the faith who can guide you. That support helps, especially when you are young or starting something new. But success is not always measured in material gain; what matters most is continuing to seek God.
exp.18:1:
This verse says that the prophet Jehu went out to confront King Jehoshaphat and challenged him with a pointed question: should you help the wicked and love those who hate the LORD? The word "seer" in the verse simply means a prophet, someone who speaks for God. The "wicked" are people who live without regard for God. Because of this, the wrath of the LORD was upon the king.

Jehu, son of Hanani, speaks on God's behalf. Jehoshaphat had just returned safely from the war, where he had joined forces with Ahab, king of Israel, who was very wicked (2 Chronicles 18). Even so, God recognizes what is good in Jehoshaphat: he removed the idols and sought God wholeheartedly.

For today: God corrects us out of love. It is worth reviewing who we ally ourselves with and what weighs on our decisions. We can be kind to everyone, but we should not compromise our faith for convenience. And if someone corrects us, let us listen with humility.
exp.10:15:
After the Levites, people from every tribe of Israel who had set their hearts on seeking the LORD their God also made their way to Jerusalem to offer sacrifices to the LORD, the God of their ancestors.

The narrator tells this after the kingdom had split. Jeroboam, king of the north, set up his own altars and priests and drove out the Levites. Faithful believers in the north did not want to follow that religion, so they went to Jerusalem, where the temple stood. This strengthened Judah, as the following verse says.

For today: seeking God wholeheartedly sometimes costs something, such as comfort or familiar customs. Ask yourself what concrete step you can take this week to draw closer to Him, even if others are not doing so.
exp.27:21:
This verse says that King Ahaz, just when he was under the most pressure and distress from his enemies, instead of turning to God became even more unfaithful. The verse's word "distress" describes being hemmed in and squeezed, and "unfaithful" means betraying trust, in this case toward the LORD.

Here the narrator of the book of Chronicles speaks, telling the story of Judah. Ahaz was under attack from several nations and also from Assyria, which he paid with treasures from the temple without receiving any help. Afterward, according to the context, he sacrificed to foreign gods and shut the temple.

For today: pressure can show us whom we trust. When difficulty comes, instead of rushing to empty solutions, we can draw near to God with sincerity and ask him for help.
exp.14:16:
Here the text says that the high places, where people worshiped on the hills, were not removed from Israel. Even so, Asa's heart was fully devoted to God all his days.

The writer of Chronicles tells of the reforms of King Asa in Judah: the covenant with God, the removal of his mother Maacah, and the destruction of an idol. Then he adds this clarification. Some think "Israel" refers to the northern kingdom, and others think it refers to places in Judah that were not removed. It is not certain which is the case. "Fully devoted" does not mean without sin, but loyal to God.

We can obey God wholeheartedly and still have areas that are unfinished. Ask him to show you which high place still remains in your life, and keep moving forward with sincerity.
exp.8:7:
The queen of Sheba blesses the God of Solomon. She recognizes that the LORD took pleasure in him and placed him on the throne. In her view, God loves Israel and wants to keep them secure forever, which is why he gave them a king. The phrase "delighted in you" means that God was pleased with Solomon, and "to carry out justice and righteousness" means that he was to rule with integrity and fair treatment.

The speaker is the queen of Sheba, who traveled from far away to see for herself the fame of Solomon. She was amazed at his wisdom and his kingdom. Her praise does not stop with Solomon but honors the God of Israel. The text does not say whether she worshiped God as the Israelites did; that is understood in different ways.

For today: if God gives us influence, success, or authority, they are meant to be used to act with justice and righteousness. In addition, the way we live should lead others to honor God, not us.
exp.12:8:
This verse is a pointed question. Abijah asks the people of the north whether they have not driven out the priests the Lord appointed, the descendants of Aaron and the Levites. In their place, they have made priests of their own, the way the peoples of other lands did. According to Abijah, anyone could become a priest just by bringing a young bull and seven rams, yet such a priest would serve things that are not gods, that is, idols with no real power.

Abijah, king of Judah, speaks before the battle against Jeroboam, king of Israel. Jeroboam had made golden calves and changed the priesthood. Abijah wants to show that Judah still keeps the worship the Lord commanded in the temple.

For today: being religious or sincere is not enough; it is wise to worship God as he has revealed himself, not according to our own convenience. Let us examine whether our faith rests on his Word.
exp.17:26:
Here the prophet Micaiah answers Ahab, the king of Israel, who had him thrown into prison and given scant bread and water. Micaiah says that if the king returns safely from the battle, then the LORD has not spoken through him. The phrase "return safely" means to come back without harm. "Take heed, all you people!" is a call for everyone to pay attention and to be witnesses of his words.

Ahab and Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, were preparing to attack Ramoth Gilead. Four hundred prophets were promising the king victory, but Micaiah announced a disaster. Ahab chose to silence the prophet rather than listen to the truth. Micaiah staked his credibility: the outcome would prove whether he spoke on God's behalf.

For today: let us not look only for words that please us. Let us learn to listen humbly to what God says in his Word, even when it makes us uncomfortable, because his truth cares for us more than flattery does.
exp.24:14:
God was very angry with Amaziah, king of Judah, and sent him a prophet. The anger burned against him, meaning it was stirred up strongly. The prophet asks him a question that shows how foolish his action was: why have you sought this people's gods, when those gods could not rescue them from your hand?

The one speaking is a prophet, sent by God. Amaziah had just defeated the Edomites, the people of Seir, and instead of giving thanks to God, he brought their gods back, worshiped them, and burned incense to them. The following text shows that the king rejected the correction with contempt.

For today: it is easy to trust in things that have no real power, such as money, success, or reputation, even after God has helped us. When someone corrects us with the truth, it is wise to listen with humility, not with pride.
exp.28:32:
This verse says that, in addition to the burnt offerings, the people brought other offerings: six hundred bulls and three thousand sheep. They are called "consecrated offerings" because they were set apart for God, and in this case they were sacrifices that were later shared within the community, as peace offerings.

King Hezekiah is restoring worship in the temple after years of neglect under his father Ahaz. He had already cleansed the house of God, and now he invites the people to bring sacrifices and praise. The people responded with generosity, and the text highlights that many gave with willing hearts. The large numbers show a real revival.

For today: when God renews something in us, the natural response is generosity and gratitude. Ask yourself what you can give to God today with joy: time, talent, or resources, not out of obligation, but from the heart.
exp.35:21:
It says that in the first year of Cyrus, king of Persia, God brought about what he had announced through the prophet Jeremiah. The LORD "stirred the spirit" of Cyrus, meaning he moved him from within and placed a decision in his heart. Then Cyrus sent out an official announcement throughout his kingdom and also put it in writing. A "proclamation" is a public announcement made aloud.

The one speaking here is the author of Chronicles, who closes the book by showing that the exile in Babylon was not the end. Judah had been taken captive, and Jeremiah had spoken of a period of seventy years. Now the time to return has come. What follows is Cyrus's decree that allows the Jews to go back to Jerusalem and rebuild the temple.

For today: God can keep his promises even by using people who do not know him. Trust that his timing is good, even when the wait is long.
exp.10:1:
This verse says that God spoke to Shemaiah, who is called "the man of God," meaning a man who belonged to God and spoke on His behalf. The phrase "the word of the LORD came" means that God gave him a direct message. The word "But" here marks a turn in the story: God steps in just as a war was being prepared.

Rehoboam had just arrived in Jerusalem with one hundred and eighty thousand soldiers to win back the northern tribes, which had separated. No one was asking what God wanted. Then He sends a prophet with a clear command: do not fight against your brothers. The verses that follow say they obeyed and returned home.

For today: before entering a fight, even when you believe you are right, stop and listen to God. His word can prevent a conflict that would cause a great deal of pain, especially among family members or brothers and sisters in the faith.
exp.17:3:
Here Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, asks King Ahab to seek the word of the Lord before going to war. The phrase "Please inquire first" is a polite request, and the word "first" shows that he wants this done before any action is taken. "Inquire" means that he should seek God's direction.

Jehoshaphat had already promised to help Ahab in the battle against Ramoth-gilead. Now he realizes that seeking God's guidance is still missing. Ahab gathers four hundred prophets who tell him what he wants to hear. Jehoshaphat is not at ease and asks whether there is any prophet of the Lord. His insistence shows that he desires a true answer from God, not just pleasant words.

Before making important decisions, it is good to seek God in prayer and in his Word, and not simply be carried along by commitments or by voices that tell us what we want to hear.
exp.24:7:
This verse tells King Amaziah that if he insists on going to war with the soldiers of Israel, even if he fights bravely, God will overthrow him before his enemies. The reason is that God has power to help and power to overthrow. The phrase "fight bravely" here means to take heart and fight with courage.

The speaker is a "man of God," a prophet whose name is not given. Amaziah, king of Judah, had paid one hundred talents of silver to one hundred thousand soldiers from Israel. The prophet warns him that God was not with that northern kingdom, and that relying on those soldiers would mean putting his trust in the wrong place.

For today: before deciding something important, ask yourself in whom you are trusting, whether in your resources or in God. Obeying him may cost money or comfort, but he can give you far more than what you lose.
exp.0:7:
Solomon speaks to God and acknowledges two things: that God showed great loving devotion to his father David, and that now God has made him king in David's place. The word "devotion" here speaks of faithful love and goodness, not only of forgiveness.

Solomon has just offered a thousand burnt offerings, that is, offerings entirely burned on the altar, at Gibeon. That night God told him to ask for whatever he wanted. Before asking for anything, Solomon remembers what God has already done. Afterward he will ask for wisdom to govern a numerous people.

Before we bring our requests, we can pause to remember God's faithfulness in our lives and in our families. Giving thanks first helps us pray with humility and confidence, and to ask with a wiser heart.
exp.0:4:
This verse says that the bronze altar, made by Bezalel, son of Uri and grandson of Hur, was in Gibeon, in front of the tabernacle of the Lord. There Solomon went with the whole assembly to inquire of God. Here "inquire" means to seek God's direction, and "assembly" means the gathering of the people.

The passage tells how Solomon's reign began. The tabernacle made in the time of Moses was still in Gibeon, while the ark was in Jerusalem, in the tent David had prepared for it. The author points out that Solomon sought God at the place of the original altar, and this prepares for the meeting that night, when God tells him to ask for whatever he wants.

For today: before making major decisions, seek God first, together with others if possible. Solomon began his path with worship, not with his own plans.
exp.18:6:
This verse says that the judges should act with respect and reverence toward God. "The fear of the LORD" means taking him seriously and not wanting to offend him. "Injustice" is unfair treatment of people; "partiality" is favoring someone because of their position or fame; "bribery" is accepting gifts to influence a decision. God does none of those things, and neither should they.

King Jehoshaphat of Judah is the one speaking. He had appointed judges in the fortified cities and reminded them that they judged on behalf of God, not only on behalf of men. He wanted a land where justice was clean, and so he warned them against corruption.

Today we can apply this by treating everyone fairly, without favoritism. Whether at work, in the family, or in the church, we can ask ourselves: am I deciding honestly, or am I letting myself be swayed by self-interest, friendship, or pressure?
exp.15:0:
In the thirty-sixth year of Asa's reign, Baasha, king of Israel, attacked Judah and fortified the city of Ramah. "Fortified" here means strengthened and built up for defense. His purpose was to block the roads so that no one could leave or enter the territory of Asa, king of Judah.

The one telling this is the chronicler, who recounts the history of the kings of Judah. Ramah was north of Jerusalem, so Baasha wanted to isolate and pressure Judah. The date "thirty-sixth year" is hard to reconcile with other texts, and scholars explain it in several ways. What follows shows that Asa looked for help from the king of Syria and not from God.

For today: when a pressure comes that closes you in, before you rush to human solutions, stop and pray. Ask God for direction, and trust that He has already helped you before.
exp.10:16:
This verse says that the priests and the faithful people who left the north and came to Judah strengthened the kingdom of Rehoboam, son of Solomon, and gave him their support. This lasted three years, because during that time they lived according to the way of David and Solomon. The phrase about strengthening is explained this way: "Strengthened" means that they gave firmness and support to the kingdom.

The author of Chronicles, who is not named in the text, tells how Jeroboam turned the north away from the worship of the LORD and set up idols. Then many who wanted to seek God went to Jerusalem. The account shows that Judah's strength came from faithfulness and from those people. Afterward, the text suggests that Rehoboam turned aside, and his strength weakened.

For today: lasting strength does not come from comfort or success, but from following God steadily. Let us ask ourselves whether we remain faithful even when the first enthusiasm fades.
exp.9:18:
This verse says that the northern tribes of Israel broke away from the house of David and went their own way. "So to this day" means that when the author wrote, that division was still in place. "Rebellion" means that they revolted and broke the unity of the kingdom.

The author of Chronicles tells how the kingdom became divided after the death of Solomon. Rehoboam, his son, refused to lighten the people's burdens, and the northern tribes rebelled. They stoned Adoram, the officer in charge of the forced labor, and Rehoboam fled to Jerusalem. This account reminded its first readers how the division began and what came of harsh and proud leadership.

For today: if you have authority in your home, your work, or your church, listen with humility and treat others with kindness. Harshness can break relationships that are very hard to repair later.
exp.24:2:
It says that as soon as Amaziah had the kingdom of Judah firmly in his grasp, he put to death the officials who had murdered his father, King Joash. "Firmly in his grasp" means his power was already secure. The "servants" here are the king's officials.

This is part of the chronicler's account of Amaziah. It is not a character speaking; the narrator explains how his reign began. Earlier it said he did what was right, though not with a wholehearted heart. The next verse clarifies that he did not kill the children of the guilty men, in obedience to the law of Moses. So his justice was real, but limited.

For today: we can seek justice without going beyond the limits God sets. And it is worth examining the heart, because a person can obey in important matters and still not give themselves fully to God.
exp.17:5:
Jehoshaphat asks whether there is still a prophet of the Lord here, someone through whom they could seek God's guidance.

Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, had joined forces with Ahab, king of Israel, to go to war. Ahab gathered four hundred prophets, and they all said what the king wanted to hear. Jehoshaphat sensed that something was wrong and asked to hear a true prophet of the Lord. Then Micaiah appears, whom Ahab did not want to hear because he never spoke pleasant things to him.

Today: it is not enough that many voices agree with me. We should seek the truth of God in his Word and listen with humility, even when it is not what I want to hear.
exp.3:11:
This verse lists part of the bronze work Huram made for the temple: two pillars, and on top of them the capitals, which are the bowl-shaped tops of each pillar. The two sets of network that covered both bowls of the capitals are described in the verse, and the verse gives no further detail about them.

The narrator is the Chronicler, who recounts the building of the temple under King Solomon. Huram, a skilled craftsman, completes the work for the house of God. The author takes care with these details because the temple was the center of Israel's worship, and remembering it gave the people hope.

For today: God values work done well, even in small and little-seen things. Whatever you do with care, whether at home, at work, or in the church, can be an offering to God.
exp.14:14:
All of Judah rejoiced over the oath, because they had sworn it with all their heart. They had sought God earnestly, and he was found by them. So the LORD gave them rest on every side.

The account tells what happened in the days of King Asa. After the prophet Azariah spoke to them, the people made a solemn covenant to return to the God of their fathers. The writer of Chronicles emphasizes that sincere obedience brought blessing and rest. The following text shows that Asa also removed his grandmother from her position because of idolatry, although not all the high places were eliminated.

Today, seeking God is not performing out of habit, but drawing near with sincerity. You can begin with an honest and simple prayer, giving him your whole heart, and trusting that he answers those who seek him.
exp.3:14:
This verse describes the Sea, a huge bronze basin filled with water, and says that twelve bronze oxen were placed underneath it to support it. The oxen formed the base that held up that great basin.

The book of Chronicles tells of the building of the temple under King Solomon. The author lists in detail the objects made by the craftsman Hiram. The priests used the water in the Sea to wash themselves, and each piece is described to remind us that the worship of God was prepared with care and reverence.

Today we can learn that God values cleanliness and preparation when we come near to Him. Before praying or serving, it is good to pause, acknowledge our faults, and ask Him to cleanse us, trusting that He receives us.
exp.29:14:
This verse tells us that the people slaughtered the Passover lamb on the fourteenth day of the second month, not the first, which was the usual date. The priests and Levites were ashamed, so they consecrated themselves, making themselves ready for service, and then they brought burnt offerings, offerings burned up completely, to the house of the LORD. The name for God in this verse is the LORD.

It is part of the account in the book of Chronicles about King Hezekiah. The writer is not speaking through a character; he is describing the great reform of Judah. Hezekiah had cleared Jerusalem of false altars, and the Passover was postponed by a month because there were not enough priests ready and the people had not gathered together yet (Numbers 9 allowed that date in certain cases).

For today: when we realize we have been careless with God, a healthy sense of shame can lead us back to Him and into action, rather than leaving us stuck.
exp.3:17:
It says that Solomon had an enormous quantity of metal articles made for the temple. There were so many that no one could determine the weight of the bronze used. "Articles" here means objects in general, not just bowls. "Furnishings" are the tools and items used in daily service.

The narrator of the book of Chronicles describes the building of the temple in Jerusalem. Earlier, Hiram, the craftsman from Tyre, who worked the metal, is mentioned. Parallel texts describe this metal as bronze (1 Kings 7:47). The author wants to show the generosity and order with which the place of worship to God was prepared.

When we serve God, it is worth doing so with generosity and without stinginess. It is not about appearing impressive, but about giving our best in time, talent and resources, with gratitude, because He first gave us everything we have.
exp.32:8:
It says that King Manasseh led the people of Judah and the people of Jerusalem astray, so that they did greater evil than the nations that the LORD had destroyed before the Israelites. To be led astray means to wander off the right path, to be drawn away from what is good. The result was that the people sank into worse wrongdoing than the nations God had driven out of the land.

The writer of Chronicles tells the story of the kings of Judah. Manasseh had set up idols even inside the temple, despite God's promise to put his name there. God spoke to them, but they paid no attention. Then punishment came: Manasseh was taken captive to Babylon, and there he humbled himself and prayed to God.

Those who have influence can lead others for good or for evil. Be mindful of the example you set at home, at work, or in church. And if you have gone wrong, remember that God hears the one who humbles himself from the heart.
exp.8:10:
This verse says that Solomon used wood from algum trees to make terraces, or steps, in the temple and in the palaces, and also harps and lyres (stringed instruments) for the singers. It states that no wood like it had ever been seen in the land of Judah. Scholars are not sure exactly what kind of tree it was; some think of sandalwood, but that is only a guess.

The book of Chronicles tells this story after the return from exile, to remind the people of the splendor of Solomon's kingdom and of the worship of God. This wood arrived together with the gold of Ophir, by the ships of Hiram and Solomon, and it is connected with the visit of the queen of Sheba. Here the author emphasizes that the best things were put at the service of the temple and of praise.

For today: the best that God has given us, such as time, talents, and resources, we can offer with joy to worship Him and to serve others.
exp.24:26:
Here is what this verse says: after King Amaziah stopped following the LORD, a plot was formed against him in Jerusalem. He fled to Lachish, a fortified city of Judah, but men were sent after him there, and they killed him.

The word "conspiracy" describes a group of people who secretly plan together against someone in authority.

The verse comes near the end of Amaziah's story, which is told in the Chronicles account. Just before this, the text describes how Amaziah brought back the gods of Edom and refused to listen to the prophet who warned him (25:14-16). The writer links his turning from God with his tragic end. The verse does not explain the details of the plot, so it is best not to assume more than the text states.

For today: turning away from God is rarely one dramatic decision. It is usually a path that leaves its marks over time. You can return to Him now, listen to correction with humility, and not wait until everything falls apart.
exp.5:4:
This verse says that, from the day God brought Israel out of Egypt, he had not chosen any city among the tribes in which to build a house so that his name would be there. He had also not chosen anyone to be ruler over his people Israel. Here "ruler" means leader or governor, and "his name" stands for God's presence and his authority.

It is King Solomon who speaks, at the dedication of the temple. He recalls what God had said to his father David. Solomon explains that God has now chosen Jerusalem as the place of his name and David as the ruler. In this way he shows that the temple and the royal line were not a human idea, but that God kept his word.

For today: God acts according to his purpose and in his own time, even when we have to wait a long while. We can trust that he does what he promises, and remember it with gratitude, as Solomon did, instead of thinking that we achieve everything by ourselves.

sum.15: When King Baasa of Israel threatened Judah, Asa took the gold and silver from the temple and the palace and paid Syria to help him, and so he got Baasa to withdraw. The prophet Hanani rebuked him for trusting in Syria instead of in God, but Asa grew angry and had him put in prison. Later, when he became sick, he also did not seek God, and he died with honor.
sum.17: Jehoshaphat allied himself with King Ahab and joined him in going to war, but he asked that God be consulted first. Four hundred prophets promised the king victory, while Micaiah, the only one who spoke the truth, announced defeat. Ahab had him thrown into prison, and he disguised himself for the battle, but an arrow struck him and he died at sunset.
sum.22: In the seventh year, the priest Jehoiada made an alliance with the commanders and the Levites to present young Joash as the rightful king from David's line. They crowned him in the temple, and Athaliah was taken out and put to death. The people renewed their covenant with God, tore down the temple of Baal, and restored worship, and the city was at peace.
sum.9: Rehoboam went to Shechem, where the people asked him to lighten the heavy burden his father Solomon had placed on them. He rejected the advice of the elders and followed the counsel of the young men, answering them harshly. Because of this, the tribes of Israel broke away from the house of David, and Rehoboam reigned only over Judah, fulfilling what God had said.
sum.26: Jotham began to reign in Jerusalem at the age of twenty-five and reigned for sixteen years. He did what was right before God, built important works, and defeated the Ammonites, who paid him tribute. He grew strong because he ordered his life before God, although the people continued to become corrupt. When he died, his son Ahaz reigned in his place.
sum.21: Ahaziah reigned over Judah for only one year and followed the wicked ways of Ahab's household, guided by the advice of his mother Athaliah. God allowed Jehu, who had been sent to wipe out Ahab's family, to kill him. Then Athaliah ordered the destruction of the royal family, but Jehosheba hid the young Joash in the house of God for six years.
sum.6:
When Solomon finished praying, fire came down from heaven and consumed the sacrifices, and the glory of the LORD filled the temple. The people saw this, bowed down with their faces to the ground, and worshiped and gave thanks to the LORD. The king and all the people offered sacrifices to mark the dedication of the temple, and they celebrated with a festival lasting seven days.

That night, the LORD appeared to Solomon and told him that he had heard his prayer and chosen this place for himself as a house of sacrifice. He promised that if his people, who bear his name, humble themselves, pray, seek his face, and turn from their evil ways, then he would hear them from heaven, forgive their sin, and heal their land. He also warned that if they turned away and followed other gods, he would uproot them from the land and remove the temple from his sight.
sum.27:
Ahaz, king of Judah, turned away from God. He worshiped the Baals, and he even sacrificed his own sons. Because of this, Judah suffered defeats and was taken into captivity.

The prophet Obed and some leaders of Ephraim made the captives wear clothes, fed them, and sent them home.

Ahaz looked for help from Assyria and from false gods, but this only pulled him further down.
sum.10: Rehoboam gathered a large army to win back the northern tribes, but God sent him a message through Shemaiah telling him not to fight against his brothers, and they obeyed. Then Rehoboam fortified cities in Judah, and priests, Levites, and faithful people from across the land came to Jerusalem. After this, his many wives and children are mentioned, and that he preferred Abijah.
sum.16: Jehoshaphat reigned over Judah and sought the God of his father David, not following the Baals or the practices of Israel. He removed the places of idolatry and sent teachers with the book of the law to instruct the people. God blessed him with peace, respect, riches, and a strong army.
sum.13: Asa reigned over Judah. He removed the foreign altars and led the people to seek God, and because of this there was peace, and they built strong cities. When the huge army of Zerah the Ethiopian attacked them, Asa cried out to God for help, and God gave Judah the victory. This chapter teaches that trusting in God brings rest and help, even when facing an enemy far greater in number.
sum.7: After twenty years of building the temple and his palace, Solomon rebuilt cities, strengthened his kingdom, and put the peoples who remained in the land to work. He also organized the priests and Levites according to what David and Moses had commanded, and kept up the worship of the LORD. In addition, he sent ships to Ophir and brought back gold.
sum.31: Sennacherib, king of Assyria, invades Judah and mocks God. But Hezekiah strengthens Jerusalem, encourages the people to trust the Lord, and prays together with Isaiah. God then sends an angel who delivers them. Afterward, Hezekiah becomes proud, humbles himself, and God blesses him, though he had been tested in his heart.
sum.23: Joash reigned over Judah and obeyed God as long as the priest Jehoiada lived, and with Jehoiada's help he repaired the temple. When Jehoiada died, the king let himself be led astray by the officials, worshiped idols, and ordered the death of Zechariah, son of Jehoiada, who rebuked him. Because of this, Syria defeated him, and his servants killed him.
sum.25: Uzziah began to reign at the age of sixteen, and he prospered for as long as he sought God. He defeated his enemies, strengthened Jerusalem, and built up a large army. But success filled him with pride. He entered the temple to burn incense, and God struck him with leprosy. He lived apart from others until his death, and his son Jotham ruled in his place.
sum.2: Solomon began to build the temple in Jerusalem, on Mount Moriah, at the place David had prepared. The chapter describes its measurements and how he overlaid it with gold, with cherubim, a veil, and two pillars called Jachin and Boaz. Everything shows the care and honor with which the house of God was made.
sum.24: Amaziah began to reign over Judah and did what was right, but he did not give his whole heart to God. He obeyed the prophet by sending home the soldiers he had hired from Israel, and he defeated Edom, but afterward he worshiped the gods of that people. Because of his pride and his refusal to accept correction, he lost to Israel and was later killed.
sum.12: Abijah, king of Judah, confronts Jeroboam and Israel, who had twice as many soldiers. He reminds them that God gave the kingdom to David and that they abandoned the Lord for golden calves. Judah cries out to God, and He gives them the victory. The text teaches that whoever relies on the Lord is strengthened.
sum.8: The Queen of Sheba traveled to Jerusalem with gifts, tested Solomon with hard questions, and was amazed at his wisdom. She praised God for placing him on the throne as king. The chapter also describes Solomon's enormous wealth and fame, and how kings came to visit him and brought him gifts. At the end, Solomon dies after reigning for forty years, and his son Rehoboam becomes king in his place.
sum.4: Solomon finishes the temple and brings the ark of the covenant into the Most Holy Place, while all Israel offers countless sacrifices. The Levites and the priests praise God with music, saying that He is good and that His mercy endures forever. Then a cloud fills the house, because the glory of the LORD was there.
sum.3: Solomon ordered the furnishings for the temple: a great bronze altar, a huge cast bronze basin set on twelve oxen, basins, lampstands, tables, and utensils of gold. Huram, the craftsman, worked the metal, and it was made in such abundance that its weight could not be measured. Everything was prepared with care to serve God in his house.
sum.29: King Hezekiah invited all of Israel and Judah to come to Jerusalem to celebrate the Passover and return to the Lord. Some mocked the invitation, but others humbled themselves and came, and God graciously accepted those who sought him wholeheartedly, even though they had not been purified. There was so much joy that they celebrated for fourteen days, something not seen since the time of Solomon.
sum.32: Manasseh was king of Judah from the age of twelve. He filled the temple with idols and led the people into doing evil. Taken captive to Babylon, he humbled himself, God heard his prayer, and he removed the idols. His son Amon returned to sin without humbling himself, and his servants killed him.
sum.1: Solomon decided to build a large temple for the name of the LORD and assigned thousands of workers to the project. He asked King Hiram of Tyre for help. Hiram sent him timber and a skilled craftsman, and he acknowledged God. Solomon admitted that no building can contain a God so great.
sum.18: Jehoshaphat returned in peace to Jerusalem, but the prophet Jehu rebuked him for helping those who hate the LORD, though he acknowledged the good things in him. Then the king led the people back to God, and he appointed judges, whom he taught to judge with the fear of the LORD, with truth, and without taking bribes.
sum.0: Solomon is established as king, and he gathers the leaders of Israel to worship God at Gibeon, where he offers a thousand burnt offerings. That night God tells him to ask for whatever he wants. Solomon asks for wisdom to govern the people. God is pleased and grants him wisdom, along with riches and honor.
sum.20: Joram, son of Jehoshaphat, killed his brothers and led Judah into idolatry, following the bad example of the house of Ahab. God did not destroy David's family because of His promise, but Elijah announced judgment against him. Joram lost his sons and died of a painful sickness, and no one mourned his passing.
sum.34: King Josiah holds a great Passover in Jerusalem. He arranges the priests and Levites and gives thousands of animals to the people, in keeping with the law of Moses. After this, Josiah goes out to fight against Pharaoh Necho of Egypt. He does not heed the warning that came from God, he is wounded at Megiddo and dies, and all the people mourn for him.
sum.19: A large enemy army attacks Judah, and King Jehoshaphat, afraid, calls the people to fast and pray, acknowledging that they have no strength of their own and that their eyes are fixed on God. God answers that the battle belongs to Him, and as the people praise Him, the enemies turn against one another and destroy each other. At the end, Jehoshaphat allies himself with a wicked king, and his project fails.
sum.28: When Hezekiah began to reign, he opened and cleaned the temple and called the priests and Levites to make themselves holy, because their fathers had turned away from God. Sin offerings were presented, the music of David was played, and the people worshiped with joy. In this way the service of God was restored, and everyone rejoiced.
sum.35: The last kings of Judah did what was evil and would not listen to the prophets whom God kept sending out of compassion. Because of this, Jerusalem and the temple were destroyed, and the people were taken captive to Babylon for seventy years. But God kept his word: he moved Cyrus to let the people return and rebuild the temple.
sum.11: When Rehoboam became strong, he abandoned the law of God, and God allowed Shishak, king of Egypt, to attack Jerusalem. After the prophet Shemaiah delivered God's message, the king and the leaders humbled themselves, and God did not destroy them, although they remained under Egyptian rule. Rehoboam continued doing evil, because he did not seek God wholeheartedly.
sum.33: Josiah became king as a boy and sought God, and he cleared the land of idols. While repairing the temple, the priest Hilkiah found the book of the law. When the king heard it read, he humbled himself and wept. Through the prophetess Huldah, God announced judgment, but he spared Josiah himself, and Josiah renewed the covenant with all the people.
sum.30: After the Passover, the people destroyed the idols and altars throughout the land, and King Hezekiah organized the service of the priests and Levites. The people responded with tithes and offerings so generous that there was a great surplus, and these were distributed faithfully. Hezekiah did what was good and right, seeking God with all his heart, and he prospered.
sum.14: God sent the prophet Azariah to tell King Asa and Judah that God is with those who seek him, but he turns away from those who abandon him. Encouraged, Asa removed the idols, repaired the altar, and gathered the people to make a covenant to seek God with all their heart. God gave them rest, though the high places did not disappear.
sum.5: Solomon blesses the people and reminds them that God kept his promise to David by allowing his son to build the temple. He then prays on his knees, acknowledging that not even the heavens can contain God, and asks him to listen, forgive, and help his people, as well as the foreigner, whenever they pray toward that place.
